ASRS:1818554.n: After taking off of Runway XXL at ZZZ, I turned 15 degrees left of the runway (per policy at ZZZ) and continued climbing. ZZZ Tower began giving me instructions to enter the pattern for left downwind XXL and I requested to return to ZZZ1. ZZZ Tower instructed me to fly a 150 heading. As I was flying on the 150 heading (I believe that I may have drifted 10 degrees off- closer to 160 heading) I saw a Piper Cub roughly a mile out and it appeared to be turning to my right, but coming straight at me still. After watching the plane, and still continuing my climb, I saw it coming directly at me (as far as human factors, the last image I remembered of the plane was it turning to my right and coming at me) so I chose to dive left immediately instead of right. Looking out the right window I was able to see the plane very clearly Turing left as well, so I steepened my dive down and to the left (after talking to a ZZZ Tower Supervisor named NAME, I found that the plane was in a 45-degree turn to join the left downwind for Runway 20L).As my adrenaline had kicked in upon seeing the plane coming at me and being left with no choice besides taking evasive action, I had missed a radio call from ZZZ Tower to turn right 20 degrees. After flying under the Piper Cub, tower explained that I was off my 150 heading instead of making a comment on the near miss, so I exclaimed that I was off my 150 heading because the plane almost hit me. Tower seemingly dismissed my comment and reiterated that I was to comply with the 150 heading immediately and I apologized and returned to the heading.Regardless of my adrenaline (which was very high for several hours after my landing at ZZZ1) I took what information I had, as I had previously seen the plane turning to my right and had to take evasive action and dive down and to the left.The inaction of ZZZ Tower in providing me or the other plane with information about each other is the most astonishing part of this event. In any pattern at a towered airport, even my times at busy ZZZ, I have always been advised if I was even within two miles of another plane in the pattern. Therefore, not being warned that another plane was on a close collision course with me would have led to a mid-air collision had I not been looking for a plane heading my direction. Even if I had been precisely on a 150 heading or if I had been 30 degrees off of the heading, I would have been on a course for a mid-air or a near miss like I had today. Upon talking with the ZZZ Tower Supervisor, he admitted that the cub had performed a non-standard pattern entry with the sharp 45-degree bank entry into it. While I do not blame the pilot of the cub, I do believe that if sharply banking into a pattern is enough to cause a near miss event, that plane and my plane should NEVER have been that close to each other.I do, however, blame the Controller in a large part, as it becomes clear that he catches his mistake when he exclaims to the cub that the traffic is one mile away and quickly tries to offer separation, but it is too late and I am too focused on trying to avoid this plane coming at me/across my field of view.Ultimately, I believe that the Controller's inaction and lack of communication with both planes is what allowed this event to occur. Aircraft X was instructed to fly heading 150, vectors for traffic. Prior to this instruction being given, Cessna 172 has requested flight following which was on a East bound heading. The reason that this vector was given was because of a Piper Cub, Aircraft Y, was inbound making left traffic for Runway XXL.I was busy issuing doing other things such as issuing wake turbulence calls and getting visual separation between aircraft on final for the parallel runway, I realized that Aircraft X was veering to the left, turning East bound. I immediately tried to correct the situation by instructing Cessna 172 to turn right 20 degrees.By this point it was too late and the Cessna had turned right into the path of the Piper Cub that was descending. I immediately issued traffic to the Piper Cub. I inquired Aircraft X about his heading to which he replied 'Yeah I was flying heading 150 but there was a plane there so I turned left to avoid.' The 150 heading exists to keep aircraft away from these exact situations. Aircraft X was an unfamiliar pilot and needed extra attention. I was busy engaging in other duties to notice that he had turned left East bound.
ASRS:1818554.s: A Cessna 172 pilot and a Piper Cub pilot experienced a near mid-air collision during climb-out at ZZZ after the controller failed to provide traffic advisories. The Cessna pilot executed an evasive left dive to avoid the Cub, which was making a non-standard pattern entry, while the controller admitted distraction caused the lack of separation.

ASRS:1818586.n: Departing JAC, [the] SIC (Second in Command) and I were given the clearance of the Geyser 5 departure procedure: NALSI, MLD, then as filed - J158 ZZZ ZZZZZ - climb and maintain 16,000. SIC and I briefed the departure on the ground in JAC and discussed the nearly 180-degree left turn at NALSI and agreed the aircraft would likely start that turn early. We briefed expediting our climb up to 16,000. We didn't anticipate any issues with that departure as the MSA on the departure procedure read 15,000. The highest terrain on the departure read 13,676. Upon departing from Runway 01 and climbing through 14,800 on autopilot, past GIYER and CFCFD on the 017 radial from JAC outbound to NALSI, the aircraft started a left-hand turn, as anticipated, to intercept the course to MLD. This turn took place approximately 10 miles from NALSI. SIC let Salt Lake Center know we were beginning the turn. The Controller said, Ok, do you have the terrain in sight, my minimum vectoring altitude is 15,800 in that area." He then said 'low altitude alert.' We were passing through 15,000 at that point and were about to enter IMC. We told the Controller we were about to enter IMC and he said expedite climb, which we did. The Controller on the next frequency gave us a phone number to call for a potential pilot deviation."
ASRS:1818586.s: Pilots departing JAC on the Geyser 5 procedure initiated a left turn early, prompting a low altitude alert from Salt Lake Center due to a 15,800-foot minimum vectoring altitude. The crew expedited their climb while entering IMC and were subsequently directed to contact authorities regarding a potential pilot deviation.

ASRS:1818590.n: We were cleared to 3,000 ft. on a wide base and a tight vector to ILS [Runway] 17L behind a heavy jet. It was very turbulent and our path put us downwind to the heavy jet. During the turbulence I lost control of the aircraft and we shot down about 500 ft. below our assigned altitude. I was in the process of correcting when the Approach Controller called out the fact we were off altitude. I told her we concurred and were correcting. I believe the issue was caused by the moderate to severe turbulence we were experiencing along with the wake from the heavy jet.
ASRS:1818590.s: The pilot reported losing control and descending 500 feet below the assigned 3,000 feet while vectored behind a heavy jet in moderate to severe turbulence. The pilot attributed the altitude deviation to the combination of turbulence and wake turbulence from the preceding aircraft.

ASRS:1818615.n: Skydiving was occurring at the field. I heard the jump plane on CTAF occasionally. The pilot who took off ahead of me called the jump plane on CTAF asking for the status of the skydivers and received no answer. I then heard that a group was being released from 14,000 feet. I had to do my run-up and checks, but I never saw them. While doing this, I heard another call for release of skydivers from 14,000 feet. I called and asked if the first group was on the ground and someone (not the jump pilot) answered that the only ones up were the ones that had just released. I thought I had a couple minutes before they would be down, so I looked around, didn't see any, and rolled onto the Runway to takeoff. As I was doing this, I heard the jump plane call. It was a very rushed transmission, so I couldn't make out exactly where he was, but I heard the Runway number and gathered that he was coming in to land. I expedited my takeoff, and as I started rolling I saw a skydiver appear from behind my wing. He seemed to be off to the side of the Runway and traveling parallel to it so I did not abort the takeoff as I wasn't sure where the jump plane was and wanted to get out of the way. Well, shortly after I lifted off, the skydiver turned right in front of me. I made a sharp turn to the right, just clearing the trees and ended up buzzing a neighborhood. I got away from the field, re-established a normal climb to altitude, and took a minute to breathe. During this, I ended up too close to final, looked up, and saw the jump plane filling my windscreen. More evasive action.
ASRS:1818615.s: A pilot taking off during skydiving operations encountered a skydiver who turned in front of the aircraft shortly after lift-off. The pilot executed sharp evasive turns to avoid the skydiver and the jump plane, resulting in buzzing a neighborhood before re-establishing a normal climb.

ASRS:1818620.n: Flying Aircraft X which is not equipped with either an electrical system nor radio, I conducted a run-up and 360-degree turn in the hammerhead of Runway 24 at Cable Airport. I did not observe any traffic in the pattern and elected to take off. I did not observe any traffic entering the pattern via the standard crosswind or midfield local entry procedures. Upon reaching the downwind abeam point, I scanned final and did not observe any traffic and began my base turn. After rolling out on final, I ended up wingtip to wingtip within a 1/2-mile of Aircraft Y. I must not have been able to see the aircraft due to ground clutter. Aircraft Y initiated a go-around and I continued to lend to prevent further conflict.
ASRS:1818620.s: The pilot of an unpowered Aircraft X took off from Runway 24 at Cable Airport and encountered Aircraft Y wingtip-to-wingtip on final approach. The pilot attributed the near-miss to ground clutter obscuring Aircraft Y, which subsequently initiated a go-around while the pilot banked left to avoid conflict.

ASRS:1818631.n: Flight started at the helicopter pads - second flight out of ZZZ for the day. This was a training flight with students. I was the Flight Instructor. I started up and prepared for takeoff as normal. The weather was IFR which required a SVFR clearance for our departure. I received weather and contacted Ground and requested the SVFR to the northeast with a present position departure from the helicopter pads. This was the expected as we had done so earlier. Initially, I was told to standby while the Controller was getting other aircraft taxiing. After the wait, the Controller came back and cleared us to the northeast at or below 1700 ft. via SVFR, which I read back. Despite still being on Ground frequency, I erroneously mistook the SVFR clearance as a clearance to takeoff as requested from present position. As such, I instructed the student to initiate the takeoff and depart, which we did.Our flight path was to the northeast which took us across Runway X, the active. As we reached 500 ft. and [was] approaching clear of the ZZZ Class 'C;' I expected a switch to Approach as usual but when I looked down at the radio I saw we were still on the Ground frequency. I quickly switched to Tower and was informed of my lack of takeoff clearance and additionally the overflight of an aircraft on takeoff from Runway X which we didn't see. Our departure flight path was at a 40-degree offset roughly 040, which put the start of Runway 8 behind us. Sitting on the right side, I didn't see Aircraft Y who was actually cleared for takeoff start their roll at roughly the same time as we did. Due to the angle, they were aft of my scan during the takeoff. Based on the info from the Controller, we passed over them by about 200 ft. as they were departing. Because we were still on the Ground frequency, we also didn't hear towers call to us when we started to depart without takeoff clearance. Unfortunately, all of this was caused by my assumption of having received a takeoff clearance and acting accordingly. Obviously, I should have been more aware and realized that it wasn't a takeoff clearance that was issued. I should have also noticed that we had not switched to Tower from Ground earlier. Not to pass blame, but an observation - it is common for a Ground Controller after issuing a clearance to push us to the next Controller, i.e., 'Read back correct, contact Tower/Ground for takeoff/taxi.' This would seem more critical, particularly for a helicopter present position departure such as this one that does not require a taxi to a specific runway. In this case, that was not stated as far as I can remember. Additionally, there has been a lot of Ground and Tower combined frequencies lately and that also could have played into the confirmation bias that led to assuming my SVFR clearance was also a takeoff clearance and not switching to the Tower frequency. In this case, Tower and Ground were on different frequencies. Regardless, I have executed present position departures many times and not had an issue like this and I definitely made a mistake which almost resulted in a collision. In the future, I will exercise extreme caution and slow down to ensure this mistake does not happen again.
ASRS:1818631.s: A helicopter flight instructor conducting a training SVFR departure from ZZZ helicopter pads mistakenly took off without clearance, assuming the SVFR instruction included takeoff authority. This error caused the helicopter to overfly an aircraft on Runway X by approximately 200 feet due to the pilot remaining on Ground frequency and failing to scan for the departing aircraft.

ASRS:1818646.n: While piloting my aircraft at Northern Colorado Regional Airport (FNL), I was holding short of Runway 33 at Taxiway A1, and I contacted the Tower and requested to takeoff Runway 33 and remain in the pattern for landing Runway 33. Tower cleared me for takeoff, advising me of an aircraft just departing ahead on Runway 33. I was instructed by the Tower to remain in left closed traffic for Runway 33.After climbing to pattern altitude, I turned crosswind, and then downwind for Runway 33. While mid-field downwind for Runway 33, I noticed several aircraft targets ahead of me to the south were all converging toward runway 33 on my ADS-B display, one from the east and one from the west, both apparently on base for Runway 33 from opposite directions, and a third target (Aircraft Y) approaching from the southeast. Spacing among all 3 appeared inadequate. The Controller told Aircraft Y from the southeast to report 3 mile final. I was scanning the sky and acquired visual contact on all three aircraft. Aircraft Y was unable to turn final due to inadequate spacing with the other two aircraft. I was unable to continue in the standard traffic pattern, as I needed to maneuver east to avoid Aircraft Y as it crossed through final from the southeast and across the downwind to the west, which I estimated to be 500 feet in front of me and 300 feet overhead. Turning east was the safest alternative to remain clear of Aircraft Y and the other two aircraft, as I had them all in sight. The Controller began shouting to all of the pilots 'I don't have radar! I see two targets converging to the south!' The Controller sounded very anxious. I immediately informed the Tower that I was maneuvering to avoid Aircraft Y now in front and above me. I recall that the Controller then called one of the other aircraft and said loudly to 'leave the pattern!', but his instructions were not clear. He then asked where everyone was located. I clearly and calmly replied 'Aircraft X, turned left base to avoid the traffic conflict' with Aircraft Y. The Controller then asked seconds later, 'Who is that on left base?', and I again replied calmly 'this is Aircraft X on mid-left base.' He then cleared me to land Runway 33, told the traffic ahead on final to turn east, and then instructed Aircraft Y (now west of the field) to return to land on Runway 33. There was inadequate traffic spacing for incoming traffic entering the pattern, and incomplete awareness by the Controller of the four aircraft positions relative to one another, followed by his distraught demeanor and very exasperated tone as he complained of having no radar feed. It is also possible that the Controller forgot about my aircraft position in the pattern and that he had instructed me to maintain closed left traffic for Runway 33. I did my best to remain clear of any traffic conflict, communicate calmly and clearly, and defuse the Controller's anxious situation, while maintaining safe spacing from all traffic in the pattern. I was cleared to land Runway 33 and did so safely, and taxied to parking as directed by the controller. No other communication took place between me and the controller.As a recommended solution, the temporary Tower at FNL needs a radar feed installed as soon as possible for better situational awareness for the Controllers. The Controller's shouting and anxious tone heightened the tension of the situation for the other pilots, which was not helpful in this scenario. A professional demeanor by the Controller with clear, yet rapid instructions would have been more effective at resolving the traffic conflicts.
ASRS:1818646.s: A pilot at Northern Colorado Regional Airport (FNL) maneuvered to avoid a traffic conflict while in the pattern for Runway 33 due to inadequate spacing and the controller's lack of radar. The pilot safely landed after the controller, who lacked situational awareness and displayed an anxious demeanor, eventually issued clearances to resolve the converging traffic.

ASRS:1818658.n: We were on an IFR flight plan in Aircraft X. We were talking to BTR Approach on 120.3 as they were vectoring us for the ILS 13 approach. The copilot was the pilot flying. We were descending through 5400 ft. when we exited a cloud and the copilot spotted two motorized hang gliders approximately 200 feet below us. The copilot immediately arrested the descent in order to avoid the hang gliders. The copilot alerted ATC of the traffic at that position. They apparently were not squawking a transponder code because ATC did not alert us and we were not painting them on our traffic system. We landed Baton Rouge without incident.
ASRS:1818658.s: The crew of Aircraft X, descending through 5,400 feet while being vectored by BTR Approach for ILS 13, spotted two non-transponder-equipped motorized hang gliders 200 feet below. The pilot flying arrested the descent to avoid the traffic, alerted ATC, and landed in Baton Rouge without incident.

ASRS:1818663.n: On Aircraft X ZZZ1 - ZZZ during final descent I noticed an oily/burning fumes that was present in the entire AFT of the aircraft but intense towards the middle AFT of the aircraft and was coming from the air vents. We communicated with each other as a crew and confirmed that all inflight [Cabin Attendants] (F1;F2;F3;F4) detected the fumes. The intensity was a Level 2: Moderate. During this phase my symptoms were the following: burning eyes, nose and throat. Flight deck was notified. After deplaning the fumes and my symptoms dissipated. Maintenance came on board and decided we would continue our next flight with same aircraft. On Aircraft X ZZZ to ZZZ1 during boarding when engines were turned on I immediately detected the oily burning fumes that were now at a Level 3: Strong since customers began to complain as well. The location started initially in the AFT of the aircraft but during deplaning was detectable throughout entire aircraft. The source was the same which was the air vents. The phase was during boarding on the ground. Flight deck was notified and they determined we had to deplane all customers. Myself and F4 were experiencing more severe symptoms. I experienced symptoms of burning eyes, nose and throat once again. I also began to feel tightness in my chest, difficulty breathing, thickness in the air, slight disoriented, and minor speech problems. Due to my symptoms I felt as though I was unable to perform my inflight duties safely. [Medical staff] was contacted when off the aircraft. Myself and the F4 were sent to the hospital.
ASRS:1818663.s: Cabin crew on Aircraft X detected moderate oily fumes from air vents during final descent, which intensified to strong levels during boarding, causing severe respiratory symptoms. The flight was cancelled with all passengers deplaned, and two crew members were hospitalized due to inability to perform duties safely.

ASRS:1818701.n: During the takeoff roll, the FA's (Flight Attendant's) dinged us twice. We continued the takeoff. Upon rotation they dinged us four times, twice before clean-up altitude. After reaching clean-up altitude I called the cabin and the FA's reported passengers seeing flames and sparks coming from the right engine, as well as hearing popping noises. The FA's reported the entire cabin lit up brightly, but that there was no smoke in the cabin. We informed ATC that we had a #2 engine fire, were returning for landing, and requested fire truck assistance. We had no cockpit indications of a fire or malfunction. Both engines were producing symmetric power and operating normally, according to our gauges. Upon landing and shutting down the engines on Taxiway XX, Fire Rescue took temperature readings and reported them in the normal range. We were towed to the gate. Incident for [the] flight [from] ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was the pilot flying. During the takeoff roll with takeoff power set, the flight attendants called the flight deck with two dings. We elected to continue to takeoff. Right at rotation speed, the flight attendants called the flight deck again, but this time with four dings. We continued the takeoff and climbing through 1000 ft., the Captain transferred the radios over to me and she started coordinating with a Flight Attendant.Flight attendants were reporting that the passengers on the right side were saying that the engine was on fire and they heard a popping noise and at the same time the flight attendants said they noticed that the cabin lit up momentarily. However, there was no smoke in the cabin, all engine indications were normal, and none of the Fire Handle Warning lights were lit. The Captain [requested priority handling] and told Tower that our #2 engine was on fire and that we needed to return for an immediate landing and requested the fire trucks. Tower cleared us for Runway XXR, I continued to climb to 3000 ft. at 210 kt. and started my turn for a left downwind for Runway XXR. On downwind, Tower cleared us for the visual and cleared to land XXR. A flaps 30 landing was conducted and we taxied off the runway on Taxiway XX where we shut the engines down. The Fire Crew inspected the engine and stated that everything seemed normal and that their heat sensors also indicated normal readings. After a short time, we were towed back to the gate.
ASRS:1818701.s: The pilot flying reported that flight attendants observed flames and sparks from the right engine during takeoff, despite normal cockpit indications. The crew returned for an immediate landing, but fire rescue found no abnormal heat or damage upon inspection.

ASRS:1818728.n: Enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Aircraft had MEL for #2 engine generator. Dispatched with APU powering #2 transfer bus. At 35,000 ft. over ZZZ2, APU failed and did automatic shutdown. We diverted to ZZZ2 due to only one AC power source remaining. Uneventful approach and landing. Multiple, unforeseen failures caused the event. Right generator was MEL'd after gate return at ZZZ. MEL required APU to be operated continuously on the ZZZ - ZZZ1 leg. During cruise FL350 the APU failed, leaving us with a single generator. Accomplished QRH items for 'APU low oil pressure' and decided to divert to ZZZ2 due to the requirement to land at [the] 'nearest suitable airport' from MEL and QRH. [Requested priority handling] in the descent due to [the] nature of [the] malfunction and overweight landing. Landed uneventfully in ZZZ2 6,000 lb. overweight. At ZZZ2 we deplaned passengers, and after a six-hour delay, the APU was repaired and overweight inspection [was] completed. Completed flight to ZZZ1 uneventfully.
ASRS:1818728.s: The crew diverted an aircraft with an MEL'd #2 generator after the APU failed at FL350, leaving only one AC power source. They landed 6,000 lb overweight at ZZZ2 due to MEL requirements, repaired the APU, and completed the flight uneventfully.

ASRS:1818754.n: During our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, Aircraft X, a flight attendant seated near the 4L lavatory reported that about 3 minutes after take off he began to notice a urine smell coming from the 4L lav. The smell began to dissipate about 15 minutes later. We suspected a contributing factor could be the high deck angle associated with the take off. This has been a continuing write up for a few weeks. Unfortunately maintenance personnel have been unable to identify and fix the exact cause. Hopefully this report will help bring together the appropriate resources to fix this problem. Our passengers and flight attendants will appreciate it.
ASRS:1818754.s: During the takeoff phase of Aircraft X, a flight attendant reported a urine smell from the 4L lavatory that dissipated 15 minutes later. The crew suspected the high deck angle contributed to the issue, but maintenance has been unable to identify or fix the exact cause.

ASRS:1818831.n: After being cleared the ILS PRM Y to Runway 10R at ORD and being cleared to land, Tower issued a go-around instruction to our aircraft. The ILS PRM Y has a 2.5 degree offset course to the runway due to the close nature of the two Runways 10R and 10C. At approximately 500 feet, we gained sight of the runway and began maneuvering to stabilize the approach on runway centerline by approximately 200 feet. The go-around command was issued at approximately 300 to 400 feet. The go-around instructions were to climb to 2,500 feet and fly the localizer course. The CRJ-200 procedure for a go around is to TOGA, advance power and set the flap to 8 degrees and initiate a climb. This was accomplished uneventfully, however, we were already approximately 0.5-1 dot left on the localizer proceeding visually toward the runway centerline. Once the TOGA is initiated, the command bars will raise to command a climb and also capture the heading the aircraft is currently on when the button is pushed. This all happened as we were transitioning back into IMC. The localizer was still displayed on both displays, however due to the sensitivity of the localizer beam at that distance from the antenna, I am not certain of our actual deviation in terms of distance to the left of course. The Tower Controller informed us we were supposed to be following the localizer course and issued a right turn to heading 140 degrees, followed by a new heading of 150 degrees. We complied and were vectored around a radar pattern to an uneventful landing on 10R.Although we could have possibly corrected faster to the localizer course to prevent the left of course deviation, I think this is an unnecessarily complicated go-around instruction. The 'button pushes' required, and the delays in the automation system before it appropriately reacts essentially rule out even using it, especially in low energy state while transitioning back into IMC. Even though we had immediately pressed the NAV button after the TOGA, the command bars did not capture the course because we had been maneuvering visually and were far enough away from the localizer course so it defaulted to 'roll' mode. This added an element of confusion and additional button pushing as we were executing the go around. Also, I have personally never been issued a clearance to rejoin a localizer course during a go-around in my aviation career, so it was definitely unexpected. I would recommend a non-breakout go-around clearance on a PRM be limited to something very simple like a heading and an altitude to climb to. This would simplify the communication and lower the overall workload in the cockpit during a critical phase of flight.
ASRS:1818831.s: The CRJ-200 crew executed a go-around at 300–400 feet while on an ILS PRM Y approach to Runway 10R at ORD after Tower instructed them to climb and fly the localizer. The pilot reported that automation delays and unexpected course capture issues increased workload, leading to a recommendation for simpler heading-based go-around clearances.

ASRS:1818853.n: CONF 1 TOGA takeoff and no APU. Normal start go #1 at the gate per non-normal start, the same for the #2 start after the push back. After-start check complete, load closeout comes. We were under PTOW (Planned Takeoff Weight) and good winds and temperatures. Normal taxi and checklist to [runway] XXC. Cleared for takeoff, CA sets TOGA. Normal acceleration Vr. Shortly after Vr, heard a loud bang - CA (Captain) says, 'I think we blew a tire.' I said, 'I agree.' CA kept flying, we left the gear down. Speed was bleeding off, and then I said 'engine failure.' [Requested priority handling] with intentions to return to ZZZ. Leveled off at engine acceleration height [and] started to accelerate, thinking the gear was up. We decided to leave the flaps at 1 to return to the field and not knowing if there was any damage. [We] completed the ECAM procedure, follow-ups. CA talked to the FA's (Flight Attendant) to prepare for a precautionary landing and made a PA to the passengers, per the OD pages. ATC asked us to climb to 4,000 ft. Then, we realized the gear was still down. [We] raised the gear [and] completed the after-takeoff checklist. Did the landing approach, overweight landing, and checklist. Briefed the approach to [runway] XXC and descent checklist. Configured on schedule, landing checklist, and landed uneventfully. After stopping, the CA made a PA, talked to ARFF (Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting), then taxed to the gate.[The cause was a] startle effect and the initial confusion of a tire failure or an engine failure. That played a significant role in the distraction of the landing gear. [I suggest to] do a max weight V1 in the SIMs. Flight planned for configuration 1 TOGA/max takeoff and dispatched with APU inop. Normal ground air-start on #1 engine per checklist. After pushback [was] complete, normal cross-bleed start #2 per checklist. After-start checklist called for and completed. Load closeout received and we were under planned takeoff weight. Normal taxi out with all checklists complete, we were cleared to line up and wait runway XXC. Subsequently cleared for takeoff and selected TOGA. Acceleration was normal and rotated at Vr.Shortly thereafter, heard a thump. I stated, 'I think we blew a tire.' Thought about not raising the gear and continued flying the aircraft and noticed rapid degradation of speed. FO (First Officer) stated, 'Engine failure.' Immediately lowered the nose and started trimming based on rudder trim to level the wings and center the rudder. Aircraft performance was very degraded but assumed it was due to heavy 321, [I] don't ever remember flying the simulator engine out near max takeoff weight or we had severe damage to the wing. [Requested priority handling] and stated intentions to return to ZZZ, thinking the landing gear was up. Elected to leave flaps at 1 and return to the field as expeditiously as possible as we were down to 1 engine and 1 generator. Completed Engine Failure ECAM procedure, ECAM follow ups, notified the Flight Attendants to prepare for a precautionary landing, and made a PA as per the OD pages. ATC asked if we could climb to 4,000 feet and said we were unable due to weight. At this point I realized the gear was still down. Raised the gear [and] completed [the] after-takeoff checklists. Accomplished the landing data for overweight landing and checklist, briefed the approach to [runway] XXC, and completed descent checklist. We were then cleared for the ILS XXC approach configured on schedule, performed the landing checklist, and landed uneventfully. After stopping, made a PA, ARFF (Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting) checked out the aircraft, and we taxied to the gate.[The cause was a] startle effect and initial confusion of tire failure versus engine failure played a significant role in distraction from raising the landing gear. As pilot flying, my attention was completely absorbed with flying the aircraft with assumed degraded performance and didn't allow for transfer of aircraft control. Additionally, lack of experience on the fleet and as a new Captain also played a significant role. Departing over max landing weight with no APU was probably not a good decision. Additionally, I think a max weight takeoff V1 cut should be added to our training. Crew coordination with the flight attendant and ATC was excellent.
ASRS:1818853.s: A new Captain and First Officer experienced a tire blowout shortly after takeoff in a heavy A321, leading to confusion between tire and engine failure. This distraction caused them to forget to retract the landing gear, resulting in an overweight return and landing after the gear was eventually raised.

ASRS:1818896.n: While flying from ZZZZ to ZZZ, we experienced a loss of pressurization about one and a half hours into the flight. We first heard a loud squeal by the main cabin door and then saw that the cabin altitude was beginning to rise uncontrollably. We [requested priority handling] and started an emergency descent to 15,000 ft. We followed the emergency descent and loss of pressurization checklist in the QRH. We calculated our range and contacted company, and formulated the plan to divert to ZZZ1. We landed in ZZZ1 about 2 hours later without any other events.
ASRS:1818896.s: The flight crew experienced a loss of pressurization during cruise from ZZZZ to ZZZ, triggered by a loud squeal at the main cabin door. They executed an emergency descent to 15,000 ft and diverted to ZZZ1, landing safely two hours later.

ASRS:1818901.n: Departed ZZZ enroute to ZZZ2. As we were climbing through FL250, we heard a loud bang and noticed that the Right-Side B Panel Window was shattered. In less than 40 seconds, the window let go and we experienced an explosive decompression. Immediately began an emergency descent with intentions of diverting to ZZZ1. During the emergency descent, ATC was unable to hear our radio calls [requesting priority handling] until we reached a lower altitude when there was less wind noise in the flight deck. It was also hard to hear crew-to-crew communication. We were able to communicate with each other utilizing hand signals. Besides glass, the only known objects that departed through the window were: Oakley Conductor 8 sunglasses and case, Clarity Aloft Headset Case, 6 ft. charging cable for Apple products, aircraft cupholder, tinted sunshade visor, energy drink, plastic Fiji water bottle, and a can of Copenhagen Mint smokeless tobacco. Approximately 15 minutes after departing ZZZ enroute to ZZZ1 while climbing through 25,000 ft., we heard a loud pop and determined that part of the copilot side aft window had cracked. We slowed our climb rate and within 30 seconds the rest of the window gave way and we experienced an explosive decompression. We immediately executed an emergency descent. Crew was transmitting our intentions but with excessive wind noise, could not establish communication with ATC. After descending to [a] safe altitude and slowing [the] aircraft to minimize wind noise, we were able to establish communication with ATC and were issued a clearance to land on a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ1. We landed and taxied in with no further issues. Emergency and medical personnel were waiting when we arrived...
ASRS:1818901.s: The flight crew experienced two separate explosive decompressions caused by shattered windows during climb phases, resulting in emergency descents and temporary loss of radio contact due to wind noise. The aircraft successfully diverted to ZZZ1, where it landed safely on a visual approach with emergency personnel on standby.

ASRS:1818995.n: While loading [the] flight, I instructed my crew to load all mail carts in the A1 compartment of the aircraft. While they were loading I noticed a box with an 'Limited/Excepted quantities' label in [the] cart. As it came up the belt I also noticed a sticker with 'ground transport only' with an aircraft and a red circle and hash mark through it indicating do not load on any aircraft. The shipment appeared to contain lithium batteries 'UN3481.' I was told by manager to make sure I load all mail. I placed it to the side and did not load.Lack of training and oversight from the contract company [is an issue]. Pressure from company management to maximize profits, complacency, lack of caring from contract company.I removed [the shipment] from [the] belt and did not load. [It was] sent back to contract mail company so [they] could transport safely.More training, more vigilance.
ASRS:1818995.s: A ground crew member identified a lithium battery shipment labeled "ground transport only" during aircraft loading but was pressured by management to load all mail. The crew member refused to load the item, removed it from the belt, and returned it to the contract company, citing a lack of training and oversight.

ASRS:1819012.n: Lost electrics in aircraft and cockpit went dark. Issue began with pulsating sounds in headset. Changed Comms 2 to 1 to see if [it was] a comm issue and [it] was not. Tried to call ZZZ Approach and had no PTT (Push-to-Talk) functions. At that time, I noticed the cockpit dimming fast. I changed comms and channels and made calls to ZZZ, Guard on [frequency], and ZZZ1 Tower if anyone could hear me. Tried to operate runway lights but had no PTT functions.[I put the] gear down and the cockpit blacked out, airplane did not react as it usually does with full gear extension. Tried to input flaps but had no reaction. Opened emergency gear handle and tried to crank with a lot of thoughts running through my head. At this point, I was in complete darkness and in a left downwind for XXL. [I] had thoughts about a Tower fly-by or diversion to another airport via ForeFlight on iPhone, but without comms inside the SFRA and in a high stress situation, I committed to landing the airplane on XXL and went with it.
ASRS:1819012.s: The pilot experienced a total electrical failure and cockpit blackout while on downwind for XXL, preceded by headset pulsation and loss of PTT function. Despite failed attempts to extend gear and flaps, the pilot manually deployed the landing gear and committed to landing at XXL without radio communication.

ASRS:1819099.n: Eighty miles southeast of ZZZ, while we we're deviating around thunderstorms, we received a call from the B Flight Attendant that we had a strong electrical smell in the aft galley. A few seconds later another call from the flight attendant said the cabin now has the strong odor and a passenger said there is a haze. We notified ATC and were cleared direct to ZZZ. We had a thunderstorm between us and the field, so this required some deviations. We elected not to don the mask because we didn't have smoke or odor in the cockpit. We briefly talked about it and didn't want the added condition. We also decided that we would don the mask at first sign of smell or smoke. Things obviously were very busy because we made it from 36,000 [feet] to the Runway in 18 minutes. By the time we were pointed in the right direction we started to run the Smoke Fire Fumes Checklist but never finished it. We were very tired from the multiple reroutes, PM trip to an AM, back to a PM. I elected not to finish the checklist because I wanted all eyes up so we could get the aircraft on the ground safely. On approach we also had a bird strike, which was a non-event and we landed 10,500 pounds overweight, also a non-event. After we cleared the runway we had the fire trucks shoot the brakes, and after we ran the brake cooling numbers found that we could taxi to the gate. At roughly XX:20 CT and at FL 360, while diverting around thunderstorms and turbulence approximately 80 miles southeast of ZZZ, we were alerted by the B-Flight Attendant of a strong electrical odor in the aft galley. Moments later we were notified that it had spread through the cabin with haze reported by a Passenger. Considering the seriousness of the issue and our #1 priority of Safety, we immediately [requested priority handling] with ATC and received direct ZZZ. The Captain turned off the galley power and advised me to alert Dispatch while he flew and communicated with ATC. We continued to get updates from the Flight Attendants/Dispatch/ATC and kept them in the loop of our emergency diversion into ZZZ. The Captain continued to deviate around thunderstorms and turbulence while I adjusted the route in the FMC, loaded the approach and got weather and landing information. We quickly discussed our arrival with overweight landing, minimum braking, and plan for fire trucks to meet us. We ran the Descent/Arrival Checklists and just started the Smoke/Fire/Fumes Checklist when, as we were now very near the airport, the Captain requested we stop the checklist as he needed me heads up with him and our focus to get the aircraft quickly on the ground. We got the airport in sight, configured, completed the Before Landing Checklist and had a bird strike on approach with a very smooth touchdown and roll out to the end of [runway] XXR. We cleared the runway, advised the Passengers to remain seated and the fire trucks evaluated us with an all clear. We ran a brake cooling with no limitations, so we taxied to the gate with the fire trucks following us. There were no damages to the aircraft or injuries to the Crew or Passengers.The short 15 minutes from first notification to landing in ZZZ was filled with the threats of task loading, additive conditions and Crew factors. It was the last leg of a four-day trip and we were both fatigued from many trip changes/delays, and I was on an FDP extension leaving ZZZ1 and two prior trip extensions. We had additive conditions of thunderstorms and turbulence to deviate around, both en route and on descent while dealing with the emergency. We had task loading with the very short period of time to assess/handle the situation/navigate/communicate/run checklists etc., and get the aircraft on the ground in minimum time.
ASRS:1819099.s: The flight crew diverted an aircraft from FL360 to ZZZ due to an electrical odor and haze reported by cabin crew while deviating around thunderstorms. Fatigue and high task loading led the crew to prioritize landing over completing the smoke checklist, resulting in a safe overweight landing with no injuries or damage.

ASRS:1819142.n: It has been brought to my attention that the 737-MAX aircraft at times sits extremely tail heavy while being loaded and/or unloaded at the gate. I'm not sure of all the details with this specific aircraft, but it is a situation that is happening often according to the line technicians working the gates. According to ramp personnel that have been asked, they have stated that their operating manual does not state that the tail stand needs to be installed. The Aircraft Maintenance Manual states at the very beginning of AMM task 07-10-08-800-801 item 1. A. 'The primary function of the tail stand is to support the airplane tail in an aft CG condition during loading and/or unloading of passengers and cargo'.
ASRS:1819142.s: Line technicians reported that 737-MAX aircraft frequently sit tail-heavy during gate loading and unloading. Ramp personnel stated their manual does not require a tail stand, despite the Aircraft Maintenance Manual specifying its use to support the tail in aft center of gravity conditions.

ASRS:1819176.n: I was the Captain operating Aircraft X. Climbing out of approximately FL280 we received the Right ENG Bleed warning message (First Officer Flying Pilot). I took the flight controls and stopped the climb. The bleed air closed before the bleed source could be selected to non-affected engine source. Initially, I did attempt to complete the procedure, However it did not work. The bleeds closed automatically leaving us with no air. We immediately put on our oxygen masks, I notified ATC and asked for a descent to 15,000. After the descent was initiated. I inquired ATC about 10,000 and terrain clearance. After reviewing terrain clearance and verification with ATC we continued to 10,000. The First Officer completed both the descent checklist and the R Bleed Duct warning check list while in initial descent. During the descent the oxygen masks deployed as both the cabin altitude and then cabin warning messages were received. The masks deployed automatically. At 15,000 the APU was started. Initially the APU would not supply air. After a second attempt to go to manual APU we obtained air on the aircraft. The flight attendants were contacted and an announcement was made to the passengers. The company was notified via ACARS.The fire trucks were requested due to the nature of the situation, initially I was very concerned about the extreme heat in ZZZ and the passengers health without air conditioning. The flight returned to ZZZ without further incident landing Runway X. The flight attendants reported all the passengers were OK and did not need assistance. I made an announcement once we were able to take the masks off at 10,000. I explained the reason for the return to ZZZ. In addition once at the gate another announcement was made apologizing for the inconvenience. Dispatch was contacted by telephone once at the gate. 2 maintenance write ups were completed at the gate: 1. R Eng Bleed Warning. 2. Pax oxygen masks deployed auto. After a delay we received another aircraft and the flight was completed to ZZZ1. I, the First officer, was assigned as the flying pilot on Aircraft X scheduled from ZZZ to ZZZ1, After a normal pushback, start up and takeoff, we received a Right Bleed Master Warning [(R(L) bleed duct] at approximately FL280. As per procedure, I stated I have the radios and controls and asked the Captain to reference QRH for R(L) Bleed Duct. However, before the Captain could perform the QRH procedure the bleeds closed and the aircraft depressurized. I also saw that the passenger oxygen light had come on indicating the passenger oxygen masks had deployed. The Captain took the controls and initiated an immediate descent. The Captain ordered oxygen mask on. Once at a safe altitude (15,000 ft as best as I can remember) we notified ATC, and I began to run the checklist for descent and QRH for R(L) Bleed Duct. Once the Captain determined it was safe, we continued down to 10,000 feet and we began setting up for a return to ZZZ. All Diversion procedures were completed and we conducted a normal approach (still with priority) to ZZZ Runway X. As per the CRJ-900 system manual and QRH, a Left or Right Bleed Duct leak will cause all bleed air sources to be closed within 30 seconds causing a loss of pressurization. This is not enough time to perform the manual bleed procedure per QRH. Therefore the manual bleed procedure should at least be a checklist item.
ASRS:1819176.s: The Captain and First Officer of Aircraft X experienced a right engine bleed warning at FL280, causing automatic bleed closure and depressurization. The crew descended to 10,000 feet, deployed oxygen masks, and returned to ZZZ, attributing the event to a system design that closes bleeds too quickly for manual intervention.

ASRS:1819178.n: On the SEEVR4 arrival FEWWW Transition to DFW descending from FL360 to FL340, in VNAV, smooth air, seat belt sign off, FO pilot flying we experienced wake turbulence from a preceding aircraft. The first encounter started with a light buffet typical of wake turbulence, then developed into a more severe rolling [motion], and eventually rolled 15-20 degrees left disconnecting the auto pilot. The First Officer stabilized the roll, selected a shallow descent in vertical speed, and reengaged the autopilot. Shortly after, a second buffeting began and the aircraft rolled left again. The First Officer implemented unusual attitude procedures disengaging the autopilot, calling 'my aircraft' prior to the aircraft rolling to the extent it did in the first encounter. After stabilizing we asked for a lateral offset and reported the wake turbulence upset to ATC saying we were unable to avoid the aircraft's wake. It was granted and no further wake turbulence was encountered. I asked if the fight attendants were ok, which they responded 'yes', and made a PA to the passengers. On landing, the No. 1 Flt attendant said that he hurt his neck trying to stay upright while standing in the aisle during the event. He had not fallen or hit anything but twisted it trying to keep his balance.I reported the event to Dispatch on landing. During descent on the SEEVR4 into DFW leaving FL360 to FL340 wake turbulence was encountered. Preceding the event the aircraft was in smooth air. Approximately passing through FL350 the aircraft encountered the wake. A slight buffet was felt followed by a bank of approximately 15 degrees to the left. An immediate recovery was made. ATC was notified and the descent was shallowed to separate from the leading aircraft. This followed with a second less aggressive encounter and a full recovery was initiated. ATC was notified and we requested an immediate lateral deviation. No further wake was encounter for the remaining flight. The Captain made an announcement and talked to the flight attendants to verify everyone was ok. At this time he was informed no one was injured. Upon landing a flight attendant informed the captain that his neck was bothering him. Stating did not hit his head but may have twisted his neck and now felt pain.
ASRS:1819178.s: During the SEEVR4 arrival to DFW, a First Officer flying a descent from FL360 to FL340 encountered wake turbulence that caused two autopilot disengagements and 15-20 degree rolls. After requesting a lateral offset, the crew stabilized the aircraft, but a flight attendant later reported a neck injury from twisting while standing in the aisle.

ASRS:1819250.n: While taxiing Aircraft X after landing, we were directed by ramp control from taxiway bravo northbound to abeam 66 blue line to gate. Well after starting our turn east to the blue 66 square, a truck drove in front of us southbound on the service road not yielding. The Captain had to apply brakes to avoid a collision. Nothing else to add. Ensure ramp personnel comply with traffic procedures.
ASRS:1819250.s: While taxiing Aircraft X after landing, a truck failed to yield on a service road, forcing the Captain to brake to avoid a collision. The pilot reported that ramp personnel must comply with traffic procedures.

ASRS:1819281.n: On a flight planned from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we were struck by lightning east of El Paso, TX, while cruising at FL400 along J74 with a clearance to deviate for weather. At the time we were struck by lightning, we were passing between two cells that were approximately 20nm north and south of us, and had been flying for several minutes inside a thin strati-form layer between two cells. The air was very smooth and our radar showed no weather of consequence beyond the two cells. The first indication that we had been struck by lightning was when there was a loud noise (bang) and the outer layer of the copilot's windshield completely fractured, with visible burn marks. We notified ATC and requested a descent to 10,000 ft and as soon as we were cleared we began a rapid descent while manually controlling the cabin pressure to reduce the differential pressure per the QRH procedure. On reaching 10,000 ft, with the cabin differential reduced to the minimum possible and the airspeed to 250 KIAS, we elected to continue to ZZZ1 where there is a factory service center. We were cleared to proceed to ZZZ with the occasional vectors to avoid high terrain and landed without incident. On a flight planned from ZZZ to ZZZ1, we were struck by lightning east of El Paso, TX, while cruising at FL400 along J74 with a clearance to deviate for weather. At the time we were struck by lightning, we were passing between two cells that were approximately 20nm north and south of us, and had been flying for several minutes inside a thin stratiform layer between the two cells. The air was very smooth and our radar showed no weather of consequence beyond the two cells. The first indication that we had been struck by lightning was when there was a loud noise (bang) and the outer layer of the copilot's windshield completely fractured, with visible burn marks. We notified ATC and requested a descent to 10,000 ft and as soon as we were cleared we began a rapid descent while manually controlling the cabin pressure to reduce the differential pressure per the QRH procedure. On reaching 10,000 ft, with the cabin differential reduced to the minimum possible and the airspeed reduced to 250KIAS, we elected to continue to ZZZ1 where there is a factory service center. We were cleared to proceed to ZZZ1 with occasional vectors to avoid high terrain and landed without incident.
ASRS:1819281.s: The flight crew was struck by lightning at FL400 east of El Paso while deviating for weather, fracturing the copilot's windshield. They descended to 10,000 ft per QRH procedures and landed safely at ZZZ1 without further incident.

ASRS:1819298.n: I returned from a short flight to ZZZ1 and ordered fuel at the FBO (Fixed Base Operator). The instructions were to top off both inboards and add 20 gal/side on the outboards - 100LL. The outboards were both empty, so this should have given me 44 gal/side in the mains and 20 gal/side in the aux (770 pound fuel load, which is my standard). I stayed with the plane to show the line person the filler locations and ensure that the fuel was 100LL. I then went into the FBO. I paid for the fuel but got no receipt, due to a change in their payment system being ongoing. I then returned to the aircraft, started it, and put it in the hangar. The next morning I returned to preflight for a trip with my entire family (me plus 4). My preflight checks oil first. This was done and OK.I then check fuel quantity using a calibrated dipstick. I then sump. I work left to right. The first dipstick goes into the left aux tank. It was completely full. I then measured the left main which was also completely full. I concluded that the line guy had topped all four fillers and the aircraft would be overweight without removal of my spares kits, my tools, and some baggage. As I was going to measure the right tanks my youngest child said he had to go to the bathroom. He is undergoing chemotherapy and my wife and I respond to bathroom requests quickly. I stopped the preflight and we took him to a bathroom nearby. I resumed the preflight upon my return, but was only 2 or 3 minutes into it when he had to go to the bathroom again. When we returned from the second bathroom trip I finished measuring the tanks and wrote the quantities in my preflight form. I wrote 'LM - 44, LA - 46, RM - 44, RA - 46.' I then sumped the fuel, which was OK. Ordinarily I would pour the sumped fuel into the right main filler but I put it instead into my power tug because I did not want one ounce of extra weight in the plane. I then did a weight and balance to reduce the weight until we were at max gross. I had to remove material from the plane that is ordinarily kept there. We then boarded and flew from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 without incident.At ZZZ2 we dropped off our 3 kids with grandparents and prepared for the next leg to ZZZ3. I always buy fuel when I stop anywhere and then dip and sump it. However, I had loads of fuel because of the over-fueling at ZZZ1 and ZZZ2 is only a 4,000 foot runway. I apologized for not buying fuel and promised to buy some when coming back through. I did not dip the tanks. I fired up the plane and my wife and I took off for ZZZ3. While in cruise, about 25 minutes into the flight, the right engine abruptly lost power. I looked and saw that it had no fuel pressure. I engaged the right boost pump. Fuel pressure returned to normal and the engine ran normally. I concluded I had lost the right engine-driven pump. About 1 minute layer it started to surge again. I switched to the right aux tank but this did not help. I still believed I had lost the engine driven pump, but I had run through the checklist and was not able to restore power. I decided not to mess with it further in the air. I went through the shutdown list and feathered the right engine. I then called Center to notify. Center suggested ZZZ and I concurred. I descended toward ZZZ, in and out of IMC. I loaded the RNAV approach as it looked like I might need it. I did a 360 at the holding point to lose altitude. I decided to make a left racetrack even though that was the unprotected side of the hold because I wanted to turn into the running engine (I was way above any obstructions).I intercepted the centerline and flew the approach on the left engine. The approach and landing were uneventful. I was able to taxi in and park on the left engine. The FBO at ZZZ told me they had already contacted ATC and informed them I was safely down. We dropped our bags at the FBO and my wife started trying to get a rental car. I went out to the plane and opened the cowlings to see if therewas anything obvious. There wasn't anything. All fuel lines (including return) were intact. I visually inspected the engine driven pump but nothing was apparent. I sat thinking through the symptoms and finally went and pulled the right main filler cap. It was bone dry. I ordered fuel. After adding fuel the engine started and once the prop spun fast enough to get out of the feather detents it returned to normal operation. There were only two possible explanations: (1) A massive fuel leak, but there was no evidence for that, or (2) The ZZZ1 line guy filled both aux tanks, and filled the left main tank, but put no fuel at all in the right main tank. I think #2 is what happened. I thought I had dipped the right main (I even wrote it on the form) but the double interruption in preflight must have meant that I started again in the wrong place and never checked the right main. After the initial ground start I again stopped to check for fuel leaks. There were none. I then did a 30 minute ground run all of which was normal. We reloaded the plane and took off for ZZZ3. The plane has had no trouble since. It was simply a dry tank. But, it was set up by the following unusual circumstances all lining up: (1) Line guy fails to fuel as directed (2) Problem not immediately caught because I was just putting it in the hangar and did not dip as per usual, (3) Lack of fuel receipt which would have shown the wrong quantity, (4) Double distraction in preflight, (5) further distraction by consternation over being heavy and having to unload the plane, (6) Failure to take fuel at ZZZ2, and (7) Failure to dip at ZZZ2 anyway.Lessons Learned: (1) If you are interrupted in preflight start over from the beginning, (2) Dip the fuel every time before you leave the ground. The landing at ZZZ2 was the first takeoff without dipping I can remember in many years. (3) With plenty of altitude under you maybe consider working the restart problem a bit longer but not much longer because it's better to work that problem on the ground. The reason for #3 is I should have been able to restart the right engine. If I had left the right selector on aux (which had about 40 gallons in it) for a minute or two I suspect the engine driven pump would have re-primed (There is no boost pump available for the aux tanks in the BE-50). Even better - I should have cross fed the right engine from the left main and used the left main boost pump to re-prime the engine driven pump. This last option would have worked and power would have been restored.On the other hand - I am glad I have done training at least once per quarter and the actual handling of the aircraft was not challenging, even though it was an IMC approach down to about 1500 feet. I think this is the main reason I thought 'Just cage the ***%@@ thing and figure it out on the ground.' In writing this explanation I want to make plain that responsibility for all these events rests with me. Line guys make errors and it is the pilot's job to catch them. It is striking to me that there were 3 separate events deviating from my normal habits of operation. Inspect fuel immediately after fueling, do not re-start a pre-flight in the middle, never take off without dipping all four fillers. Had I conformed to my normal habits on any of the three, this would not have happened. Lastly, I feel a bit bad about declaring and tying up resources. However I would do it again. ATC was just as helpful as you would expect and it was nice to be able to offload distractions, looking up weather and frequencies, when I was single engine in IMC.
ASRS:1819298.s: The pilot reported a right engine power loss during cruise from ZZZ2 to ZZZ3 caused by an empty right main tank due to improper fueling at ZZZ1 and a missed preflight dipstick check. The pilot successfully feathered the engine, flew a single-engine IMC approach to ZZZ, and landed safely after confirming the tank was dry.

ASRS:1819346.n: This was both pilots' second flight on the MAX Aircraft since its return. We briefed a single engine taxi, in order to save gas, due to carrying an alternate in ZZZ1. We determined to start the engine once we determined what the lineup was for takeoff. As we turned the corner, approaching taxiway, we saw that we were #4, and due to the long start of the MAX, we began to start the #1 engine. This turned out to still be almost too late to start the engine and ensure 3 minutes of stabilization at idle prior to takeoff. The engine was started by the time we turned onto taxiway, but both of us were very closely monitoring the time and taxiing slow as we were now #2 for takeoff. After stabilization, we remembered that we had also talked earlier in the trip about trying to remember to do the new VNAV programming procedures in order to build habit patterns. Having a minute to go before our three-minute stabilization time, we decided to program the computer for the practice. This was one more distraction added to that of watching the engine time. About the time we finished, we were cleared for takeoff with 30 seconds to go before three minutes. We saw that we were going to be good on the time, so acknowledged the clearance, turned on the lights, took the runway and took off. Only on climbout, after having cleaned up, did we realize that we had failed to run the Before Takeoff Checklist. We immediately checked in with the Flight Attendants, who confirmed the fact that we had not notified them of the takeoff clearance as required by our flows and the checklist. Due to the length of taxi, however, they were all seated with everything stowed, and nothing unfortunate occurred. The rest of the flight went uneventfully. Distractions piled up, due to being in a somewhat unfamiliar aircraft and trying to accomplish new programming procedures for climbout. While everything was being done to try to be procedurally correct in accordance with what the Company wants done, being out of normal habit patterns caused us to miss a checklist. I would suggest that regarding the MAX, until we are all much more familiar with the timing required to start the engines with motoring and still get the three minutes, that we minimize the times that we single engine taxi, doing so only when there will be an excessive amount of ground time anticipated. Beyond that, if we do accomplish a single engine taxi, and we approach the runway without the time required, rather than focus on slowing down to get the time, simply tell Tower we need a minute to allow for the three minute and accept the delay. Further, the timing for the VNAV programming needs to be codified. It can only be accomplished after the numbers are received from ATIS which is when everything is happening quickly to get us off the gate. It might be worth adding a 'VNAV Climbout programmed' step to the Before Push or Before Taxi Checklist, to prevent distractions later on. Second flight in the MAX 8, since its return to service. We taxied out single engine and saw the lineup was minimal for takeoff on [Runway] XXL. Began engine start, after exiting the ramp. Because of the slow engine start with the MAX, we were closely watching the timing to ensure we got three minutes after engine start. Engine was started as we turned onto taxiway, and the aircraft in front of us was cleared for takeoff. We taxied slowly, as it looked like we would make our engine warmup time with a slow taxi. We decided to load the new VNAV Takeoff Programming Procedures. Got that loaded, just as our engine time was completed and Tower cleared us for takeoff. We rolled onto the runway and had an uneventful takeoff and climbout. Because we were distracted, we failed to accomplish the Before Takeoff Checklist or ding the flight attendants. Loading of VNAV takeoff programming should be accomplished earlier than approaching the end of the runway. I'm not sure where the best time is to load the VNAV takeoff procedure, since we are very busy after we get our numbers. This would minimize distractions at a critical point in the taxi out. MAX engine start is slow. If it looked like we needed more time for engine warm up, we should not hesitate to let Tower know we need more time.
ASRS:1819346.s: Pilots on a second MAX 8 flight missed the Before Takeoff Checklist and failed to notify cabin crew due to distractions from single-engine taxi timing and late VNAV programming. The aircraft took off safely with no adverse outcome, though the crew noted the need to adjust procedures to prevent such distractions.

ASRS:1819365.n: Conditions were VMC and more that 10 statute miles visibility within the area surrounding ZZZ. Upon seeing and confirming the ZZZ airport to our Northwest, ATC cleared us for the visual approach. After clearance was provided I entered the downwind and both descended to and leveled off at approximately 2300 to 2400 feet. Now this altitude is about 145 to 245 feet higher than traffic pattern altitude. This additional altitude decision was due to the understanding of elevated terrain in the area as described in our company published page that was current and wanting to have what I felt was an adequate but slight additional safety buffer between the aircraft and this terrain. In level flight the aircraft had a GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) warning occur one time for a moment and then disappear nearly immediately. When the warning occurred both pilots were already heads' up and eyes out with a clear visual of the area and the airport. At such time when the warning occurred it was determined that the best course of action was to hold altitude for the moment and the warning disappeared. Upon the disappearance of the warning and the CRM (Crew Resource Management) of the situation, the Visual Approach was continued to a successful landing and positive result.Now as I do not recall the complete details of the event I can only speculate on a possible cause for this while in level flight. It may be due to not being on a perfect line for the downwind and sporadic changes in terrain within proximity of the aircraft for the safety system catch that change and to alert. Our company page does advise caution when conducting visual approaches into ZZZ due to elevated terrain and that GPWS warnings do occur in early descents and if one does occur to take appropriate action to ensure the safe completion of the flight. I believe the CRM with this situation was handled appropriately with respect to this publication. The company page for ZZZ states that the safety department has noticed a high rate of GPWS warnings with respect to landing in ZZZ. With respect to this a possible suggestion could include a little more detail on the pages for the area of the airport with recommended altitudes, or possibly change approach procedures in to the airport entirely to help combat these occurrences.
ASRS:1819365.s: Pilots flying a visual approach to ZZZ in VMC held 2300–2400 feet due to elevated terrain, triggering a brief GPWS warning. The crew maintained altitude until the warning cleared, then completed a successful landing, attributing the alert to sporadic terrain changes and noting the airport's known high rate of such warnings.

ASRS:1819466.n: Cruising at 10,000 feet, without warning the number 2 engine failed. First Officer called out 'Power Loss' on number 2, Memory Items and QRH were completed. ATC and Dispatch was advised. ZZZ was chosen as nearest suitable airport, single engine approach and landing completed without incident.Engine failure inflight without warning. No indications or warnings that could lead to cause inflight.As per Company EMB-120 training, we completed the memory items and QRH procedures for engine failure inflight and single engine approach and landing. Notified ATC and dispatch. I was the Pilot Monitoring and Captain Name [was] Pilot Flying. While cruising at 10,000 feet MSL approximately 60 nautical miles south of ZZZ1 (destination) my Captain and I experienced the right engine fail. The airplane yawed and banked to the right, and I immediately pointed out 'right engine failure' on the engine instrument stack. The Captain and I immediate went into our emergency action items, then I gave the radios to the Captain while I performed the 'Engine Failure Inflight' checklist in the QRH. The checklist was completed and the engine secure, then we made our diversion decision to ZZZ considering factors of single engine performance, distance from the destination and the availability of a nearer airfield on our filed route of flight. After making the appropriate calls to ATC I ran the 'Single Engine Approach and Landing Checklist' in the QRH. I paused the checklist at 'Landing Gear.....Down' to give the Captain time to brief the approach into ZZZ, ILS XX. I took controls from the Captain and maintained proper coordination, speed and altitude while he briefed the approach. I handed back controls to the Captain when he was ready and let approach control we were ready for the approach. The remainder of the paused checklist was then completed and we made a seamless approach and landing on a single engine. After landing the emergency vehicles did an exterior check of the aircraft and confirmed we were safe of harm and we taxied under our own power to the civilian FBO and shutdown/secured the airplane. Aware at approximately XA:53, immediate yaw and bank to the right as the number 2 engine failed. The only aural warning was when the NH dropped below 50% and ELEC illuminated on the MAP (Multiple Alarm Panel). Do not know [cause] entirely. Waiting for diagnosis from maintenance.
ASRS:1819466.s: The crew of an EMB-120 experienced an unannounced right engine failure at 10,000 feet, causing yaw and bank. They completed emergency checklists, diverted to ZZZ, and executed a safe single-engine ILS approach and landing while awaiting maintenance diagnosis.

ASRS:1819468.n: At 7,000 feet approximately 4.5 miles of the ZZZ VOR, pilots observed a large two piece drone, black in color, with camera equipment at 11 o'clock fly over the wing, clearing the aircraft's wing by what seemed like 1-2 feet. No evasive action was taken as pilots had no time to react. ATC was immediately notified and advised of drone's altitude, position and description. Flight continued to ZZZZ without incident. As soon as drone was spotted. Drone being flown on active airway. Advised ATC of description and location of drone activity. Suggestion: Drones not being flown in areas of heavy aircraft traffic.
ASRS:1819468.s: Pilots encountered a large black drone with camera equipment at 7,000 feet on an active airway, which passed within 1-2 feet of the wing. No evasive action was possible, but the flight continued to ZZZZ without incident after ATC was notified.

ASRS:1819490.n: Passengers boarded & travelled from ZZZ to ZZZ1. In ZZZ1, the passengers then boarded a [make/model aircraft] and boarded through the aft with their carry on bags. I saw their bags and let them know they were too big to fit in the overhead bin. Passenger stated they were told to bring them onboard as a carry on. FA A and I were trying to accommodate the bags and were then told by the Gate Agent they were smart bags & since the battery couldn't be removed, the bags would need to come off. The pax were deplaned along with their bags. FA A stated the passengers were with us (along with their bags) on the previous flight. I did not see them board with their bags on the original flight.
ASRS:1819490.s: Cabin crew encountered passengers with oversized smart bags on a [make/model aircraft] at ZZZ1. The Gate Agent required the bags to be removed due to non-removable batteries, resulting in the passengers deplaning with their luggage.

ASRS:1819509.n: My student pilot and I had just entered the pattern from a 45 degree leg to left downwind when a call on CTAF addressed us by call sign, asked our intentions, and said we were 'all over the place'. I looked to my right and saw another airplane about 500 feet from us, also on left downwind. The pilot said on CTAF that he had just turned from crosswind to downwind and was aware of our entry from the 45 based on our position reports. He said he would extend downwind to allow us to land ahead of him. I can think of three factors that contributed to my failure to see the traffic until so late.First, the CTAF frequency for ZZZ is shared by numerous airports in the area. While I was talking my student through the pattern entry, we were hearing calls for at least four different airports without any silence, so we had to talk to each other over these calls. In such a situation it was easy to miss the one call we needed to hear.Second, the frequency was congested shortly before the traffic conflict by a lengthy and non-standard position report ending with, 'could any traffic in the area please advise'. This may have been the pilot of the aircraft that conflicted with me, or it may have been an unrelated call at another airport that blocked the frequency. A colleague who had just landed at the same airport later told me that the same pilot had also called him on CTAF while he was on final, asking his 'intentions after landing'. Third, my student had become disoriented while making a teardrop turn to the 45 degree entry, and I was distracted by helping her get reoriented to the airport and make a correct pattern entry.
ASRS:1819509.s: An instructor and student pilot on a left downwind entry at ZZZ nearly collided with another aircraft due to late visual acquisition. The reporter attributed the conflict to congested CTAF communications, non-standard position reports, and distraction from assisting a disoriented student.

ASRS:1819510.n: We were cleared for visual approach Runway 21 at FWB. Our FMS was programmed and engaged on the RNAV(GPS) RWY 21. On the LPV VNAV glide slope, at 2,000 feet MSL, our GPWS [alerted] 'too low terrain, pull up'. We were still VMC with no terrain concerns, and we continued for a normal landing. I am concerned that the top of the trees may be interfering with the approach clearance area. Also, taking off from Runway 21, resulted in a momentary GPWS warning when below 500 feet during climb.
ASRS:1819510.s: The flight crew received a GPWS "too low terrain" alert at 2,000 feet MSL while on an RNAV(GPS) LPV visual approach to Runway 21 at FWB. The pilot attributed the false warning to potential tree interference and noted a similar momentary GPWS alert during a previous takeoff below 500 feet.

ASRS:1819514.n: Potomac TRACON Chesapeake Sector always issues the BWI altimeter, regardless of the destination of the IFR flight within the sector. This occurs whether the pilot is calling with an initial check-in or being cleared for an approach. TRACON always issues the BWI altimeter, even though they are provided the ESN weather data (Tower/ASOS). Note that BWI and ESN altimeters rarely are the same. When cleared for an instrument approach to ESN, a pilot should be given the ESN altimeter and not BWI's. As a local pilot, I am keenly aware of the discrepancy in altimeter settings provided by the TRACON, therefore, I ignore the altimeter setting given to me by the TRACON. However, transient pilots may overlook the discrepancy and subsequently descend below minimums on an IAP into ESN. I have talked to Chesapeake Sector supervisors about the problem but haven't been successful in convincing TRACON management that their procedures should be changed.
ASRS:1819514.s: A pilot reported that Potomac TRACON Chesapeake Sector issues the BWI altimeter instead of the correct ESN setting for instrument approaches to ESN. The pilot warned that transient pilots might descend below minimums due to this discrepancy, despite unsuccessful attempts to change the procedure.

ASRS:1819524.n: I had to turn off all electronics, including taxi Light, landing light, anti-collision lights, navigation lights, ADS-B, transponder, and radios. Due to a discharging battery state. I was worried I was not going to have the power to bring down the gear. I continued on the flight at 5,000 feet to get to ZZZ1. I let Approach know by phone, as that was the only number I had easy access to in the air, and they let the Center know of the issue and my plan and location. I had 2 iPad's and a smartphone to stay on a new course and stay out of any controlled airspace and followed a route around the western side of the Class B airspace. Route was ZZZ to ZZZ1.Then after clearing the northwest side of the airspace, I went direct to ZZZ1. Once I got less than 10 miles away from ZZZ1 I turned on my electronic system to bring down the landing gear. The backup plan if the gear was not going to go down was to go to ZZZ2. I told them I was planning on calling them no later than XA:30 PM of my plan or if I was on the ground. I got on the ground safely in ZZZ1. Approach called, and I told them I was on the ground safely. The major worry I had was my NAV lights or anti-collision lights at night and the point of this report. I decided to continue the flight and land in ZZZ1 over any other airport because I knew that was the safest place for me to land at night with no lights or radios. I had people waiting, and they turned on the airport lights for me. At any other airport, I was worried it would have ended badly. The different idea was to turn around to ZZZ, but there was flight training with multiple airplanes in the pattern. There was no damage or any injury. I still had all primary flight instruments the whole flight.
ASRS:1819524.s: The pilot experienced a discharging battery at 5,000 feet, forcing the shutdown of all electronics including radios and lights. The flight continued to ZZZ1 using visual navigation, where ground personnel activated airport lights to ensure a safe landing with no injuries or damage.

ASRS:1819532.n: While on an IFR flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, we were sent 'direct ZZZZZ' to begin the RNAV Approach into ZZZ1. About a mile from ZZZZZ1, we were advised by ATC of VFR traffic that seemed to be on the other feeder route for the approach. After making visual contact with the pointed out traffic, we announced 'traffic in sight' and proceeded with the approach.
