The traffic in question was a Cirrus SR22 doing 152 knots, so we slowed down to our approach speed of 90 knots and expected them to continue the approach, at which point we would either continue behind or request delay vectors. The Cirrus unexpectedly turned outbound towards us and we had to take evasive maneuvers. The situation resolved with both parties taking evasive action in the form of a right turn, as stated by the FAA's right-of-way rules
ASRS:1819532.s: During an IFR RNAV approach to ZZZ1, the crew encountered a Cirrus SR22 on a feeder route that unexpectedly turned outbound. The crew executed evasive right turns to avoid a collision, resolving the conflict in accordance with FAA right-of-way rules.

ASRS:1819534.n: I was flying along the highway at 1,500 feet AGL with the mountains to my north and the ocean to my south. I took the plane on a personal flight out to Location. I was returning to my home base airport ZZZ and was 5 miles out when the engine started to cough/quit very erratic. It was apparent that I needed to land immediately as the plane would not be able to hold altitude. My landing options at 1,500 feet in this area were limited. The tide was in so there were no beach options along the ocean and the mountains were cliffs down to the road. I landed the aircraft on the highway with the motor still coughing. After safely landing the plane with no damage to aircraft or risk to other traffic on the road I shut down the motor and pushed it off on a shoulder. It appeared to me that I was having a fuel delivery issue and that was causing my motor to choke. I had 12 gallons of fuel in the plane and was operating with 1.25 hours remaining. I sumped the fuel and was unable to find contaminates at the time. I poured 3 each 5 gallon travel bags of fuel into the wings and sumped the fuel again. After 40 minutes of inspection, I started the motor up again, It ran rough for short period of time and then came back to full power and normal operation condition. I departed right after traffic was momentarily stopped on either end and returned to my home airport without further issue. I have scheduled a full mechanical inspection of the fuel tank plumbing system. I suspect the vent caps and/or vent lines for the new fuel tanks are not venting as fast as the motor is sucking fuel when the tanks get down to 12 gallons remaining.This is an experimental aircraft which received a new wing and fuel tank system and I have only flown the new wing for approximately 60 hours. We will also retest each tank to verify usable fuel in each tank and make determination if fuel indicating lines need to be re-placarded for usable. Plane will not be returned to service until root cause has been identified with mechanic.
ASRS:1819534.s: The pilot of an experimental aircraft experienced erratic engine power and altitude loss during the return leg at 1,500 feet AGL, forcing a highway landing. The pilot suspects a fuel venting issue with the new tank system, as the engine recovered after refueling and inspection.

ASRS:1819564.n: Removed and replaced HYD pump on engine and noticed that this engine and all the others don't have safety wire on the HYD tubing where it should be. Has bothered me ever since and ended up being one of the reasons that I am not employed there. I was told that they don't safety the large intake and return lines on the engine driven pumps even though there is clearly a place for it.
ASRS:1819564.s: A mechanic replaced a hydraulic pump and found missing safety wire on engine-driven pump tubing, contrary to design. The mechanic was subsequently terminated after reporting that the employer refused to install safety wire on large intake and return lines despite available attachment points.

ASRS:1819625.n: Per the NOTAMs for RDM, daylight savings hours for Tower Operations begin at 0600L. 10-7 information just has 0500L as the opening for RDM Tower.
ASRS:1819625.s: A pilot reported a discrepancy between RDM NOTAMs, which state Tower Operations begin at 0600L during daylight savings, and ATIS 10-7, which lists the opening time as 0500L.

ASRS:1819718.n: While on approach into ZZZ, an aircraft on the ground reported an APU fire message they had on approach and that they believed there was no fire. While we were on short approach into ZZZ a fire vehicle pulled out of the fire station and up to the hold short line and said they were going to cross the runway. We made two radio calls stating we were on short final and the fire vehicle stated that they know we are on short final and that they will be off the runway momentarily. We performed the balked [landing] in ZZZ at about 100 feet because the fire vehicle was still on the runway. We then returned back to the field and landed.[There was a] possible fire for [an] aircraft on [the] ground on the opposite side of [the] runway fire station. [It was] night time with rain that possibly lowered visibility from the ground, but flight visibility was at least 10 miles [and the tower was closed]. Enhanced training for operators of ground vehicles that may operate on the runway [is recommended].
ASRS:1819718.s: A pilot on short final into ZZZ executed a balked landing at 100 feet after a fire vehicle entered the runway despite radio warnings. The vehicle was responding to a reported APU fire on another aircraft, and the pilot subsequently returned to land safely.

ASRS:1819754.n: While supporting a Metro pilot as a non-acting crew member on the ZZZ-ZZZZ run who was unfamiliar with the specifics, we were returning to ZZZ and found the airplane in a near-miss with VFR Traffic. The pilot, was instructed to fly direct to the IAF. The controller alerted us about VFR traffic, later instructing to expedite descent to 4,300 feet. I continued to watch for traffic as it was on my side of the aircraft. I found the traffic and alerted the Captain that it was at the same altitude, heading in our direction of flight. Being unfamiliar with the aircraft I'm not sure if there is proper TCAS, but we received an alert and immediately descended to avoid the near-miss with VFR traffic. The pilot flying then told the Approach Controller his action and intent, and the controller repeated twice 'below MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) climb to 4,300 feet but we were unable due to the VFR traffic we were avoiding. After successfully avoiding the traffic the Captain climbed to 4,300 feet and continued the approach. I saw the VFR/colliding traffic at the airplane's 3 o'clock, the side of the airplane I could visually see from my observation seat. Lack of vectoring instruction from ATC for two airplanes on a collision course. Captain immediately descended to avoid collision with VFR traffic. IFR traffic and VFR traffic needs better observation from ATC. Though I was a non-acting crew member on this flight the Captain and I worked as a team and executed proper CRM to avoided a mid-air collision. I was operating Aircraft X to ZZZ, as the Captain and Pilot Flying. Onboard I had a Brasilia First Officer, who flew down to ZZZZ with me to assist with customs and all the paperwork associated with the run. ZZZ-ZZZZ was his regular run, and I was covering it for the day. The additional crew member was not an active crew member during the leg, but he was on headset with me helping to monitor the flight. It was towards the end of the flight, and we were being vectored by Approach. We were flying towards the Initial Approach Fix for the ILS Approach and descending to 4,300 feet. During the descent, ATC called out VFR traffic to our 3 o'clock position several miles away, at an altitude of 4,500 feet. During the descent, ATC has also told us to expedite our descent. Initially, we saw traffic in that direction and called 'in sight' to ATC, but I quickly realized we had identified a 737 climbing, not the VFR traffic we were looking for. I decided to use the First Officer and asked him to continue to look for the VFR traffic. He told me he had it in sight, and he helped me locate it. At about that same time, the transponder gave an aural alert 'traffic, 1 mile, same altitude'. When I saw the traffic, we were very close and a couple of hundred feet below it. The other aircraft had little relative motion on the windscreen, so I knew our flight paths would cross very closely. At that moment, I made a split-second decision to exercise Pilot in Command authority, and I deviated from our altitude by initiating a descent. I immediately advised ATC that I was deviating due to traffic, and I was descending to 3,500 feet. The weather was VFR, so I felt like descending was the safest option for the flight. The controller responded that I was below his Minimum Vectoring Altitude and needed to return to 4,300 feet. I told him that we would go back to 4,300 feet when able. I stayed around 3,500 feet until I felt like we were clear of the traffic. The controller asked if I was responding to an RA. I told him, no. I'm not sure if was explained that the aircraft was not equipped with a TCAS. Eventually, we returned to 4,300 feet, got a visual on ZZZ, flew a Visual Approach to the field, and continued the flight without further abnormalities. We were aware of the event the moment it occurred through active monitoring. I think the instructions we received from ATC were the primary factor in this event. I deviated from our assigned altitude to create a safe amount of separation between our aircraft. I should have queried the controller more about the traffic at 4,500 feet as he was having us expedite our descent. That could have given him an opportunity to change his instruction for us. I thought his plan was to get us further below the traffic.
ASRS:1819754.s: The Captain of an IFR flight descending to 4,300 feet deviated below Minimum Vectoring Altitude to avoid a near-miss with VFR traffic at 4,500 feet after ATC failed to provide adequate separation. The pilot attributed the event to insufficient ATC vectoring and traffic observation, though the crew successfully avoided collision through immediate descent and CRM.

ASRS:1819860.n: While maneuvering near ZZZ airport, another aircraft was on a similar flight in the same general vicinity. My instructor and I made at least six radio calls to the other aircraft by its tail number to attempt to determine its intentions, but received no response to any of them. Said aircraft did make occasional radio calls, but they did not reflect its actual flight path or maneuvering intentions. On two occasions, the aircraft maneuvered directly into our immediate vicinity, although we were able to remain clear of it in the course of our maneuvering. On the third instance, we had announced our intention to follow the other aircraft as we were both returning to ZZZ airport. We had maneuvered well outside of the traffic pattern because of other traffic in the area, continuing to follow the other aircraft. Said aircraft then announced a right turn to increase its clearance from us and other traffic, but instead initiated a descending left turn directly into our path of flight. At this point we were approximately 1,000 feet, and were forced to initiate an evasive descent of about 350 feet. We estimate the lateral distance between our aircraft and the other to be approximately 150 feet, as its registration was clearly legible. Prior to these events, our aircraft was on a short final approach as part of a practice landing, at which point the other aircraft in question cut in front of us to take off. We had announced our position and the other aircraft had responded that it was holding short of the runway, but did not do so. Throughout the duration of our flight, the aircraft in question appeared to operate without regard for us or other aircraft in its vicinity, and had we not taken the evasive action that we did, a collision would have been highly likely.
ASRS:1819860.s: A student and instructor near ZZZ airport were forced to descend 350 feet at 1,000 feet to avoid a collision with another aircraft that ignored radio calls and executed an unexpected descending left turn. The other aircraft also cut in front of them on short final despite claiming to hold short, operating without regard for traffic.

ASRS:1819866.n: Chain of Events:Advised by Tower upon approach that a runway inspection was being conducted, cleared to overfly the runway at 800 feet MSL, then make left pattern until runway inspection was completed. I descended to the 800 feet but, upon level off, was subsequently blinded by the sun (I was flying west and it was approaching evening). As a result, I was sun-blinded and didn't see the altimeter for a few moments -- when I could see it again it was unwinding toward 450 feet as I approached the runway. I immediately added power and pulled up to regain the assigned 800 feet I was to overfly the runway. No violation occurred as I did cross the threshold (and did overfly the runway) at the assigned 800 feet. Apparently the tower controller concurred, remaining cheerful, friendly, and very helpful in cutting short my pattern to expedite my arrival as the runway inspection was concluded (I was allowed to turn downwind, cleared to land, after only needing to overfly a few feet of the runway).Human Performance Considerations:I was sun-blinded upon level off, as the sun then appeared suddenly in my flight path after being shielded by the roof line in the descending approach. I had not yet trimmed the aircraft for level flight, so it seems the manual pullback on the yoke was relaxed without my awareness while being distracted/blinded by the sun. I was aware of the hazard and tried to look to the side for orientation while reaching to block the sun with the visor and my hand, whereupon I regained sight of the altimeter and corrected.What can be done to prevent recurrence:Remember to preemptively pull down visor in such an approach. (It is my habit to do so, but didn't this time because it didn't seem quite late enough to worry about it.) I'm sharing this to alert others to this potential problem.
ASRS:1819866.s: A pilot flying a westbound approach was cleared to overfly the runway at 800 feet MSL but descended to 450 feet after being sun-blinded and losing sight of the altimeter. The pilot immediately corrected the descent to regain the assigned altitude, successfully overflew the runway, and was subsequently cleared to land.

ASRS:1819894.n: Aircraft X was inbound to ZZZ from the ZZZ1 airspace. I verbally coordinated a 360 heading with the north controller because I was vectoring off the arrival for sequencing. I took a handoff on Aircraft Z at 10,000 feet direct ZZZ2, at the same time I had two ZZZZZ departures that I was worried about being a factor. I was vectoring Aircraft A off of the arrival as well as Aircraft B. I was trying to make sure there was enough room for Aircraft A because he was a heavy and [I had to] get Aircraft B behind them. I wanted to group the 3 small transports together and get them to final before the next set of arrivals. I turned Aircraft X. I then turned my attention back to the final and didn't notice Aircraft Y, who was controlled by the north controller at 4,000 feet inbound to ZZZ3. As soon as I noticed there was going to be a loss of separation i turned Aircraft X northeast and climbed them. It is very hard to get used to the traffic after Covid. This was the first day I had to take every aircraft off the arrival in years. I was so concentrated on my feed to final that it caused me to lose track of other aircraft away from the airport. I think there should have been stricter Traffic Management Unit (TMU) numbers in because both of my sessions I was vectoring over 20 miles off the arrival. If the sector was not combined that would have helped too.
ASRS:1819894.s: An air traffic controller lost separation between Aircraft X and Aircraft Y while managing multiple arrivals and departures. The controller attributed the incident to high workload, inexperience post-pandemic, and excessive vectoring distances caused by insufficient Traffic Management Unit restrictions.

ASRS:1819904.n: This is once again another report about the Steelhead MOA/ATCAA. Area X Controllers were briefed that the Steelhead ATCAA (Air Traffic Control Assigned Airspace) was going to be active from 29,000 feet to 31,000 feet from XA:00-XD:00. There would be numerous military aircraft in the MOA (Military Operations Area) due to the VIP being in TVC. When I sat down at the sector, there was already confusion. There were 3 tanker aircraft wanting a clearance into the MOA but it was not yet active. I tried to call the Minneapolis Center military desk and Black Talon (as I've repeatedly been told to do after these reports). Cleveland Center's 'fix' is to call those two facilities. There was no answer at either line. I tried having my Assist call. No answer. I had the Supervisor call. No answer. I called the Minneapolis Center controller at TVC high sector to try to coordinate a new altitude block of 25,000 to 31,000 feet and was denied. The tankers were given vectors until the airspace went active. At that time, I cleared the tankers into the MOA. During this live operation, the tankers repeatedly asked for more vertical airspace. The supervisor coordinated it and it was granted.I told the Operations Manager (OM) that a dangerous situation was occurring and has been occurring with the Steelhead MOA/ATCAA. He stated that he didn't really know how it worked, but the aircraft controlled the airspace and that he did not think there was an air traffic controller working the airspace. Later on, the OM talked to my supervisor who spoke to me. The supervisor said that Black Talon is only the coordinating agency and they simply schedule the airspace but are not controllers. As the day went on, the tankers were asking to join up and were asking for permission to climb and descend. This is not the procedure for military airspace. In MOA/ATCAA, the aircraft are not under the FAA's control. Whose control are they under? I am still unclear. However, they were soliciting separation services. I didn't even have flight plans for these aircraft any longer. Their radar services had been terminated. I advised them that they are responsible for separating themselves and I was not providing separation services. They informed me that Aircraft Y told them that they had to ask my permission for altitude changes inside the Steelhead ATCAA. There were also several spillouts involving these aircraft. At least 2, I personally saw.After another break I came back to a cap and anchor drawn on the screen. Cleveland Center's military guy had come in and drawn a cap and anchor but had told the controllers it 'wasn't official'. Basically, what it seems happened is someone made a cap and anchor in the Steelhead MOA at 29,000 to 31,000 feet. Cap and anchors are typically inclusive vertical altitudes. The cap and anchor, however, were not in the confines of the Steelhead MOA hence the spillouts. To be clear, the Steelhead ATCAA was active just apparently with a cap and anchor that no one forwarded down the line. The aircraft were making altitude and time adjustments real time, not in advance. It went from FL290B310 to FL200B310 and from XA:00-XD:00 to now XA:00-XG:00. Very last minute changes.To make this matter even worse was that I was controlling the VIP aircraft. I had sent the VIP aircraft through this (at the time) unknown cap and anchor because I wasn't told about it. Every pilot and every aircraft is important to me, but the VIP aircraft was placed in an unsafe proximity to randomly maneuvering military aircraft that were not radar identified, who I no longer had flight plan information on, and who were not on my frequency. It was only after the VIP aircraft flew through that a 'not official' cap and anchor was drawn which not only penetrated Cleveland, but Minneapolis and Toronto Centers as well.The Steelhead MOA/ATCAA seems strangely still very confusing. My supervisor and Operations Manager were unclear, and still are unclear, about it. Does Black Talon coordinate it through the Minneapolis military desk? Does Aircraft Y control it? I give pilots a frequency for Black Talon so maybe there is a controller there? Someone needs to find this stuff out. I personally volunteer for the mission. I will be medically disqualified for weeks and I would spend that time and my own money to travel to wherever or Zoom meeting whoever to figure this out. This has been an on-going issue that was especially perverse today. I have been raising the alarm for quite some time and am passionate about it and would like to personally get/set the record straight so that all aircraft and pilots or safe. I hope this will be met with the serious spirit with which it's written. As a Supervisor in Area X at Cleveland Center, I spent my morning attempting to coordinate and discover why the aircraft were not following what we were briefed on. Area X was briefed that due to the TFR for VIP at Traverse City, Steelhead ATCAA would be activated from 29,000 to 31,000 feet for tanker and E3 activity. These altitudes and ATCAA (Air Traffic Control Assigned Airspace) were supposed to encompass all AEW (airborne early warning) and supporting activity. The ATCAA was activated from approximately XA:45Z to XE:00Z, however aircraft showed up before it was active and then requested it to remain active past it's finish time.From the start, every single aircraft requested different altitudes than what was coordinated. I attempted to get information from Minneapolis Center, our military desk and Black Talon and was unable to get any answers. Eventually, we extended the Steelhead ATCAA from 23,000 to 31,000 feet to accommodate. Later, a tanker aircraft requested a block altitude of 20,000 to 22,000 feet and a controller gave him those until established in the lateral boundaries of Steelhead, at which point the controller understood the aircraft would climb to within the altitude limits of Steelhead (FL230-FL310). The aircraft never climbed. The controller then coordinated with Minneapolis Center blocking 20,000 to 23,000 feet to accommodate the aircraft. I then coordinated with our military coordinator to extend Steelhead to include these altitudes.When any aircraft are cleared into the Steelhead complex, radar service is terminated and the aircraft track gets dropped. This occurred during this session, as we were briefed to treat the aircraft as we normally would with Steelhead. However, while Steelhead was active, we had multiple occasions where an aircraft went outside of the lateral bounds of the Steelhead complex. After trying repeatedly to find out why this was happening, we discovered that the Sentry track was not fully inside of the Steelhead complex as we were briefed. At this point I called on the phone to Minneapolis Center supervisors desk, Toronto Center sectors Hamilton and Centralia to warn and pass along that we discovered that our information was incorrect. VIP Aircraft traveled through our airspace around XB:00 Local time estimated. Having no Controller in Charges on the entire day shift, I asked the Operations Manager to cover the Supervisor position while I plugged in and monitored the VIP movement. VIP Aircraft's course traveled about 4 to 5 miles west of the Steelhead ATCAA. During this time we kept a close eye on any tracks within Steelhead due to their previous spillover events (We were not aware at this point that the Sentry was not fully enclosed within Steelhead). All tracks were on the East side of Steelhead and not in conflct with the VIP aircraft, however that potential did exist due to the Sentry course that we were not aware of.In addition, multiple aircraft called at the Peck sector to request join ups and altitude changes while within the Steelhead ATCAA. The aircraft stated that Aircraft Y told them to do so. I had the controller inform the aircraft calling that Cleveland Center could not provide control instructions within Steelhead ATCAA. I also told the controller to state that they were not providing any separation services within Steelhead and that it was Aircraft control. At this point the floor walker was involved as well and verified that what we were doing was correct and was able to inform us why aircraft were spilling out of Steelhead. Also, we discovered around XD:00Z that the end time of XE:00Z would not be correct. This was only because I prompted my controller to ask detailed and blunt questions about if the aircraft within Steelhead would want it open longer. The aircraft's intention was at XD:45Z to ask to extend Steelhead which in no way is enough time for coordination and planning! It was only because I pressed the controller to ask aboutan ambiguous statement from an aircraft within Steelhead that we discovered this!There is probably more that I have left out, this was all very fluid and unorganized. Nothing occurred how we were briefed it was to occur and answers/information were slow and hard to get.[Recommend] Coordination/communication. The military did not do anything that was expected. They did not request any of the altitudes that were originally blocked for Steelhead. They did not communicate far enough in advance to extend Steelhead. Once their abnormal requests were received, there was nobody to call to get answers. Black Talon is the controlling agency, there were no Whiskey alerts called and information was very slow and untimely to be of use to us. I recommend that if Steelhead is active, Black Talon needs to be monitoring the airspace. We need a direct call/shout line for them to inform us of any Whiskey events, or us to ask questions and perform point outs in case of weather, deviations, emergencies or TCAS events.
ASRS:1819904.s: Cleveland Center controllers and military tankers experienced confusion and spillouts during the Steelhead MOA/ATCAA activation due to uncoordinated altitude changes and incorrect boundary data. This lack of communication placed a VIP aircraft in unsafe proximity to untracked military traffic while controllers were unable to obtain timely coordination from military desks.

ASRS:1819915.n: While working the radar position, I accepted an automated handoff on Aircraft X, an IFR flight inbound from the St. Louis area to one of our satellite airports. Several minutes later I received a transmission from Aircraft Y. Because I was not expecting to hear from this aircraft--looking back, it appears they mistakenly took the frequency change meant for Aircraft X--I queried their position and they said they were in the vicinity of the STL VOR. I advised them that they were well outside my airspace and suggested they contact St. Louis Approach (T75) on the 'Low North' position frequency 124.2. I then realized that, if they were close to the STL VOR, they probably were not looking for initial services but were already in contact with ATC. I immediately reached out again, asking if they had been talking to a T75 Controller before contacting me, but they had already changed away from my frequency. I reached out to the Low North Controller on the landline and told them what had happened, and that the aircraft was no longer responding to me. They said they were trying to get in contact with the aircraft and there may have been an NMAC over the airport. Eventually they told me they had re-established contact with the aircraft. Additionally, while this was happening, Aircraft X flew beyond radio coverage of the T75 Low North position without contacting me. Eventually they reached out on my frequency and I advised the Low North Controller that the aircraft was no longer NORDO. That was the end of it until, while going home, I thought over the situation again and realized I wasn't certain if I had suggested that Aircraft Y contact St. Louis on 124.2 or 124.3. 124.2 is the correct frequency for the T75 Low North position, while 124.3 is the frequency for ZKC Sector 58, which borders the east/southeast side of both our airspace and T75's. I can't remember which frequency I suggested, if I did suggest the wrong one that would have contributed to the confusion and extended the amount of time the T75 Controller was unable to properly control the aircraft. If I had kept the pilot on my frequency while I reached out to the T75 Low North controller, I would have been able to issue a confident 'contact' instruction instead of 'suggest you contact.' If I had issued that instruction I would have been less likely to make a slip and say the wrong frequency. It is also surprising to me that the frequencies 124.2 and 124.3 are used in immediately adjacent sectors. This is a potential cause of confusion for controllers and pilots alike.
ASRS:1819915.s: An air traffic controller reported a potential NMAC involving Aircraft Y, which mistakenly contacted the wrong frequency, and Aircraft X, which became NORDO. The controller attributed the confusion to issuing a suggestion rather than a direct instruction and noted that adjacent sectors using similar frequencies (124.2 and 124.3) contributed to the error.

ASRS:1819919.n: Aircraft Y departed ZZZ VFR and wanted to overfly the downtown before picking up his IFR [clearance] and proceeding on course. I told him to proceed on course and advise when he was ready to be on his way. When Aircraft X departed, Aircraft Y was circling over Downtown about 8 miles north of the airport below 4,000 feet. This is a typical spot and generally not a factor for departing jets as they climb above that area. I issued traffic to Aircraft Y since he had no restrictions and he reported Aircraft X in sight. Unfortunately, at this time Aircraft Y had also just exited his circling and had started to fly southwest and begin a climb. This was not apparent to me yet and I was unsure what direction he was headed due to his maneuvering and equipment refresh rate. I was also unable to turn Aircraft X more than 15 degrees due to our departure/terrain limitations and neither 15 degrees left or right seemed prudent for the uncertain course of the traffic. Since Aircraft Y had Aircraft X in sight, I did not believe he would continue a climb directly towards him, but he did, and I issued an immediate right turn to Aircraft Y. Altitude restrictions wouldn't have worked here since the MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) is 5,000 feet in that area. Unfortunately this turn was not timely enough and Aircraft X had to respond to an RA by descending.Although an altitude restriction would not have helped, asking the pilot to advise prior to climbing could have been the heads up I needed to give him a heading to avoid the traffic, or to ask him to delay his climb for traffic. Another option could have been to have Aircraft X remain clean of the class charlie, as this would have also potentially prevented the climb into traffic. It's clear I did not take action soon enough. Aircraft X should have been given a traffic call, on initial call-up ideally. A traffic alert should have been issued at a minimum to Aircraft X since I was able to turn him. Aircraft X had just reached the minimum altitude for a turn at that moment. Aircraft X departed and conflicted with Aircraft Y orbiting VFR. I observed the event in the departure corridor while on the Tower Controller In Charge Only position. Aircraft Y finished a left turn toward the runway centerline and flew straight towards the departing Aircraft X. As the aircraft converged I noticed the altitudes decreasing in separation. Then subsequently noticed a turning descent of Aircraft X under the Minimum Vectoring Altitude descending to 4,300 feet (estimated). After no factor Aircraft X climbed and departed to the NE. Aircraft Y departed to SW. Recommend larger Class C, due to great increase in ZZZ traffic. Class C 10 mile ring down to surface.
ASRS:1819919.s: Air Traffic Controller observed VFR Aircraft Y circling downtown below 4,000 feet while IFR Aircraft X departed, resulting in a conflict when Y climbed toward X. The controller's delayed right turn instruction for Y was insufficient, forcing X to descend in response to a Resolution Advisory.

ASRS:1819922.n: Aircraft X was on the STAR going into ZZZ airport. I descended him from 5,000 to 3,000 feet. I turned him base while he was descending to 3,000 feet. When I turned him on the approach he descended through 3,000 to 2,700 feet. The MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) in that area is 3,000 feet. I told him to maintain 3,000 when I cleared him for the approach. He climbed back up to 3,000 feet.
ASRS:1819922.s: An air traffic controller vectored Aircraft X on a STAR to ZZZ airport, instructing a descent from 5,000 to 3,000 feet. The aircraft descended below the 3,000-foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude to 2,700 feet before the controller issued a maintain 3,000 feet instruction, prompting the pilot to climb back to the assigned altitude.

ASRS:1820049.n: Complete right side brake failure upon landing in ZZZ. Brake line became detached. Failure of some sort after brakes had just been replaced on #3 and #4. Surprised that entire right side brakes failed. One brake line detaching should not have resulted in complete right side failure.
ASRS:1820049.s: The pilot reported a complete right-side brake failure upon landing in ZZZ caused by a detached brake line. This occurred shortly after brakes on wheels #3 and #4 were replaced, with the pilot noting that a single line detachment should not have caused total system failure.

ASRS:1820065.n: During push with brake set, started the Right Engine. Immediately after the engine started, we received an APU Limit checklist indication. We ran the checklist which stated an exceedance had occurred and directed us to shutdown the APU, which we did. Shortly after shutting down the APU with the overhead switch, the ground mechanic stated on the intercom 'APU fire, shutdown the APU.' I then stated 'no we do NOT have an APU fire indication in the cockpit, but did get an APU limit checklist, which we ran and shut down the APU already.' He acknowledged the radio and I believe at this point went to the back of the airplane for a closer look. I assumed any smoke he had seen was from the limit exceedance and decided not to fire the APU bottle since we did not have an indication of an APU fire. After taking care of the switches in the cockpit, I went outside to investigate what had occurred and found two mechanics at the rear of the airplane with the APU compartment open, as they investigated the APU from a cherry-picker stand. From the ground, I could see no evidence of any fire either inside the APU compartment nor on the exterior of the tail section. When finished with their examination, the mechanics came into the cockpit to explain what they found. I had great difficulty understanding their English and exactly what they were saying, except that they would now MEL the APU. I understood them to say they thought it was from fluid leaking in the APU. I only found out after talking to the operations director on a phone patch on the ramp in ZZZZ, that the mechanics had used a fire extinguisher during their inspection. They did not tell me this or perhaps both my First Officer and I misunderstood them. I did not witness them using a fire extinguisher and it must have occurred prior to me leaving the cockpit to investigate. I made a write-up in the logbook. No emergency was declared because it seemed well under control. Better communication between crew and mechanics over what they did, as they should have told the Captain that a fire extinguisher was used! Now perhaps they did attempt to tell the crew and we did not comprehend what they were stating.
ASRS:1820065.s: During pushback, the crew received an APU limit indication and shut down the APU, while a ground mechanic reported a fire and used an extinguisher without clearly informing the flight deck. The crew found no visible fire, and the APU was deferred due to suspected fluid leakage, highlighting a communication breakdown regarding the extinguisher use.

ASRS:1820104.n: I accepted a ferry flight for Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1. This flight was accomplished as a single pilot operation. It was a perfectly clear day, with light winds from the south. Aircraft X required a special ferry permit due to an inoperative stabilizer trim position indicator, coupled with an inoperative out-of-trim warning system. Essentially, the pilot was unable to determine the position of the elevator trim from inside the flight deck, and there was nothing to alert the pilot that the trim was set outside of the takeoff range during takeoff. I was thoroughly familiar with this discrepancy because I had recognized it and alerted Maintenance of the need for repair the night before this event. The stabilizer trim itself had functioned normally.I felt comfortable accepting this flight, as I had been flying Aircraft X for many days prior to the aforementioned maintenance issues, and was familiar with this specific aircraft. Before starting the engines, I re-trimmed the horizontal stabilizer by making adjustments on the flight deck and confirming the position of the trim visually from outside the aircraft. Confident that the airplane was ready for flight, and assured that the trim was working, I started the engines and taxied to Runway XXL for takeoff.After experiencing no abnormalities prior to V1, and reaching the predetermined rotation speed, I took the plane airborne. After attaining a climb and retracting the landing gear, I attempted to make my first adjustment of the stabilizer trim since starting the engines. There was no response to my input. My first reaction was to ensure that I had not switched the stabilizer trim off inadvertently, as the switch rests immediately adjacent to my right knee. The switch was still positioned to the Captain's side. At this point I quickly recognized the gravity of the situation, which was that I was now flying a nearly 11,000 pound airplane, and I had no mechanical assistance to maintain a level flight attitude. During the climb out, my yoke weighed approximately 70-80 pounds.In my initial radio communication with Departure, I informed the controller of my altitude and that I had no elevator trim. I did not explicitly declare an emergency. When asked if I needed assistance, I requested the most direct radar vector possible to join a visual approach at ZZZ1. I knew from my preflight planning that they were landing to the south at that airport and Runways XXL and XXR were in use. This meant that from the point at which I began my first turn to the point at which I joined final approach was a straight line just under 15nm long. This reduced the physical burden on me significantly versus returning to ZZZ, as flying the airplane became noticeably easier in straight and level flight.I also requested a lower altitude than the 9,000 feet MSL that I was cleared to. Departure requested that I maintain 8,000 feet MSL as there were military aircraft operating in ZZZ2 airspace at 7,200 feet MSL. The vector I was given took me directly over the top of the military airfield. I visually observed several military fighter aircraft engage in sharp right turns to remain clear of me laterally. During level flight, I allowed the airplane to accelerate to approximately 215 KIAS. Every bit of airspeed I gained translated into a lightening of my controls, and made it possible to continue flying without exhausting the strength of my arms. It is possible that while at this speed, I descended under the Class B airspace into the Class E airspace that lies north of ZZZ1 and west of ZZZ2. Meaning, under my authority as PIC of an aircraft under 14 CFR 91.3, I may have inadvertently violated 14 CFR 91.117 as it pertains to the maximum speed of an aircraft in Class E and Class D airspace. The conclusion of this flight was a safe landing at ZZZ1, followed by an uneventful taxi to the company maintenance hangar. I believe that I conducted this 8 minute flight as well as could be expected of any pilot with a similar level of knowledge and experience. My familiarity with the aircraft and the surrounding area, my current level of physical fitness, as well as the timely response and assistance from air traffic control led to the safe outcome of the flight.
ASRS:1820104.s: A single pilot flew Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1 with an inoperative stabilizer trim indicator and warning system. After the trim failed during climb, the pilot manually controlled the aircraft at 215 KIAS, received direct vectors from ATC, and landed safely despite the heavy control forces.

ASRS:1820122.n: On climb out from ZZZ, we noticed engine oil quantity on engine #2 had gone to 0. We notified ATC and returned to ZZZ. All other indications were normal. The landing was uneventful and we taxied to the gate.
ASRS:1820122.s: The crew reported zero engine oil quantity on engine #2 during climb out from ZZZ. They notified ATC, returned to ZZZ, and completed an uneventful landing and taxi to the gate with all other indications normal.

ASRS:1820170.n: It was my second day on the line. This was a repositioning flight with two other crew members in the back who I was taking to ZZZ to fly their lines. I was on standby for the first half of the day and I had just flown ZZZ to ZZZ1 then to ZZZ2 and was in IMC from take off to landing on each flight. I was unaware upon leaving ZZZ1 that they had scheduled me to fly these other pilots to ZZZ after reaching ZZZ2. So I operated the flight and all went according to plan except I had an unstable approach into ZZZ. Using the auto pilot for the approach I ended up descending below minimum altitude for the final approach fix and continued well below glide slope until I was approximately 1200 AGL at which point I disconnected autopilot, increased power to help arrest the descent rate, caught up to the glide slope and hand flew the rest of the approach. I relied too heavily on the autopilot and lost situational awareness. I also could have asked one of the other pilots to act as copilot.I think it would be safer to not have new hire Captains fly without an FO (First Officer) in hard IMC for multiple legs even if it is just a reposition flight. And if there is a crew member on board they should sit right seat.
ASRS:1820170.s: A new hire Captain flying a repositioning flight in IMC experienced an unstable approach into ZZZ, descending below minimums and the glide slope to 1200 AGL while using autopilot. The pilot attributed the event to over-reliance on automation and lost situational awareness, noting the absence of a First Officer in the right seat.

ASRS:1820203.n: In weight and balance data, no dry ice was listed. Arrival airport Ramp called Name and told him that there were approximately 44 kg of dry ice in 2L due to [medical supplies], but no listing as such. Notified by Operations Control that 44 lbs of dry ice was on our airplane in position 2L. Had two packs and no pneumatic MEL's. Dry ice limits not exceeded. HAZMAT paper work stated ' no DG on board'. Continued safely to destination.
ASRS:1820203.s: The crew discovered 44 kg of unlisted dry ice in position 2L after the ramp reported it, despite HAZMAT paperwork stating no dangerous goods were on board. With no pneumatic MELs and limits not exceeded, the flight continued safely to the destination.

ASRS:1820243.n: The flight was cleared for the ILS Runway XX in ZZZ with VMC conditions. On final approach, at approximately 4.8 DME a drone was sighted along the final approach course, approximately 200 or 300 ft. below the aircraft flight path, and slightly right of the localizer. Drone in Class B airspace without clearance. [I suggest] continued public education on the proper use of drones. Limitations on the selling of drones to qualified individuals.
ASRS:1820243.s: The flight crew sighted an unauthorized drone in Class B airspace while on final ILS approach to Runway XX in VMC. The drone was located 4.8 DME from the threshold, 200–300 feet below the flight path, and slightly right of the localizer.

ASRS:1820263.n: Aircraft X departed ZZZ1 for ZZZ behind schedule due to a deferred APU and excessive cabin temps. Prior to descent crew performed arrival brief discussing the landing on Runway 26 at ZZZ. As part of the brief crew extended a 3.5 NM extended final at approx 1,000 feet and programmed the FMS for the corresponding VNAV guidance. Flight was being vectored for approach and landing when crew was taken off arrival into ZZZ. Crew had airport in sight and proceeded visually to airport with FMS back up. The plan was to be fully configured, on speed at the created waypoint at 1,000 feet AGL. During vectors it was determined the flight was going to be heavy for landing, crew extended drag to help with landing within the maximum safe landing weight. At that time, crew became distracted with weight, terrain and visually flying to the final approach course when crew descended prematurely below our briefed 1,000 foot AGL waypoint. Crew was still approximately 3 miles on an extended base leg. Crew maintained visual separation with terrain. It was identified that we descended below 1,000 AGL down to 800 AGL. Crew initiated corrective action and climbed back to 1,000 AGL. Upon reaching 1,000 AGL, crew proceeded to turn final and land without further issue.In this scenario, crew became distracted with managing landing weight, flying a non standard visual approach without guidance in the vicinity of terrain. For the next time, I would've fixed the landing weight issue prior to beginning the approach. In this case the amount was so small that a simple delay vector would've solved our issue. The crew could've then focused on the visual flight path to the runway. Also for the future I would, I'd also incorporate more of the autopilot until at a safe altitude to help with workload management. For the future maintaining the altitude and autopilot until approaching a base to final turn could resolve premature descents. In the future I could also be more specific and clear about which altitudes and how soon I expect to descend to those altitudes and waypoints when transitioning below 10,000 MSL building a better shared mental model.
ASRS:1820263.s: The flight crew of Aircraft X descended prematurely to 800 feet AGL while flying a non-standard visual approach due to distraction from managing landing weight. They corrected by climbing back to 1,000 feet AGL and landed safely, attributing the error to workload management and lack of autopilot use.

ASRS:1820291.n: Received GPS jamming, indicated by ADS-B OUT L, TERR POS, NAV UNABLE RNP". Jamming started at XA:25Z N4850 E4304. Ended XA:54Z N5241 E 3919. In southern Moscow airspace skirting Ukraine just south of us. [Caused by] jamming of satellite signals by unknown entity."
ASRS:1820291.s: The crew experienced GPS jamming in southern Moscow airspace near Ukraine, indicated by ADS-B OUT L, TERR POS, and NAV UNABLE RNP messages. The reporter attributes the signal loss to satellite jamming by an unknown entity.

ASRS:1820307.n: AVL [Runway] 35 PAPI's [Precision Approach Path Indicator] unreliable. Gives on course indication 1 to 1.5 dots low on glideslope including GLIDESLOPE" annunciation by GPWS. Appears 2nd light from runway is misaligned. NOTAM PAPI's out of service until fixed and flight check. Also call Jeppesen and demand they put the antenna's new height on our ILS 35 approach charts. Actual antenna is higher than company pages."
ASRS:1820307.s: The pilot reported unreliable PAPI lights on Runway 35, which indicated a low glideslope despite the aircraft being on course. The reporter attributed this to a misaligned second light and noted that Jeppesen charts incorrectly list the ILS antenna height.

ASRS:1820342.n: Lithium batteries are not being removed from bags.
ASRS:1820342.s: The reporter states that lithium batteries are not being removed from bags. No specific aircraft, phase of flight, or personnel involvement is mentioned in the narrative.

ASRS:1820375.n: Hazmat was found in ZZZ on XX month 2021 while conducting the facility inventory. Looking at the [Cargo Record] it looks to have arrived in to ZZZ on the evening of XX/month -1/2021, so it looks like it may have arrived off flight from ZZZ1. The piece is noted as UTL [Unable To Locate] on XY month -1 2021 in ZZZ1 as per the remarks. This is a Class 3, Packing Group III, Flammable Liquid n.o.s (1-Methoxy-2-Propanol, 4-Chloro-a, a;a-trifluorotouene), UN1993, PI 355, with 0.1L in volume.
ASRS:1820375.s: Ground staff discovered a Class 3 flammable liquid hazmat item during a facility inventory at ZZZ. The package, likely arriving from ZZZ1, was previously marked Unable To Locate at that origin station.

ASRS:1820409.n: Notified ATC and diversion due to burning smell inside flight deck. Passing through FL310 Captain asked First Officer (FO) if he smelled anything out of the ordinary. FO stated he smelled something like burning toast. Captain rang flight attendant and asked the same to which she stated burnt toast as well. Captain notified ATC and we diverted to ZZZ. During descent smell went away but reoccurred intermittently. Performed overweight landing smoothly and stopped on runway. Confirmed smell was gone with flight attendant and taxied to gate while fire rescue followed. Passengers deplaned. Maintenance met us at gate and we were able to duplicate smell when packs were turned on using APU. First Officer flew aircraft while Captain performed checklist. We landed without further incident. Captain and FO spoke and initially felt okay to continue on [from] ZZZ. However as time passed and adrenaline wore off fatigue set in. We spoke again and both determined that we could not safely operate the flight [from] ZZZ. When climbing through 31,000 feet, both the FO and I noticed a distinct odor that smelled like burning toast. We immediately asked the FA if she smelled it as well and she did. I then [requested priority handling] with ATC and the FO initiated a descent as we diverted to ZZZ1. Once we descended through 31,000 feet, the smell dissipated. Throughout the flight, we smelled the burning order intermittently for short durations of only a few seconds. Once we landed, we came to a stop on the runway and assessed the situation. The odor was gone so we taxied back to our gate under our own power with fire trucks in tow. When at the gate with the door open and APU bleed and packs on, the odor came back and intensified. Maintenance was able to reproduce this on the ground.
ASRS:1820409.s: The flight crew and flight attendant detected a burning toast odor at FL310, prompting a diversion to ZZZ1 and an overweight landing. Maintenance later confirmed the smell originated from the air conditioning packs when powered by the APU, leading the fatigued crew to cancel the return flight.

ASRS:1820413.n: Captain (CA) was Pilot Flying. During climb going through FL180, windshield 1 heat fail message showed in the EICAS, message went away. A few seconds later PACK 1 valve closed (cyan message) showed on the EICAS, CA recycle the pack. Both CA and First Officer (FO) observed a boringness smell after pack was cycled. Crew was notified by the Flight Attendant (FA) that there was smoke in the cabin. CA and FO donned the oxygen mask and gaggles and started an emergency descent and turning back towards airport of departure. FO notified ATC. Crew was cleared by ATC direct ZZZ. [The briefing] was done between crew and FA. FO was able to get landing data and set up the FMS for the RNAV RWY XX in ZZZ. CA landed and exited the runway safely, parked at a ramp shutdown engine #1 and opened the main cabin door. CA used engine #2 for power and chose to not start the APU since the crew wasn't sure about the integrity of the system. On climb through 21,000 ft crew received a windshield heat fail message, CA (Captain) pulled out the QRH but the message cleared. Moments later the crew received a cyan PACK 1 valve close message. CA selected pack one off and then reset. Shortly after the crew both smelled smoke in the flight deck. Seconds after the smell of smoke the FA (Flight Attendant) called notifying crew of smoke filling up the cabin. The crew put on oxygen and smoke goggles and the CA initiated an emergency descent, the FO notified ATC and requested direct ZZZ. ATC assigned 15,000 ft direct ZZZ. Crew established that the CA will fly and the FO will work the radios and FMS. The FO informed ATC of the souls on board and fuel on board and requested visual for Runway XX from the final approach fix (ZZZZZ). FO got landing numbers for Runway XX, and verified the aircraft would not be overweight. The crew checked in with the FA 3 times before landing back at ZZZ, each check in the FA stated the smoke is slowly dissipating. Upon landing the crew exited on [taxiway] and had trucks follow them on A to an empty ramp area. The crew shut down engine 1 and opened the main cabin door, engine 2 was kept running to maintain radio contact. The APU was not started because the crew was not sure of the systems integrity. After aircraft was inspected and safe, the aircraft was brought back to the gate and deplaned.
ASRS:1820413.s: During climb through FL180, a windshield heat failure and PACK 1 valve closure caused smoke in the cabin, prompting the crew to initiate an emergency descent and return to ZZZ. The aircraft landed safely, and the crew shut down engine 1 while keeping engine 2 running to avoid starting the APU due to uncertain system integrity.

ASRS:1820446.n: After a 5 hour maintenance delay to change a flat tire, we departed for ZZZ1. We executed a normal, flex, CONF1 takeoff from [Runway] XXL in VFR weather with light winds and a light aircraft. I was PF (Pilot Flying) and was hand-flying the departure. At approximately 1,000 AGL I heard several loud bangs from the right side of the aircraft. My first thought was bird strike but the CA (Captain) called out 'engine failure.' I called out 'my aircraft' and we determined there was a problem with the #2 engine. I don't recall any ECAMs but I do recall seeing the #2 EGT was high. I was continuing to hand-fly and CA suggested we reduce thrust to idle on the #2 engine. I agreed and we reduced the thrust and the surging and vibration ceased and the engine parameters went into the green. CA suggested an immediate return to the departure field and [advised] ATC and coordinated a downwind turn and level-off. I engaged the autopilot and prepared for a return to runway XXL with an ILS approach. CA set the FMGC up for the approach and I flew the downwind and base. CA advised the FAs (Flight Attendants) to prepare for a precautionary landing and gave a short PA as well. ATC vectored us to the ILS and cleared us for a visual approach once I had the field in sight. I executed a normal landing on XXL and we taxied clear on taxiway 1 and had the fire department inspect the aircraft. CA made several PAs instructing the passengers to remain seated and that the situation was under control. I noticed the #2 EGT was increasing and approaching the upper limit and we shut the engine down as the fire department was inspecting the engine. CA coordinated with operations a return gate and once the fire department was done and deemed the aircraft safe to taxi we returned to gate. The passengers deplaned normally. CA then called Dispatch to advise them of our return.We both determined the safest course of action was to get the aircraft back on the ground as soon as possible. This was made easier with good weather, no air traffic, and being below max. landing weight. We were only in the air ten minutes and this didn't give us time to do much troubleshooting or communication with anyone except ATC and the flight attendants. I was 100% busy flying the aircraft the entire time, but due to excellent ATC and constant communication with the Captain/PM, I felt in the yellow most of the time and in the green for the final approach and landing. I only felt I was 'in the red' for the few seconds between when the engine began surging until the CA said 'engine failure.' That statement immediately told me what was happening and I snapped into our trained procedures. We continued to discuss the plan and agreed that a quick return to the field was best throughout the short flight. Since the engine seemed stable at idle and we had no ECAMs we decided not to complicate things by troubleshooting but rather execute a quick precautionary landing. I feel our combined experience in the Airbus as well as constant precise communication and exchange of ideas led to the successful outcome. We backed each other up, trapped errors, and executed our plan efficiently and effectively. I don't see this event being preventable, but I think our training and emphasis on SOP and communication made for a good outcome. On takeoff, at approximately 1,000 feet AGL #2 engine compressor stalling with high EGT. We brought the thrust lever to idle and stalling stopped. We [notified] ATC and returned to field. Firefighters inspected the airplane and it appeared normal. Taxied to the gate.
ASRS:1820446.s: The Pilot Flying and Captain experienced a #2 engine compressor stall with high EGT at 1,000 feet AGL during departure from runway XXL. They reduced thrust to idle, returned for a precautionary landing, and taxied to the gate after a fire department inspection found the aircraft normal.

ASRS:1820448.n: Requested priority for flight control malfunction on descent into ZZZZ. For approximately 5 minutes I was unable to comply with assigned altitude and course while regaining control of the aircraft. We received 3-4 STAB OUT OF TRIM Level 2" alerts. Alert would be presented for 15-20 seconds, disappear, then return after a minute or two. Reviewed stab out of trim level 2 in QRH. Late in the descent, roughly simultaneously, AP1 (Autopilot 1) failed to capture final approach altitude of 2,600 feet, descending and FO (First Officer) reported LSAS (Longitudinal Stability Augmentation System) "ALL FAIL" alert, which I was unable to confirm as I was simultaneously manually arresting the uncommanded descent, close to ground, IFR, night in moderate turbulence and rain, slow, configure, determine what if any stab trim was available, and navigate the aircraft to final. Disconnected AP, slowed and configured the aircraft with FCP speed commands and the pedestal long trim handles. Flew the rest of the ILS XXL manually in approach/ land. Stopped on taxiway for inspection by fire personnel, nothing noted, taxi to gate."
ASRS:1820448.s: The pilot reported a flight control malfunction and STAB OUT OF TRIM alerts during a night IFR descent into ZZZZ. After AP1 failed to capture 2,600 feet and LSAS failed, the crew manually arrested an uncommanded descent, flew the ILS manually, and landed safely with no damage noted.

ASRS:1820450.n: My First Officer noticed while checking the hazardous cargo pallet, there was a '4.3 DANGEROUS WHEN WET' box loaded on the very bottom of the pallet, with several boxes of other DG (dangerous goods) on top. It had been raining steadily for several minutes during loading, so the pallet had about a half inch of water or more that had puddled on the floor of the metal pallet. The pallet had plastic wrapping around all the boxes and of course the plastic was also wet due to the rain. But since this box was loaded on the bottom we couldn't tell if it was totally wrapped in plastic or bare to the pallet flooring. Also if there was a rip in the plastic, it could get the box wet. So I told the ramp agent I needed to see bottom of the box. The Ramp and DG Agent did not understand due to language issues and initially they put styrofoam under the box. My First Officer used Google translate and they finally understood. When they took the box off the pallet and showed it to me, it was wet on half of the bottom of the box, the box had absorbed a good bit of water as it looked darker. We had them remove that small box from the plane. It would have been easy to over look this!! My First Officer deserves a recognition for his attention to detail!! The DG Specialist most importantly needs to understand this could have been a very serious issue! I believe the package contained Lithium Phosphorus. 'Dangerous When Wet' DG should never be on the bottom of the pallet for this very reason. The cause was a poorly built DG pallet and a misunderstanding of how this box could easily get wet in the conditions presented. Ensure DG specialist at ZZZZ understand this issue and re-train as necessary.
ASRS:1820450.s: The pilot and First Officer discovered a "Dangerous When Wet" box on the bottom of a wet cargo pallet during loading at ZZZZ. Due to language barriers and poor pallet construction, the box absorbed water, prompting its removal to prevent a serious safety incident.

ASRS:1820481.n: Right after takeoff, Flight Attendant Name and myself smelled a strong odor. Smelled like chemical/acetone to me. I went out into cabin, the odor was strong for about 5 rows from back galley. I asked the passengers if they had used anything like nail polish, or anything with chemical base. Everyone said no. I asked if they smelled it, they said yes. I looked and felt in overhead bins found nothing. My eyes were burning. I went and told Name that I couldn't find the source of odor. She called Captain to report what was happening. The Captain said she'd get back to her. We then notified the number one flight attendant. Then the Captain made a PA announcement that we were returning to the airport. And that we'd be landing in about 15 minutes. I'm still out in cabin trying to find anything that was causing the smell. After Captain's announcement, passenger in 25F hands me a open wipe packet with the used wipe in it. She said she used it right after takeoff. It was the exact smell. It had a concentrated eucalyptus oil in it. I asked her why she didn't tell me this when I first came out into cabin. She said she didn't hear me. There is no way she didn't hear me. To prove my point, when the Captain said we were returning to airport, giving no reason why. This passenger then hands me this wipe packet. She did hear me but for whatever reason didn't admit she had used this product right after takeoff. Now that she realized the repercussions of the situation, she admits to using product. I took used packet to Name to let her smell it, we both agreed this was the odor, F/A called to tell Captain. But everything was already in motion to go back and land. The Captain makes an announcement to passengers that we are returning due to a odor in cabin. And that it needs to be accessed. At the gate firemen came on with meters to test the air. It was all good. Name showed them the eucalyptus packet. We followed procedures in every way. Climbing out of ZZZ at approximately 12,000 MSL we got a call from the aft flight attendant. She reported a gaseous odor similar to kerosene, that was making her eyes water. The Captain and I elected to return to ZZZ. We [requested priority handling] and conducted and overweight landing without any further cause for concern. Upon arrival at the gate, the flight attendant determined that the cause of the odor was an 'herbal cleaning wipe' that a passenger had brought on the aircraft to clean their respective seat. The flight attendant's overreaction and hasty response to the cleaning wipe created an unnecessary divert.[Reporter suggested] Flight attendants should be vigilant but also patient and reasonable.
ASRS:1820481.s: Flight attendants reported a strong chemical odor during climb from ZZZ at 12,000 feet, causing the crew to divert and land overweight. The odor was caused by a passenger's eucalyptus cleaning wipe, which the reporter suggests led to an unnecessary diversion due to the crew's hasty response.

ASRS:1820579.n: While I am submitting this report late, let it be known that I began drafting notes on the below report on the afternoon of Date when the events were fresh in my mind. Please accept this report even though it is late. It would have been submitted in a timely manner but I have been consumed with caring for my health and that of my fellow Flight Attendants.I have a varied work history which includes [professional medical experience]. Before I was furloughed [on] Date and after I returned from furlough, I flew high time, however, I am an inexperienced Flight Attendant, as I only have approximately 800 hours of flight time. I find myself often relying on my recollections from training when I am faced with events that are out of the ordinary. In my short time as a Flight Attendant, I had not previously experienced a fume event. While I remember them being discussed very briefly in training, I feel that I was personally ill-prepared on how to handle the situation that happened to me and my crew on Date. I was in possession of a lanyard card from the union regarding fume events that I was able to reference as a guide during the situation, however, the actions the card indicated were not sufficient in protecting my crew that day. I believe I failed in my duty as a Flight Attendant to protect the crew and passengers in the incident that happened onboard Aircraft X on Date due to my inexperience and also due to incapacitation which was caused by the inhalation of fumes.On Date I was scheduled to work Aircraft X ZZZ to ZZZ1 on Boeing 737. At approximately XA:20 during taxi out after the safety demo Flight Attendant 2 Name and Flight Attendant 4 Name 1 called the forward cabin indicating that they smelled a strange odor in the aft galley. They could not describe the odor so I (Flight Attendant 1) went back to check it. I did not detect any unusual odor as I made my way through the cabin. In the aft galley I removed my face mask but did not detect an odor. Flight Attendants 2 and 4 indicated that they could still smell a faint odor but I could not. Flight Attendant 4 indicated that she had recently (within the last 3-4 weeks, I believe she stated) experienced a fume event and that 'it smelled the same.' Flight Attendants 2 and 4 indicated the odor was/had been coming from aircraft left, specifically the aft-most aircraft left corner of the galley. I took deep breaths in the area they indicated the odor was coming from in an attempt to detect it. They said it smelled like 'a dirty bathroom mixed with gasoline.' I did not smell anything unusual but they insisted that they did. I continued to attempt to smell the odor because I could sense that they were very concerned. I called Flight Attendant 3 Name 2 and requested that she come to the aft galley. She came back and immediately said that she smelled something unusual, describing it as 'hot dust on electrical wires.' I was still unable to detect any odor but I informed Captain of it via the interphone in the aft galley. I gave him the descriptions of the odor per the other Flight Attendants (FAs) and added that I could not smell it. He indicated that we had 'passed through a lot of exhaust from other aircraft.' I informed him that none of us smelled exhaust. I again relayed what the other FAs had smelled. He said we would return to the gate. I immediately returned to my jumpseat at the forward entry door. While we were still taxiing back to the gate my nose started running which was approximately 5 minutes after I had been in the aft galley. This was somewhat alarming to me because it was very sudden and profuse, and I became worried for the FAs 2 and 4 in the back. I called to check on them but I cannot recall what they said. We arrived at the gate at approximately XA:35, disarmed the doors and did the all call. At this point the order and timing of events is slightly unclear to me as I believe I was incapacitated to the point where my decision-making abilities were negatively affected, I am aware that we were on the aircraft for quite some time until at least XE:00 but I think it was closer to XE:30 when we deplaned. My sense of time was off from around XA:25 when I called the Captain to report the odor until after we deplaned. The event felt like a blur but I have recalled everything accurately. During this period of time I felt slow, like I was hiking at a high altitude. I was not thinking clearly. I had difficulty articulating the situation to passengers and I felt like I was at a loss for words, which is abnormal for me. Throughout the incident I recall the FAs 2, 3, and 4 having to sit in the flight deck behind the Captain (CA) at times due to lightheadedness, and they all appeared ill. I regret not putting them on O2 immediately and I regret not insisting they get immediate medical attention, especially for FAs 2 and 4 who both looked particularly ill. FA 3 also at times appeared glassy-eyed and like she did not feel well. FA 2 told us that she felt nervous and lightheaded as she was doing the safety demo, she had been in the aft galley the longest. FA 4 had also been in the aft galley for a significant period of time.After we arrived back at the gate and did the all call, I believe FAs 2 and 4 immediately came to the forward galley. I recall FA 2 sitting in the flight deck. She appeared glassy-eyed and her eyes were red and watering. She indicated that she did not feel safe on the aircraft. I told the Captain that my nose was running but that I had not smelled the odor. FA 4 and FA 2 answered the CA's questions as a report was filled out. Two maintenance employees boarded the aircraft. I relayed the information regarding the odor's location and description that the other FAs had given. I told them that I did not detect an odor but that my nose was running. They proceeded to the aft galley. Approximately 20 or 30 minutes after exposure I began to feel a raw burning sensation in my throat and my voice became hoarse. I indicated this to the Captain. I had the urge to cough but tried not to so as not to alarm passengers as they were still onboard, but I coughed several times onboard (also after we deplaned and on the way to the hospital, and occasionally still have the urge to cough). While onboard I started to develop a light headache in spite of having taken ibuprofen earlier that morning and again at XB:00 for reasons unrelated to this event. In hindsight I believe I was incapacitated as my decision-making abilities were questionable by this point.Passengers began to question whether or not it was safe for them to been the aircraft since the Captain had made an announcement about an unusual odor. I advised them that it was, which I now regret. No voluntary deplaning announcement was made. At one point, a Flight Service Manager expressed concern for us FAs, indicating that we looked like we needed fresh air and that it was unfortunate that we had to remain on the aircraft due to passengers being onboard and minimum crew requirements. More passengers eventually started complaining about still being onboard the aircraft. FA 3 indicated to me that she did not feel safe on the aircraft. I asked the Captain if we were going to deplane. He said, 'it's not up to me. They've got to make the call.' It was my impression at the time that he was referring to the gate agents when he referenced 'they' but I did not ask him to clarify. I was not thinking clearly and vaguely wondered why it was not up to him as he was the Captain. I regret not pressing the matter further and I failed my duty to keep the crew and the passengers safe. At one point a passenger asked for a snack. I did not feel comfortable going to the aft galley but I did not want the other flight attendants to go back there either because their complaints of their symptoms were worse than mine (they reported shortness of breath, feeling so faint that they had to sit down while I was comfortable standing up, and tingling lips and limbs, burningtongue, etc., and I could see their eyes were glassy and watering) and they had been in the aft galley longer than me. I tried to hold my breath as I entered the aft galley to retrieve the snack for the passenger but I was not able to hold it for more than about 10 seconds which struck me as abnormal. Those passengers in the aft-most part of the cabin questioned whether or not they were safe being on the aircraft due to the odor the Captain had mentioned on the PA. I do not recall what I told them but I think I indicated that it was safe to be on the aircraft which I now deeply regret. As I made my way forward from the aft part of the galley, more passengers started complaining about being kept on the aircraft. When I returned to the flight deck I indicated to the Captain that the passengers had been on board (since boarding) the aircraft for over two hours without food or water. I again asked the Captain if we were going to deplane and he said he stated that the aircraft was 'going to be taken out of service soon.' I regret not pressing the matter further.At one point the flight attendants and I were the only employees at the forward part of the aircraft and I believe the only employees on the aircraft. I was nervous about this because I felt like no one should be on the aircraft. I called the gate multiple times but the line was busy so I called Ops again. I believe I told them that the passengers had been held on the aircraft for over two hours with no food or water and that we should deplane but I can't remember if I said this to Ops or to the gate agent (when I finally reached them after my call to Ops), or both. Either Ops or a gate agent told me at one point on the phone: 'Tower says you guys are going back out' or something along those lines. I did at one point get ahold of the gate agent and I indicated that passengers had been on the aircraft for over two hours without food or water. I believe he said that the Captain and the chief pilot were at the gate discussing the matter. This gate agent indicated to me that he agreed that passengers should have been deplaned as soon as we returned to the gate and that we had been held on the aircraft too long, and he stated that if it had been up to him the passengers would have been deplaned immediately upon returning to the gate. I again regret at this point not insisting the passengers be deplaned for their safety and for the safety of the crew. I regret not initiating an emergency deplaning which I believe would have been advisable given the state of incapacitation of me and my fellow crew members.Throughout this entire time all three FAs told me multiple times that they did not feel comfortable on the aircraft and that they believed passengers should not be on the aircraft. Prior to deplaning my runny nose resolved but my raw/burning throat did not. At one point I noticed my hands trembling slightly for no reason but I minimized this symptom and did not mention it to anyone. I regret not speaking up when the other FAs expressed their concerns to me. Eventually we deplaned somewhere between XE:00 and XE:30. We were advised that the flight had been re-crewed and I believe he said that there would be an aircraft swap. I then heard an announcement at the gate after we deplaned that there was to be no aircraft swap. I was gravely concerned for the oncoming crew but I wrongly assumed they would ultimately not take Aircraft X. I told one crew member that 'I didn't smell any odor but I'm having symptoms' as I walked by her at the gate but I did not have time to elaborate, as we were going to immediately seek medical treatment. I assumed that the aircraft would not go since the Captain had stated earlier to me that the aircraft was 'going to be taken out of service soon'. I assumed the fume report would be or had been filed. I assumed the new crew would not be put in any danger. I regret not staying at the gate and speaking up, and I feel it was my duty to try to protect the On Date I boarded Aircraft X servicing route from ZZZ to ZZZ1 around XA:30 as the #2 Flight Attendant on a 737 aircraft. I got straight to work in the back due to the flight basically starting to board right as we arrived to have a delayed departure time of XB:07. I believe the original departure time was XA:00. I set up all my carts and did everything I needed to get done throughout the boarding process, we then armed our doors and cross checked and proceeded to go off to do the Safety Demo once we pushed back. It was at that time I started to feel very lightheaded and didn't feel too well. I ignored it and figured it would go away. Once we did our final safety checks we all sat down in our jumpseats and proceeded to inform Flight Attendant (FA) Name I was feeling light headed just so she would be informed. About two minutes later I started to smell an odd odor, the only way I could best describe it is a dirty bathroom smell mixed with gasoline. I wanted to make sure I was really smelling what I smelled so I asked FA Name if she smelled it and she did not. She came over to my jumpseat and immediately did smell it. We both wanted to be sure so we called back FA 1 Name 4, she did not smell anything and continued to keep smelling to be sure, she saw our concern and took into account that I was also lightheaded so she called FA 3 Name 3 back to see if she could smell it. Right away FA Name 3 did smell what she described as a burning electric smell. FA Name 4 made the call to the Captain and told him of the odor we were all smelling, he informed us we had just passed a lot of planes and exhaust, we informed him that was not what we smelled. So we proceeded back to the gate.Upon arrival to the gate, Captain informed the passengers that the flight attendants smelled an odor that was off so we would be returning to the gate. After we verified and disarmed doors and cross checked we proceeded up to the front. At this point I was extremely light headed and it had felt like I was moving very slow. FA Name and myself sat in the flight deck and answered all of Captain's questions that he had for the report he was filling out. At this point all four flight attendants were experiencing symptoms (shortness of breath, light headed, sore throat's, running noises and tingly lips.) we all clearly did not look well. For some reason we did not deplane and I regret not seeking medical attention when we got to the gate due to my heightened symptoms. I was pretty out of it so I wasn't really sure what exactly was going on between the gate agent and Captain. I do recall Captain saying he had no say on if we could deplane the aircraft (which was kind of a shock to me due to this being his aircraft). I did notice that passengers wanted to get off the aircraft due to them being held on it for so long without food or water. FA Name 4 was doing a great job handling the passengers during all this even though she too was having symptoms of her own. All in all I believe the passengers and the crew were held on this aircraft for two hours. I then with glossy eyes proceeded to tell the Captain that I needed to get off the plane due to feeling like I might pass out. At this point nothing was done to get us off. Name 5 from inflight came down and said he wished he could let us off because we clearly needed fresh air but due to FAA minimum crew we could not do that. I did hear that the plane might be going out of service but then I also heard from the gate agent that this plane was going to pushback soon. I informed FA Name that I did not feel safe on this plane and she said the same thing. We all got together and said that we would not be taking this plane back out due to how ill we have all become. Finally around XE:30 the gate agent came on and told everyone to deplane and that there would be a crew swap and an aircraft swap. As we got our bags to leave we headed up to the gate where we heard the gate agent say that there indeed was not going to be an aircraft swap and that did not sit well with me.
