FA Name 4 and myself quickly warned one of the crew members that were going to work the plane to ZZZ1 that we are all ill and going to seek medical attention, I also told her to please stand her grown with this. We did get in contact with that crew and you will be receiving reports from them that will describe what happen to them. At this point we are walking to go to the onsite clinic to get us checked out, halfway through terminal I grabbed onto the wall and almost passed out. Inflight manager Name 5 got me a wheelchair and told me to take deep breaths and we proceeded to the clinic. The nurse said to get blood work done we should go to the nearest emergency room. Name 5 tried to set up transportation from the numbers we were given but he could not reach anyone so we ended up taking an Uber. At the hospital we all were given chest X-rays, EKG and arterial blood work for carbon monoxide. FA Name, myself and Name 4 all came back clear since the incident had been so long ago but unfortunately FA Name 3 did still have carbon monoxide in her blood, she was then put on 100% oxygen for 40 min and more blood work was done until she was also cleared to be discharged. The next morning we went to catch our deadhead to go home and we all were clearly completely out of breath from just walking from TSA to our gate which is very abnormal. Date 1 after we all got home I received a message from FA Name 4 that she was back in the emergency room due to her heightened symptoms and that the nurse told her to go. The next day Date 2 we received a message from FA Name that she too was back in the ER due to stomach pains. Later that day I became very dizzy and was having trouble breathing so I called FA Name 4 and she drove me to the same ER she went to after I called the nurse and gave me the all clear to do so. I was put on a breathing tube to help open up my airways and was prescribed and inhaler, FA Name 4 who was with me also was prescribed an inhaler for her too. We are now all at home Date 3 resting and we cannot return to work until symptoms are completely gone. I have a note stating I can't go back until Date 10 and if needed to extend because not fully recovered the doctor will extend it. This 737 should have been taken out of service after seeing what it did to us four flight attendants. Instead they put four new flight attendants in clear danger. We did come in contact with two FAs that worked that flight and I will let them tell their own stories but at least three out of the four are seeking medical attention and one had to call off mid sequence for feeling so ill. It's a complete shame that this aircraft is still out there flying and will continue to fly and affect so many more people. A fume event is not to be messed with and I hope the company will do something about this and take this seriously.
ASRS:1820579.s: During taxi out on a Boeing 737, cabin crew reported a fume odor in the aft galley, causing symptoms like lightheadedness and burning throats. The reporter attributes the crew's incapacitation and delayed deplaning to their inexperience and the fume exposure, which they believe compromised their ability to protect passengers and crew.

ASRS:1820618.n: Went to land at ZZZ and while in the middle of the downwind engine cut out. I was at roughly 900 feet. I instantly switched fuel tanks and made sure that the fuel pump was on. I then assessed the allude and came to the conclude that I wouldn't be able to make the runway. This was because I was centered in the middle of the downwind so I was unable due to altitude to turn and make the landing. After I decided that I couldn't make the runway so I turned right and had to put down the aircraft into a field. I had to make sure to avoid hanging electric lines. There was no damage to property or to myself. And I walked away from the plane.
ASRS:1820618.s: The pilot experienced an engine failure at 900 feet on downwind while landing at ZZZ. Unable to reach the runway due to altitude and position, the pilot executed a forced landing in a field, avoiding power lines with no damage to the aircraft or injuries.

ASRS:1820640.n: En route to FHR approximately 30 NM south of the airport, escaped a near mid-air collision with a plane coming from behind/overtaking us. We received a traffic report from Whidbey Approach of traffic 300 feet above at our 6 o'clock a few miles behind. Next transmission was 'traffic descending to same altitude gaining speed'. We diverted 10 degrees left of course for traffic avoidance, however they also followed our left course. Whidbey transmission 'traffic right behind you/on you 6 to 5 o'clock'. I spotted them nearly hitting our wing and diverted into a steep 50 degree turn left to avoid the collision'. Upon later confronting the other pilot, he said 'he didn't move even though he saw us because he was making position reports on the UNICOM'.
ASRS:1820640.s: The pilot reported a near mid-air collision en route to FHR while being overtaken by another aircraft. The other pilot failed to maneuver despite seeing the threat because he was making position reports on UNICOM, forcing the reporting pilot to execute a steep 50-degree turn to avoid impact.

ASRS:1820651.n: Busy day at the airport in the ZZZ traffic pattern. I heard a slightly garbled message about a Piper Cub entering a tear drop for the 45 to Runway XX as I was turning crosswind. I continued looking for the cub but did not see it and made my downwind turn and radio call. About halfway through downwind TCAS alerted me that there was something closer than a mile about 300 feet below me even though I was at TPA (Traffic Pattern Altitude). Worried I was over top of another aircraft I turned left and then right aggressively to check under the wings and nose for an aircraft and I did not see anything. Passed the numbers on downwind and started my descent to base. Called my base turn, heard something garbled. Then heard someone calling 'the Diamond' to which the pilot said I had gotten within 100 yards of him and that I should watch for traffic better. I did look, I had been in the pattern practicing all morning, I made clearing maneuvers to make sure there was nothing in a blind spot but at the end of the day I did not see him. While radios are not required, he obviously had one. Some of the hardest things to see while in the air are airports and other planes. It also would have been beneficial had the Piper Cub been at published TPA and even though not required, when within a very busy non towered airport, clearly announcing his position.
ASRS:1820651.s: A pilot flying a Diamond in the traffic pattern at a non-towered airport experienced a TCAS alert and a subsequent near-miss with a Piper Cub. The reporter attributed the incident to the Cub's failure to maintain Traffic Pattern Altitude and announce its position, despite the reporter performing clearing maneuvers.

ASRS:1820674.n: Engine roughness that resulted in the instructor taking over controls, [notified ATC] and making a precautionary landing a ZZZ. Engine didn't want to stay running at anything less than full power, Carburetor heat was applied but didn't seem to help the problem. Maximum power was 2100 rpm in straight and level flight.
ASRS:1820674.s: The instructor took controls of an aircraft experiencing engine roughness and low RPMs during flight, applying carburetor heat without success. The crew notified ATC and executed a precautionary landing at ZZZ because the engine would not run below full power.

ASRS:1820677.n: Preflight and runup was normal. Engine operation was good. Began taxiing on the runway. Full power was applied and engine instruments were all in the green (RPM, pressure, and temperature). Airspeed was increasing slowly initially at first, but RPM increased as airspeed increased and I reached rotation speed of 60 to 65. I reached my normal Vx speed of 65 to 70 MPH. I had seen the climb-out of another aircraft and it appeared to be windy so I decided to add a little more speed to that as a buffer for safety. I had briefed this prior to takeoff and was aiming for 70 to 75 for the climb out, for obstacle avoidance and wind buffer. I also had briefed and prepared for a wind shift as I got above the trees, as this is a standard precaution that I have regularly made at this airport (because of the location of the trees) and was prepared to expect it (as is regularly briefed for an eventuality such as this). This is a part of my normal before takeoff emergency brief. As soon as I got nearing the tops of the trees I felt the lift reduce and the stall horn began. The controls were sluggish and I knew instantly that I needed to lower the nose to prevent a stall. I lowered the nose and tried to nurse it back up but very quickly realized something needed to be done as the runway was reducing and I didn't feel comfortable in the lift being generated being able to take me over the trees. I made a quick decision to reduce the power and attempt for an aborted landing. I pitched over, touched down, and hit the brakes. I realized that the runway was coming to an end and the hill was going to slope down. So I attempted to turn the aircraft using the rudders and was successful in slowing the aircraft and not going down into the sloped hill. Then, managed to stop the aircraft at the end of the runway. Once the aircraft was stopped, the engine was running, I pulled the mixture, switched the mags to off, and turned off the master. Post-incident inspection showed apparently minor prop damage (a ding in the prop) and nothing else appeared to be damaged. Postflight discussion with the pilot of the initial observed aircraft and he stated that he also felt the wind shift and was struggling to climb. The climbout seemed a little low to me, but it was not readily apparent to me that it was solely because of the winds. I surmise that a windshear event occurred from the changing wind direction because of the trees. Luckily, I had briefed for this eventuality and knew what to do. Things that went right:- Proper brief prior to takeoff which covered a change in wind due to the trees- Proper speed-wind buffer: this resulted in the lift that WAS available at that time and contributed to a safe landing without exceeding the critical Angle of Attack. - Managed to stop the aircraft with minimal damage, and no occupant damageThings that went wrong:- Initial observation of the struggling climb of the aircraft on departure should have resulted in more hesitancy to depart to begin with
ASRS:1820677.s: The pilot aborted a takeoff due to a suspected wind shear event caused by trees, which triggered a stall warning and reduced lift. The aircraft was stopped safely at the runway end with only minor propeller damage after the pilot lowered the nose and applied brakes.

ASRS:1820737.n: I experienced a ground loop. Wind was 260 at 8kts, and tower had me land on Runway 16. My plane has conventional gear. I got my right wheel down, then the left wheel, then the tail wheel, retracted flaps. Suddenly the plane turned right into the wind, despite my pressing left brake.We ended up in the weeds of the runway safety area, about 50 feet from the runway but facing towards it. I did not drag a wing tip or strike the prop. Neither I nor my passenger suffered any injury. Got grass between the left tire and the rim, and a shallow gouge in the tire's inner sidewall where it took off the brake bleeder valve. No other damage to the aircraft. Could start up, but could not taxi straight. Operations / Fire towed me back to my hangar. I called Tower with a report as requested, and gave a report to the Operations / Fire agent. I suspect I failed to keep the control stick into the wind on roll-out.
ASRS:1820737.s: The pilot of a conventional gear aircraft ground looped on Runway 16 during rollout in 8-knot winds, suspecting a failure to hold the control stick into the wind. The aircraft ended up in the runway safety area with minor tire damage but no injuries or structural damage.

ASRS:1820753.n: We were on a repositioning flight to ZZZ on an IFR flight plan in VFR conditions. Upon being handed off to Approach, ATC instructed us to descend to 2000 feet and fly a westerly heading to join a right downwind for Runway 9 at ZZZ. We reported the airport in sight for the visual. ATC said that we would fly for several more miles to allow for a departure. ATC then instructed us to fly a heading of 360, cleared us for the visual approach, and to contact ZZZ tower. We complied with all instructions. As we turned a 5-mile base to final, we attempted to contact the tower three times as we continued our descent. At 900 feet, the tower finally responded and told us to immediately turn to a heading of 120 and climb and maintain 2,000 feet. As we began the turn and initiated a climb, tower announced several times in the same radio call that we needed to expedite our climb as there was traffic at 1,000 feet at our 12 o'clock, less than a mile. We aggressively climbed from 1,000 feet to 2,000 feet and was instructed to contact Approach for further vectors. ATC vectored us to a 9-mile right base and once again cleared us for the visual approach. We landed without further incident. After clearing the runway and asking ground control for a phone number to speak with the manager. The controller asked if it was about what just happened. We replied yes. She stated that it was Approach that gave the suggested heading of 120 that put us in direct conflict with the GA traffic that was at traffic pattern altitude on the right downwind for Runway 9. She said that it was Approach's fault and offered the TRACON phone number if I wanted it. I declined and informed her that I would file a NASA report and that the midair was entirely too close.
ASRS:1820753.s: During a visual approach to Runway 9 at ZZZ, the crew received conflicting vectors from Approach that placed them in a near-midair conflict with traffic at 1,000 feet. The crew executed an aggressive climb to 2,000 feet to avoid the collision, and Ground Control later confirmed Approach issued the erroneous heading.

ASRS:1820754.n: I was scheduled to fly over an event on the coast of ZZZ. I arrived about 20 minutes early and began orbiting nearby. The visibility was excellent and the air was smooth. I could see the mountains in the distance and the pier about 8 miles to the southeast. Rather than continuing to orbit, I decided to fly along the coast past the pier and back. I visually cleared the route from my location to the pier and turned on course, level at 1,200 feet MSL. I began a shallow descent off shore. As I descended through about 800 feet, suddenly, there appeared a banner tow aircraft just barely above and slightly to the left. I pushed down and to the right narrowly avoiding a midair collision.After the event, I realized that I had made a mistake. Even though I had visually cleared the area in front of me, I should not have flown a shallow, wings level, straight-ahead descent. I should have made one (or more) S-turns during the descent to scan for traffic ahead and below my flight path.
ASRS:1820754.s: A pilot flying a shallow descent at 800 feet MSL near a coastal event narrowly avoided a midair collision with a banner tow aircraft. The pilot attributed the near miss to failing to perform S-turns during the descent to scan for traffic ahead and below.

ASRS:1820768.n: I am the owner of a Mooney M20E and have >300 hours in this plane. The flight in the late afternoon was a demonstration flight for a friend of mine who is considering beginning pilot training. He has done informal training many times over several years including with me, and has excellent instincts and innate skills that indicate he will be an excellent pilot. In addition, he has significant knowledge about airplanes, airplane systems and general aeronautical/ aviation information. Weather conditions were VFR and not challenging in any way. There were some mild clouds and precipitation in the area but we had no difficulty avoiding them throughout the flight.I flew left seat and handled all engine controls and critical phases of flight, takeoffs, landings, radio calls, etc. He had controls for much of the enroute time and legs of traffic patterns. We did standard maneuvers, mostly practice traffic patterns and landings at ZZZ1, which is close to ZZZ and is the most commonly used training field for many pilots out of ZZZ, including myself. We did three touch and goes and one full stop/ taxi back at ZZZ1. There was no indication of a gear problem for any of these several extensions or retractions. I have very recently done solo training flights with similar or greater numbers of gear extensions and retractions in a similar span of time with no indication of problem. After close to an hour of flying, we returned toward ZZZ for our final stop. We entered a long right base for Runway XXR, and at the appropriate time put the gear switch down. For the first time ever in this plane that I know of, there was a gear extension problem. The gear motor activated and could be felt extending the gear. It seemed mostly normal, but perhaps a little louder/ more forceful than usual. It stopped abruptly, it seemed to have taken a usual amount of time, but the gear on this plane do normally extend quickly and I could not be certain the motor had run as long as usual. The two gear down lights (one on the panel and one on the floor) did not illuminate. The gear actuator circuit breaker had popped out. I tried resetting the circuit breaker twice, but it did not stay in. The gear switch had no effect at this point, as expected with the circuit breaker tripped. The feel of the plane in flight felt as though the gear were down with the expected amount of drag.I advised ZZZ tower that we were breaking off the approach for troubleshooting of a gear problem, and headed generally north of the field in coordination with the controller. I pulled out the Owner's Manual, and my passenger assisted in reviewing the manual gear extension procedure, with which I am very familiar. I have practiced this on the ground a few times over the years at the time of annual inspection with the plane on jacks. I have also practiced it in the air at least once in this plane.With my passenger reviewing the steps out loud for me, I extended the gear manually. The hand crank did not reach a stopping point and the gear down lights did not illuminate. I checked the visual floor indicator, which is there as a backup in case of electrical failure, and the 'GEAR DOWN' sign was visible as normal when the gear extend, with the alignment bars lined up normally as per my memory of how they typically line up. Many additional cranks on the manual extension handle on several more tries had no further effect on anything that I could tell. We were concerned we might have a broader electrical problem of some type leading to failure of the indicator lights, even though the gear appeared to be fully extended. I checked another indicator light on the panel in the same cluster as the 'Gear Down' light (the 'Ram Air' light), which was working properly. I could find no other signs of electrical failure on board. There was no smell or sign of smoke.At this point, I contacted ZZZ tower and coordinated a low pass down Runway XXR to get a visual check of the gear. The tower controller was ableto see the gear well and reported all three appeared to be fully extended. The plane was performing well and maintaining control was not an issue. I was able to aviate, navigate and communicate easily and without difficulty, and to go through the appropriate manual gear extension procedure with plenty of time and focus. My passenger remained very calm, focused and helpful throughout. Neither of us became anxious or nervous, and we were able to communicate well and work together well. He was an asset to me functioning as part of the crew, even without formal pilot training. The ZZZ controller(s) likewise were extremely responsive, helpful and professional.I did not seem to have any additional options to try to get the 'Gear Down' lights to illuminate. I was fairly confident that the gear were fully extended. We were in no immediate danger, and there seemed to be no other emergency reason to land prematurely, although the possibility of some larger electrical system problem remained in my mind. As such, I decided that spending extra time in the air for additional attempts at troubleshooting was no longer wise and that we should land safely while conditions were good.The landing on Runway XXR was smooth, well controlled and uneventful. The wind was nearly straight down the runway and was light. I most often land with no flaps, and chose to do so in this case as well. I made sure to land with excellent technique, touching down gently just above stall speed, well aligned with the center line and with minimal control inputs. I made sure not to use the brakes, and I elected not to use the elevator for aerodynamic braking, as I wanted to avoid any unnecessary forces on the gear. I allowed the plane to roll out long on the runway, and all appeared to be going well. I let the tower know that I intended to roll out long due to the unknown status of the gear. Runway XXR is 7,500 feet long, I touched down not far past the numbers, and rolled out nearly to taxiway 1 for a total rollout distance of about 3,500-4,000 feet.After we had dissipated most of our forward speed without incident or sign of additional problem, I began a very gentle right turn toward the 'high speed' exit for taxiway 1. At that point, the plane began to settle toward the ground toward the left, with the front and right settling down very quickly after. The prop struck the runway and the engine quit, the plane skidded about 30 feet and came to a stop at a mild angle off center line. The impact with the runway was surprisingly soft from our standpoint. I quickly shut off the master switch, magneto switches, and fuel selector, and we exited the plane quickly and easily. There was no fuel spillage, smoke or fire. Neither of us sustained any injury of any kind.Using a heavy boom truck, we were able to gently lift the plane off the runway via the engine mount. I was able to easily manually extend the gear fully, and again was unable to get the 'Gear Down' lights to illuminate despite the gear being verified fully down, and the manual floor indicator properly aligned. While being towed away, the plane again settled to the ground toward the left when initiating a fairly gentle slow turn to the right. This time, only the left gear folded.At the time, shortly after, and for the next day or two I believed that I had properly pushed the crank forward to engage the manual gear extension mechanism and allow the handle to work properly. This is one of the basic few steps needed in the manual gear extension procedure, and I had done it many times. It is a small handle and lever located at approximately the left side of the left pilot's knee, and is easily reachable with your left hand. After reflecting on the events and going back to visit the plane, in fact I had not properly pushed that lever all the way forward. It appears that the manual gear extension mechanism will apply enough lowering force even when not properly engaged to allow the gear to fully or nearly fullyextend, but without the crank properly engaged it appears that you cannot get enough force to fully lock the gear in place.At the time of the [event], although I and my passenger were under good control and responding well to the situation, I was approaching or beyond 14 hours since I had woken up and gone to work early that morning. I believe that pushing the end of my duty day, as well as familiarity with the procedure and not double checking myself that I had followed every step properly were contributing factors in my failure to fully lock the gear. I believe I could have prevented the gear collapse had I followed the checklist and double checked every step.We have not yet jacked the plane and examined all of the relevant components. Whether or not there is some other structural damage to the gear extension mechanism or any of the components involved, and whether or not we are able to ultimately demonstrate that the gear down lights were or were not in fact working, it does not change the fact that I did not properly complete one of the necessary steps on the checklist for manual gear extension. I also failed to catch this omission with a thorough review of the procedure and circumstances after the gear lights failed to come on. I allowed myself to give too much weight to the possibility of an indicator failure and did not continue to troubleshoot more when I have the ability to do so. I also believed that my familiarity with the procedure was sufficient that I did not consider that I might have omitted or failed to properly complete a step.As I reflect on this, it gives me a sense of humility and a reminder of my own fallibility, and reinforces that I need to double check checklists and critical steps at all times. My belief that my left hand had done what it was supposed to with respect to the one missing step was simply inaccurate. I could have and should have caught the error with a careful review of the circumstances, and there was not an emergency pressing need to get the plane on the ground immediately. I will carry this lesson for the rest of my life. Fortunately, no one was injured, and the mechanical and financial damage to the plane are the only costs. But it is still a humbling fact that I did a basic part of managing my aircraft incorrectly and caused damage as a result. In another circumstance, I or someone else could have been hurt with such an error. I will redouble my efforts to be meticulous for procedures, checklists, and review of critical items at all times. In addition, I will be more careful with respect to aircraft operations beyond 12 or 13 hours since waking up in the morning on any particular occasion.
ASRS:1820768.s: The pilot of a Mooney M20E experienced a gear extension failure during landing at ZZZ due to an improperly engaged manual extension lever. Although the gear appeared down, they failed to lock, causing the aircraft to settle and the propeller to strike the runway during a taxi turn, resulting in no injuries.

ASRS:1820769.n: On takeoff roll while training a Multi Engine Instructor (MEI) in a standardization course, Left Hand Engine RPM exceeded limits. Instructor Pilot-in-training reduced power lever and it went to normal (which is normal procedure). When he reestablished full power it returned to abnormal range but we reached Vr and rotated. Instructor Pilot conducting training took flight controls to check the condition and confirmed it was a malfunction. Thus requested a return to the field for landing. After a few minutes, when it was confirmed that even with significantly reduced thrust, the engine was still malfunctioning, [we advised ATC] and landed. Did not shut it down because the engine was still producing useful thrust. Landing was uneventful, and taxied back to the ramp.
ASRS:1820769.s: During a standardization training takeoff, the instructor pilot-in-training experienced a left engine RPM malfunction that persisted despite power adjustments. The training instructor took control, requested a return to the field, and landed safely with the engine running to utilize its remaining thrust.

ASRS:1820785.n: Flying a 0.055 lbs fixed wing RC in an open park space in early morning. An unleashed dog came running up and created a distraction for a few seconds, at which time the aircraft drifted about 200 yards downwind over nearby residential area. Steered the aircraft back, but at one point the wind and turbulence became too much and the aircraft went down over the residential area. It has so far not been relocated. The winds were much too close to the limits for such a light aircraft.
ASRS:1820785.s: A pilot flying a 0.055 lbs fixed-wing RC aircraft in an open park was distracted by an unleashed dog, causing the aircraft to drift 200 yards downwind over a residential area. Strong wind and turbulence subsequently caused the aircraft to crash in the residential area, where it remains unrecovered.

ASRS:1820801.n: While turning south from Taxiway B onto the ramp I noticed a (Service Driver) type vehicle traveling west on the vehicle service road. He was traveling at a high rate of speed and I mentioned it to the First Officer. As we approached the vehicle service road the driver passed through the yield sign painted on the road and drove right in front of our aircraft. I stopped the aircraft and we watched him drive by, looking to the south, paying no attention to us. After he passed by, the First Officer called Ground and told the Controller what happened.
ASRS:1820801.s: The pilot stopped the aircraft on the ramp after a service driver ignored a yield sign and drove in front of the plane at high speed. The First Officer subsequently reported the incident to Ground Control.

ASRS:1820885.n: Coming from the DYMND Arrival for visual/ILS backup to [Runway] 28L. ATC cleared traffic onto 28L for departure. We were around 800 feet on the approach as they began their takeoff roll. Separation looked tight and we mentioned the possible go around. As they rotated and began their climb, we incurred wake turbulence which pushed our limits on a stable approach and would have led to a landing outside of the touchdown zone, a go around was commenced. Returned and landed uneventfully on 28L.
ASRS:1820885.s: The crew on a visual/ILS approach to Runway 28L encountered wake turbulence from a departing aircraft at 800 feet. This pushed the approach limits, forcing a go-around to avoid landing outside the touchdown zone, followed by an uneventful landing.

ASRS:1820895.n: First, the biggest threat to the flight was that I hadn't flown in a little over a year, zero hours. This was due to COVID related reduction in flying at my airline. This flight was my first flight on Operator Experience (OE).We were cleared to line up and wait on Runway XXY at ZZZ. A regional jet was also cleared to line up and wait on Runway XXZ. The tower frequency was busy due to landing traffic on the crossing runway and communication between tower and a previously departed aircraft reporting bird activity. I haven't flown at ZZZ for a long time and had forgotten that they normally clear the smaller aircraft to takeoff before the heavy due to wake turbulence. Tower cleared the regional jet for takeoff and in the busyness my brain processed the clearance as ours. The last factor for me was we were right in the middle of transferring the aircraft from the captain to me and so the radio call, acknowledging the takeoff clearance I thought I heard, got dropped. I don't recollect making it. In addition, I failed to verbalize, verify and monitor the clearance with the captain.When tower saw us begin our takeoff roll prematurely, they cancelled our takeoff clearance and we rejected the takeoff at very low speed...I estimate 50 knots. We acknowledged, cleared the runway and taxied back to XXY. The following takeoff was uneventful.Lastly, we noticed on our second takeoff that red lights on the runway were illuminated in front of us prior to getting takeoff clearance. They extinguished when we received takeoff clearance. The lights were not used for our first takeoff.
ASRS:1820895.s: A pilot with zero recent hours mistakenly initiated a takeoff roll at 50 knots after misinterpreting a clearance for another aircraft during a busy transfer of control. The tower cancelled the clearance, prompting a rejected takeoff, while the crew later noted runway lights illuminated only after receiving the correct clearance.

ASRS:1820978.n: Attention Mangers and Chief Dispatcher;I am currently working desk X. In my opinion the workload on my desk is currently unmanageable. I am requesting immediate assistance due to increased activity. At this point I had one flight holding, multiple reroutes, a MTOW /reroute issue in ZZZ that would have resulted in involve bumping 30+ passenger if unable to get a route approved by the command center. This was all in addition to my normal flight following duties. The amount of flights on the desk, combined with summer weather, ATC proficiency, and crew staffing, have us all operating in the yellow on a continuous basis. I had no choice but to stop issuing releases to avoid going into the red and losing operational control. The manager was able to have another dispatcher prepare some releases for me, but the flights were never actually pulled from my desk.Management is putting too many flights on desks.Once and for all, come up with a joint solution for a workload model that puts safety first.
ASRS:1820978.s: A dispatcher reported unmanageable workload at desk X due to summer weather, staffing issues, and excessive flight volume, including a critical MTOW/reroute issue. To prevent losing operational control, the dispatcher stopped issuing releases until a manager assigned another dispatcher to assist, though flights remained on the original desk.

ASRS:1820979.n: Flight was signed and released by morning shift without applying the MEL fuel penalty of MEL 28-XXA. After flight release and review, the afternoon shift noticed the error, corrected it, and re-released the flight with MEL 28-XXA applied correctly.This MEL was missed due to incredibly high dispatch desk workload, and un-forecast hazardous weather in every part of the country. These factors and the resulting task saturation lead to an incredible amount of additional flight planning time that was rushed due to the demand that flights which do not actually calculate for up to an hour past morning shift end time are signed with that dispatchers name.Workload is excessive and borderline disorienting leading up to and through shift turnover. At no point should there be any more 15 flights airborne per desk at one time, and yet 16-25 flights airborne at once has become the norm in the past few months. Perhaps the threshold for signing un-calculated flight plans should be 15 minutes past end of shift. This should allocate plenty of time for the oncoming dispatcher to review the work of the A.M. shift and sign the plan with their name. This alleviates the turnover workload, and provides the A.M. shift time to review their work and flight follow. I reported for duty, 15 minutes in, I noticed that flight had a wing tank aft fuel MEL (28-XXA). This MEL calls for 5,000 lbs of MEL fuel. In error the previous dispatcher failed to allocate that fuel as MEL fuel. I sent a revised release and the flight departed without incident. I have advised the dispatcher to file a report as well.
ASRS:1820979.s: The morning shift dispatcher failed to apply the MEL 28-XXA fuel penalty due to excessive workload and task saturation. The afternoon shift corrected the error by re-releasing the flight with the required 5,000 lbs of MEL fuel, and the aircraft departed without incident.

ASRS:1820981.n: We were descending from 6,000 ft to 4,000 ft on an IFR flight plan. As we passed through about 5,500 ft the Pilot Flying (PF) saw an aircraft at our 1 o'clock. They appeared to be climbing. The PF disconnected the autopilot and stopped our descent and turned left. We missed the glider but were able to see the other pilot. The glider did not show up on our TCAS and approach was unaware of any aircraft operating near us. After passing the glider we returned on course and continued our descent. Approach was unaware of our deviation. We did report the near miss to approach.
ASRS:1820981.s: During an IFR descent from 6,000 to 4,000 ft, the Pilot Flying manually stopped descent and turned left to avoid a climbing glider at 1 o'clock that was not on TCAS or known to Approach. The crew reported the near miss after passing the glider, noting Approach was unaware of both the glider and the deviation.

ASRS:1820996.n: After takeoff in ZZZ, received a 14th stage right duct warning. Shortly after we received 'Jetpipe overheat.' We turned right and stayed in the pattern and returned to ZZZ to land. I ran the 14th Right Duct checklist. I queried the Captain about declaring an emergency, but he told me we had 'priority handling' and that he didn't see the need. We went back to the gate and deplaned. According to Maintenance, the right engine was new and the wiring for the fire loops was creating friction and causing the sensors to alarm. Better training [recommend] for Maintenance. One of the Mechanics said a smell that the Flight Attendant pointed out during her preflight was 'normal.' It wasn't, and this whole situation could have been avoided, had the mechanics took their time to analyze what was going on. Staffing is a huge issue in ZZZ the ground crew told us they were not prepared or staffed to handle an emergency situation. I would not feel comfortable having an emergency in ZZZ based on this experience with the current level of staffing.
ASRS:1820996.s: The crew received false engine warnings after takeoff at ZZZ due to new engine wiring friction, prompting a return to land. The reporter attributed the incident to inadequate maintenance analysis and insufficient ground staffing, noting a missed preflight odor and lack of emergency declaration.

ASRS:1821087.n: Due to being sick from this flight, this is my first chance to write this report. I was on standby from XA:00am-XG:00 on Date in ZZZ. Crew Scheduling called me at XF:06 to work a 1-2-1 three day trip. They assigned me position 1 and the first leg of the trip was to ZZZ1. I switched positions with Name and became the #3 because I don't like being #1. While walking to the gate flight service called to check on us (they thought they were calling the #1 from the original crew but instead called me by accident) and informed me that the original crew was being taken off this trip due to a fume event. When we arrived at the gate, our flight had begun deplaning. We were told that they had sat out on the tarmac for 2 hours before they were able to get to the gate and deplane so the aircraft could be checked out. During deplaning, Name 1 (the #4) and Name 2 (the #2) called the union and Name 3 to talk to them because we were very nervous about flying on this aircraft after it just came back to the gate and had to have us re-crew it due to a fume event. We did not know the original crew personally but as they deplaned they warned Name 2 and Name 1 that we should not get on that aircraft because something was wrong with it and that they were on the way to the hospital. They were shaken up, pale, and were visibly ill. One of the girls even had to get a wheelchair to wheel her out of the terminal. I immediately felt very unsafe about proceeding forward on this trip. Seeing the crew so visibly ill from a fume event and then being expected to take that aircraft right back out and move on like nothing happened is extremely terrifying and irresponsible of the flight deck. Our health and safety clearly was not a first priority in this instance. After original crew and passengers deplaned we were immediately sent down to the aircraft and the agent wanted us to check our equipment so we could board again and get this flight out as quickly as possible since it was so delayed. I was the first FA on the jet bridge, and I ran into the maintenance man on his way out. He told me he did an inspection of the aircraft and it was cleared to fly. He said he could smell stuff in the aft lavs but that everything was clear. He told Name 2 when he saw her that it was all good and to not get on and break anything. This was all happening so fast that it was hard to process it all and I was very uneasy and felt pressure to work this flight. After I got on the flight, the Captain was dismissive of the event. He informed me that he thought the previous crew was being overly cautious because two of the four flight attendants had just recently been through an incident on one of their trips that they had not been able to fully recover from, so that is why they turned around, but he did not think there was a serious issue to be concerned with. I interpreted this as the Captain thinking the previous crew was overreacting and that he did not take their concerns seriously. He and the First Officer said they attributed the fumes to there being a lot of aircraft congestion on the way out and that they thought it would be fine this time around. They said to let them know if we experienced anything this time, but it seemed as though the flight was going no matter what based on the flight deck's attitude. They continued to dismiss our fears before boarding started again saying it was fine to fly on this aircraft and that maintenance didn't see a problem. I was hesitant with this news because maintenance was on their way out not even 5-10 minutes after deplaning took place, and I did not think that was a substantial amount of time to do a thorough check of the aircraft. After the Captain informed me of this, my other crew members got on board and they asked me what he said. Name 2 was especially nervous because she has a health concern that if mixed with a fume event could be life threatening, so she went into the cockpit and had a long talk with the Captain. I'm not exactly sureof what he said to her because I was out of earshot but she told me he was dismissive and also mentioned what he said to me about the other 2 flight attendants from the other crew being overly cautious due to their past experiences on a trip. Name 2 told me that the Captain also made a joke when she expressed her concerns about how his mother thought he was the smartest guy in the world but there is always a chance that I'm wrong. We re-boarded passengers on the flight without there being a substantial amount of time to pass after it was deplaned the first time (like 15-20 minutes). During boarding, passengers kept asking me if it was safe to fly, and I told them that the Captain had told me he thought it was due to congestion from other aircraft that caused the smell the first time and that maintenance had cleared us to fly. The Captain never once made an announcement to the passengers to update them on the situation and reassure passengers once they re-boarded. Name 1 called Name 3 during boarding and asked Name 1 to ask the Captain if he had filled out the cabin odor fume report. Name 1 called me since he was in the back to ask. Name 2 had come to the front during boarding and she ended up being the one to ask the Captain. The Captain's response was that he had never heard of the cabin odor fume report before. There was another report that the union wanted us to ask about (the report is named with numerics) and when Name 2 asked the Captain about this he said he was going to pull it up but we never actually saw him do it. He then changed the subject with Name 2 to talk about his vacation that he was going on at the end of the trip. I had COVID back in Month and ever since I recovered, my taste and smell have not returned, so I am not a good judge on if there was an odor in this aircraft. However, Name 1 and Name 2 mentioned they smelled something gross in the back of the aircraft. Once in the air, Name 1 and I started feeling very light headed. Name 1 and the #1 Name 2 also started having a bad headache. During the middle of the service, there was moderate turbulence that continued the duration of the flight. We ended up having to suspend service because it was too dangerous to be in the aisle. I even felt like I caught some air at one point. We hurried to secure the carts and ourselves in the back. This is not what this report is about, but I think you should know that the Captain did not communicate with us the entire time about the turbulence or when it would end. We had to call him to ask if the turbulence would continue the rest of the flight and if there was a different altitude we could try because we were all feeling whiplashed in the back and queasy. He said we should suspend service and that he would make the announcement to the passengers about it. Name 1 then had to call him about 15 minutes later after the initial call to see if he was still going to make the announcement because he had yet to do it. He finally made the announcement to the passengers that we would not be completing the rest of the service due to the turbulence. However, he called the #1 Name 2 to make sure she had completed first class service because he wanted to make sure the customers were getting what they paid for. The Captain's unprofessionalism and lack of care for the flight attendants and our safety was astounding. Once we landed he and the First Officer were one of the first ones off the aircraft and they left to go straight to the van for their layover. These pilots ran off right when we landed. It was evident that the Captain was in a hurry to start his layover and had no concern for health and safety of his flight crew. He never once checked on us or asked us how we were feeling from the fume event or the turbulence. Now you have at least two flight attendant crews sick and a Captain and First Officer that could care less. Was this airplane truly airworthy? Name 1's headache continued for the next 3 days. On the second day of ourtrip, after we worked from ZZZ1-ZZZ2 Name 1 had to call out because he threw up mid flight, had a horrible headache, and had an upset stomach. He said his symptoms started that first flight from ZZZ-ZZZ1 and only continued. We had to get a standby from ZZZ2 to finish the trip with us. I have felt extremely lethargic ever since that flight. It feels like I took 10 Benadryl. I have had a very foggy brain and have slept non-stop. Writing this report is the longest I have stayed awake since I got home from that trip. I have also had shortness of breath. Name 1 and I went to the ER on Date 3 and got our hemoglobin levels tested and our chest x-rayed. Our hemoglobin levels were normal but that is to be expected since we went 48 hours after exposure. We called out on flight because we felt so sick and unable to fly. I talked to nurse when I called the number and after describing my symptoms she told me she was going to have me stop right there and recommend that I go get checked out at the ER and call her back within the next few days after I was checked out. I am still experiencing extreme brain fog, exhaustion, and shortness of breath. At the end of the day, we felt forced to get on an aircraft that had an issue and work Aircraft X to ZZZ1 because the union told one of the other flight attendants if we didn't we would get in trouble with the company and a refusal to fly. We have been given points against us when we were injured on the workplace in a fume event of some sort and now we are having our jobs jeopardized by points. The points are penalizing us for being sick and being taken to the hospital on a work injury/fume event. Why would a company that I give my time to penalize us for a work related injury? I want to recap that you have 2 crews that are sick with a Captain who was absolutely unprofessional, unsafe, and dismissive. This is a serious safety issue, and with this aircraft still flying you are risking the safety and health of passengers and crew members. Train your pilots and ground staff (the Tower and Ops) on how to handle fume events. We should have never taken this aircraft after knowing that 4 flight attendants were taken to the hospital sick and now we are all sick. At the end of the day, this flight deck crew and the company is responsible for our illnesses. I have not received any calls from our department. It is like no one cares how sick we are. This is my first fume event and I have had no guidance on how to handle this and proceed from here. Communication is key. I was on standby on Date at XA:00 sign in & was called at XE:15 to work the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was assigned position 4 on the trip with 3 other crew members. I made my way to the gate & as I arrived there were still passengers getting off the aircraft. I went over to the side & started talking to the crew that I was going to be working with. We saw the other crew come off & they did not look okay, the crew came over to us & said that the airplane had just had a fume event & that it wasn't safe for us to fly. We continued down the jet bridge after scanning in with the agent, upon arrival to the aircraft I saw that Maintenance was on board & talking to the Captain. As we got on we asked the Captain what had happened & if the airplane was safe to fly. He began to say that the other crew was just smelling fumes from the congestion on the taxi way & that it was nothing to be worried about. As I got to the back of the aircraft I smelt a terrible pee smell which seemed to be coming from the aft lavatory's. I informed the Captain but he said he was aware of the situation in the back. Our number 2 made sure to go up front & ask a bunch of different questions to the Captain about the aircraft & what had just happened. The Captain didn't give us much information with the plane & so I called the union. As I called the union, I was told to ask for a cabin air quality check, upon asking the Captain for this he said it was not necessary & that he wasn't needing one done. We tried our best with not feeling safe going on this aircraft, we boarded up & began pushing back. Upon push back, I was informed that 3 of the 4 flight attendants on that flight before us were headed to the hospital & one had to be wheeled out in a wheelchair. We were already taxing & there was nothing we could do at this point. We got up in the air & I started to have a terrible headache, later in the flight the number one came to the back & said that she was having a headache as well. We thought nothing of it for the most part, we then began to all feel light headed. We continued onto ZZZ1. The headaches continued onto the next day when we were working our flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2. About 30-45 away from landing I began to feel super nauseous from the flight & ended up getting sick on the flight. I proceeded to call the Captain to call tracking & have a standby waiting at the gate for me because I wanted to get off of the trip because I started feeling so sick. I got off the trip went to my hotel & slept for 12 hours before waking up. I was foggy & very out of it, very unlike me in any way. I still had my headache even after I had taken my medicine that I had been given by a doctor a while back for pain. The headache continued through the night & I was deadheading on a flight the next day, I was very very exhausted & short on my breath. I got on the plane not thinking much about it. As we were in the air I started to feel light headed, like I was going to pass out once again. Upon landing I got a message from the other crew informing me that 2 of the 4 had been in the ER still. One of the flight attendants did test positive for carbon monoxide poison. I proceeded to call the injury number and report everything to them. I was informed that I needed to go to the hospital & get checked out. Me & the number 3 flight attendant ended up going to the hospital together to get checked out, all of our tests came back normal but the doctor said that was to be expected since it was so long after exposure. He said there was a very good chance that is what it was but the test didn't show it. He gave us a note & recommended us stay rested & healthy. I don't believe that I should be punished with points for the company's inability to properly check the aircraft & deem it not safe. I should not be receiving any points for the situation as it was an injury on duty & was reported to the company in a timely manner. The points should not count against us in this event since it was a fume event. The points are given to us for being proactive about our safety & well being, Why would a company that I work for & give most of my time, want to give us points for a situation we believe is linked to an unsafe aircraft. We now have 2 crews who have been sick & however many after the fact. You have a Captain who was not in charge enough to say he wanted an air quality check of the aircraft for the safety of his crew & passengers. You still have this aircraft in service & are potentially putting other people's life & health at risk. Pilot & airplane need to be taken out of service for endangering passengers & crew members.
ASRS:1821087.s: A flight attendant crew boarded an aircraft previously returned due to a fume event after maintenance cleared it, despite the original crew's illness and the captain's dismissal of concerns. During the flight, crew members experienced headaches and light-headedness, while the captain failed to communicate about turbulence or check on the crew's well-being after landing.

ASRS:1821139.n: I was flying with a private pilot student to practice landings at ZZZ1. We departed ZZZ, and arrived midfield at ZZZ1 at XA:40 local time according to my ADSB track log. Other traffic in the pattern was using Runway XX, so we made right traffic for XX. The student and I completed two laps in the traffic pattern for XX. On our third lap in the pattern, we were flying in front of another Skyhawk in the pattern, Aircraft Y. At XA:57 we turned base to final for runway 26 and made a radio call on CTAF. We heard Aircraft Y call base behind us. At XA:58, just past the numbers of Runway XX, I saw Aircraft Z low and climbing towards us. I could see his tail number. I called my controls and executed a go around and a turn to the right. I attempted to raise Aircraft Z on the radio, but had no answer. Aircraft Y responded to my calls and advised me that the aircraft appeared to be making a left crosswind turn and exiting the pattern to the north. I attempted to raise the pilot on 1XX.X, in case he maybe just had the frequency wrong, but this did not work to raise a response. My student and I exited the traffic pattern to the north to gain altitude. Then, re entered right traffic for [Runway] XX with a 45 degree entry to the downwind. We continued to make our radio calls for the traffic pattern. As we turned base for XX, I observed on my ADSB that Aircraft Z had made a 180 degree turn from his heading and was now headed directly for us, 300 feet high and descending. I took the controls and called a go around, extending the base. The aircraft was now at my altitude, close and lining up for the base to final for Runway XX. I had not heard any radio calls from the aircraft. We exited the ZZZ1 area and departed to another area until we could contact approach to get clearance back in to ZZZ for a landing. After the incident, I called the pilot of Aircraft Y to confirm what had happened. The pilot mentioned that they had landed at ZZZ1 and talked to a mechanic who witnessed the incident and talked to Aircraft Z after he had landed. According to the mechanic, the pilot of Aircraft Z said that they had a radio failure. It is unknown to me what transpired with the aircraft after that.
ASRS:1821139.s: The instructor and student in a Skyhawk encountered Aircraft Z twice while practicing landings at ZZZ1, forcing two go-arounds due to Z's conflicting path and lack of radio communication. The reporter later learned from another pilot that Aircraft Z's pilot claimed a radio failure, though no response was received during the incident.

ASRS:1821153.n: I was involved in a rapid decompression event of an aircraft. I was acting as pilot in command of a reposition flight. We were filed under an IFR flight plan. At the time of the event we were cruising at FL410 and on frequency with ZZZ Center. While in cruise flight, roughly 1:10 into the flight we started experiencing a loss of pressurization in the cabin. I made my First Officer aware of the decompression, immediately donning the oxygen masks and requesting a descent from ATC. The frequency was cluttered with radio chatter and I was having trouble transmitting to ATC that we needed an immediate descent due to the loss of pressurization. Due to the hazardous nature of our situation I began a descent without being able to communicate with ATC. My First Officer immediately input the emergency squawk code of 7700 into our transponder to relay to ATC that we had an emergency. ATC saw our descent and queried us 'Aircraft X verify level at FL410.' I replied with 'We need a descent now.' ATC then cleared us to FL240 where we began running checklists and were able to stabilize our cabin altitude.Once we had the situation under control we informed ATC that we were no longer [in need of priority handling] and that we had our cabin altitude stabilized. My copilot and I agreed that the situation was under control and that our cabin altitude was stabilized enough to where we could safely continue our flight to our destination at FL240. We flew the remainder of the flight and landed safely without other incident.
ASRS:1821153.s: The Pilot in Command of an IFR reposition flight experienced rapid decompression at FL410. Due to radio congestion preventing immediate clearance, the crew initiated an emergency descent, squawked 7700, and stabilized cabin altitude at FL240 before landing safely.

ASRS:1821159.n: I received flight following enroute to ZZZ. After ATC approved my frequency change and squawk code change to 1200. I switched to CTAF frequency and AWOS. I made radio calls that I was approaching airport from several miles away and would be doing a 45 degree entry for [Runway] XX, full stop. I then made my radio call for a 45 degree entry on the 45 degree entrance for Runway XX right traffic. Preceding traffic did an entry via base leg and landed on Runway XX without incident. I proceeded to enter via 45 degree entry and made my turn to downwind right traffic at about 1;006ft MSL. I continued to make radio calls that I was right turn downwind XX for ZZZ. I heard nor saw no other traffic in the pattern nor making radio calls for ZZZ. No traffic appeared on my ADS-B in Stratus 2I unit either. Abeam numbers of Runway XX, I reduced power and start about a 500/min descent and was scanning for traffic and scanning for proper distance for a turn to base. As I descended a silver high wing banner towing aircraft came into view coming from the opposite direction slightly above me on downwind (maybe 35 feet above me) and was transitioning through the traffic pattern of ZZZ towing a banner. There was no time for a radio call at the closing rate of the two aircraft and I abruptly made a descending right turn to avoid a head on collision. The banner tow plane did not turn initially but made a right turn after I called on the radio letting him know he flew through the downwind leg of in the opposite of the pattern at ZZZ and nearly collided with me. He then made a right turn and proceeded to fly west toward the bay to avoid the pattern. He said he had no idea what I was talking about and was cursing on the radio. I then realized that he never saw me. I continued to make my base leg radio call and final approach radio call and landed without any other problems. This collision was avoided.
ASRS:1821159.s: The pilot flying a general aviation aircraft on downwind at 1,006 feet MSL at ZZZ nearly collided head-on with a banner tow aircraft entering the pattern in the opposite direction. The pilot executed an abrupt descending right turn to avoid the collision after the banner pilot failed to see the aircraft or make radio calls.

ASRS:1821169.n: Planned flight for the day was to ZZZ1 (for fuel) then to ZZZ. Preflight planning conducted with assistance from ForeFlight mobile application. Departed Runway XX. Climb to 1500 MSL, 14 min cruise to ZZZ1 with landing. Landed at ZZZ1. The flight was conducted satisfactorily. The aircraft was then fueled as necessary.Secondary preflight planning was completed. Satisfactory takeoff and climb out to 7,500 MSL. Approximately 29 minutes, started to notice engine roughness with a significant drop in tachometer RPM. The Pilot in command (PIC) took over as sole manipulator of control and emergency checklist for engine failure in flight initiated. Looked for suitable landing area. Increased in engine RPM occurred and became within glide distance of ZZZ. Engine roughness and drop in RPM began again and ZZZ Tower contacted, advising of need for precautionary landing due to engine roughness. Decision was made to not [get priority handling]. Smooth and satisfactory landing made at ZZZ. After slowing and attempting to turn off Runway, the aircraft did not have any right turning authority. Airplane would only turn left in circle when power applied. Suspected right tire or brake malfunction. Contacted the Tower and asked for permission to shut down aircraft on runway to inspect aircraft.Aircraft was satisfactorily shut down on Runway XY with airport crew arriving for assistance. On post flight walk around, it was found that the right tire became flat, no other external damage grossly observed. Also found to have fluid leak within right pilot side inside firewall. Aircraft was towed to FBO for diagnostics of engine and repair of right tire. When asked if needed to report anything to Tower or FAA, the ZZZ airport crew stated nothing was needed. Furthermore, the Tower did not mention of any need to provide any post flight report during communications. No accident or serious incident occurred.There were a few factors found on post-flight that may have caused the problems:1. Engine Roughness: The engine was new with approximately 28 hours on the engine. Engine during break in period was using Aeroshell 100W. Furthermore, this flight was conducted with cruise altitude at 7,500 MSL. Miscommunication and ill-information about any special procedures regarding aircraft break in were not discussed between aircraft owner and PIC. PIC was told to use 100W oil from previous aircraft owner (box in back of aircraft). Furthermore, the aircraft owner did not provide engine overhaul information or procedures needed for aircraft. On mechanic review, it was found that the left magneto was rotated 17 degrees causing the engine to overheat, an oil line by the firewall was damaged causing a leak, cylinders were glazed, induction air leak, and some crankcase oil leak. Overall a combination of these factors is what probably lead to engine roughness. Post flight testing, the engine performed within specifications 2250 static RPM, 600FPM climb, 2350 dynamic RPM. Engine oil consumption has increased, likely due to glazed cylinders, and is being sent to Company1 for re-honing. Furthermore, the magnetos are being sent in to [Company] Magneto to be re-checked.2. Right Flat Tire: No noted gross evident issues on pre-flight inspection for tires, struts, fairing, or braking systems. Landings was smooth and satisfactory. Theory for tire damage could be due to stuck break after landing and prior to right turn out to taxiway, in conjunction with weak spot on tire and/or a foreign object on runway and/or other. Tire was satisfactorily repaired at ZZZ. Reviewing this scenario there are a few factors to consider. There needs to be improved communication between aircraft owner and operator (PIC), especially during critical times where specific procedures are needed (such as a new engine break in). The right tire flat is a chance occurrence, and I do not think that the flight could have been handled different to prevent. The pilot did all in power to safely shut down the aircraft and immediately check out airplane to prevent any further damage.I have had a clean pilot record, commercial license and CFI. I will use the lessons from this flight for myself and all future students for the purpose of discussing complete airplane maintenance with airplane owners (especially new airplanes), what to do when engine becomes rough, and procedures to follow with a flat tire.
ASRS:1821169.s: The pilot experienced engine roughness and a flat right tire during a flight to ZZZ, caused by a misaligned magneto, oil leaks, and a tire failure. The aircraft landed safely, but post-flight inspection revealed the engine required re-honing and the tire needed repair.

ASRS:1821177.n: While on right downwind at Traffic Pattern Altitude (1000 MSL) to land runway XX at ZZZ, I reduced power abeam the arrival end of runway XX and started my descent. I was momentarily looking at the airport runway as I reduced my power. I then returned my vision to straight ahead and spotted a high wing airplane towing a banner approximately 100 feet below me, coming directly at me from my 11-12 o'clock position. He was less than 1/4 mile away when I first spotted him. At that time my altitude was approximately 950 feet. I immediately added power and pulled up as he passed no more than 100 feet below me and no more than 100 feet to my left. After he passed under me, he turned out to the west and departed the area at the same altitude. I made a radio call to the aircraft telling him he nearly hit me but he did not respond. Prior to that time, I had made 5 radio calls announcing my position and intentions beginning 8 miles north of the airport.The banner tow plane flew right through the ZZZ traffic pattern, directly opposing downwind traffic on the right downwind and between 100 and 150 ft. of traffic pattern altitude. He should not have been flying through the traffic pattern and was not communicating with aircraft in the area on the CTAF. He was initially in my forward blind spot, just under my nose. I spotted him when I lowered my nose to start my descent for landing on the downwind leg. He was a high wing aircraft (fabric body, silver colored) and likely did not see me above and slightly to his left. The approaching banner tow aircraft was not spotted until he was less than 1/4 miles ahead. Contributing factors were:1. His position in my forward blind spot below the aircraft nose. 2. A second factor is that the banner towing aircraft was approaching head on and provided a small profile for both the aircraft and the banner.3. He was flying through an active traffic pattern with aircraft actively communicating on the CTAF.4. He was not communicating his position or intentions on the CTAF while operating in the airport traffic pattern5. He was flying a non-standard traffic pattern leg, i.e., opposed to downwind traffic.6. He was approaching from a position that was at first spotting, slightly outside the traffic pattern. Aircraft in the traffic pattern are dividing attention between the traffic pattern and the runway environment. My attention was diverted toward the runway for a few seconds just prior to the time the aircraft was first spotted.7. The banner towing pilot has a dangerous habit of flying through the traffic pattern at this airport as described in the additional incident below which occurred earlier on the same day. Additional Relevant Information:Earlier that day another pilot had a near miss with the same aircraft at the same location. He also had to take evasive action to avoid the aircraft. In his case, he was on right base for runway XX and the banner towing aircraft was just above his altitude.
ASRS:1821177.s: A pilot on right downwind at ZZZ airport executed an evasive climb to avoid a banner tow aircraft flying head-on through the traffic pattern at 100 feet below. The near miss occurred because the banner pilot was not communicating on CTAF, flew a non-standard opposing leg, and was initially obscured in the reporter's forward blind spot.

ASRS:1821187.n: While enroute operating IFR, deviating around buildups, we received an altitude alert from ATC. We immediately initiated corrective action and returned to our assigned altitude. At the time of the altitude alert we were off altitude by roughly 400 ft. While deviating around the buildups, we were experience moderate turbulence as well as continuous changes in updrafts and downdraft. I believe this was the cause of the deviation.
ASRS:1821187.s: The pilot reported an altitude deviation of approximately 400 feet while enroute IFR and deviating around weather buildups. Moderate turbulence and continuous updrafts and downdrafts caused the deviation, which was corrected immediately after an ATC alert.

ASRS:1821200.n: Aircraft X was issued a descent to 2500 feet but as soon as I said 2000, the pilot started to read back 2000. This caused the 500 (of the 2500) to be blocked and when I un-keyed, I just heard the call sign portion of the transmission. The aircraft descended to 2000 feet and asked for an altimeter setting and I noticed the aircraft below the 2500 minimum vectoring altitude (MVA) and assigned altitude. I issued low altitude alert and instructed them to climb to 2500 feet. I missed the read back. This all stemmed from the aircraft departing ZZZ with a known mechanical issue and low on fuel. They had diverted to ZZZ earlier (unknown to me) and was trying to reposition back to ZZZ1.They departed ZZZ1 minimum fuel and would not accept an approach at ZZZ1 that was consistent with the flow of traffic. I should have [requested priority handling] for the pilot immediately and handled it as one. The pilot put the FAA in a tough situation as I was trying to do my best to help the pilots who were in a bind, but I also missed many things I should have done.I did not ensure the aircraft had the weather and NOTAMs at ZZZ1, [request priority handling] for the aircraft, advise them of their position when vectoring them on to the localizer, allowed them to intercept the localizer inside the final approach fix. I did not catch the lack of read back when I issued 2500 MVA altitude and they over keyed me with a read back of 2000. Issue a brasher to the pilot. I need to make sure all the phraseology and regulations are followed on our side (ATC)However, Aircraft X's principle operations inspector needs to investigate if the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 was conducted legally and safely. It was very apparent the urgency to land immediately after taking off from ZZZ. This should not have happened. This caused me to make shortcuts and put the FAA at risk of liability as well as put the pilots at risk of missing something like landing on runway XX at ZZZ1, a closed runway. The pilots were wanting to land on runway XX at one point. Upon departure from ZZZ to ZZZ1, a short 5 minute or so flight, we were given a heading and an initial altitude of 3000 feet on initial departure. Given we were taking the plane in for maintenance, the plane had enough fuel to meet the minimum FAR requirements for an IFR flight. While setting up for the approach at hand, we were told by the controlling facility to descend and maintain 2,000 feet which was read back. A couple minutes went by as we were being vectored in for the approach and ATC gave us a low altitude alert followed by a command to 'descend and maintain 2,500 feet MSL'. Having already been cleared down to 2000 feet initially after we asked for lower, we read back the instruction for 2,500 feet followed by a 'we were initially cleared down to 2,000 feet MSL'.At that point, the controlling facility told us that they weren't going to debate over it and we instigated the climb to 2,500 feet. We only meant to reiterate the initial 2,000 foot altitude instruction for clarification purposes, not for argumentative purposes, as that was the initial instruction given to us after all. After landing, we received a phone call to contact the appropriate controlling facility to clarify the situation. We pulled the tapes from the appropriate controlling facility at the time of the incident and the tapes coincide with our initial hearing of '2,000 feet MSL;' not '2,500 feet MSL'. The altitude is clearly heard as 2,000 feet being the instruction given and 2000 feet being the instruction read back, not '2,500'. In order to keep a situation like this from reoccurring, an articulate tone should be adopted in order to hear and say the correct altitude assigned. Given that a weather system was rolling through as well, that added extra workloads on both us, the pilots, along with the controlling facility.
ASRS:1821200.s: An air traffic controller and pilots of Aircraft X experienced a descent conflict where the controller issued 2,500 feet but the pilot read back 2,000 feet due to overlapping transmissions. The aircraft descended below minimum vectoring altitude, prompting a low altitude alert and climb instruction, which the pilot attributed to a misheard clearance and high workload.

ASRS:1821201.n: Aircraft X was on a vector descending to 5,500 feet for the GPS approach. Aircraft X read the heading and altitude assignment correctly. Aircraft X was issued a base turn heading 060. After traffic passed below Aircraft X at 4,000 feet, I began to Precision Turn Altitude Clearance (PTAC) Aircraft X for GPS Approach. It was at the moment when I finished transmitting that I realized Aircraft Y was leveling at 5,000 feet. Immediately, the pilot read back the clearance. However it was incorrect due to the pilot stating 'maintain altitude until established in the localized... I immediately told the pilot to disregard the PTAC and to climb to 5,500 feet. I then told the pilot to 'check their altitude immediately' and that the MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) in the area was 5,400 feet. I received no response so I repeated the climbing instruction with an amendment to maintain 5,400 feet instead. I then asked the pilot to read back the altitude assignment. The pilot did not read back the numeric altitude. I then instructed Aircraft X to join the final approach course upon reaching 5,400 feet. I observed Aircraft X reach 5400 feet quickly and safely. Aircraft X was cleared for the RNAV/GPS Approach and landed without incident.I recommend having a quarterly conversation with the local flying community around BTV's airspace. There are a multitude of flying clubs and academies that can benefit from a conversation with BTV ATC. The format for these conversations could include in person tours, sit-downs, or e-mail correspondence. Events like this can be avoided, in my opinion, by explaining the importance of understanding altitude assignments, approach information for our lengthy, step-down, ILS and RNAV/GPS Approaches and expectations. Most of the flying community around BTV flies in and out of uncontrolled airports."
ASRS:1821201.s: An air traffic controller issued a PTAC to Aircraft X descending for a GPS approach but realized Aircraft Y was leveling at 5,000 feet. The controller immediately cancelled the clearance and instructed Aircraft X to climb to 5,400 feet, which the pilot achieved safely before landing without incident.

ASRS:1821230.n: RNO was using Runway 16L. Neither Pilot had used this runway during previous flights. It was noticed that there are arresting cables depicted on Runway 16L on the Jeppesen diagram (page 10-9). Pilot Monitoring called RNO Tower directly during the arrival to ask about the cables and give time for the crew to make a plan. RNO Tower stated that there are not any cables installed on Runway 16L. Arrival was continued without issue.While taxiing to the gate, the Controller told the crew that Airfield Operations was asked about the cables and responded that cables had not been installed in a long time. The incorrect depiction on the Airfield Diagram created an additional distraction to the crew during the arrival.
ASRS:1821230.s: The crew of an arriving aircraft at RNO contacted Tower regarding arresting cables depicted on the Jeppesen diagram for Runway 16L. Tower and Airfield Operations confirmed no cables were installed, but the incorrect chart depiction caused an unnecessary distraction during the arrival.

ASRS:1821266.n: Currently the ALB VORTAC is out of service, and there is a FDC NOTAM that requires its use for a Missed Approach Procedure because the CAM is also out of service. While our aircraft is equipped with RNAV capabilities, the clearance limit in the current NOTAM MAP is not valid using normally equipped aircraft through July XXth.
ASRS:1821266.s: The pilot reported that the ALB VORTAC and CAM are out of service, requiring VORTAC use for the Missed Approach Procedure. Although the aircraft has RNAV capabilities, the NOTAM clearance limit remains invalid for normally equipped aircraft until July XXth.

ASRS:1821271.n: Climbing out, Autopilot/Flight Director would indicate an overspeed and the plane would pitch up violently. Disconnected Autopilot and reestablish. 5 minutes later same thing. Happened 50-60 times during flight. Aircraft would not capture NAV. Flight Level Change (FLCH) would not engage. Could only fly in Heading (HDG) mode and Flight Path Angle (FPA). FADEC never shifted from TO mode with the Automatic Takeoff Thrust Control System (ATTCS) armed. Checked Emergency Procedure Checklist (EPC) but could not find a checklist that would pertain to us. Decided to return to ZZZ. At decision time it indicated we would be 3000 lbs over landing weight so we initiated procedures to minimize overweight landing and returned to ZZZ. Landed approximately 750lbs over weight. Aircraft landed fine and there were no additional issues. Upon return I wrote the airplane up. Priority handling was not requested as the aircraft was still controllable with no Autopilot or Flight Director.
ASRS:1821271.s: The pilot experienced repeated autopilot overspeed warnings and violent pitch-ups during climb and cruise, preventing NAV and FLCH engagement while FADEC remained in TO mode. The crew returned to ZZZ for an overweight landing of 750 lbs after determining the aircraft was controllable without autopilot or flight director.

ASRS:1821280.n: After 30 minutes of flight cruising at FL330 right engine began to compressor stall with multiple thumps and erratic engine indications. Right throttle was brought to idle and we ask for a lower altitude. All engine indications at idle were normal. Continued the remainder of the flight with right throttle at idle until beginning the approach. Elected to divert to ZZZ. Once on the approach, advanced right throttle and all indications were normal through the approach and landing.There were no casual factors. Followed SOP.This was a normal flight with no outside factors involved. Flight from ZZZ2 to ZZZ3 was normal to FL 330 about 15min into cruise flight compressor stalls on right engine with 4 bangs. We reduced the throttle to idle and the ECAM went away. We kept the throttle at idle and descend to FL240 and diverted to ZZZ which was approximately 100 miles away and landed safely.[Caused by] Engine compressor stall[This was] a maintenance issue alone.
ASRS:1821280.s: During cruise at FL330, the right engine compressor stalled, prompting a throttle reduction to idle, descent to FL240, and diversion to ZZZ. The crew attributed the incident solely to a maintenance issue, landing safely after normal engine indications returned on approach.

ASRS:1821291.n: Cleared DARAN1A into MEX, during cruise check of points noted altitude constraint at DARAN was different in the bow than on the chart. We initially had the DARAN2B loaded. Chart or database not accurate. NOTAM or new database update required.
ASRS:1821291.s: The flight crew, while cruising in a MEX arrival, discovered an altitude constraint discrepancy at DARAN between the FMS and the chart. The pilot attributed the error to an inaccurate chart or database, recommending a NOTAM or database update.

ASRS:1821337.n: I have noticed that there are a number of taxiway signs at SeaTac airport that have taxiway identifiers on only one side of the sign. For example when taxiing northbound on [Runway] 34C the right turn for Taxiway M is not shown. However, when taxiing southbound on 16C Taxiway M is depicted on the taxiway sign.
