There are numerous signs that exist, with information on only one side, or possibly a sign needs to be installed for some of these turnouts. This is becoming more noticeable as ATC is frequently parking aircraft on taxiways holding short of 16L/34R when their gates are occupied. This can be especially problematic to see a taxiway that is a reverse high speed in the dark and in the rain. Have the Port of Seattle install taxiway signage that is appropriate for each taxiway regardless of the direction of travel so taxiways are easily identified regardless of direction of travel.
ASRS:1821337.s: A pilot reported that taxiway signs at SeaTac airport display identifiers on only one side, making turnouts like Taxiway M invisible when taxiing northbound on Runway 34C. The pilot attributed this visibility issue to the sign orientation and requested double-sided signage to improve safety during night and rain operations.

ASRS:1821354.n: During an 18-hour duty day with multiple discrepancies, write-ups, MEL's, a rejected takeoff, a turnback to the gate, and other issues, we departed Runway XXL at ZZZ for the ZZZZZ RNAV departure. We had just finished 5 hours on the ground dealing with a hydraulic 3 elevator shutoff valve and inoperative 3-2 non-reversible motor pump, and had briefed the possibility of an associated flight control problem on departure. During the initial climb, we were instructed to maintain 250 kts and acknowledged. Our speed did not require a high-speed climb. Repeatedly during this event (prior to slat retraction, and intermittently all the way to final cruise altitude), we got am amber-boxed engine 1 compressor vibration indication, averaging 4.5 units of vibration. This required retarding power on engine 1 (up to one knob-width, and up to 7-10% N1 reduction), to bring the vibration out of the amber range. When reaching 3,000 feet and just beyond ZZZZZ1 on the ZZZZZ, we began the clean-up process on schedule, and upon slat retraction, the airplane rolled left. I countered with considerable right aileron. The strong rolling moment occurred coincident with slat retraction. Shortly after, we got a master caution and two level 1 EAD messages (SEL LSAS LOB OFF, SEL LSAS RIB OFF), for which I called for the [Relief Pilot] and FO (First Officer) to address and confirm before selecting off. As that occurred, we got a caution light with a lateral fuel imbalance (LAT FUEL UNBAL), which occurred three more times (four total), along with a 2,000 kg drop in fuel quantity (repeat write-up). While focused on the control issue, I allowed airspeed to increase briefly above the 250 kts limit, estimated to be 270 kts, before decreasing speed again to maintain 250 kts to 10,000 feet ATC did not mention the overspeed, but the [Relief Pilot] did call 'airspeed.' The ZZZZZ departure includes a restriction to remain below 3,000 until ZZZZZ1, then a climb to 15,000 or above, by ZZZZZ. My priority was addressing the control issue, but adjusted pitch per the flight director to return to 250 kts. No further variations from the speed schedule occurred during the remainder of the climb, or flight. Additional distractions occurring in series (except the engine vibration indication, which occurred intermittently throughout the event), one after the other, did not cause the airspeed excursion, but certainly worked to divert attention, and increase cockpit workload.I became aware of the amber boxed vibration indication about the time we entered the 1100 ft. ceiling, departing ZZZ. I became aware of the rolling moment immediately upon slat retraction, and the airspeed excursion upon the 'airspeed' call by the [Relief Pilot]. I did note the pitch attitude below that commanded by the flight director, and noted speed increasing, but the intent was to increase airspeed through slat retract speed to 250, and I focused on the immediate concern, the rolling moment. I did not notice the speed exceed 250 until the [Relief Pilot] brought it to the crew attention with the 'airspeed' call. At that time, I observed approximately 270 on the airspeed indication, and increased pitch to the flight director pitch bar to reduce speed. The FO was occupied retracting slats, and performing the follow-up flow associated with my call, 'slats retract, after takeoff checklist.' Aside from being distracted by the rolling moment, the illumination of the amber compressor vibration indication on engine 1, subsequent LSAS failure, and fuel imbalance were contributing errors to detection, and detection was voiced by the [Relief Pilot]. I became aware of the LSAS issue, and the lateral fuel imbalance issues, with illumination of the master caution light. The LSAS issue caused loss of autopilot 2. I delayed autopilot engagement until the series of issues were addressed, given that they included flight control and subsequent autopilot engagement problems. Once those were addressed and we were outside the busier airspace, the enroute climb and remainder of the flight until descent, were largely uneventful, except for continued monitoring and adjusting of engine 1 throttle position to prevent high compressor vibration. The period of time between detection of the event and the filing of this report is accounted by the end of a long duty day, the necessity of filing another report on the previous leg rejected takeoff in ZZZ1, and then flying home.We had briefed the possibility of a flight control problem, given the return to the gate for the system 3 Hydraulic elevator shutoff valve, and associated 3-2 non-reversible motor pump. The fix on the ramp had been to add another two gallons of fluid to system three, with the explanation that 'maybe the gauge is just reading high.' I did not find that explanation satisfactory, but following an engine run in which the problem did not reoccur, maintenance was satisfied, the write-up was signed off, and we departed. About the time we entered the cloud layer, the amber-boxed engine 1 compressor vibration alert illuminated, and power was reduced on engine 1 slightly (up to one knob width) to reduce the vibration indication. This indication came and went, as we climbed, necessitating further slight reductions in power. The flight control problem which occurred after departure (strong left rolling moment, coincident with slat retraction) did not match the potential problem (possible elevator shutoff valve actuation and NRMP malfunction), but did merit attention, during which time I let the airspeed slip. I focused on leveling the wings and reduced angle of attack. I should have maintained pitch with the flight director, but divided the task of roll and pitch to prioritize directional control, while addressing the uncommanded rolling moment. Additional subsequent illumination of the master caution with the LSAS failure, and the lateral fuel imbalance level 2 warning and master caution illumination, were peripheral distractions, as was the engine vibration issue. I was hand flying at the time, and believe it was better to be hand-flying with the potential to feel a problem, than have it masked by the autopilot. Had the autopilot been flying, the speed excursion would likely not have occurred, but we may not have seen or felt the rolling moment as much, if at all. I did feel a shift in the controls when the LSAS was selected off, but couldn't say afterward exactly what I'd felt. In retrospect, the best course would have been to focus on the flight director while addressing the roll. The natural tendency when experiencing that event (rolling moment), for me, was to decrease angle of attack slightly, which I did, which resulted in the excess speed as we accelerated while cleaning up. The rolling moment was caused, I am certain, by asymmetric slat retraction, the degree of asymmetry I couldn't say, but it was significant in feel and the amount of aileron deflection needed to counter the roll. There was no buffet. It was significant enough that on arrival in the ZZZ2 area, we briefed the possibility of the same event when extending slats, and I hand flew the descent and arrival, configuring slats early. A rolling moment did occur, but not to the same degree as departing ZZZ. (We also experienced a strong rolling motion that resulted in heading change, with autopilot engaged, when deploying speed brakes, and observed speed brake asymmetry on the configuration synoptic page, and determined not to use speed brakes further on the subsequent ZZZ2 arrival). These aircraft discrepancies, while important, should not have detracted from the basic task of flying the airplane, or maintaining the assigned/required 250 kts. on departure from ZZZ. Additionally, the subsequent illumination of the master caution light several times with LSAS failure and lateral fuel imbalance issues served as peripheral distractions. The tendency for engine 1 compressor vibration to show high with amber-boxed indication, repeatedly, and to require the engine power to be retarded repeatedly, was also a distraction. Retarding power on the no. 1 engine further caused a slight yawing motion, and subsequent potential rolling moment. Flying all night and then a five hours of trouble shooting on the ramp in a hot airplane didn't help, prior to this takeoff.My reaction to the high compressor vibration indication on engine 1 was to retard the No. 1 throttle slightly, the problem was known and a recurring one which had become a repeat write-up. My reaction to the 'airspeed' call was to note the speed and increase pitch to the flight director pitch bar, after observing airspeed in excess of 250 kts. I followed the flight director command while re-acquiring and holding 250 kts, and flying the departure. My reaction to the subsequent master caution illumination was to direct the First Officer and [Relief Pilot] to work together, specifically on the LSAS issue, because with one FCC affected, I wanted confirmation on selecting the correct switches off. The lateral fuel level 2 warning was familiar, as it keeps happening and keeps being written up on this airplane. On arrival, I wrote it up again. The engine vibration was a repeat write-up that was squawked multiple times, and was subsequently written up again on arrival in ZZZ2. On arrival in ZZZ2, the [Relief Pilot] asked if I thought we should file an report, and I advised that yes, I thought it prudent. I advised the crew to file what they saw, individually. After that, I was occupied discussing multiple discrepancies and write-ups with Maintenance, and with the incoming crew as they arrived. It was a very long night and day, and a full duty day. We had a rejected takeoff, ATC directed, at ZZZ1 on the first leg, and I had to write a report for that, after arriving at the hotel. I made that report, and the next day flew home, where I slept for an extended period. This report is submitted outside the 24-hour window, when I had rested adequately to be awake to write it. I did write up the flight control issues, to be addressed by Company Maintenance Personnel.My actions were my own, and my responsibility. I was the Pilot Flying, and the Captain, and I was hand flying, and regardless of distractions, should not have allowed the airspeed excursion to occur. That said, we should not be seeing so many discrepancies and issues, especially on one flight (let alone one phase of flight simultaneously or subsequently in close succession, and especially not items which have been written up multiple times). These issues ranged from multiple flight control issues to fuel system indications and issues, engine vibration, and even a TCAS fail during the initial climb. The subsequent issues that occurred on the flight including multiple items that were repeat write ups, including a level 2 fuel lateral fuel imbalance several times during the departure. The LSAS failure is also a repeat write-up. I do not include these as excuses for failing to maintain the airspeed at 250 kts, as that was my responsibility, but these are certainly things which do not need to be happening on every flight, as a regular part of flight operations, and this can be fixed. So far as preventing this specific event from occurring again, my counsel is to point my finger at myself and what I would say to anyone else: 'fly the damn airplane.' I need look no farther than myself as the reason for failing to maintain 250 kts as cleared, and as required by the regulation, and as the captain, the buck stops with me. We can prevent it, in my cockpit, by my not allowing it to occur again. The question will arise why the autopilot was not engaged earlier in the series of events. I had briefed a hand-flown departure. The engine vibration, while a distraction, did not rise to the level of needing automated intervention, and was familiar, having occurred previously and been a repeat write-up. The rolling moment was not something I wanted masked by engaging the autopilot; After getting handed off to approach ATC instructed us to limit our speed to 250 kts. However because of multiple issues going on and the flight deck our speed had increased to 300 kts. Once I called airspeed the Captain and then proceeded to reduce the speed to 250.Use auto pilot in airspace in which is busy and cockpit work load is heavy.Have a proper scan and use auto pilot when workload is heavy.
ASRS:1821354.s: During departure from ZZZ, the crew experienced an uncommanded left roll upon slat retraction, attributed to asymmetric slat retraction, alongside engine vibration and LSAS failures. These distractions caused the pilot to briefly exceed the 250 kts speed limit to 270 kts while prioritizing directional control.

ASRS:1821370.n: About 55 minutes into flight and about to finalize the beverage [and] snack service [myself] and the Flight Attendant C discovered a strong smell of electrical burning fumes in the cabin. I immediately went to aft galley to conduct a thorough inspection of all compartments, coffee makers, circuits, closets and under toilet sink. There was no visible fire but there was a faint white haze of smoke in cabin. I proceeded to inform the pilots of our situation that we had also pulled the circuit breakers and he pulled the power to both galleys. At XA18 hours we initiated a rapid descent into ZZZ and landed 17 minutes later XA35 hours.Aircraft was met by [Fire Department] and followed us to the gate for safety measures in case our landing gear or brakes became hot due to overweight landing.Once customers deplaned the Maintenance Technician inspected aircraft and later he stated the re circulation fan under the floor board had charred. [Name] at the [Company Communications System] called me for details of what had occurred and stated we would Dead Head in the morning. Following morning was a an XK30 report with under 8 hours of rest and made to work flight back to ZZZ1.
ASRS:1821370.s: Flight attendants detected electrical burning fumes and smoke during beverage service, prompting a rapid descent and overweight landing. Maintenance later identified a charred recirculation fan under the floorboard as the cause.

ASRS:1821446.n: I went to the ZZZ area to pick up a Super Viking that a customer wanted me to fly/train with him to ZZZ1. The aircraft was coming out from an annual inspection and I inspected it as an airplane out of serious maintenance. I noticed some play in the prop blades but it was consistent on all blades, and coming out of inspection, I assumed that it was the way the prop was.When we landed in ZZZ, I had the prop inspected by a mechanic who found the prop 'questionable' and recommended not to fly the aircraft. Prop was dismounted and sent to a prop shop which found the prop non airworthy. I had never seen a broken prop and I pride myself to inspect and teach to inspect CS props very carefully. Maybe we should have more documentation about props.
ASRS:1821446.s: A pilot inspecting a Super Viking after annual maintenance noticed propeller blade play but assumed it was normal. A mechanic later deemed the propeller questionable, and a prop shop confirmed it was non-airworthy, grounding the aircraft.

ASRS:1821458.n: While returning to ZZZ from the south after an instructional lesson, we made a radio call approximately 10 miles out reporting our intentions, around the same time I heard a non flight school aircraft report they were departing but the call was very weak and had a lot of interference with it (I believe this to be the conflicting aircraft but did not hear any type/callsign). We continued to report our position as we got closer to the airport and reported our intention of entering a 45 to downwind for Runway XX at ZZZ and while we entered and were on the 45 to downwind. While on around 3 NM I noticed an ADS-B target departing Runway XX and was climbing so I tried to look for them in case they were remaining in the pattern. After about 5-8 seconds of looking and not seeing them I returned my focus to ahead of the aircraft, it was at that time that a small high wing aircraft (appeared to be a piper cub), was at our 12 o'clock and level at the same altitude heading straight towards us. I immediately took the controls from the student (who was flying at the time) and entered a rapid descent and began banking the aircraft to the right. Well after we began to maneuver away from the aircraft I noticed them start to climb and turn (to their right). It appeared that the other aircraft did not have us in sight until our maneuver.I did not hear any radio calls from the other aircraft at any point before (except possibly as mentioned above) nor after the event.ZZZ is in need of a Control Tower, it is an unsafe airport with the type of flight operations, how much activity there is. There seems to be close calls for various types of events nearly every day.
ASRS:1821458.s: A flight instructor and student in a training aircraft experienced a mid-air conflict with a departing Piper Cub while entering the downwind leg at uncontrolled airport ZZZ. The instructor took control and executed an evasive descent after the other aircraft, which had not been seen or heard on radio, appeared head-on at the same altitude.

ASRS:1821478.n: I was doing student training in the vicinity of ZZZ at FL270. The clouds were building in the area and climbing up through our flight level in a relatively short amount of time. The ATCAA (ATC-assigned Airspace) was just south of our position and went hot while we in the area. Center restricted our working airspace clearance to remain north of the ZZZ airport and we accepted. The weather and high clouds were just a few miles north of ZZZ and started to severely limit our maneuvering airspace and we were getting boxed in between staying out of the weather and complying with the airspace clearance. During crew swap, I briefed the incoming pilot about the weather/high clouds and the requirements to stay north of the ATCAA. I also advised him that it was probably time to depart the area as it was becoming unworkable due to the building weather. I showed him that my student was currently on a heading that was pointing in the direction of the weather (approximately 040 heading) and he would need to turn south before the aircraft entered the cloud and possibly picked up ice. I did not specify, but I intended for the turn to be made to the right where there was still clear air. It also should have been a manual bank heading to steepen the bank angle enough to avoid flying into the ATCAA. I assumed he understood what I wanted him to do, but I did not get any communication from him that he was confused about my instructions. He said he's got it and then proceeded with the crew swap and dismissed my student from the flight controls. After the incoming pilot sat down, he commanded a left turn with the autopilot (14 degrees of bank) and turned right into the clouds. The aircraft began picking up icing and he [contacted] Center to avoid flying into more weather/icing. Upon my student exiting the ground control station, I began talk to him about his handover briefing and I did not notice the aircraft turning left until it was already in the weather. I debriefed with the incoming pilot later and he told me at the time of the crew swap, he had no idea where the clear air was and therefore was forced to exit the area immediately which resulted in him eventually [contacting] Center in order to get clear of the weather.
ASRS:1821478.s: During student training at FL270 near ZZZ, an incoming pilot turned left into clouds and icing after a crew swap, contrary to the instructor's intended right turn. The incident resulted from the pilot's lack of situational awareness regarding clear air, forcing an immediate departure and contact with Center to avoid further weather.

ASRS:1821480.n: I was working Ground Control 1 when Aircraft X notified me that an airlines [ground vehicle] came into contact with their right scimitar winglet. The incident happened while Aircraft X was taxiing eastbound on taxiway 1 just east of taxiway 5. I reached out to city operations, who typically monitor the frequency. I was not able to reach city operations, and neither was the Controller in Charge. I noticed Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting (ARFF) vehicles in the area so I reached out on the emergency frequency and got hold of ARFF-2 and send them to investigate. A few minutes later, city operations came on frequency and I advised them what happened. While moving traffic around the incident, I noticed that planes were not departing. I asked Traffic Management Unit (TMU) about it, as they had not informed me of their intentions. He said that departures were stopped. I asked why had I not been informed and he stated 'you should have known.'It seems like there are more issues with [ground vehicle] than there should be. A more rigorous training program may be in order.Also, TMU needs to be more active in the communication of their positions and advise everybody of their intentions.
ASRS:1821480.s: Ground Control 1 reported that an airline ground vehicle struck Aircraft X's right scimitar winglet while taxiing eastbound on taxiway 1. The controller contacted ARFF-2 after failing to reach city operations, while noting communication failures with the Traffic Management Unit regarding the subsequent departure stoppage.

ASRS:1821482.n: I was assigned D-side to Sector 02/17 after a 40 minute break from position. By the time I sat down on position the R side was already too busy to give me a briefing and we already needed a tracker which we did not receive for 30 minutes. The Warning Areas were active up to FL 500 with an aircraft doing air work at FL450. There was a line of extreme precipitation from ORL to the warning areas which did not allow any northbound traffic. The northbound traffic was deviating from the adjacent sector to the west (Sector 65/68) and eventually they started handing them off to us on vectors climbing into the weather while we had opposite traffic southbound head on. Meanwhile, while this was happening ZJX KEYSTONE and ST AUG Sector (J58/J76) told us that they could not take the aircraft northbound if they were going to enter the warning areas. I started pointing the aircraft out to the military so ZJX could take them and they still refused and had us vector the aircraft out in an attempt to not violate their airspace. Meanwhile I was told by my CIC (Controller in Charge) to tell ZJX that we are unable to take any more aircraft and that they need to hold their aircraft. I was also told to tell the adjacent sectors (J58/J76) that we were unable any more point outs or handoffs from them due to saturation and unsafe operation. Also because of tropical storm X the Atlantic routes were closed essentially cutting us off from north bound traffic. We had no way to take aircraft northbound because the Atlantic routes were closed, the military had airspace up to FL500 and there was a line of extreme precipitation stretching across the northwest side of the sector. We were trying to point aircraft out to the military and ZJX. Unfortunately between the tracker/CIC/and an additional tracker, I was being given multiple commands from all around and it was impossible to know where the exact airspace violations occurred. I know there were a few from sector 65/68 and I am sure there were a few into ZJX and the military as well. This was a result of poor planning with aircraft being launched from the ground with routes filed into and lack of communication between controllers in adjacent airspace and facilities which led to the result of multiple sectors putting aircraft into one sector with no available altitudes and no airspace.Recommendation: REOPEN UP THE PIT AT ZMA!!!!! This would allow Traffic Management Unit to reroute aircraft before they even took off from the airport on good filed routing away from Weather/Military airspace/ and closed routing.
ASRS:1821482.s: An air traffic controller in Sector 02/17 reported multiple airspace violations during saturation caused by extreme precipitation, active military warning areas, and closed Atlantic routes. The controller attributed the unsafe conditions to poor flight planning, lack of inter-facility communication, and conflicting commands that prevented safe traffic management.

ASRS:1821487.n: Sector 32 was placed in a highly dangerous and unsafe situation. I was training a D-side and had to jump in and take over, the sector was overloaded with traffic and extremely complex and warranted a CPC, [Certified Professional Controller] D-side and an L-side. There was moderate to extreme precipitation in Bay 2 and TMU [Traffic Management Unit] decided to route their traffic through our sector with little to no restrictions. We were working three flows of PHL arrivals with no in trail spacing. One flow from Bay 6, one from ZTL, and one from sector 36. Blending these three flows in to one with aircraft deviating was proving to be very difficult and complex. We were also working two flows of DCA's and BWI's with no restrictions. We were told that there would only be 2 or 3, but we ended up being overloaded. We had coordinated that aircraft to enter the sector level at FL250 and in trail, but we were getting multiple flows with aircraft descending from high altitudes. During this time we were also dealing with a massive departure push, moderate chop/turbulence and frequency congestion.There were 45+ aircraft in the EDST [En Route Decision Support Tool], and the sector was alerted red and overloaded;however we were receiving no help from TMU. At one point an L-side had to plug in because the sector was getting out of hand and there were so many aircraft that it was difficult to see where aircraft were going. This was compounded by the fact that the other sectors in bay 5 were also overloaded. There needs to be better planning, and restrictions put in place to avoid overloading sectors. The strategy of pumping all traffic through a single sector/point is dangerous.
ASRS:1821487.s: An air traffic controller training a D-side trainee reported that Sector 32 became dangerously overloaded with 45+ aircraft due to TMU routing multiple unrestricted arrival flows through the sector without adequate spacing or restrictions. The situation required an additional L-side controller to intervene as the sector turned red, highlighting the risks of pumping all traffic through a single point without proper planning.

ASRS:1821532.n: On the RNAV Stadium Visual to runway 29 we were vectored behind an Airbus 321 on the ILS to 22R. We joined the visual at GIMEE with the airport and the [A321] in sight. We had been cleared to land prior to crossing GIMEE. Tower reported winds calm, ATIS had winds 200/6. Prior to SLIMR we were configured and slowing to approach speed. At approximately 1,500 ft AGL I called for the landing check and called to the FO that [the A321] appeared to be crossing the numbers and spacing looked good. Continued in LVAV/VNAV till the autopilot rolled us out on final at about 1,000 ft AGL. At this point PAPI showed slightly high and corrected to visual glide path. A rapid right roll was encountered just prior to touchdown causing contact of the right main. This slowed the roll but aircraft was still rolling right. Immediate left aileron was applied along with deployment of the auto speed brakes quickly caused the left main to touch down. Roll out was normal from this point. Wing drop was so rapid that I thought the right gear leg had collapsed. The event occurred so quickly that there was not even time to consider a go-around. The application of power and lifting off again would likely only have exacerbated this situation placing us at a bank angle at low speed with an at the time unknown problem. During debrief we determined that the event occurred just prior to the intersection with Runway 22R and was likely a wake turbulence event. An ACARS generated report showed a max bank angle of 6.9 degrees with a predicted wing tip strike at a bank angle of 7.5 degrees. The FO inspected the aircraft for possible damage, none was found. The event was reported to Tower, but they did not seem concerned. I contacted Clearance Delivery to get more information on the preceding aircraft. CD took more interest and sounded like it would be reported.
ASRS:1821532.s: The flight crew experienced a rapid right roll and right main gear contact during the final approach of an RNAV Stadium Visual to Runway 29, likely caused by wake turbulence from a preceding Airbus A321. No damage was found after the aircraft was stabilized, and the event was reported to Tower and Clearance Delivery.

ASRS:1821548.n: During preflight in 44C temperature day cargo smoke detectors were acting erratic and not testing in various configurations of the panel. Maintenance thought it might be heat related and ducted conditioned air into forward bin. The forward bin abnormalities stopped ;either by cooling the bin or exercising the detectors switches. The aft bin wasn't cooled and the mix meld the aft cargo smoke detector system. Plane is signed off and we push back. With 2 engines running and the APU on for a bleeds off takeoff, we started to taxi out to runway X Left full length. Bleeds were configured eng1 off, APU on, eng2 on. Isolation valve closed and packs on. About 4 minutes after engine start near [intersection] the aft FA calls the flight deck. FO answers call and I stop the plane. I turn on service interphone switch to hear an FA saying electrical/ burning plastic smell in the aft galley. I grab phone and ask where she is smelling it from, initially she doesn't know and says it is faint but getting stronger. I asked her to pull all of the circuit breakers in the galley. I decided to return to the gate and we advised ATC. During taxi back we started smoke;fire;fumes checklist. The utilities/ife were switched off transfer bus off recirculating fans off WiFi off. The FA calls back and says it is coming out of the gasper vents in the galley and it was getting stronger after I turned off the recirculating fans. We were waiting for parking crew at this point and in 44c temps I was trying to keep as much cool air as possible. Eng bleeds were both turned off. APU bleed on , left pack high , iso closed. We could not smell anything in the front, so I figured it wasn't from the left pack or APU. At the gate, ground air was hooked up and the second the jetway was up and door opened I instructed via the pa for all passengers to grab their belongings and exit the plane. After the passengers deplaned, I went to the back and could smell the residual coming from the gasper. It was a melting plastic smell. It faded, to my dismay, before the maintenance technician got to us. They turned on all systems, and even performed an engine run to find the cause. As they were unable to duplicate the smell, they signed it off as such. By this time the fuel was up to 54C and we were unable to operate that flight due to time. We were put on another flight and a separate crew operated on a different plane.
ASRS:1821548.s: The flight crew aborted a takeoff due to a melting plastic smell in the aft galley, likely originating from the gasper vents. Maintenance could not duplicate the issue despite high fuel temperatures, leading to a flight cancellation and crew reassignment.

ASRS:1821599.n: I was operating as First Officer and pilot flying on our morning flight out of ZZZ. As soon as the gear came off the ground we heard a ding and received two EICAS messages, LG AIR/GND FAIL and ENG1-2 REV DISAGRE". In the climb out the captain ran the QRH and advised dispatch through ACARS of the situation and that we would continue to our destination which not only had the longest runway but also maintenance. We [requested priority handling] with ZZZ1 Center and asked them to advise ZZZ2 that we would need the center runway for our landing. ATC was very helpful. Upon arrival the trucks were standing by just in case. The flight was uneventful and was conducted normally. The [priority handling request] was precautionary just in case there was an issue. We executed a normal landing. As soon as we got the message we knew that there was an issue and that we would need to [request priority handling] at our destination. As soon as we received the messages we were unsure of the cause but attributed it to possibly having something to do with the fact that the plane had been in short term storage.We reacted appropriately by flying the plane first and then once at a safe altitude ran the QRH and worked as a team to troubleshoot the problem. As mentioned above we decided the best course of action and most conservative approach was to [request priority handling] and continue to our destination which was most suited for this type of situation."
ASRS:1821599.s: The First Officer reported that shortly after takeoff, the aircraft received LG AIR/GND FAIL and ENG1-2 REV DISAGREE EICAS messages, possibly due to short-term storage. The crew requested priority handling, continued to a destination with maintenance, and executed a normal landing with emergency trucks standing by.

ASRS:1821604.n: I elected to perform a high speed aborted takeoff due to pop up severe weather conditions. Prior to departure, the weather was VFR and clear. Small thunderstorms were developing around the area north of the airport, but nothing was seen while taxiing to the runway. Both crew members engaged weather radar with an upward tilt, with nothing indicating the possibility of weather impacting departure. ATC issued a takeoff clearance for runway XX and advised us of a small cell of extreme precipitation north of the airport, and said it didn't appear to be a factor. We were lined up on Runway XX, facing south, and could not see any adverse weather around us. After initiating the takeoff roll, at around 100 knots, we encountered immediate extreme precipitation and wind forces. Visibility was reduced to 0 (I could not even see the nose of the aircraft). Simultaneously, ATC advised of 40-60 knot windshear over the runways and of a micro burst. Due to being unable to see out of the windshield and feeling the wind forces coupled with the windshear and micro burst warning, I elected to abort the takeoff. I estimate that the abort was initiated at 115 knots accounting for the reactionary delay of retarding the thrust levers. The flight attendant verified no one was injured. Aborted takeoff procedures were followed, and after a follow up with maintenance, dispatch, we were able to depart normally after the cell had passed.The conditions were not present at the time of takeoff, and no one (flight crew nor ATC) had a way to predict such a rapid, immediate change. We used wet takeoff numbers as a precaution since there were storms in the forecast while at the gate. I believe all parties involved functioned proficiently. We were clear to take off runway XX in ZZZ. Weather was clear, and winds calm. A little bit of rain on the East side of the airport while our takeoff roll at 90 knots, Captain (CA) and the First Officer (FO) lost sight of the runway due to extreme precipitation, and simultaneously the Tower Controller came on line and reported a Wind Shear alert on all runways, and a gain and loss of 25-30 knots. Winds went up to 50 knots. Captain decided to abort the takeoff. We initiated the abort at 117 knots. Our V speeds were as follows: V1: 129, Vr: 131, V2: 136. We stopped on the runway safely, made sure everyone in the back was all right, passengers and Flight Attendants. Tower asked us to exit the runway at the next available taxiway to our right, and stated that he did not have visual on us. We exited the runway on taxiway D, and did the after landing checklist. Tower then asked us to taxi to the run up pad of runway XX. Once at the pad, the CA contacted dispatch, talked to maintenance control and operations. We received our amendment, and we were cleared to takeoff again. The rest of the flight was uneventful.
ASRS:1821604.s: Flight crew aborted takeoff on Runway XX at 115–117 knots due to sudden extreme precipitation, zero visibility, and ATC-reported windshear and microburst. The aircraft stopped safely with no injuries, and the flight departed normally after the weather cell passed.

ASRS:1821612.n: En route from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 we were directed by the physician on call to divert to ZZZ which we had just passed at FL350. The Captain gave me controls of the aircraft and radios and began the fix strategy. We were given a heading direct to ZZZ and began a descent to the airport. We began the approach on a visual right downwind as there was a cell to the north and west of the airport we wanted to avoid. Selected speed was chosen as we slowed down, however, when managed speed was selected the aircraft accelerated because I had not activated the approach. We captured the error, however, these few seconds caused us to be high and fast. Given the already high-altitude airport and compressed diversion time for the medical issue, we elected to do a visual left 360 and rejoin final. We had selected the final approach fix altitude, however, when we did our left 360 turn it took us away from the airport. The Tower Controller alerted us that he had an altitude alert and we climbed back to the 7,200 feet altitude for the fix we were now joining the ILS. We continued the approach without further issue.Cause - 1. Compressed, high pressure with the medical emergency of passenger with 60/40 blood pressure.2. Out of sequence normal approach and landing with the diversion that greatly compressed our time from top of descent to landing. 3. Choosing ZZZ - high altitude/high terrain as a divert airport.4. Loss of situational awareness as we made the turn away from the airport.Suggestions -1. Take vectors out for a longer final approach.2. If possible, choose diversion airports that have less threats. 3. If a turn for an airport is needed to descend or slow - make them towards the airport not away as altitude is less likely going to be an issue with regards to terrain avoidance. During a medical divert we were high and fast. On approach we accomplished a left 360 to descend. We initially had 7,300 feet set and when we turned inbound and had the field insight we began a descent to 6,300 feet the final approach fix altitude. Approach received a low altitude alert and informed us. We climbed and continued the approach visually. We never descended below 6,300 feet before the FAF.Visual approach, high and fast resulted in loss of situational awareness. Avoid visual approaches when in unplanned situations, get vectors for an instrument approach.
ASRS:1821612.s: During a medical diversion to a high-altitude airport, the crew became high and fast after selecting managed speed without activating the approach mode. A subsequent visual 360 turn away from the airport triggered a low altitude alert, forcing a climb before rejoining the ILS.

ASRS:1821671.n: We experienced the wake turbulence encounter on the descent through FL300, initial uncommanded roll 15 to 20 deg left followed by 25 to 30 deg to the right, rolled out and escaped from the encounter. We asked Center what type of aircraft we were flying behind. The reply was a Boeing 757, which we had on screen TCAS at about 10 miles ahead of us. However there was another aircraft farther ahead of the 757 that we could also see on screen. The Center Controller allowed us to take a heading off course to remain clear of the threat. However we ran into the wake again in the vicinity of GLAVN, and was not as much of a problem during that encounter. and I thought it was strange I have never had a 757 wake encounter roll the aircraft like that. Shortly after we were on approach control into Atlanta airport we discovered that the 757 was what appeared to be slightly less than 10 miles in trail of a heavy B787.I find it unusual to be in that type of upset due to 757 wake turbulence. We followed them all the time. I think it could be possible that the 757 was so close to the preceding aircraft that the heavy aircraft's wake was not a problem for the 757, but became one for us. Given the current conditions the winds were pushing the wake in our direction [so] obviously more spacing would've helped. I don't mind a vector off course. I would greatly appreciate more spacing behind heavier aircraft.
ASRS:1821671.s: The crew encountered severe wake turbulence during descent through FL300 behind a Boeing 757, which was following a heavy B787 less than 10 miles ahead. The pilot attributed the uncommanded rolls to the B787's wake affecting the 757 and subsequently the crew's aircraft, recommending increased spacing behind heavy aircraft.

ASRS:1821674.n: We were talking to Ramp Control and were cleared into the ramp to gate via [Taxiways] K3, J, and hold short of spot 10A for further instructions. The taxi was briefed between the Captain and I and we were going along Taxiway J looking for spot 10A. However, there is no depiction on any of the agc or apc charts of where 10A is including the temporary agc and apc charts. Also, along Taxiway J there are multiple construction sites and construction vehicles. We continued on Taxiway J and stopped at the mouth of the gates and inquired Ramp when we saw the reverse 10A spot assuming that we were in the right spot. However, we were told that we had passed it. We then completed a series of 180 degree turns to hold short of the other spot 10A that wasn't clearly visible or centered on the taxi centerline of Taxiway J. This was due to construction and barricades moving the taxi line over from the original. A recommendation would be to add spot 10A to be depicted on the charts to help identify where it would be during construction. This would be helpful because it can be easily missed with the construction traffic and not being centered on the taxi line. There were no other aircraft involved or inconvenienced.
ASRS:1821674.s: The flight crew missed gate spot 10A while taxiing on Taxiway J because the location was not depicted on charts and obscured by construction. They performed 180-degree turns to reach the correct spot, which was displaced from the centerline by barricades, with no other aircraft involved.

ASRS:1821685.n: The FO was flying a visual approach to Runway 33 in BGR. He was descending to 2,300 feet between ELSUH and CUVOT intersections and got terrain warning. There are towers on top of these small hills near the course. He turned the autopilot off and climbed a little with some extra power and the warning went away.
ASRS:1821685.s: The First Officer flying a visual approach to Runway 33 in BGR received a terrain warning while descending to 2,300 feet between ELSUH and CUVOT due to towers on nearby hills. He disengaged the autopilot, applied extra power, and climbed slightly, which cleared the warning.

ASRS:1821703.n: During taxi out the APU on the aircraft failed with only one engine running. We then returned to the gate and the captain requested all passengers deplane while we waited for the MEL for the APU because the cabin temperature was becoming extremely unsafe. An air cart was attached to the aircraft because the bridge air was not cooling the aircraft, but this did not make a significant impact on the cabin temperature. We reboarded the aircraft and pushed back, but due to the remnants of Tropical Storm Name, there were significant departure delays and we need up with a 64 minute taxi-out. After we were airborne FA4 asked the Captain what the cabin temperature reached while we were waiting for departure and was informed that the cabin reached 96 degrees F. We were not re-catered with water or ice as requested and this made a significant impact on our service once airborne.Perform an aircraft swap if an APU goes INOP during the summer months. It is completely unacceptable and unsafe to expect passengers and crew to endure temperatures that high.
ASRS:1821703.s: During taxi out, an APU failure on a single-engine aircraft caused unsafe cabin temperatures reaching 96°F, forcing a return to the gate and a 64-minute delayed departure. The crew reported that inadequate cooling and lack of re-catering negatively impacted service, recommending aircraft swaps for summer APU failures.

ASRS:1821728.n: During the preflight of the aircraft, my student performed the inspection. He called me in when he was having trouble removing the oil dipstick of the right engine to inspect oil level since it was secured very tight and was hot to the touch. I came out there with a napkin to use as an insulator for our fingers and managed to loosen the dipstick by using both my hands. I checked the oil level and handed the dipstick to the student for him to do the same. He placed the dipstick back in and secured it, and I doubled checked that the stick was secure by loosening and retightening it. I then proceeded to run my own quick check of the aircraft by verifying the oil in the left engine and checking the fuel quantity onboard. We found no issues with the aircraft and proceeded with the flight.About an hour into the flight, we were in the south practice area performing Vmc demo with the student at the controls. During the maneuver, I had noticed an oil slick starting to form off the right engine. For the maneuver, we were operating the right engine at full power while the left was idle. To make sure we are all on the same page, I pointed out the slick and had him start turning back to ZZZ. I instructed him to scissor the throttles, go full power on the left engine and idle the right engine. I immediately called up our dispatch and informed them of our engine trouble while they coordinated preparations at the school, airport, and rescue services as part of the company procedures. About three minutes after we idled the right engine, the oil temperature was rising to the limit. Since we were holding 3,000 feet at the time with an idling engine with good performance, and I did not want to risk having a seized engine I elected to shut the engine down and feather it. We informed dispatch, and then followed the appropriate checklist. And elected to continue to ZZZ since they still needed time to prepare the field for our arrival with emergency services, familiarity, and long runways available. On the way back, I shifted my attention to the student and briefed what happened, and what we are going to do from now. During this time, I had him at the controls flying while I ran the checklists with him. I briefed that I would have him fly to ZZZ but once we start maneuvering, I will take the controls for descent and landing. As we were nearing the field, dispatch called us requesting we circle the field if performance allows for a few minutes while they still waited for rescue to arrive. Once we were about 3 miles south at 3,000 [feet], dispatch called again telling we do not need to circle anymore, and that the airport will not call rescue. I really did not want to stay in the air longer than we needed to, and changing the plan now would have increased risks, I opted to continue to land. I took the controls at this point, and since we needed to lose altitude, I decided to fly a normal pattern and flew down to make a normal 45 entry for runway 20. Runway 20 was the longest runway with most favorable wind conditions. The landing was successful. The airport was closed for our recovery, and we planned to shut down on the runway and get a tow, but I was nervous about another aircraft behind me on short final, so I used the remaining speed of the aircraft to turn off onto the taxiway at about 10 knots.During the post flight inspection, we could not see anything out of place other than the oil streaks. We checked the dipstick and saw that it had slightly loosen but appear to be seated. But when maintenance performed their inspection, they determined the oil dipstick was cross threaded. They determined this was the most likely source of the oil leak. Only about a quart of oil was lost in flight.I think obviously the biggest factor here was the dipstick not secured properly. I was not aware how easily the dipstick could be cross threaded. The biggest learning moment for me was paying closer attention to how the dipstick is seated. In the specific aircraft, the dipstick sits directly on the engine block, and you can only easily see the dipstick from a top view unlike other aircraft I operate such as the other [aircraft type] where the dipstick is sits on a pipe that protrudes from the engine where the dipsticks cap is visible from the side. I think what also did not help was the fact we used a napkin to hold the dipstick during the preflight, which also visibly covered it. I think from here on out I am going to make sure some gloves are accessible and emphasize to my students the potential risk of cross threading.However, I am concerned about the airports handling of this situation. It was revealed when we landed, the airport management seemed to have not deemed our situation important enough to call in fire rescue as a precaution. They also have seemed to do a poor job of closing the airport as aircraft were still taking off and landing even when they announced multiple times over the radio the airport is closed. When I landed, a aircraft was flying not too far behind us in the pattern, and I had to move the aircraft on a single engine off the runway out of concern they would land on top of us which added the risk to us. But in the end of the day, the aircraft made it back in one piece, and most importantly my student and I made back safe.
ASRS:1821728.s: During a Vmc demonstration, the instructor and student experienced an oil leak caused by a cross-threaded dipstick that had been difficult to secure during preflight. The crew shut down the right engine, landed safely on a single engine, and noted that airport management failed to properly close the field or dispatch rescue services.

ASRS:1821741.n: Experienced a partial power loss and expedited landing beginning at about 800-1200 AGL. I had turned a high final and noticed that engine RPM was at approximately 1,000. I advanced the throttle in an attempt to add power but the engine did not respond. I pitched for best glide and tried to troubleshoot. I attempted to engage the starter again with no response. I noticed that the display on my comm 2 had disappeared. I tried to declare an emergency but I believe that I was not able to reach ATC. On my comm 1, I requested priority on my CTAF frequency, not having time to dial a new frequency. I landed on the Runway without incident. Maintenance determined that the starter wiring/switch had an issue and was fixed in such a way that it was permanently on. Therefore, whenever the master was on, it would engage the starter.
ASRS:1821741.s: The pilot experienced partial power loss during final approach due to a starter switch fault that kept the starter permanently engaged. After failing to contact ATC, the pilot executed a priority landing on the runway without incident.

ASRS:1821744.n: During climbout from CGZ airport on a dual CFII flight we noticed a helicopter quickly approaching us at the same altitude from our left. They initially appeared to be flying away from us deviating to the right. I knew the right away rules said they should give way to us and I believed they were initially. Shortly after though I noticed they were continuing to fly toward us so I chose to quickly execute a rapid climb. I did not think it was safe to descend or turn away as we had mountains below us the helicopter was approaching us rapidly. I believe the helicopter passed 500 feet below us.
ASRS:1821744.s: During climbout from CGZ on a dual CFII flight, a helicopter approached rapidly from the left at the same altitude. The pilot executed a rapid climb to avoid a collision, estimating the helicopter passed 500 feet below due to terrain constraints preventing descent or turns.

ASRS:1821753.n: After conducting an aerobatic practice flight, I entered the pattern on the 45 degree leg to downwind behind two other aircraft, a Cherokee and a C182. The Cherokee was operated by the local flight school and was in front of the C182. The C182 was flying a wider than normal downwind, 3 times the size recommended by the airport. The Cherokee did the same and flew a 1.7 mile long final with no other traffic in front of him. This caused me to perform two 360 degree turns to increase spacing. I also performed S-turns on final but got too close to the C182 so I went around. During the go-around the C182 announced that he was disabled on the runway. I orbited and then started to divert to ZZZ1 but realized that I did not have enough gas to get there. I returned to the ZZZ pattern, declared a fuel emergency on CTAF and landed without incident on taxiway A. My low fuel state was caused by two factors: the excessively large traffic patterns flown by flight schools causing two 360 deg turns, s-turns, and a go-around, and the limitation of the Extra 300/S to prohibit aerobatic flight with fuel in the wing tanks limiting the amount of fuel on board to 12.9 gallons.The FAA must push flight schools to fly tighter traffic patterns. The ZZZ airport requests GA traffic to fly a 1/2 to 3/4 mile downwind and flight schools typically fly 1 to 1.5 mile down winds.
ASRS:1821753.s: The Extra 300/S pilot executed two 360-degree turns, S-turns, and a go-around due to flight schools flying excessively large traffic patterns, causing a fuel emergency. The pilot declared an emergency and landed safely on taxiway A after determining insufficient fuel to divert.

ASRS:1821761.n: While flying on an IFR flight plan from to ZZZ1 at 4,000 feet the Controller contacted me and asked for my altitude. I responded that I was at 4,000 feet and he told me he showed me at 6,600. We had a discussion that resulted in him asking me to turn off the altitude transmitting feature on the GPS. I attempted to do so but was unable and called back to ask about the weather at ZZZ. When I learned I could get in without having to shoot an approach I asked to be vectored and stated that I was not declaring an emergency at the time. I was cleared direct and informed he would call ahead to advise of the situation. I was unable to acknowledge as my Garmin 650 would not transmit, nor would the Narco that's our COMM2. I squawked 7600 and hit IDENT. I was able to hear the controller trying to raise me but couldn't respond. The GPS screen went black about a minute later so I decided to descend to get below the clouds. I continued towards ZZZ with no electronics. I next connected my cell phone to the blue tooth on my headset and called my father who is also a private pilot and asked him to telephone the Tower, tell them I'm requesting priority and that I will be landing on Runway 23 in about 15 minutes and that I was experiencing an electrical failure. I noticed electrical sparks coming from under the co-pilot side of the panel when I was about 2 miles out so I killed the master power and the alternator immediately. My landing was largely uneventful and actually better than I was expecting, given the conditions.
ASRS:1821761.s: A pilot flying IFR at 4,000 feet experienced a GPS altitude discrepancy followed by total electrical failure, including loss of transponder and radios. The pilot squawked 7600, descended below clouds, used a cell phone to coordinate a priority landing, and killed the master power after seeing sparks before landing safely.

ASRS:1821768.n: UAS was being flown for photographing the sunset under section 44807 for recreational use. The app used for controlling UAS and verifying an appropriate flying location was the DJI Fly app. The DJI Fly app has geofencing capabilities and has shown on multiple occasions that certain areas are restricted and will prevent the user from taking off and flying in restricted areas. I did not know at the time that this app does not restrict flying in certain areas that require authorization to fly in. At this particular location the altitude restriction on the app is set to 400 feet, there were several 'altitude zones' and restricted areas nearby that limited altitude and the geofencing software would stop the UAS from entering these areas and I avoided them. While the UAS was around 400ft altitude and 300 feet away, maintaining VLOS, I noticed a vehicle approaching my location. They informed me that they were contacted by Naval Air Station about an unauthorized UAS flying in their airspace and requested that I not fly at this location. The location in question, I found out later is Class D airspace with a grid altitude of 0 feet. The DJI app was in conflict with this information saying it was 400 feet. Following the incident I spoke with the FAA in order to find an appropriate location to fly my UAS and was informed about completing TRUST training, using the B4UFly app, and not relying on geofencing from the DJI Fly app.
ASRS:1821768.s: A recreational UAS operator flew a drone to 400 feet in Class D airspace near a Naval Air Station, relying on conflicting DJI Fly app geofencing data. The flight was terminated after the operator was contacted by the base regarding the unauthorized intrusion and subsequently advised by the FAA to use B4UFly and complete TRUST training.

ASRS:1821771.n: Working 4 sectors combined, and Controller in Charge. SLC was in a South Operation, Visual Airspace, Visual Approaches. Weather was VMC but visibility was diminishing and was marginal. There are thunderstorms throughout the sectors in my airspace. Lightning reported on the finals to all Runways, airspeed fluctuations reported on final, audible Wind Shear Alerts continuous all runways, 15 knot wind shift approaching the SLC Airport. Light to occasional moderate chop reported in the area. Tailwinds on final.Aircraft Y vectored to a 15 mile right base, cleared for Visual Approach to Runway 17 at SLC, switched to Tower. Aircraft X at 210 knots given descent to 8,000 feet abeam the SLC Airport, expecting Runway 16R, on the RNAV arrival being sequenced with other traffic within my sector(s) and on final. Traffic Management Unit calls down to TRACON through speaker in the Supervisor's console that Aircraft Y had a Lightning Strike and coordinated a heading 270 at 9,000 feet. I responded Radar Contact. Tower initiated the Heading 270 on a 9 mile final at 9,000 feet, which you never do, however, Aircraft Y was coordinated at 9,000 feet. I kept Aircraft X expediting to 6,000 feet, which would not be an issue as long as Aircraft Y leveled at 9,000 feet. This was not the case as I observed Aircraft Y continuing descent through 8900 feet and continuing. Recognizing this immediately, Aircraft Y appeared to be an Emergency aircraft not knowing what altitude he would be stopping at, I issued traffic to Aircraft X followed by a Traffic Alert with a heading 270 immediately to avoid a mid-air collision, all the while I was still not talking to Aircraft Y performing evasive maneuvers in my airspace.As soon as Aircraft X was past Aircraft Y I would then have divergence. I turned Aircraft X to heading 340, and issued a Low Altitude Alert and climbed him immediately to 7800 feet, while doing so I see Aircraft Y turning to the same north heading 340 at 8000 feet, with Aircraft X just West of Aircraft Y on a parallel course, and not talking to Aircraft Y in my airspace, not having lateral separation, I immediately turned Aircraft X to heading 310, all the while trying my best to achieve some sort of radar separation, and avoid a collision, until I find out who is talking to Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y at 8,000 feet is not what coordinated nor approved by me in my airspace, and a Heading 270 off the finals is never performed, for this exact reason. This is an unsafe operation with traffic in the downwind. Aircraft Y at 8,000 feet leaves no options at all.After determining the adjacent sector controller, who is only certified on those positions, was working Aircraft Y, in which Tower switched him to my airspace, when I had conflicting traffic. The adjacent sector controller provided zero communications to me, even though I repeatedly asked who was working Aircraft Y and what is he doing? After I had Aircraft X squared away, they just happened to say 'Aircraft Y had your Aircraft X in sight and was maintaining visual separation.'This would have been nice to know.When an aircraft is coordinated to be 9,000 feet then have the aircraft be at 9,000 feet, not at 8,000 feet, which leaves the final sector Controller absolutely no way out. No attempt was made to by Tower who assigned 8,000 feet, or by the adjacent sector who received the aircraft at 8,000 feet to advise the sector who owns the airspace with an aircraft in direct conflict. When a heading of 270 and 9,000 feet is coordinated with another sector, a Departure Only Sector, then make sure he enters the airspace for which that specific coordination was originally made, and not another sector that has conflicting traffic with that type of coordination.No coordination or even a point out was attempted to be made to the appropriate sector in which the vital coordination directly impacts. When Visual Separation is applied between two aircraft that are in direct conflict with each other, it is absolutely a top priority to ensure that all parties involved receive this valuable bit of information.When a Controller takes it upon themselves to accept the responsibility of an aircraft in someone else's airspace at an altitude that is in direct conflict with an aircraft that you are not in communication with and at a different altitude than what was previously coordinated, then it might be a top priority to advise Controller working the aircraft in his own airspace that he is in direct communications with that visual separation is being applied. When a controller is taking evasive actions to prevent a mid-air collision with an aircraft that you are talking to, that is not in your airspace, and you are providing control instructions to, don't sit quietly when you hear 'Who is talking to Aircraft Y'?
ASRS:1821771.s: An Air Traffic Controller reported a near mid-air collision between Aircraft X and Aircraft Y at SLC during visual approaches in marginal weather. The conflict occurred because Tower and an adjacent sector failed to coordinate Aircraft Y's descent to 8,000 feet, forcing the controller to issue emergency traffic alerts and evasive headings to avoid collision.

ASRS:1821787.n: IFR departure, advised ATC upwind due to engine failure. I asked if he wanted to stay on my frequency and stay in the pattern to land. He said yes, so I issued him right traffic. I didn't solicit a cancellation of IFR, or ask if he could maintain terrain and obstruction clearance.
ASRS:1821787.s: An ATC controller managed an IFR departure with an engine failure, allowing the pilot to remain on frequency and land in the pattern. The controller issued right traffic but failed to solicit an IFR cancellation or verify terrain and obstruction clearance.

ASRS:1821814.n: Approach flashed (handed off) Aircraft X departing ZZZ going to ZZZ1 to me. The aircraft was out of 8,500 feet when I took the handoff and checked on out of about 9,400 feet climbing to 16,000 feet. I climbed the aircraft to 2;6000 feet as I had no traffic in the area. The majority of my attention was focused on the south side of the sector where I had a VFR aircraft inbound to ZZZ2, an IFR aircraft inbound to ZZZ2 who was just out of 40,000 feet 45 miles from the airport as well as an additional VFR aircraft who was climbing and descending that needed lost communication procedures. Shortly after climbing Aircraft X, he reported that he needed to level off at 100 feet due to traffic above at 10,500 feet, I looked and I did see the numbers XXX on the scope but the target associated with these numbers was obscured by the target from Aircraft X.I was trying to figure out if there was actually traffic there and if there was traffic there why I had not received any kind of CA (Conflict Alert) indication (nothing was flashing at all) and since this was well within the lateral and vertical confines of Approach's airspace why they had climbed the aircraft into traffic within their airspace. I acknowledged Aircraft X and approved his request to level off, at that point he told me he was responding to an RA. I was surprised by this, but just asked him to report on course and when he resumed his climb. A few minutes later he told me that he was going to report the incident. At that time I responded trying to calm him down and let him know that I had already notified the supervisor that he had responded to an RA. A few minutes after that, Aircraft X pilot informed me that he was going to report it as a 'near midair'. Again I attempted to defuse this situation, informed the Controller in Charge and told him I would contact Approach to find out more details. We then gave him the information to contact the Center Operations Manager in Charge as well as the Approach Control Supervisor. Approach Control should have called the traffic and not shipped me the aircraft until they were clear. The Conflict alert should have been going off for several minutes, which would have alerted both myself and Approach Control to the unusual situation. At that point I would have seen the non-associated VFR target and called the traffic. We should have better staffing so that we aren't working 6 day work weeks and running 2 under on busy shifts. Everyone is burnt out, exhausted and probably not as sharp as they would be. On departure out of ZZZ, we received a RA after encountering a near mid-air collision. The event occurred around around 30 to 40 miles south of ZZZ. The Captain was Pilot Monitoring and the First Officer was Pilot Flying. The First Officer was hand flying at the time of the event. We were climbing to 16,000 feet as instructed and talking to Departure Control. 16,000 feet was our initial altitude assigned on the ground in ZZZ. We received a handoff climbing through approximately 8,000 feet and contacted Center. After we checked in with Center, I noticed traffic straight ahead at 10,700 feet depicted on the scope and we were climbing toward them. We were not notified by ATC of any traffic and once myself (First Officer/Pilot Flying) noticed the traffic at 5 miles, I called 'traffic 5 miles 10,700, I'm going to level off' and began to level off immediately around 9,000 feet and did not climb above 10,000 feet.We got a TA, and I began a slight left turn as I noticed on TCAS that traffic was crossing left to right of our course. As the Captain was calling Center to ask about traffic in the area we got a visual on the traffic and immediately started a descending left turn to avoid traffic, simultaneously we received a descending RA and complied. The converging aircraft passed off our right wing and appeared to make a left turn also to avoid our converging course. We never saw the converging aircraft change altitude more than a few hundred feet. We notified Center of the RA event and returned to normal flight. Prior to departure, we briefed General Aviation traffic as the biggest threat in the departure briefing and I think that helped our awareness.General Aviation traffic not on a IFR flight plan or talking to ATC. Departure or Center not notifying of traffic. Timing of handoff from Departure to Center occurring at the event. Suggest attentiveness to traffic.
ASRS:1821814.s: A pilot and air traffic controller were involved in a near mid-air collision during Aircraft X's departure from ZZZ while climbing to 16,000 feet. The pilot reported an RA after encountering uncoordinated General Aviation traffic, attributing the event to a lack of ATC traffic advisories, obscured radar targets, and controller fatigue.

ASRS:1821822.n: The EFP (Engine Fail Procedure) for Runway 31 out of COS is very confusing and or incomplete. It states 'Reaching BRK R-218 (All Eng-delay turn until 7200 ft. Eng Fail After 7200 ft. Right Turn H125) or D5.6 ILPI LEFT turn H125. Min Cleanup 7187 ft.' We were cleared the SPRINGS 6 Departure, which calls for a RIGHT turn to H050. It does not say to wait until 7,200 ft. until turning to heading 050. If we lost an engine below 7,200 ft. in the turn to heading 050 what is the appropriate EFP path to follow? My F/O and I discussed at length but came to no clear answer. It needs to be more clearly written with appropriate 'EFP decision points' if needed.
ASRS:1821822.s: The pilot reported that the Engine Fail Procedure for Runway 31 at COS is confusing and incomplete regarding the SPRINGS 6 Departure. The narrative highlights a conflict between the departure's right turn to heading 050 and the EFP's requirement to delay turns until 7,200 feet, leaving the crew without a clear path for an engine failure below that altitude.

ASRS:1821848.n: [Personnel were brought to] PTKK to finally fix the PAPI lights that have been inoperative for months. The Runway 4 PAPI was no longer NOTAM'd out. However, upon arrival [to] PTKK, we tried multiple times to turn them on to no avail. We asked TKK Radio to try and he was unable to turn them on either. Then arriving PTSA, the PAPI was inop for Runway 5 with no NOTAM. Then arriving [to] PKWA the Runway 6 PAPI is also NOTAM inop with shortened runway construction. So now we have the three shortest runways PTKK 6,000 ft., PTSA 5,700 ft., and PKWA (now down to 6,000 ft. with construction) having inoperative PAPI lights for the prevailing wind runway. Add this to PGSN not having PAPI/VASI installed even though the Jeppesen Approach chart indicates there are VASI, and we have 4 airports in the Guam region with no visual guidance. Poor trend, especially for night time operations and new crews coming on board. Unsatisfactory trend. [We're] lucky we have light and empty airplanes with very few passengers allowing for short landing rolls. I write this not relating to a specific flight but relating to a safety issue at PTKK airport. For the past 2 years, the PAPI at PTKK Runway 4 has been out of service. Sometimes this is noted on the NOTAMs and sometimes it is not. The safety issue is that PTKK is the proverbial 'black hole' airport which gives very limited visual reference. This makes flying a visual approach very challenging. In fact, an article 'Black Hole Approach' concludes with the statement 'The best way to combat these often subtle and insidious factors (relating to the Black hole effect) is to avoid straight-in, visual approaches at night without glide slope guidance, especially when overflying the infamous black hole.' Engineers conducted an extensive study of the problem. The results were published in a report entitled, 'Flight Deck Work Load and Night Visual Approach Performance' They concluded that the problem is exacerbated by many factors but the factors that stood out to me are those that are present on nearly all PTKK approaches. They are:1. A runway length/width combination that is unfamiliar to a pilot. PTKK is 6,000 ft. long with absolutely no overrun on either end. It is shorter than most runways and that effect is amplified by the fact that there is no paved safety area on either end. SNA is famed for being short but it is 5,700 ft. long PLUS over 1,000 ft. of paved safety area on the approach end to Runway 2L. It actually has almost 7,000 ft. of pavement. PTKK only has 6,000.2. Substandard runway and airport lighting. PTKK has had broken PAPI for at least 2 years. The only other airport lighting is the runway edge lights and some taxi lights. There are no MALSR lights. There is no big city lights to help with visual reference. 3. Peering through a rain-soaked windshield can convince a pilot (because of refraction) that the aircraft is too high and can result in an error of as much as 200 ft. of altitude per nautical mile from the runway. It is very common to have an island induced rain shower right off the approach end of Runway 04 at PTKK. Now we are flying this approach late at night, windshield covered in rain, poor lighting, and absolutely no backup source of glide path information as I will explain later due to the way the RNAV approach is built. 4. An airport that is situated at a slightly lower elevation and on a different slope than the surrounding terrain. This is PTKK. The runway is on the northwest side of the island at sea level. The island rises quickly to the southeast to an elevation of 2,700 ft. in less than 1 mile. 5. An approach over water or unlit terrain means that the visual reference points are at a distance where altitude and sink rate are more difficult to judge. This is PTKK. Absolutely no ground reference from the IF of FIGBY until the runway nearly 10 miles away. The problem is further exacerbated by the fact that the only approach we have to Runway 4 (most commonly used because of the prevailing trade winds from the NE) is the RNAV (GPS) Runway 4 approach. Everything works fine with VNAV and LNAV until we reach the missed approach point of HAMAX. Notice that HAMAX is 2.2 miles from the end of the runway. So here you are, flying the approach as usual in VNAV and LNAV and you have the usual rain shower between FASPO and the runway. You are tired because it is now after midnight and you are over the dark ocean with no ground lights in sight and the PAPI's are not working as usual. You approach the waypoint HAMAX and the flight director bars (your only vertical guidance at this point) suddenly command a pitch up and a turn to the left. Why?? Because you have hit the missed approach point and the guidance tells you to go around. This isn't common for most approaches. It throws off even seasoned pilots. You can see the runway lights through the rain soaked windshield but again with no PAPI, you have now lost all vertical guidance. You are now at 660 ft. above the ocean and continue based on a fuzzy view outof the windshield. Are you stable for that 500 foot callout? I guess so, hard to tell if we're on the vertical path...Is this safe? I would submit that in my opinion that this is the most dangerous flight we operate. Why do we do it in the middle of the night? I am not talking about the hopper. That is daytime and is doable. We don't currently have an aircraft availability problem like we did when we were busy. Why not do this flight in the daylight? Why not get those PAPI's fixed? They've been broken for 2 years! Why not get the RNP approach finished. That would solve the whole problem if we actually had vertical guidance to the runway instead of losing it right at 660 ft. where we really need it.
ASRS:1821848.s: A pilot reported that PAPI lights at PTKK Runway 4, PTSA Runway 5, and PKWA Runway 6 are inoperative without consistent NOTAMs, creating unsafe night visual approach conditions. The lack of glide path guidance at PTKK, combined with rain, short runway length, and RNAV approach limitations, forces pilots to lose vertical guidance at 660 feet, increasing the risk of unstable approaches.

ASRS:1821910.n: Suspected GPS jamming between LOGMU and ROKUB on T561 XA:17Z-XB:03Z. EICAS alert for NAV UNABLE RNP. Followed checklist and used radio/IRS updating during the event. Was able to resume normal GPS ops for remainder of flight. Most likely some crazy militants in the area. Perhaps pay the big bucks and fly over Siberia on this route. Most likely less GPS jamming and probably more efficient for flight planning. Although I appreciate the longer rest opportunities on these double crewed flights.
ASRS:1821910.s: The flight crew experienced suspected GPS jamming between LOGMU and ROKUB on route T561, triggering a NAV UNABLE RNP alert. They followed checklists using radio and IRS updates to resume normal GPS operations, attributing the event to local militants.

ASRS:1821911.n: During Cruise we received an ACARS message from the company [Dispatch] that they had left 1768kg (initial message said 1768lbs but was later corrected) of Dry Ice off the DG manifest. We began to send follow up messages back and forth to confirm the location and total quantity of the dry ice. It was determined that the total quantity was 1884kg vs the DG manifest value of 166kg. Basically, 2 cans worth of Dry Ice had not be accounted for on the DG manifest. The crew deployed the Drager CO2 monitoring system immediately and was also directed to do this from the company. We also ran the QRH for this event. Upon further review, it was determined by crew and Dispatch that the dry ice quantity on board not only exceeded normal FOM limits, but was over the supplemental limits in the FOM. I began a conference call with the Dispatcher, DO, and Flight Operations. Based on all the information, they recommended we deploy the CO2 monitoring system and keep a close eye out for any elevated CO2 levels, but that we should be able to continue safely to our destination which was another 8 or so hours away. We knew if the levels were elevated we could follow the QRH and use oxygen to breathe safely and divert if needed. We also knew that we were flying right over ZZZ1 in about an hour which we could just divert to immediately to remedy the problem. This would give us time to get ready for the divert and allow us to burn enough fuel to get below maximum landing weight. So basically our options were 1) continue or 2) divert. We woke up the Captain to provide him all of the data so he could make the decision. With all the data and the opinions of the crew, he decided we should continue. The decision was supported by the crew and Dispatch. The rest of the flight was uneventful. Obviously, undocumented hazardous materials is a big deal and could have serious safety concerns. Luckily everything worked out here. Once the issue was identified, Dispatch was a little slow to get us all the info and to provide input. I believe this was because the Dispatchers had a shift change. I think this led to information slowly being provided to all parties. The cause was someone [erred] in the chain of [custody] during loading, documenting, and manifesting must have made an error which led to this dry ice not being manifested. Approximately 20 minutes into flight, we received a message via ACARS from Dispatch that 1768lbs of dry ice went on the aircraft unmanifested and to please use supplemental dry ice procedures. At that time the RFO was in the jump seat and he retrieved, turned on and distributed a Drager monitor to each crew member. Once established in cruise, CA proceeded to the CRM as planned/briefed and RFO took the left seat. Subsequently we received message that the unmanifested dry ice was 1768kg, not lbs. We confirmed with that the 1768kg was on the main deck along with the 116kg that was manifested , for a total of 1884kg of dry ice on the main deck. The main deck limit is 1814kg.
