DO stated that he and dispatch agreed, that with all systems on the aircraft functioning properly and with FOM 10.37 DRY ICE SUPPLEMENTAL PROCEDURES in place, we were OK to continue to destination, however, if Captain desired to divert that would be appropriate as well given the over-limit situation. At that time, we had just passed the east coast of [State]. Diverting to a [company name] base at that time would have required dumping fuel in order to land under MAXLGW. FO and RFO discussed and determined that we would arrive overhead ZZZ1 on current flight planned route at MAXLGW and that if a divert decision was made, ZZZ1 was the most appropriate divert base. One hour prior to arriving overhead ZZZ1, FO awakened the CA in the CRM and informed him of the situation and [Dispatch's] deferral to him on a divert decision. CA agreed that continuing on was appropriate. FO/RFO informed [Dispatch] via ACARS of decision to continue to [our destination] using dry ice supplemental procedures. Rest of flight was uneventful. A [contributing] cause was it had something to do with this being a chartered/non standard flight.
ASRS:1821911.s: During cruise, the crew discovered 1,884kg of dry ice on board, exceeding limits due to a loading and manifesting error on a chartered flight. After consulting Dispatch and reviewing procedures, the Captain decided to continue to the destination using supplemental monitoring, resulting in an uneventful flight.

ASRS:1821926.n: GPS jamming encountered between XA21Z and XA52Z at 33,000 feet. Jamming resulted in immediate loss of ADS-B and GPS left and right. Once jamming ceased all system function returned to normal. Informed ATC immediately of the jamming and then again informed ATC when our actual navigation performance was going to require vectors. As soon as I notified ATC that we were at the point of navigation degradation beyond acceptable performance, the jamming ceased immediately. I believe the parties responsible were monitoring ATC frequencies. [Cause was] Some form of GPS Jamming - extremely long period. It usually happens for much shorter periods that is less than 3 minutes. Identify the parties responsible and remove them from the equation.
ASRS:1821926.s: The pilot reported GPS jamming at 33,000 feet between XA21Z and XA52Z, causing immediate loss of ADS-B and GPS systems. The jamming ceased after the crew notified ATC of navigation degradation, which the pilot attributed to responsible parties monitoring ATC frequencies.

ASRS:1821938.n: While on our first attempt to land at COD we were vectored onto the RNAV to Runway 4 visual conditions prevailed and we were using the RNAV primarily for additional terrain clearance continuous moderate turbulence and windshear persisted on the arrival. ATC vectors and my attempts to maintain an airspeed that buffered against the rapid ups and downs of the green line and the rapid fluctuations of the indicated airspeed left us high and fast on our first attempt so we initiated a go-around missed approach. There was a significant tailwind down the valley that sheared to a headwind at the surface this contributed to us being high and fast.While we were climbing out we were instructed to climb and maintain 15,000 feet and were given vectors back to TOCUD. Approaching TAKBE the Captain requested a turn direct to TAKBE from ATC. Being at 15,000 [feet] we couldn't lower the flaps [so] the Captain instructed me to set 12,200 [feet] for TAKBE and start down. I complied with these instructions and as we dropped below 15,000 [feet] we began lowering the flaps and configuring.Shortly after starting our descent ATC issued a low altitude alert and stated that his minimum vectoring altitude was 15,000 [feet]. We were visual with both the mountains and airport in sight but failed to get proper approval from ATC for the visual approach before descending. As a side note we were being shook pretty good by the continuous moderate turbulence and I was really having to work the thrust levers to maintain a safe airspeed. We informed ATC that we were visual and we were cleared for the approach to Runway 4. We successfully landed on our second attempt. At no time was the safety of the fight or terrain clearance an issue and no EGPWS cautions or warnings were issued.Confusion on my part of the Captains instruction to 'sneak / start down'. It was the last leg of long hot sweaty day with multiple Captain swaps delays and MX issues, heat fatigue and dehydration were setting in and the turbulence and windshear created a very challenging flight environment.Once we goofed up and should have made sure that we were cleared for the visual prior to initiating a descent from a clearance altitude. The clearance to turn direct to TAKBE was not a clearance to descend even though we were visual. Mountain airports and strong winds are a difficult mix and other than adopting overly restrictive limits these difficult approaches will continue to be part of the job.
ASRS:1821938.s: The flight crew descended below 15,000 feet at TAKBE without ATC clearance for a visual approach, confusing a direct routing instruction with descent authorization. This occurred during a challenging arrival at COD involving turbulence and windshear, though the crew subsequently received clearance and landed safely on the second attempt.

ASRS:1821957.n: While climbing out at approximately a little over 10,000 feet we received a pitch trim caution. I was hand flying the aircraft as we were maneuvering around some build-ups in order to avoid unnecessary turbulence, the caution light came on when I used the trim to command more nose up trim to properly trim the aircraft for the climb.The First Officer ran the Pitch Trim Caution E&A checklist. This would not clear the malfunction and the checklist confirmed that our pitch trim was jammed in position and we would have no AutoPilot for the remainder of the flight. The aircraft was trimmed for a climb at approximately 200 knots at a 5 degree nose up attitude. I contacted Dispatch and advised them of the situation and spoke with Maintenance (MX) control. When discussing what my intentions were, myself and Dispatch agreed that we would continue to ZZZ for the moment but I'd evaluate the situation a little closer to ZZZ1 once we were in cruise flight.Once we reached our cruising altitude of FL240 it became apparent that the amount of nose down force that needed to be maintained on the control column was substantial. Furthermore in order to minimize the amount of nose down forces required on the yoke to hold altitude and to comply with the E&A checklist the airspeed had to be maintained at just over 200 knots IAS, greatly increasing our time enroute to ZZZ. The First Officer and I had a discussion as to the wisdom of continuing the flight all the way to ZZZ under these conditions and determined that the more prudent course of action was to divert to ZZZ1. I also believed that the pace of ATC operations into ZZZ1 were much more favorable for an abnormal landing than in the busy airspace of ZZZ. I called Dispatch and the Dispatcher agreed with my decision and we diverted to ZZZ1. We followed the E&A procedure for this landing and landed without incident in ZZZ1 and taxied to the gate. After landing in ZZZ1 and speaking with the MX personnel waiting for us I debriefed the crew with the exception of 1 FA that had already left the aircraft before I could get to the back (approx. 5 minutes or so after deplaning ended) in order to make her DH back to ZZZ1. I also spoke with [NAME] and we debriefed the flight.This was a situation that I hadn't seen pop up before as either a FO or a CA on the Dash 8-400 and I might be mistaken but I'm not sure I've seen this particular situation in the SIM either. Although the situation was certainly manageable it might be a good scenario to incorporate into future SIM sessions just so pilots can get an idea of what the aircraft feels like when the pitch trim is inoperative.
ASRS:1821957.s: The Captain and First Officer of a Dash 8-400 experienced a jammed pitch trim during climb at 10,000 feet, causing a loss of autopilot and requiring substantial nose-down control force. They diverted to ZZZ1 due to high workload and airspeed restrictions, landing safely without incident.

ASRS:1821974.n: We executed a reduced power departure. Passing through 400 feet AGL immediately after takeoff and upon beginning to execute our assigned heading with a right turn to 155 degrees, the right engine experienced a significant compressor stall with an immediate over temp. The CA (Pilot Flying) immediately applied the appropriate steps to deal with the loss of thrust. I (Pilot Monitoring) immediately referenced the QRC and began to run the Engine Fire/Engine Severe Damage or Separation checklist. The EGT continued to climb and exceeded limits (712 Max) with no signs of recovery with the throttle moved to idle. We subsequently continued the QRC and secured the right engine. We then completed all steps of the checklist upon continuing with the flight manual and coordinated for an expeditious return to departure airport. We cleaned up the aircraft to flaps 5 and 210 KIAS, began cross feeding fuel, climbed to 3,000 feet, calculated landing distance and completed vectors to a single engine landing utilizing the ILS. Weather was not a factor and winds were approximately 10-12 knots. I was able to coordinate with the FAs per the FOM and then conveyed the situation to the passengers. We stopped straight ahead on the runway and coordinated for Fire/Rescue forces to inspect the aircraft for any signs of further fire or damage that would limit our ability to clear the runway. We were given the all clear and subsequently taxied to parking. Shut down was normal. Upon a thorough debrief, we believe we accomplished all required checklist and emergency action items, as well as used excellent CRM to back each other up and set up the aircraft for the immediate return and recovery. As we were climbing through 400 feet and starting our right turn out we heard a loud bang followed by the right engine displays going to zero. We both called out engine failure and then followed up with our engine failure procedures. We [contacted] Tower and they offered us runway XXR for landing, but we elected to use XYL as that would give us more time to complete all the checklist and set up for the approach. We had the emergency equipment waiting for us and I elected to stop on the runway so that they could look over the aircraft. Once they gave us the all clear we taxied back to the gate.
ASRS:1821974.s: During a reduced power departure, the right engine suffered a compressor stall and over-temperature at 400 feet AGL while turning right. The crew secured the engine, returned to the departure airport, and executed a single-engine ILS landing with no injuries or further damage.

ASRS:1822073.n: On departure, aircraft failed to pressurize. Leveled off. Ran appropriate checklist from QRH. Unable to manually control pressurization. Returned to field.
ASRS:1822073.s: During departure, the aircraft failed to pressurize and leveled off. After running the QRH checklist and finding manual pressurization control impossible, the crew returned to the field.

ASRS:1822078.n: Upon receiving approach clearance for the ZZZZZ XX Approach, [the] FO (First Officer) disengaged autopilot and began [a] gradual descent on approach while configuring to Flaps 20 and slowing to 170 kt. As I read back approach clearance to ATC, we crossed ZZZZZ1 and I heard the trim clacker activate. I thought that this was [the] FO adjusting to nose down trim as we were descending and configuring. After a few seconds, I asked if he was commanding the abnormally long trim down and he replied that he wasn't. The trim then stopped and appeared to remain stable. It then started a nose-up motion uncommanded. I verified that [the] FO did not inadvertently have his finger on the trim switch, and I [was] certain that mine was not. I then realized that this appeared to be a stab trim malfunction and went through and verbalized the immediate action items.Upon successfully disconnecting the stab and Mach trim, I asked [the] FO if he needed assistance in adding extra pressure on the controls and he informed me that they felt fine, just marginally heavier than normal. I elected to continue the approach as the uncommanded action was no longer occurring and I determined that an approach to landing would have been the safer, more stable option over quickly changing configuration and executing a go-around in a nose-down trim. We continued and landed without further incident. I sent Dispatch a text informing them of the event, and contacted Maintenance Control following entering a discrepancy in the aircraft maintenance logbook.
ASRS:1822078.s: During the approach phase, the crew experienced an uncommanded stabilizer trim malfunction while configuring for landing. The Captain executed immediate action items to disconnect the trim systems, elected to continue the approach, and landed safely before reporting the discrepancy to maintenance.

ASRS:1822093.n: While conducting the cockpit setup, we received an ACARS message stating, 'No Dangerous Goods Planned.' On taxi out, we sent Load Planning a Late Weights message. The response from company was, 'Hazmat Needs To Be Secured. Ramp Does Not Have Enough Bags.' We were both confused by this message as we were not aware that any Hazmat was loaded. After about 20 minutes, Ops instructed us to return to the gate to have the Hazmat secured. I asked if Ops had been advised what the Hazmat was. They could not provide that information. I told Ops that I was refusing the Hazmat and upon gate return, I wanted it removed. I contacted the Asst. Manager of Ramp Operations, [name], by phone and advised of the safety implications of what had happened and of my refusal of the Hazmat shipment. Two large red bags and two large boxes were removed from the forward pit and we departed.My main safety concerns are that we were out of the blocks for almost an hour with no idea that we had Hazmat aboard, Ops couldn't tell us what the Hazmat was and Hazmat was not properly secured by the ramp crew. If we had had a cargo fire or smoke or fumes, I had no information to provide to the [ARFF] crews.I refused the Hazmat for two reasons. 1) I had no information about the shipment and 2) I didn't want to subject the passengers to any additional delays for this issue.
ASRS:1822093.s: The flight crew discovered unsecured hazardous materials during taxi after receiving conflicting ACARS messages from operations. The captain refused the shipment, returned to the gate to have two red bags and two boxes removed, and cited a lack of cargo information and improper securing as safety concerns.

ASRS:1822107.n: We were cleared to depart on the ATUMA3B. The chart depicts climbing on the CAT 092/15.0 and above 8,000 ft. then turning to a 315 heading. This is also what is depicted when selecting the departure in the FMC. However, the narrative below says to fly out the CAT 092 until 8000 and then turning to a 315 heading. It does not say to fly to the fix depicted on the chart only to turn once passing 8,000 ft.
ASRS:1822107.s: The pilot reported a discrepancy between the ATUMA3B departure chart and its narrative text regarding the climb to 8,000 ft and subsequent turn to heading 315. The chart and FMC indicate turning at the CAT fix, while the narrative instructs turning only after reaching 8,000 ft without specifying the fix.

ASRS:1822116.n: I was taxiing on ZZZ Taxiway XX from the north, having landed on XXL. A rain shower had just passed through the airport. I was taxiing at 15 kt. on the straightaway, brought the thrust levers to idle, and began braking to slow down for the 1st turn. The 1st turn is about a 30-degree angle. When I started the turn, we were at about 12 kt. and slowing, [and] then began hydroplaning, I had no nose wheel steering or braking. I continued to turn the nose wheel to the right hoping to gain traction and [to also] keep the airplane on the taxiway. After that turn, the airplane gained traction and the nose wheel steering was able to steer the plane to the right. However, I still did not have braking available. I was able to steer the plane back to the centerline and [to] stay on the taxiway. We were taxiing in from landing on Runway XXL in ZZZ. During the approach there was moderate rainfall. Our taxi instructions were to taxi via Taxiway XY, Taxiway XZ, Taxiway XA, Taxiway XX, hold short of Runway XXC at Taxiway XX. As we turned onto Taxiway XX from Taxiway XA, the moderate rain had started to subside. The Captain was taxiing slower than usual due to the contaminated taxiway conditions - standing water. [At] the first bend on Taxiway XX as it turns from a south to a southwest heading, the aircraft almost completely lost traction. The nose wheel understeered and the aircraft continued straight ahead even as the taxiway turned. The Captain applied braking and the main tires also lost traction immediately. I also applied the brakes on the First Officer's side because I thought we were going to depart the taxiway. The aircraft skidded approximately 15 feet and nearly departed the prepared surface. At the last second, the aircraft slowed enough to allow the nose wheel to regain some effectiveness. The Captain was able to steer the aircraft back toward the centerline. There was a short, but secondary loss of traction [and] as we overshot the taxiway centerline, the aircraft was still in a partial skid.I have never seen an aircraft moving that slowly lose traction on a wet taxiway. I estimate the aircraft was moving at 15 kt. when the turn began. Both the Captain and I agree that this was something neither of us expected or have ever seen in our combined experience on the 737. I do believe any prudent pilot would have taken the turn at the same speed considering the conditions. It's my feeling that there was some issue with drainage or that [that] stretch of pavement is unusually slick during rainy conditions. I notified the Ground Controller of the event and reported braking action as fair to poor. I asked them to inform other aircraft of the slippery conditions on Taxiway XX between Runway XXL and XXC.
ASRS:1822116.s: The Captain and First Officer of a Boeing 737 hydroplaned on wet Taxiway XX while turning at 15 knots after landing, losing nose wheel steering and braking. The aircraft skidded 15 feet near the edge before regaining traction, which the crew attributed to poor drainage or unusually slick pavement conditions.

ASRS:1822164.n: While in cruise at FL370 the cabin altitude began to rise quickly. Noted that both packs were tripped/amber. [Requested priority handling] and initiated an descent. The PAX O2 mask deployed at 14,000 cabin altitude. We were at about 16,000 MSL at that time. About 3-5 minutes after mask deployment the FA's reported smoke, electrical smell and heat in the cabin. Diverted to ZZZ. Had AARF check aircraft that was stopped on the runway for indications of fire. None noted. Taxied to the gate X. Deplaned the PAX and filled out the AML.I suspect an open MEL (#1 eng HP bleed) played a role. I think the reported smoke, smell and heat were a combination of the PAX O2 generators plus an unpressurized vessel flying in warm ambient conditions. Plus the O2 generators read 200 degrees Fahrenheit at gate with the AARF equipment. If this turns out to be the case training on this would be helpful. Flight ZZZ1 to ZZZ2. Level FL370 for about 10-15 minutes just short of ZZZ3. Pressure page came up on lower ECAM and we saw that cabin pressure was rising quickly above 8,000 PSI. Both packs were amber. CA [requested priority handling] with ATC and we immediately began priority descent. FO was PF, CA was PM. We donned our O2 masks. ATC was very helpful and we were cleared to 9,000 ft quickly. CA was able to call FAs and tell them to sit and briefly what was happening. Cabin pressure was climbing as we descended, so that as we descended through 16,000 ft the cabin pressure reached 14,000 feet and the cabin oxygen masks deployed. We were level at 10,000 less than one minute later. Initially we were cleared to 9K and then lower, but I leveled at 10K due to weather and vectored toward ZZZ. CA and dispatch had discussed returning to ZZZ1. We had plenty of fuel and could transit at 10K. However, 3-5 minutes FA's called to complain about smoke and electrical smell in cabin, especially aft, so CA requested direct ZZZ. CA took over as PF and ATC gave us direct to ZZZ. CA requested single frequency approach and I requested AARF. We made normal visual (ILS back up) approach into ZZZ. Landed and stopped on RWY XXC. AARF looked for indications of fire/smoke. There were none. We taxied to gate X and AARF followed. All passengers were deplaned and firefighters boarded to check for fire indications. Aircraft had MEL XX-XXB for HP Valve. #1 Eng Bleed was placarded INOP.Do not send old aircraft with known MELs flying.
ASRS:1822164.s: The flight crew diverted Flight ZZZ1 from FL370 after a rapid cabin altitude rise triggered oxygen mask deployment and subsequent smoke reports. The pilot attributed the incident to an open MEL for the #1 engine HP bleed valve combined with oxygen generator heat in warm ambient conditions.

ASRS:1822179.n: At XA:30z [Dispatch name] received a phone call from [Ramp name] [who] said that there was undeclared Hazmat on Aircraft X. [Ramp name] relayed the info to me and I send the crew an ACARS message letting them know that there was 60 kg of dry ice in position X, can number YYY. They were not above the max so no other actions were required. Advised the crew that I was going to submit an [company] report and it wouldn't hurt if they did as well. We let the manager on duty know.
ASRS:1822179.s: Dispatch received notification from Ramp regarding 60 kg of undeclared dry ice on Aircraft X. Since the quantity was within limits, no further action was required, though the crew was advised to submit a report.

ASRS:1822205.n: There had been a ground stop for passing storms to the east, which were now 1/3 of the way between ZZZ and ZZZ1. The Captain gave a briefing and asked the Flight Attendants to remain seated the entire flight due to the cells we'd be flying around and the potential for turbulence. He also made this part of his welcome aboard announcement.We took off and were given a 090 heading, transitioning north of the group of cells. This group of cells gave us a small option north toward ZZZ2 VOR and a small option south between cells. Neither path had a significant advantage over the other.Once we were abeam the northern track, ATC gave us a hole they depicted on their radar to our 1 o'clock position. We opted to continue straight, but ATC said straight looked worse to them. We conversed back and forth with them and the hole appeared to our right and clear skies on the back side. We maneuvered right, then left to make a perpendicular path through the hole. The bottom of the hole was higher than our altitude and we were given a climb from 17,000 to FL210. We tried to establish this climb at 250 kts. to stay slow for possible turbulence. This was made difficult by the fact we had an MEL for the speed bug. The speed bug jumped from the upper 200s into the lower 300s, back and forth throughout the flight. It was distracting and was the first time either of us had experienced this particular anomaly in nearly four years. Just prior to penetration, we could see heavy lightning coming from the cells immediately left of our path, extending toward the area we were originally going toward.As we climbed to FL210, we penetrated the lower portion of the hole and into IMC. Throughout the encounter, we had moderate turbulence and heavy to extreme rain. Our ice detection caution message activated, as well.We estimate the pass took 30 to 45 seconds to transition. I tried to transmit to ATC not to send anyone behind us, but never received a response.Once in clear air, I tried ATC again and they said they'd been trying to reach us to say the hole had closed up on their scope. We never their transmission either.In discussion after passing into clear air, neither of us felt we'd encountered hail. The sound of the rain striking the window and body of the aircraft were consistent with heavy to extreme rain.I checked on the Flight Attendants to make sure they were ok and to make sure the passengers were ok, and everyone was. We landed without incident and discovered damage during the walk around.The first area I noticed was the radome. There were extensive areas where the paint had been removed and the composite material underneath was exposed. There were three areas where horizontal slices in the composite material were visible. There was at least one area where a circular area was compromised. Most of the damaged paint and material were on the upper half of the radome. There was one hole that was previously covered during the preflight inspection that was now exposed due to speed tape coming off the aircraft. We conducted numerous, slow and methodical visual inspections of the exterior of the aircraft over the course of the next two hours. The only other damage was an unidentified antenna on the top of the aircraft. It was located aft of the VHF 1 antenna and forward of the upper beacon. POH and PRM (Pilot's Reference Manual) searches failed to produce an identity to this antenna, and might possibly be a wifi antenna installed after manufacturer documents were printed.The Captain notified [Maintenance Control], the Chief Pilots, and Dispatch and briefed them on the incident and the status of the aircraft. Our Contract Maintenance arrived about an hour later and began making an evaluation of the damage. Our return flight was eventually cancelled and we rode the brakes for Ground Personnel while they repositioned the aircraft. We left the aircraft with Maintenance and proceeded to the hotel. After the flight, the Captain and I debriefed our flight and the incident. The flight attendants and the passengers were secured at the time due to crew briefings and the announcement that the seat belt sign would stay on and the flight attendants would remain seated throughout the flight. As previously noted, we had north and south options that were basically equal. Since our radar conflicted somewhat with ATC, we applied their observations into our decision making process in accordance with good CRM procedures. We had convection on our left and right sides and clear blue skies ahead. Our ability to climb over the IMC we entered could have been better facilitated if we began our climb sooner, however there was a small layer that obstructed our view and we were too close to the hole when the height of that IMC was determined. Again, this was further complicated by not having our heading bug to help with pitch reference and avoid a lower than desired speed or increasing over the turbulence penetration speed.
ASRS:1822205.s: The flight crew penetrated a storm cell while climbing from 17,000 feet to FL210, encountering turbulence, rain, and ice despite ATC radar guidance. Subsequent inspection revealed extensive radome damage and an exposed antenna, leading to flight cancellation and maintenance evaluation.

ASRS:1822302.n: I was assigned a service check on Aircraft X while doing the check on the log book I had a inbound write up in the log book gasper vent above storage compartment forward side #3, 4 popped out [of] business class. The job was not a monitor and challenge item. While trying to gain access to the air outlet distribution valve I looked at the AMM and the instructions were not sufficient enough so I looked for some type of access so I opened the cover for the r2 escape slide inflation reservoir bottle and saw small access though that compartment while sticking my arm though the compartment the inflation reservoir bottle was deployed.
ASRS:1822302.s: A mechanic performing a service check on Aircraft X deployed an R2 escape slide inflation reservoir bottle while reaching through its cover to access an air outlet distribution valve. The deployment occurred because the AMM instructions were insufficient, leading the mechanic to use an unintended access point.

ASRS:1822310.n: Left off email list from [Manufacturer's] EHM (Engine Health Monitoring) engine notification of potential EGT (Exhaust Gas Temperature gauge) error. The EGT thermocouple leads were found to be loose on all four probes causing erratic readings. No ready visibility on this modification. The desktop was acting up beyond being slow, multiple windows opening and some closing or moving resulting in very slow response with any usable information. The cause was found to be a screen saver disable function that had to be shut down by IT.
ASRS:1822310.s: A mechanic reported loose EGT thermocouple leads on all four probes causing erratic readings, while a separate IT issue with a screen saver function caused desktop performance problems. The engine error was corrected, and the computer issue was resolved by disabling the screen saver.

ASRS:1822314.n: Prior to [the] flight, I was coming off of a previous flight that was on maintenance delay and right after that, lunch. Due to the tight assignment that I was assigned, I was stressed out. This caused me to forget to do my arrival walk around. Once plane arrived, I immediately scanned the offload. After completion of offload I sent two of my agents to run [flight load]. This left me to start the onload with one agent. Once I started the on load, it was weight restricted. I proceeded to load the plane according to the load plan. Upon completing F1 & F2, I started to the aft eventually running out of space, due to restriction. I directed my team to go to the fwd bin, in which I myself moved bags accordingly from F1 to F2. I proved to load the remaining bags in F1. Once I finished the on load I had to call [Manager] due to weight restrictions. I also directed one of my agents to notify the Captain to release the parking brake and let them know that I was contacting [Manager] for weight restriction. After talking to [Manager] for about 5-10 minutes, I immediately got into my push back and proceeded to push the flight out while forgetting to do my walk around.I realized the event occurred, once being notified my Management. The event occurred due to one of my agents placing a vitamin water bottle on the main landing gear upon arrival.The aircraft had to do an emergency landing due to the water bottle being on the main nose gear, which caused the tires not to go in. [Management] notified my crew and I and told us what happened and why it happened. One of the agents admitted that she placed the water bottle upon arrival but forgot that she placed it there.
ASRS:1822314.s: A ramp agent placed a vitamin water bottle on the main landing gear, preventing the nose gear tires from retracting and causing an emergency landing. The reporter admitted that stress from a tight schedule led to skipping the arrival walk-around, which would have detected the obstruction.

ASRS:1822343.n: On a flight intended for ZZZ to ZZZ1, I noticed a little way into the cruise portion of the flight that my hydraulic pressure was low. I confirmed that the hydraulic pump switch was in the ON position, and then cycled the switch to see if this would resolve the problem. When I did that, the radio stack lost power with the switch in the ON position and the pump did not activate. Moving the switch to the OFF position, the radio stack returned to life. I performed this action again with the same results: with the pump switch in the ON position, the radios died, but in the OFF position the radios returned to life. I imagined that the pump system had shorted out somehow and left the switch OFF and used the manual pump handle to restore pressure. At that point, I decided not to fly all the way to ZZZ1 but instead to ZZZ2, which was somewhat closer (although still an hour ahead) and where the propeller was scheduled to be inspected the next day, thinking to repair the pump at that same time.Flight continued normally after this for some time, until I noticed that the landing light switch was in the ON position, and I moved to turn that switch off. When I turned off the landing light switch, the radios again failed. Recycling the landing light, radio master, and master switches did nothing. The next day, the Mechanic discovered that the battery terminal connector was broken, not the hydraulic pump, and it was this that explained the electrical failures.The problem had actually started before the flight: the landing immediately prior to this flight had resulted in a significant nose wheel shimmy due to the castering nose wheel not being aligned with the longitudinal axis of the plane (This can happen in this plane when the nose wheel has been down in the water and it casters, during a water takeoff there is no runway to naturally realign it). The shimmy had probably caused a pre-existing crack in the terminal connector to nearly, but not completely, open the circuit. So the engine start, taxi, takeoff and climb were normal, but additional vibration and heat caused the crack to spread until finally it broke completely. So at first there were wonky partial failures and then a total failure later in the flight.
ASRS:1822343.s: The pilot experienced electrical failures during cruise caused by a broken battery terminal connector, initially misdiagnosed as a hydraulic pump short. The connector failure resulted from vibration due to a nose wheel shimmy on the previous landing, which widened a pre-existing crack.

ASRS:1822382.n: Forgot to look for landing traffic. I have never done that before. Got distracted? Pulled out onto the runway with a small aircraft on very short final. He did a go around. It was very close. Glad one of us was awake. I pulled off the runway onto the grass.
ASRS:1822382.s: A pilot forgot to check for landing traffic and entered the runway while a small aircraft was on short final, causing the other pilot to execute a go-around. The pilot attributed the near-miss to distraction and subsequently exited the runway onto the grass.

ASRS:1822407.n: I was holding short of the runway and heard a radio call that a small aircraft was on a 2 mile final straight in. I thought I heard Runway 31, and I was holding short on 31 and had no visual sight of the small aircraft. I heard him call again a 1 mile final, and I still had no visual sight. I looked up and down the runway both ways made sure we were clear and felt I had plenty of time to takeoff before he came into land. As I took off on Runway 31 I saw him inbound on Runway 13. Immediately I turned right and got out of his way.Reflecting on it, I should not have taken the runway. Even though I could not see a plane in either direction, knowing there was a plane on final I should've held short and waited for him to land. I haven't had a chance to review the recording, if possible, so even though I heard Runway 31, and I knew that I had plenty of time to takeoff based on the visual site to final, it may have been confirmation bias. The pilot may have said 13, and I heard 31. Regardless, I will never again take the runway when someone is on final.
ASRS:1822407.s: The pilot holding short of Runway 31 took off after hearing a small aircraft on final, believing it was for Runway 31, but discovered the aircraft was actually landing on Runway 13. The pilot immediately turned right to avoid a collision and attributed the error to confirmation bias regarding the runway clearance.

ASRS:1822421.n: I am a Private Pilot working on my commercial ticket. I need dual time in complex so my Instructor and I decided to fly from ZZZ1 to ZZZ, do a full-stop taxi-back and return to ZZZ1. I picked up VFR flight following en route and talked with ZZZ2 Approach and ZZZ3 Approach. Approximately 10 miles from ZZZ, ZZZ3 switched me to advisory so I called ZZZ Tower. Tower instructed me to enter a right base for Runway XX and report a 2 mile right base. There was one other aircraft also intending to land at ZZZ, who was also going to be reporting a base.I don't recall exactly what Tower said when I called my 2 mile right base, but was instructed to look for traffic. I assumed the traffic would be closer to the airport than me, considering that they had entered the pattern prior to my arrival in the Class Delta airspace. They had reported a 2 mile base before I reported mine. I looked 12:00 to 3:00 (straight ahead and along to the numbers) but could not see any traffic. I glanced at the ADS-B traffic on my iPad but did not see any markings there to indicate traffic (aircraft do not require ADS-B in the area at ZZZ). Finally, I saw traffic a few hundred ft. away from me, at my 11:00, at just a slightly lower altitude. This traffic was flying a significantly wider base than is standard (more than 1/2 to 1 mile from the runway threshold). I initiated an immediate 90 deg left turn, then flew a 270 right turn to enter the final approach.When Tower asks me and other traffic to report a 2 mile right base, I am assuming that I will have a 1/2 to 1 mile final, and that I am just on an extended base leg. I'm wondering if the other pilot flew to a 2 mile final, and then called that as their 2 mile base. I know ZZZ is a Class Delta, but I don't believe they get any supporting radar from ZZZ3. If they were using their eyes to sequence us, then their advisories were unhelpful at best. I don't believe that ZZZ Tower had any accurate idea of where the traffic in the air was at any moment. ZZZ was unaware of how close we came to a collision, and didn't seem to care when I told them I was turning onto a downwind, and then doing a 180 to final. I am the Pilot in Command so [I] take full responsibility for my actions, which were correct in that moment to avoid a collision, but I received no further instructions, which would have been an issue if there had been anybody on a straight-in.In the future, I will be more cognizant of scanning left and right when looking for traffic ahead on a right base. I will be less dependent on Towers with no radar backup to provide me with accurate traffic advisories, or any at all. I believe that Tower Controllers need to be more cognizant of where the traffic is in the air so they can provide better traffic advisories. If they aren't sure where an aircraft is, they should be telling the number 2 airplane to keep a wide scan, rather than acting like everybody is flying a standard pattern.
ASRS:1822421.s: A private pilot and instructor flying a complex aircraft into ZZZ experienced a near collision with another aircraft on a non-standard wide base leg. The pilot attributed the incident to the non-radar tower's inability to accurately sequence traffic and the other pilot's deviation from standard pattern entry.

ASRS:1822426.n: I departed runway XY to rejoin XZ pattern which was the active runway & pattern. On the crosswind leg at approximately 400 - 500 ft a significant coolant leak was detected in the cabin and coolant was observed running down side of fuselage & door on pilot side. I turned 180 degree and declared an emergency. With an assumption of complete coolant loss, low altitude, and a potential loss of engine I announced and proceeded to land on Taxiway C as the best and safest option. I know this airport well and Taxiway C is rarely ever used. Any other option would have required another 90 degree turn.
ASRS:1822426.s: The pilot departed runway XY and detected a significant coolant leak at 400–500 ft on the crosswind leg. Declaring an emergency due to potential engine loss, the pilot turned 180 degrees and landed on Taxiway C to avoid further maneuvers.

ASRS:1822443.n: We spotted a drone going in the opposite direction of our plane. We were about 2 miles north of CCR at 6,500 ft. MSL and the drone was about 500-1000 ft. below us and about 1000 feet horizontally from us flying south.
ASRS:1822443.s: Pilots reported spotting a drone flying south approximately 1,000 feet horizontally and 500–1,000 feet below their aircraft while at 6,500 ft MSL, 2 miles north of CCR. The drone was traveling in the opposite direction of the plane.

ASRS:1822445.n: I landed and was given taxi instructions to the ramp that included two runway crossings while still rolling on the runway. I was told to exit on [Taxiway] 1 and cross [Runway] XXL on [Taxiway] 2 and hold short of [Runway] XXR. I exited and rolled to hold short of XXL and verified that I was cleared to cross. I crossed and continued on 2 to XXR. Before XXR, I asked if I could taxi via 3 [and] 4 to the ramp, which was incorrect. I needed to taxi to 4X. I didn't recall getting instructions beyond holding short of XXR prior. After resolving some confusion, the tower controller told me to taxi on XXR and 4X to the ramp. That is what I heard. I read it back and was partially stepped on and someone said something else. The tower controller said 'what' then proceeded to talk to other traffic. At this point I was taxiing on the runway and was slightly thrown off. I exited the runway and was on the non movement area ramp. I continued to monitor the frequency until shutting down and didn't hear my callsign again. It was a confusing sequence from getting the instructions on the rollout and given two different runway crossings with two different instructions. It would have been nice to have been given time to clear the runway and then take down instructions when I wasn't still focused on the landing during a critical phase of flight. Simple taxi instructions such as one taxiway to the ramp or one runway crossing isn't too hard to remember but still hard during a critical phase of flight. However, two runway crossings while rolling and complex instructions were confusing. The controller had a high work load and asking for conformation on the runway crossing probably didn't help her but I felt like I needed to verify. Then the confusion on my end didn't help crossing XXR. Being told to taxi via XXR weren't the instructions I was thinking of getting and made me second guess crossing the runway. Coming to a stop and asking for more clarification on frequency would've been the best thing to do. XXR wasn't a runway in use at the time and I cleared the area so I felt comfortable to cross, along with being told to taxi via XXR, I believed I had been cleared onto the runway.
ASRS:1822445.s: The pilot received complex taxi instructions with two runway crossings while still rolling after landing, causing confusion. Miscommunication regarding the route led to the pilot taxiing on an active runway before exiting to the ramp, though no collision occurred.

ASRS:1822464.n: I was practicing my aerobatic routine in Aerobatic Practice Area (APA) waivered airspace just north of HGR and had a ground observer. The airspace NOTAM was active and the area is depicted on a sectional chart and is in software for current navigational systems. However, my concern is that I'm getting traffic coming through the airspace.I feel there are a few things that could be done to enhance the safety of my current operation. I'm writing you because I'm concerned the FAA will just close it down if I suggest there is a safety issue. The current waiver requires me to monitor Potomac Approach during my operation. That possibly may help, but sometimes there is so much chatter that it would be difficult to catch a call and their main purpose is to keep IFR traffic out of my waivered airspace. In the past I would monitor HGR Tower and they were more helpful because they would look for traffic and be able to warn VFR traffic that they were communicating with also. My aircraft does not have the ability to monitor 2 frequencies simultaneously, so I'm currently only monitoring Potomac Approach as required by the waiver. As you know, TFR's are depicted boldly on digital navigational software devices. Could 'Hot' APA's also be depicted boldly like TFR's? That would be a more obvious warning to other aircraft than just a drawing on a chart. Obviously, all pilots should be familiar with published NOTAMS in their route of flight, but we know that doesn't always happen. Also allowing HGR Tower to call out possible traffic conflicts would be helpful but please don't let the FAA close the area again for months until they have time to amend the paperwork! I did contact a representative from Potomac Approach about my concern and am waiting for a reply. Even if he is able to allow me to monitor HGR Tower instead of Potomac Approach, it would still be helpful if Hot APA's could show up as obvious as TFR's on digital navigational aids. Your consideration in this matter would be greatly appreciated. Thank you.
ASRS:1822464.s: A pilot practicing aerobatics in a waived Aerobatic Practice Area north of HGR reported concerns about VFR traffic entering the airspace. The pilot attributed the risk to limited frequency monitoring capabilities and requested that "Hot" APAs be displayed more prominently on digital navigation systems like TFRs.

ASRS:1822465.n: I was flying on an instrument flight plan from SEE in San Diego to ZZZ1 outside of Denver and filed via Foreflight. The flight plan of direct was accepted but I assumed a SID. Given that SEE was MVFR I studied the departures including the Mission Bay Two (obstacle) Departure which seemed the most likely. I noted that this was a procedure which required tracking multiple radials of different VOR's, and I know from experience that modern glass panels (Garmin G600 and Garmin GTN 750) do not recognize these departures and they must be manually configured tuning the VOR's and radials.Shortly before departure, Foreflight via cellular connection gave me an expected route which was an odd route as it contained over 20 waypoints, but I programmed it into the Garmin GTN750 after engine start. There was no SID assigned. Normally when a SID is assigned its included in the expected route. So, I assumed SEE direct the MZB VOR. The weather was good VFR. So, I did not brief terrain clearance. When I called Ground Control, I was told it was a complicated route and asked if I was ready to copy it all down. I also advised that I had also received the route electronically. To make it faster I wrote the expected route on my knee board and followed along as the Controller gave it to me. I believe the route was the same, but I cannot rule out confirmation bias. I read the route back and received a 'readback correct'I took off on runway heading and noted that if I made an immediate turn to MZB I would not be able to out climb the terrain so continued on runway heading. It was VFR and I had the terrain in sight at all times. When I was handed off to Departure I was asked by the Approach Controller why I was not turning right. (presumably to follow the obstacle departure). She further immediately called a terrain alert. I advised the terrain was in sight and was not a factor. The Approach Controller then directed me to fly a heading and advised of a possible pilot deviation. It [is] possible that the Controller specifically called out the obstacle departure and I missed it due to confirmation bias. However, I believe the obstacle departure was not mentioned either due to it being a VFR day or common practice for the field and part of an unduly complicated clearance. The obstacle departure definitely did not populate as the Foreflight expected clearance like other SID's. I have screen shots of this. As a corrective action, I believe that obstacle clearances need to be built with waypoints and published like any other SID so they worked with automated clearance delivery mechanisms and integrated avionics
ASRS:1822465.s: A pilot departing San Diego (SEE) in VFR conditions followed a complex electronic route instead of the required Mission Bay Two obstacle departure due to avionics limitations and confirmation bias. This resulted in a terrain alert and a possible pilot deviation when the pilot failed to turn right as expected by the Approach Controller.

ASRS:1822469.n: After entering Runway XX for takeoff, stopped on runway to align aircraft to center line, released brakes, applied throttle gradually to ensure aircraft stays on center line. When applied full throttle, the aircraft turned left (due to left turning tendency), to correct that applied right rudder correction. However the aircraft turned more left towards the edge of runway and felt risk of takeoff. So pulled throttle off completely, applied brakes and steered safely into grass.Tower contacted me immediately to check, I was safe. Then asked me to check if any of the tires were flat/punctured. I confirmed looking at both the tires, they were not flat/punctured. Tower provided progressive taxi to parking. After parking, control tower provided a contact number for flight instructor to contact them. Also a person from rescue team came and checked with me about what happened and noted my information, checked tires and aircraft for any visible damage. Everything was found ok. Also there were no damages to airport property. My student pilot lost directional control of the aircraft during the takeoff roll on Runway XX at ZZZ and ended up rejecting the takeoff, however, he ended up in the grass on the side of the runway before coming to a complete stop. He was on a solo cross country flight ZZZ1-ZZZ-ZZZ2-ZZZ1.I was immediately contacted by my student who notified me of the event and he told me to contact the ZZZ Tower, which I did as soon as I was done talking to him. The controller said that it appeared as if my student lost rudder control. He also said that neither the aircraft nor the airport property sustained any damage.My student informed me that the aircraft was veering to the left slightly and he tried to correct it with right rudder. After the application of right rudder, the aircraft veered even further left, which is when he decided to abort the takeoff by pulling the throttle to idle and applying brakes. The aircraft was turned too far left to safely turn it back to the runway center line while applying brakes and therefore, the aircraft ended up in the grass. My student then taxied back onto the runway and exited at the next taxiway. The controller gave him progressive taxi to parking where the aircraft was inspected.Based on the description of this event from both the controller and my student, I suspect that my student inadvertently tapped the left toe brake while applying more right rudder to keep the aircraft on the runway center line. As a result, the aircraft quickly veered to the left.
ASRS:1822469.s: A student pilot lost directional control during takeoff on Runway XX at ZZZ, veering left into the grass after applying right rudder and inadvertently tapping the left toe brake. The takeoff was rejected with no damage to the aircraft or airport property.

ASRS:1822478.n: I was on Ground Control and Clearance Delivery, I read clearances as normal and coordinated flow times. The facility both Tower and Radar were evacuated and went to ATC Zero for COVID-19 Cleaning. I instructed all IFR aircraft on frequency to contact ARTCC for IFR services and broadcast it on the ATIS frequency. I did not specifically tell the IFR aircraft that had already been read clearances while the airport was controlled to hold for release. After the facility had been evacuated and the airport deemed uncontrolled, an IFR aircraft departed without coordinating with ARTCC. I would recommend a procedural amendment to the local contingency plan to broadcast that all IFR aircraft that had been issued IFR clearances to hold for release and contact ARTCC or FSS to coordinate their departures prior to taking off. Received pre departure clearance from ZZZ clearance. Clearance informed us the Tower would be closing due to the Tower getting cleaned. Departures/Arrivals and Ground and Tower would be closed. They asked if we would be gone before then and we said probably not. They did not give us a hold for release instructions. They gave us Center frequency before the tower closed. We finished, pushed back and broadcast over CTAF we would be taxiing out. We attempted to contact Center several times before departing. We called in the blind on CTAF as we took the runway and departed. We contacted Center at around 1,500 feet and continued on our way. 10 minutes later Center informed me to contact Center via the telephone for a possible pilot deviation. It is unknown what the actual deviation may have been if there was a pilot deviation.
ASRS:1822478.s: Ground Control and an IFR pilot were involved during a facility evacuation for COVID-19 cleaning. The pilot departed without a hold-for-release instruction after the tower closed, contacted Center at 1,500 feet, and was later notified of a possible pilot deviation.

ASRS:1822494.n: On approach in to ZZZ, we were cleared direct ZZZZZ intersection and to descend to 3,000 feet There was a thunderstorm cell between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 (Final Approach Fix) on the approach to Runway XXR to ZZZ. We asked ZZZ TRACON (Approach Control) for direct ZZZZZ1 to avoid the thunderstorm cell. We were anticipating a visual approach to Runway XXR because the most recent ATIS (weather report) was reporting only Few and Scattered clouds at the airport with adequate visibility for a visual approach. The TRACON Controller asked if we would be able to 'get the airport?'My First Officer and I were slightly confused by his phraseology and tried to discuss what the Controller meant. At that time, we were within a few miles from ZZZZZ and just about to level off at 3,000 feet. The Autopilot Mode Control panel was in Vertical Speed (Altitude Acquire) and LNAV to ZZZZZ. I was anticipating going to ZZZZZ1 and was ready to change the altitude to 2,800 feet in MCP for the autopilot. We were then cleared on a 160 degree heading to join the final approach course of 128, and cleared for the approach. I didn't hear the Controller say 'maintain 3,000 feet until established.' I selected VOR/LOC and dialed 2,800 feet into the autopilot Mode Control Panel. Because we were in a descent and in Altitude Acquire, the autopilot continued to descend towards 2,800 feet.My First Officer said we were supposed to maintain 3,000 feet. I had missed that part of the clearance so I dialed 3,000 feet into the Mode Control Panel, but by that point the aircraft had descended below 3,000 feet and was continuing to descend and would not ever capture 3,000 feet. I was also trying to slow the aircraft and get it to capture the localizer. Seeing that we weren't going to level off, I tried to use Vertical Speed to make the aircraft climb back to 3,000 feet, but it was continuing to descend. Our descent was exacerbated by the fact that I still had the speedbrakes deployed almost to the flight [descent]. ZZZ TRACON (Approach Control) said he he had a low altitude alert and his MVA [Min Vector Altitude] was 2,800 feet. We were now at about 2,300 feet. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottles, started a climb and we decided to go missed approach. I finally stowed the speedbrakes, climbed to our clearance altitude and we then got re-vectored by ZZZ TRACON for another approach to Runway XXR and landed safely. We were being vectored around some weather coming into ZZZ and were given a descent to 3,000 feet and direct ZZZZZ outside of ZZZZZ1 on the ILS XXX. There was some confusion as ATC asked if we would be able to get the airport. I wasn't sure if he meant visually or altitude wise. After a pause, as I pondered his meaning, I responded that we were IMC. At the time, I didn't think we were high, so I assumed he meant visually. Just a couple miles outside of ZZZZZ, Captain asked for a turn to ZZZZZ1. I paused because I was anticipating a vector shortly to intercept the final approach course. I then asked ATC for the turn inbound, and ATC responded that he was just about to give us a vector and then provided the clearance. We were given a 160 heading to join and maintain 3,000 feet until established and cleared for the ILS to [Runway] XXR. This extra communication ultimately caused a delay in getting turned in. Because it all got really busy, I didn't see that Captain dialed in 2,800 feet. So, I don't think it acquired 3,000 feet and was now descending below it. Then I think 3,000 feet was reset into the MCP and yet the aircraft was still descending. All of this was happening while I was replying to ATC and I didn't realize what happened until after we talked about it later. We triggered a low altitude alert, and ATC informed us that we were to maintain 3,000 feet until established. I responded that we were correcting. Captain was climbing back up to 3,000 feet and we were slightly south of the localizer. I figured by the time we got back to 3,000 feet, we would then be high for the approach and not being established on the localizer, I said we should go-around. Captain agreed, and we did. This whole thing took me out of the Green, made me feel rushed and got behind in my responsibilities. A go-around was the best decision.
ASRS:1822494.s: During an ILS approach to Runway XXR at ZZZ, the flight crew descended below the cleared 3,000 feet due to autopilot mode confusion and delayed speedbrake retraction. This triggered a low altitude alert, prompting a missed approach and safe re-vectoring for another attempt.

ASRS:1822507.n: I was a bit frustrated that the Ops Agent wanted to leave 60+ plus customer bags due to the broken carousel at the front of the airport. Even with Dispatch approval for 10 late departure, the Ops Agent said higher ups wanted the flight to leave on time. It seemed a bit arbitrary. I believe I mistakenly released the parking [brake] during rudder pedal adjustment. I don't know what caused the aircraft to roll backwards. I applied [brakes] and the aircraft stopped about 12 feet back from original position. I observed no damage to Captain's pitot probe or angle of attack sensor. Ground Crew confirmed no damage. Safety walkaround completed. No damage. No injuries. No call from ATC. I am self-reporting to improve safety.
ASRS:1822507.s: The pilot reported that while adjusting rudder pedals, they likely released the parking brake, causing the aircraft to roll back 12 feet during pre-departure. A safety walkaround confirmed no damage to the aircraft or injuries, and no ATC contact was required.

ASRS:1822540.n: Primarily, en route ATC was task saturated the entire day working multiple frequencies while providing speed and vector control, versus sequencing traffic on the arrivals. On the leg from ZZZ to ZZZ1, we were handed off to ZZZ near the waypoint ZZZZZ. After multiple failed attempts to reach ATC, we returned to the previous frequency to try an alternate frequency. This frequency was very busy as ATC was working multiple frequencies and also providing multiple aircraft with vectors and speed control. We were given 10 degrees left. ATC told us to expect direct ZZZZZ1. As we approached ZZZZZ2, we tried multiple times to reach ATC on the frequency assigned. Unable to reach them we tried the alternate frequency multiple times with no success. Shortly after those attempts, ATC transmitted on Guard frequency for us to turn south immediately. We replied that we are turning south and had attempted to reach them multiple times on two separate frequencies. Their reply was, 'Yeah, right!' On (date) at approximately (time), we lost communication with Center, while on a vector and ended up in Special Use Airspace. About 10 minutes prior, we were switched to a frequency from previous Controller. We were unable to get contact on this frequency, so we went back to our previous assigned frequency and were given a new frequency. We were able to contact Center on this frequency. While with Center on this frequency, we were given a vector for spacing with an expectation to rejoin our arrival. After a few minutes, without hearing anything we began to query the Controller. We had no contact. We tried a few times, when the Captain said we should try the other frequency we were given earlier. As we switched over, we hear Center simulcasting on Guard, to come up. As we contacted Center, the Controller asked us where we had been and we explain that we were up on the frequency where they were talking to us earlier. The Controller then proceeds to give us a vector and tells us that we are in Special Use Airspace. Once we cleared the Airspace we continued with the arrival uneventfully.
ASRS:1822540.s: Pilots lost communication with en route ATC while being vectored, causing an inadvertent entry into Special Use Airspace. The incident resulted from ATC task saturation and frequency management issues, requiring a Guard frequency transmission to re-establish contact and exit the restricted area.

ASRS:1822554.n: Aircraft was dispatched to operate out of ZZZZ, a high altitude airport (+7900') in mountainous terrain with a faulty pressurization system. A subsequent failure of the Alternate channel during Takeoff or initial climb would NOT provide enough time to address the problem causing O2 mask deployment and a divert to an airport not currently served by the airline (assuming airport is not affected by volcanic activity). A return to departing airport would exceed oxygen/altitude time requirements for passengers making it impractical.
ASRS:1822554.s: The pilot reported that an aircraft with a faulty pressurization system was dispatched from high-altitude ZZZZ. A potential Alternate channel failure during takeoff would force an oxygen mask deployment and a divert to an unserved airport, as returning would exceed passenger oxygen time limits.

ASRS:1822583.n: Tonight I almost got hit by a plane. Before the incident happened, I was pulled off to the side in front of the gates, away from the roadway. I waited in front of the gates because I was waiting for a plane to cross the main taxi lane. I checked around me and the only thing by me was a fuel truck. All of a sudden, I heard a faint honking sound. As soon as I turned my head, I saw a plane turning in, right in front of me. I quickly pressed on the gas and drove as fast as I could. Once I cleared the airplanes path, I was really close to its wing tip. There were no wing walkers outside, or any signs of warning. I had no warning that a plane was coming in. The plane turned in without any clearance. As soon as I pulled into a safe spot, the wing walkers came out and told the plane to stop. Thankfully I didn't get hit, but knowing that my life was right before my eyes, terrified me to death.
ASRS:1822583.s: A ground vehicle driver nearly collided with an aircraft turning onto a taxi lane without clearance or wing walkers present. The driver accelerated to avoid the wing tip after hearing a faint horn, noting the plane entered the path without warning before being stopped by ground crew.

ASRS:1822603.n: During approach to Runway 2 into BMI, there are four bright lights approximately 0.5 miles from the approach end. They appear to be part of a sports complex. The lights appear to be PAPI lighting and in IMC conditions, such as low ceiling and/or visibility, and may cause spatial disorientation. Due to the proximity to the airport, we momentarily thought the runway environment was in sight. After cross checking flight instruments, we continued down another approximately 200 feet to where we saw the actual PAPI lights and runway environment, at approximately 800 feet. We landed following a stabilized approach and without further incident.There are four bright white lights approximately 0.5 from the approach end of runway 2 that appear to be PAPI lights on the same side as the real PAPIs. Suggest a NOTAM, remark, comment, or other publication should be made available to all airmen wishing to use the ILS, LOC, or RNAV (GPS) to Runway 2 at BMI.
ASRS:1822603.s: Pilots approaching Runway 2 at BMI mistook four bright lights from a nearby sports complex for PAPI lights in IMC conditions, causing momentary spatial disorientation. After cross-checking instruments and descending to 800 feet to locate the actual runway environment, they completed a stabilized landing without incident.

ASRS:1822607.n: After takeoff, in our climb, smoke was detected in the cockpit. The smoke was coming from the First Officer's yoke. We also started to have BAT DISCHARGE caution light come on multiple times. Followed appropriate check list and QRH procedures. Decided to go back to the airport. We got clearance to go directly to the airport and got vectors for ILS. All the appropriate procedures and check list were completed before landing, with verification of speeds and weight. After an uneventful landing, we did not need any further assistance, and went to our parking spot. Advised ATC due to smoke in cockpit. Returned to [departure airport]. QRH was read, approach was briefed and setup. Checklists were followed. Uneventful landing was made under maximum weight. Battery discharge light annunciated several times during the event. First Officer smelled electric burning, then noticed smoke. Caution light annunciation and battery discharge light noticed during normal scan. I should have waited and asked ATC to standby before announcing the aircraft condition. This would have given time for the crew to evaluate all resources and outcomes before making a decision.
ASRS:1822607.s: The crew detected smoke from the First Officer's yoke and battery discharge lights during climb, prompting a return to the departure airport. They followed QRH procedures, received ILS vectors, and executed an uneventful landing at maximum weight without requiring assistance.

ASRS:1822656.n: Landed 27L, exited on Y1. Directed to taxi on D4, then left on Bravo, then right to Mike. Delta taxiway is before Bravo and parallels it. We turned on Delta erroneously and was corrected by ground who gave us alternate taxi back instructions to turn right on MD-1, then MD-2 to Mike. No other implications noted.Signage was a factor and I misprioritized my tasks by completing after landing check before getting on long taxiway. After landing we exited 27L on taxiway Y1. We were given instructions to taxi left on D1, left on B, and then right on M to spot M. Instead of turning left on B, we turned left early on D. ATC caught the error at the same time we did and we received new taxi instructions to spot M. There was no conflict with other aircraft traffic. Bad crew situational awareness, bad signage in LFPG, language barrier. More situational awareness on the part of the crew. Better signage in LFPG.
ASRS:1822656.s: The flight crew erroneously turned onto Delta taxiway instead of Bravo at LFPG due to poor signage, language barriers, and misprioritized tasks. Ground ATC detected the error and issued corrected taxi instructions to reach the stand without traffic conflict.

ASRS:1822709.n: A full aircraft and all lavatory inop being told under 16,000. This violates the DOT requirement to have operable lavatories anytime an airplane is on the tarmac.
ASRS:1822709.s: The reporter stated that a full aircraft with all lavatories inoperative was held below 16,000 feet. This situation violated DOT requirements mandating operable lavatories whenever an airplane is on the tarmac.

ASRS:1822772.n: I was coming in to land. The landing seemed like it was going well until I hit the ground and turned to the left and ended up in the grass right next to the runway. Tower contacted me and I taxied out of the grass. My student did a solo and went off the runway. Maintenance had said they looked at the aircraft and it was fine to fly back. We flew back and later on [realized I] did [not] have any hard written conformation that the airplane was OK to fly. Currently maintenance department is trying to get a hold of the mechanic that did the inspection to get a written statement.
ASRS:1822772.s: The pilot and student landed an aircraft that veered left into grass, and the student later went off the runway during a solo. Although maintenance verbally cleared the aircraft for return flight, the pilot realized no written confirmation existed, prompting an investigation to obtain a written statement from the inspecting mechanic.

ASRS:1822783.n: After flying a stabilized RNAV RWY XX practice instrument approach to ZZZ and a normal flare and landing, the fixed nose gear of the airplane collapsed and the plane skidded to a halt on the runway. I believe that the landing gear failed because the strut suffered metal fatigue at or near its weld adjacent to the engine frame.
ASRS:1822783.s: The pilot landed an aircraft on Runway XX after a stabilized RNAV approach when the fixed nose gear collapsed, causing the plane to skid to a halt. The reporter attributes the failure to metal fatigue in the strut weld near the engine frame.

ASRS:1822798.n: When unloading airmail from Aircraft X staff discovered potential DG. The parcel has not been forwarded from ZZZ1, but is hold back until further notice.What is your opinion of the cause?It could be an old box reused, but we have to react on those label.I do not understand how this could be sent without any attention when it was placed on the pallet.What is your suggested corrective action?Please inform staff not to put boxes like these on pallets. When unloading airmail from Aircraft X staff discovered leaking oily substance from a parcel.The parcel is military mail, and it is not long ago we have had the same problem.The parcel was removed from other airmail, but have leaked on 3 other parcel. We will hold back the parcel at our warehouse until further notice.What is your opinion of the cause?It is potential dangerous with leaking oily substance in aircraft and shipper must know not to send oil like this.What is your suggested corrective action?Please inform shipper not to send parcel like this on passenger aircraft.
ASRS:1822798.s: Ground staff discovered a leaking oily substance from a military mail parcel while unloading airmail from Aircraft X, contaminating three other parcels. The reporter attributes the cause to improper shipping by the shipper and recommends holding the parcel while informing shippers not to send such items on passenger aircraft.

ASRS:1822799.n: During climbout we deviated multiple times to avoid convective buildups, which is normal and air traffic control helped us greatly. We experienced intermittent light turbulence in the climb as we deviated around heavy precipitation and convective cloud build ups that we were observing on weather radar.Our filed altitude was 41,000 feet, we were cleared to climb to 40,000 feet and were informed we would be cleared to climb once we were clear of some conflicting traffic.We leveled off at 40,000 feet and were clear of the convective thunderstorm buildups but were still in Instrument Meteorological Conditions (IMC). FO and I were discussing potentially climbing to 45,000 to get on top of the IMC. Approximately 30 minutes into the flight as we were level at 40,000 feet I heard a pop, looked up and saw the right forward windscreen was completely shattered. FO noticed it at the same time and I said get our oxygen masks on immediately. We donned our masks, advised ATC and asked for a descent and requested a diversion to the nearest airport with emergency services. Air traffic informed us it was ZZZ and we elected to divert there. We informed our passengers of the situation, to please be seated with the seat belts securely fastened and requested that if the oxygen masks deploy to please don them. I continued flying the aircraft as FO ran the QRH Emergency Checklist for a shattered windshield. FO then set up our flight management system for approach and landing into ZZZ as I guided us in.The rest of the descent, approach and landing went without incident. During climbout we deviated multiple times to avoid convective buildups, which is normal and air traffic control helped us greatly. We experienced intermittent light turbulence in the climb as we deviated around heavy precipitation and convective cloud build ups that we were observing on weather radar.Our filed altitude was 41,000 feet, we were cleared to climb to 40,000 feet and were informed we would be cleared to climb once we were clear of some conflicting traffic.We leveled off at 40,000 feet and were clear of the convective thunderstorm buildups but were still in Instrument Meteorological Conditions (IMC). The Captain and I were discussing potentially climbing to 45,000 to get on top of the IMC. Approximately 30 minutes into the flight as we were level at 40,000 feet I heard a pop, looked up and saw the right forward windscreen was completely shattered. We noticed it at the same time and I said get our oxygen masks on immediately. We donned our masks, advised ATC and asked for a descent and requested a diversion to the nearest airport with emergency services.
ASRS:1822799.s: The flight crew experienced a shattered right forward windscreen at 40,000 feet while in IMC during cruise. They donned oxygen masks, diverted to ZZZ, and landed safely after following the emergency checklist.

ASRS:1822806.n: The trouble started on a busy arrival into ZZZ trying to comply with approach's request to descend over 2,000 FPM for a crossing altitude of 11,000 [feet] at ZZZZZ from 17,000 [feet] at that point the trim actuator failed trying to comply. At that point it caused a warning horn affecting the ability to hear well in the cockpit. I missed a frequency. I heard and read back XXX.XX but I programed XXX.XY. After getting on XXX.XX I was given what I though was 2,000 [feet] and read back 2,000 [feet]. It was really 2,600 [feet]. I descended to 2100 as approach was clearing me for the approach and caught the low altitude. Approach told me low altitude alert and to maintain 2,600 [feet] until established on the localizer. I immediately climbed to 2,600 [feet]and joined the localizer.
ASRS:1822806.s: During a busy arrival, the pilot's trim actuator failed while descending, causing a warning horn that led to a frequency programming error and a misread altitude clearance. The pilot descended to 2,100 feet instead of 2,600 feet, triggered a low altitude alert, and subsequently climbed to the correct altitude before joining the localizer.

ASRS:1822808.n: When flying left traffic patterns for taxiway parallel [Runway] XX with a student pilot, a plane taking off a parallel Runway XX turned an early left crosswind at 300 AGL after we had turned our crosswind at 300 AGL in a helicopter. Upon hearing the radio call, I glanced over my left shoulder knowing their relative location upon climbout. I found them almost directly above and to my left making a left hand turn that was leading into our course. I immediately descended to approximately 150 AGL to build separation from the craft and turned to the right to avoid a collision course. I called out upon the radio to connect with the the other aircraft and no response was received from the other pilot, who I came to find out was a solo student. The plane was flying extremely tight patterns cutting off the flow of helicopter traffic that is typically flying on the adjacent taxiway. With two flight schools based at ZZZ, there is a lot of student traffic. Procedures and policies have been put in place, but lack of situational awareness from students causes a lot of mishaps such as the events of today.
ASRS:1822808.s: A helicopter instructor and student flying left traffic at 300 AGL descended to 150 AGL and turned right to avoid a solo student pilot in a fixed-wing aircraft who turned early left at 300 AGL. The reporter attributed the near collision to the student's lack of situational awareness and tight pattern flying.

ASRS:1822817.n: On takeoff, we were told to fly heading 230 (runway heading) to 3,000. As a new pilot flying, I was at the controls in the right seat flying the airplane to our directed heading and altitude. Upon reaching 3,000 feet, the autopilot gave all indications of capture and blew through its selected modes. The climb rate maintained over 2,000 before the controls were taken by the Captain. Upon reaching 3,300 feet we entered at steep turn to a heading of 160 and attempted to continue a descent as the trim was running all the way to the trim up position and airspeed was increasing. We slowed the aircraft down while simultaneously disengaging the autopilot and gaining positive control of the aircraft. This was critical because an aircraft with lost communications was above us at 4,000 feet. Once we cleared of the traffic the flight went smooth for the rest of the way. An improvement that would have helped this situation is more automation management as well as a full panel on the copilot side which would have helped notice the climb rate continuing rather than capturing. We later perceived the autopilot to failed and continued the flight without any further issues. Copilot was flying on autopilot. Alt sel was armed. Gave all indications of capturing but did not. I took control and returned to the correct altitude. Approach Control Supervisor advised there was no conflict in airspace with other traffic. Remainder of flight was uneventful.
ASRS:1822817.s: The copilot flying on autopilot during takeoff experienced a mode failure where the aircraft overshot 3,000 feet to 3,300 feet despite altitude capture indications. The captain took control to correct the climb and trim issues, avoiding a conflict with traffic at 4,000 feet, and the flight continued uneventfully.

ASRS:1822822.n: About 1-1:15 hours before landing into Country I smelled a strong pungent smell and therefore called my co-worker to come up and smell the odor. She smelled odor, we contacted Captain and we then continued to check first class passengers electronic devices for overheated batteries etc..and asked passengers to check their bags in the overhead compartments.We checked ovens and coffee makers and odor was not concentrated in that area. The odor was concentrated in fwd aircraft left jump seat area and lavatory. As we were descending the odor got stronger. The odor was not electrical more like an overheated odor sweet but irritating to the eyes, throat. I had a headache very quickly and nauseous. Very pungent on descent. Couldn't breath had to get on oxygen. At descent, odor entered cockpit. During time in Country, mechanics were looking for problem. They discovered catering papers behind coffee makers that looked brown and smelled liked burned paper this could have caused a fire midair however that was NOT the odor I smelled. This would have been another issue.
ASRS:1822822.s: Cabin crew detected a strong, irritating odor during descent into Country I, which entered the cockpit and forced the reporter to use oxygen. Mechanics later found burned catering paper behind coffee makers, but the reporter stated this was not the source of the odor experienced in flight.

ASRS:1822842.n: On short final, we received a 'Too Low Flaps', I directed a go-around, subsequent landing was uneventful. We discussed what contributed to event and agreed that the lack of depth perception of the flap gauge for the MAX versus the NG gauge made it difficult to synthesize. I now point to the gauge to bring extra attention to the gauge.
ASRS:1822842.s: The flight crew received a 'Too Low Flaps' warning on short final and executed a go-around, followed by an uneventful landing. The pilot attributed the event to the MAX flap gauge's lack of depth perception compared to the NG, prompting a new habit of pointing to the gauge for verification.

ASRS:1822860.n: It is impossible to egress the jetway at Gate XX at MYR.
