The jetway doors lock from the inside, and there is no exit button or push bar that will allow you to exit the jetway into the terminal. These codes are obviously not available to Passengers or even Crew Members. You must enter the security code to exit the terminal door even from the inside. Same thing for the door to the ramp at the bottom of the jetway. These are the only jetways in the system that I am aware of that lock you in at the top of the jetway. In the event an evacuation from the aircraft is necessary for a fire, smoke or some other emergency, people are going to pile up in the jetway with no means of escape into the terminal. Exit buttons that unlock the terminal doors from the inside allowing egress from a jetway that has become dangerous should be installed immediately.
ASRS:1822860.s: Crew members reported that jetway doors at Gate XX, MYR, lock from the inside without accessible exit buttons or push bars, trapping occupants. The reporter stated this design prevents escape into the terminal or ramp during an emergency evacuation, creating a safety hazard requiring immediate installation of internal unlock mechanisms.

ASRS:1822878.n: During landing roll out, using max autobrake, transfer of control, stowing the thrust reversers, at a relatively high speed, Tower issued taxi instruction of turn left on Taxiway 1 hold short of Taxiway 2. As I was concentrating on flying the airplane (decelerating on landing rolling out) I only heard Left on 1 and 2. As I vacated the runway on Taxiway 1 Ground called us but was stepped on and was unreadable. When vacating taxiway 1 and clearing the hold short line for the runway there is barely room to even hold short of taxiway 2 thus, I never expected for that to even be a possibility. I taxied out onto taxiway 2 and then saw Aircraft Y under tow on taxiway 2. He was far away and there was no threat of a collision but there was a conflict now on 2. Ground advised us we were supposed to hold short of 2, sounded annoyed, and then told the Aircraft Y tow crew to pull into the run-up area which they did and told us to continue which we did with no further complications. Receiving taxi instructions during a landing roll out while a pilot is still 'flying' the jet and concentrating is definitely a threat I will address moving forward in my briefings. Daytime/VMC arrival into ZZZ. Normal landing/rollout, aircraft decelerating brakes MAX, Tower issued clearance to exit via Taxiway 1, hold short Taxiway 2, contact Ground. Clearance heard/understood/read back accurately by First Officer, misheard/misunderstood by Captain as 'exit Taxiway 1, Taxiway 2, contact Ground.' First Officer unaware of misunderstanding. Clearing runway, VHF 1 switched to Ground. Ground transmission blocked by simultaneous transmission of third aircraft, essentially unreadable to First Officer. Captain still exiting left on 1, continued left turn onto 2. First Officer assumed transmission heard/understood sufficiently by Captain to continue taxi. Turning onto 2, CA noted Aircraft Y under tow opposite direction on Taxiway 2, stopped aircraft well short of conflict. Reprimanded by ground for failing to hold short Taxiway 2. Tow crew directed to turn into holding pad, allow Aircraft Y to pass. Conflict resolved, ground directed taxi to parking via 2.Breakdown in CRM/communication/First Officer verification. Contributing factors included: ATC taxi instructions issued during high workload period (short field landing, brakes MAX, transfer of controls). Minimal length of Taxiway 2 resulted in a) limited area to clear runway and still hold short taxiway A, and b) insufficient time to query ground regarding blocked transmission and/or verify with Captain understood taxi instructions.
ASRS:1822878.s: During landing rollout, the Captain misheard a Tower instruction to hold short of Taxiway 2 and entered it, causing a conflict with a towed aircraft. The incident resulted from high workload, a blocked Ground transmission, and a breakdown in Crew Resource Management where the First Officer failed to verify the clearance.

ASRS:1822920.n: On the night of July XX, the lavatories stopped working. I made the decision to divert the aircraft to ZZZ to get the lavs serviced. Once on the ground in ZZZ I was contacted by NAME and the manager on duty of Operations Control. NAME was not professional during the call, placing all of the blame on me for the situation. I unfortunately had to deal with the situation because the lavatories were never serviced in ZZZ1. I was upset, annoyed, and disappointed by the attitude of the director of Operations Control. I was berated and interrogated by him for the decision to divert. What was needed in this situation was assistance from Operations Control and Dispatch so the flight could continue. Due to the unprofessional attitude from Management and the blame being placed on me for the situation I was unable to sleep soundly when arriving in ZZZ2. when we departed ZZZ2 I felt fine, but as the flight continued I started to become fatigued. When I landed in ZZZ1 I called Crew Scheduling and told them I was fatigued for Flight XXXX to ZZZ3, and removed myself form the flight for the safety of the passengers. This was caused by ZZZ not servicing the LAV, leading to a diversion, and the lack of professionalism from Operations Control leading to lack of sleep.
ASRS:1822920.s: The pilot diverted due to inoperative lavatories, but Operations Control blamed the decision and failed to arrange repairs, causing sleep loss. This fatigue led the pilot to remove themselves from the subsequent flight for safety reasons.

ASRS:1822957.n: We got to the plane and had found out the ramp was closed due to storms in the area. The plane was hot so we started the APU to cool it off. Boarding had already started. We right away started to smell dirty sock smell. We went to the aircraft odor in the QRH. It had us turn bleed and packs off. Plane was getting hot. Called MX and they had us Aircraft Smoke Odor Fumes report. We asked to deplane. Once the pax were off, we assess the crew. Pilots were fine. All flight attendants had some symptoms reported in that form. Paramedics were called and recommended they get assessed at the hospital. On predeparture at gate in ZZZ with passengers boarding flight attendants called flight crew complaining of dirty sock smell from APU. We ran the QRH Aircraft Odor/ Toxic Substance/ Volatile Liquid checklist on page XX-XY. We then deplaned the passengers. While deplaning we called maintenance and filled out Report. Flight attendants complained of symptoms so we called paramedics to aircraft. Paramedics assessed flight attendants in jetway and elected to have them escorted to hospital for medical evaluation. Flight crew obtained a different aircraft and new flight attendants and departed for ZZZ1 almost 3 hours later.
ASRS:1822957.s: During pre-departure boarding at ZZZ, flight attendants reported a "dirty sock" smell from the APU, prompting the crew to execute the Aircraft Odor checklist and deplane passengers. Maintenance was notified, paramedics assessed symptomatic flight attendants and recommended hospital evaluation, and the flight departed three hours later with a new aircraft and crew.

ASRS:1823021.n: Passengers in XX3/4 repeatedly removed their mask during flight. Male passenger in XX3 removed his mask twice during the flight and had to be told to put it back on. He also removed it during deplaning. I had to make an announcement and he also put it back on. Passenger in XX4 removed his mask 3 times during the flight. When I first noticed his mask off I asked him to pull it backup and he did. (Gaiter style mask). During takeoff while I was in my jumpseat he removed his mask again. I decided to wait until the chime to ask him to pull it up again. However, it appeared the passenger behind him had asked him to pull his mask back up and he was starting to argue. (I was unable to hear the actual conversation.) In order to prevent conflict/escalation I got up and told him he needed to put his mask back on. He did. After service, (he did not eat or drink) during trash pick up - I noticed he had his mask under his nose. When he saw me looking at him he pretended to be asleep. I called the pilots and told them I need to issue a notice to the passenger and told them what seat. I went back and handed him the notice and he pulled his mask back up when I 'woke' him. I came back a few minutes later to make sure he was still complying and retrieve the card. He looked shock and made gestures asking me why I had given it to him. I told him that he needed to keep his mask on. He sarcastically pulled it up to his eyes and asked if that was OK. I said yes, took the card and left. There was no additional interaction for the rest of the flight. The Captain called and asked if the issue was resolved and we told him yes.
ASRS:1823021.s: Cabin crew managed multiple passengers in seats XX3 and XX4 who repeatedly removed or improperly wore masks during flight and deplaning. After verbal warnings and issuing a formal notice to one passenger, compliance was achieved without further escalation, and the Captain was informed the issue was resolved.

ASRS:1823045.n: Cleared for the RNAV 05 Approach. Instructed to cross FOVOJ at or above 2,500 feet. Set Altitude on A/P for DH. Aircraft started down and action was taken at 1,300 feet MSL. ATC called me as well. It would not have occurred had I done a proper instrument scan.
ASRS:1823045.s: The pilot, while executing an RNAV 05 approach, descended below the 2,500-foot crossing restriction at FOVOJ and initiated a recovery at 1,300 feet MSL. The pilot attributed the incident to an improper instrument scan.

ASRS:1823047.n: My student and I were cleared to takeoff of Runway XXR this afternoon. We entered the runway, and my student began the departure roll. Seeing the left turning tendencies begin, I told my student to input some right rudder. My student over corrected by putting too much pressure on the rudder. I stated my controls and tried to maintain control of the plane but was unsuccessful. When I was trying to stay on the centerline of the runway, I noticed his foot was still stiff on the rudder causing us to veer to the right. I closed the throttle immediately and prepared to go off runway. As we got off the runway, I applied aft pressure on the yoke to try prevent damage to the prop and nose gear. I informed ATC that we went off the runway, possibly hit a light, and I would need to be towed. Moving forward, in order to be fully on the controls better I think I will be more assertive with my students so that they do not freeze up on the controls. I told my student this was a good learning experience for the both of us. We both learned from this event.
ASRS:1823047.s: An instructor and student veered off Runway XXR during takeoff after the student overcorrected rudder input, causing the instructor to lose control. The pilot aborted the takeoff, exited the runway to protect the propeller and nose gear, and reported a possible light strike requiring a tow.

ASRS:1823085.n: In traffic pattern doing touch and go landings. 1 other Cessna 172 was ahead of my aircraft and I was number 2 for touch and go. After other aircraft performed touch and go ahead of me and was climbing out I then performed my touch and go. Estimated time between other aircraft landing/taking off and my plane landing/taking off was 1 minute. After taking off I had lowered the nose to an 80 knot initial climb speed for cooling of the engine and better visibility. I climbed to approximately 1,400 feet before beginning my crosswind turn. I had not seen the aircraft ahead of me since it took off as there was significant haze. Upon beginning my turn the ADB-B TCAS (Garmin GTN 750) in the cockpit alerted me to an aircraft 100 feet below me and extremely close. I looked to the left and below my aircraft and spotted the other Cessna very close and going much slower than my plane. I turned 20 degrees right, reduced the throttle, applied full flaps in order to gain distance from the other aircraft. I then notified the controller that I was going to be slowing down in the pattern to give the other aircraft additional spacing.
ASRS:1823085.s: A Cessna 172 pilot executing a touch-and-go in haze lost sight of a preceding Cessna 172. A TCAS alert at 1,400 feet revealed the other aircraft 100 feet below, prompting the pilot to turn right, reduce throttle, and deploy full flaps to increase separation.

ASRS:1823119.n: I was the Pilot Flying on the ZZZZZ 1 Arrival into ZZZ. ZZZ TRACON asked us what approach we wanted to [Runway] XXR into ZZZ. We requested the RNAV visual to [Runway] XXR. We were cleared to 7,000 feet and cleared to intercept the final approach course for [Runway] XXR after ZZZZZ. We thought we were cleared for the approach so we set the next altitude of 4,000 feet in past ZZZZZ. After crossing ZZZZZ the aircraft started descending to 4,000 feet. ZZZ TRACON informed us of a Low Altitude Alert and had us climb to 7,000 feet, then he Immediately cleared us for the visual. Told us to take down the phone number for possible pilot deviation. Both our first time to ZZZ. We were cleared to intercept final segment. We said to each other, 'ZZZZZ is IAF;' and then we determined it was the final course we were supposed to intercept. We should have asked ATC to repeat, but we put 4,000 feet in the autopilot, as in VNAV, to continue published approach, but 7,000 feet was still our clearance limit. On the published segment it continued down, inside ZZZZZ, below 7,000 feet. ATC queried us at 6,000 feet and told us to climb. We had the field in sight and ATC then cleared us immediately for the visual.I was so focused on terrain and being in VNAV. As Pilot Monitoring, I should have questioned the clearance and any confusion we had. I am sure what we heard, thought we heard and what ATC said were all different.
ASRS:1823119.s: The Pilot Flying and Pilot Monitoring on a ZZZZZ 1 arrival descended below their 7,000-foot clearance limit to 4,000 feet after misinterpreting ATC instructions. This triggered a Low Altitude Alert, requiring a climb before ATC issued an immediate visual clearance and noted a potential pilot deviation.

ASRS:1823130.n: Climbing through 7,000 feet on the ZZZZZ SID, the aural warnings for airspeed, fire and pressurization came on. The First Officer and I scanned the flight deck for unreliable airspeed, fire warnings and any possible pressurization problems. We were in agreement that none were present and could not locate the source of the warnings, I elected to disengage the autopilot and auto throttles, to verify control of the aircraft. The First Officer and I searched again for any indication of fire or airspeed issues. We found none. With the fire bell still sounding we elected to return to ZZZ and request priority. ATC was notified and vectors given back to Runway XX. Having just departed and well over the gross landing weight, we planned the longest runway available. I notified the A Flight Attendant, to prepare the cabin for landing and that we had about 10 minutes to touchdown.The First Officer computed the landing data and a visual approach was planned. Landing weight was XXX;000 pounds, and the Ref Speed 1XX. ATC provided vectors to a base leg and we were cleared for the visual approach. The landing and rollout were normal and I elected to let the aircraft roll to the end and turnoff, stop the aircraft and allow CFR to inspect for fire. As soon as I stopped the aircraft, I made a PA to the Flight Attendants and Passengers to remain seated. Ground was contacted and we spoke directly with fire command. No evidence of fire was found to exist. The First Officer computed the brake cooling module for and potential issues that would prevent us from parking at the gate or cooling required. None were found. Coordination with ZZZ Operations as to our situation and a gate was completed and we taxied to gate X. At the gate we were met by the Fire Crew, ZZZ Maintenance and Ground Operations. The warnings continued to sound and were not able to be silenced by Maintenance Personnel. I made two logbook entries for the discrepancies and the overweight landing and gave a debrief of the event to the Maintenance Personnel. Dispatch was contacted and informed of the situation and we agreed to talk later as my main focus was still dealing with passengers and Ground Ops. After passenger deplaning, the aircraft was handed over to maintenance and the First Officer and I went to the Crew lounge, where we contacted Dispatch and conducted a debrief of the events with the Chief Pilot. This event occurred while departing ZZZ from Runway XX, climbing out on the ZZZZZ Departure at about 7,000 feet. I was the PM, and had just completed the final flap retraction and a radio hand off to ZZZ Departure. All of a sudden, numerous alarms/warnings sounded on the flight deck and were extremely loud. The PF stayed focused on flying the aircraft in the high density environment. I quickly started to scan all of the panels, Master Caution and Warning indications, pressurization panel, cargo fire panel, fire handles, flight instrumentation, airspeed, AOA, and standby indicators. There were NO indications of any light or malfunction anywhere on the flight deck and all aircraft flight parameters seemed normal.The Captain made the decision to advise ATC and return to ZZZ, on Runway XX. Meanwhile all aural alarms continued to sound very loudly which made communication difficult. We discussed the situation. We had just about every major aural alarm sounding at once, with the exception of wind shear. With no other indications presently indicating any kind of system malfunction, we concluded the best option would be to get the aircraft on the ground. This would be an overweight landing by about XX;000 pounds, on a long runway in day VMC conditions. The Captain coordinated with the cabin and operations. We computed landing data, briefed, and ran checklists. We were cleared a visual approach and the Captain completed an excellent uneventful landing to Runway XX. We cleared the runway at the end. I coordinated with CFR (Crash Fire Rescue equipment) and requested them to thoroughly evaluate the aircraft for any fire/smoke issues. I also ran the numbers for any brake cooling issues. The CFR Chief stated there were no indications of fire or smoke. There were no brake cooling issues. ZZZ Ops cleared us to gate X. We resumed taxi to the gate, with CFR following us to ensure absolute safety.We parked the aircraft at the gate and were met by Maintenance and the Fire Chief. THE ALARMS WERE ALL STILL SOUNDING. Maintenance came on board and tried to figure it out, to no avail, prior to us leaving. Passengers were safely deplaned and sent to another gate for continuation to ZZZ1. With the alarms still sounding at the gate, the Captain and I both commented on how fortunate we were to have on noise cancelling headsets, otherwise communication would have been nearly impossible. This was a very unusual emergency and I hope that we are provided follow-up with the cause of the malfunction.
ASRS:1823130.s: During climb on the ZZZZZ SID at 7,000 feet, the crew experienced simultaneous aural warnings for airspeed, fire, and pressurization with no visual indications. They returned to ZZZ for an overweight landing; post-landing inspections found no fire or system faults, yet the alarms persisted and could not be silenced by maintenance.

ASRS:1823143.n: New Captain was PM, LCA (Line Check Airman) was flying from right seat on arrival into IAH. Approach kept us so high the entire time we had to get approval to miss the altitudes. Aircraft on other arrivals were holding and we were expecting the same. We were cleared to descend via the GUSHR arrival, and had to use full speed brakes the whole time but we made 10,000 at 250kts, and were able to make the bottom altitude at GUSHR at 6000 and 210 kts. Big rain shower at 15 miles out on the final of 8L. By the time we went by the rain shower it was mostly north of our course but there was rain and lightning coming out of the shower. TCAS showed traffic on 8R behind and above us. We could see him out of our window. We were told to hold 200 knots till about 10 mile final. At this time, traffic somewhere, behind us we think, said they needed to go around because of rain and lightning. Approach gave us a frequency and switched us to tower and told us to tell them our speed. We switched to the Tower frequency but must have put it in wrong, and when we tried to check on to what we thought was tower, another approach told us it was the wrong frequency. To go to the Tower, we looked up on the Jepp chart and the Tower frequency for 8L was 120.725. We called Tower on 120.725 and they cleared us to land. On final after that, a monitor came on and told us to change to 119.82. We switched to 119.82 and it was the same Tower Controller as 120.725 and she cleared us to land a second time. After landing we were told to contact ATC for possible pilot deviation. We had no idea why. We contacted the ATC Ops Manager who said there was a possible conflict with the traffic on 8R as that traffic was so close that had he not seen the airport and been given a visual we would have been too close and had a separation issue.1. We were cleared for an ILS. There was no PRM operations being used or advertised.2. The tower frequency they were using, 119.82 is nowhere on the IAH 70-9 page, dated 16APR21, effective 22APR21. ATC Ops Manager said Houston has been using frequency 119.82 as Tower for a few weeks because coverage was poor on the other frequency in some areas, but that frequency (119.82) is not published anywhere. 3. After talking with ATC Ops Manager, we verified in the NOTAMs there was nothing about 119.82 being used anywhere.4. Why is approach cramming the planes on approach so close that a momentary loss of communication results in loss of separation?
ASRS:1823143.s: A crew on arrival into IAH experienced high altitude vectors and a frequency confusion involving an unpublished tower frequency, resulting in a potential separation conflict with traffic on runway 8R. The ATC Ops Manager attributed the near-miss to tight spacing and the use of an unlisted frequency, prompting a pilot deviation inquiry.

ASRS:1823160.n: Jetbridge trainer and trainee on Jetbridge XXX, moving off XX. Trainee called for ramp guide person, guide person standing directly under Jetbridge XXY Door XY. From below the [Door] XY door, the guide person guided us back as Jetbridge went to our right toward the engine, guide person not moving from below [Door] XY door, Jetbridge XXY. Heard someone on the radio transmit you need to go forward and straight back, you're close to the engine". While trainee still at the control, trainer looked out the right side of Jetbridge. It appeared the Jetbridge was less than a foot away from the aircraft engine. The Ramp (lead?) on the tug directly behind us was advising us by radio to stop and move forward. With no guide, trainee moved Jetbridge forward and stopped then trainee proceeded to move Jetbridge backwards to the 6 o'clock direction and then the same guide person appeared below us at Jetbridge XXX [Door] XX." I was guiding the jetbridge back I was telling the jetbridge driver to go to the left but she was not following my directions. She kept on going back towards the engine almost making contact with the engine. So I told her to stop same time as my ramp lead saw what was happening and had to call the jetbridge driver to make her go forward so she would not hit the engine, but the whole time she was looking at her screen and was not following my directions.
ASRS:1823160.s: A jetbridge trainee operating Jetbridge XXX nearly contacted an aircraft engine while moving off the gate because she ignored a ramp guide's directions and focused on her screen. A ramp lead intervened via radio to stop the movement and prevent the collision.

ASRS:1823198.n: During the climb out we experienced a L BLEED DUCT warning message. The First Officer was the Pilot Flying. He remained on the controls and radios while I ran the appropriate checklists and made the necessary communications to the crew, the passengers, and the company. [We advised ATC] and we were given priority handling back to land at ZZZ. The temperature in both the cabin and the cockpit reached 40 degrees Celsius because we were unable to maintain an open engine bleed valve. The warning occurred at approximately 12,000 feet MSL. We immediately got a clearance to descend below 10,000 feet MSL as pressurization could not be maintained. We then only had ram air to cool the cockpit and cabin. We landed safely on runway and taxied directly to gate where the passengers were deplaned through the normal method.
ASRS:1823198.s: During climb out at 12,000 feet, the crew received a L BLEED DUCT warning, causing cabin temperatures to reach 40°C due to an inoperative engine bleed valve. The aircraft descended below 10,000 feet using ram air for cooling and landed safely at ZZZ for normal deplaning.

ASRS:1823199.n: As Captain, I was the Pilot Monitoring and the First Officer was the Pilot Flying for this flight. On the take off roll at approximately 90 to 100kts, I hear the First Officer make the comment 'There seems to be a lot of airflow through this window'. I glanced over and to see from my point of view that the window appears to be closed. I shift my eyes back to the runway centerline, airspeed and engine instruments while thinking about what he said. At approximately 110kts, it becomes loud with high airflow into the flight deck. The First Officer shouts 'My window is open'. I quickly glance over to his side to see he has his left hand on the control wheel and is holding the R 2 flight deck window closed by the window lock lever with his right hand. I immediately took the controls. At this time we are approximately 120kts just prior to V1 (129). I took a quick glance at my First Officer and back to my instruments, I saw that we were Vr + 8 to 9kts. I then rotated. I saw a positive rate of climb and shout 'gear up'. The First Officer assumed pilot monitoring and raised the landing gear. I shouted 'Can you crank the window closed at all?' He responded 'No, it won't close'. At this point, Tower had advised us to contact Departure. I selected the Center Autopilot, VNAV & Heading Select with a heading of 360 as assigned. I opened the speed window and remained at Flaps 5 to prevent the airplane from accelerating. I figured the faster we would go, the louder the flight deck would be and the more the First Officer would struggle to hold the window in position. The First Officer shouts 'I can't hear anything from ATC.' Around 3,400 ft. I contacted Departure and informed them that we need to stop climb and return to the airport because we have a flight deck window opened. We were given a left heading of 270 and to maintain 4,000. We performed the after takeoff checklist. My First Officer states 'I can't hear anything from ATC but what do you need from me?' I responded 'ATC is giving us vectors back to ILS RWY XX. If you can, get flight deck performance for Runway XX and set us up for the ILS RWY XX, I'll do a quick brief, then we will do our Descent and Approach checklist.' With one hand still on the window crank, the First Officer did just that and along with his flow. ATC gave us another vector and asked if we need more time. I told ATC that we were not ready and asked to continue heading at 270 and 4,000. Once we were set up, briefings and checklist were complete, I advised ATC we were ready for the approach. Since I was flying while doing the radios myself and the First Officer with only one free hand available, I decided it would not be prudent to be heads down and message Dispatch through ACARS. I felt the priority was to fly the plane and get us safely on the ground. I informed ATC 'We [request priority], 2 souls on board and approximately 4 and half hours fuel on board'. ATC asked the nature of the [situation] and I replied 'We have a flight window cracked'. I meant to say cracked open, however, the noise from the airflow was a little distracting. ATC gives us an intercept heading of 100 and clears us for the approach. We were stable, fully configured, and all checklists were complete prior to the final approach fix. At 800 feet AGL we broke out of the clouds. I had the airport in sight and disengaged the autopilot. A normal landing was made at approximately 265,000 lb. We informed Tower that we did not need assistance and taxied to parking. Upon taxi in, I do not know if the First Officer closed the window or left it in its previous condition from flight, opened. Perhaps he left it alone so that Maintenance could inspect. I wrote up that the First Officer R2 flight deck window opened on takeoff/climb and I waited for them to inspect. There was no damage or defects noted.I honestly do not know if it was a Flight Deck Window malfunction or if it was ever truly locked. Both of us had opened our Flight Deck Windows on the ground during preflight because the APU was off and the temperature was in the 70's. About 30 minutes prior to block out, I started the APU and we closed our windows. In the Before Start portion of the checklist, I verified my flight window was closed and locked with strut at a 90 degree position. I heard the First Officer respond 'Closed and locked'. I could see his Window Lock Lever was in the forward and locked position, however, I could not verify if his decal showed 'CLOSED' nor if the strut was at a 90 angle simply because of the angle from where I was sitting in the Captain's seatI think that in the moment, the First Officer did a great job of prioritizing aircraft control in such a critical phase of flight. To be in the high speed regime of takeoff, so close to V1 and to keep 'aviating' while a huge startling distraction occurred was commendable. He also, kept his head in the game and jumped to the pilot monitoring duties without delay. He prompted me for the after takeoff checklist as we were about to level off at 4,000. If I could have done one thing over, I would have shouted 'My controls' in a louder voice. I didn't take into consideration that the First Officer could not hear well at that point.I'm also appreciative of our Company training video made by Boeing of a flight with the flight deck window opened. I'm glad that I was shown to me during my 767 upgrade training. I never thought I would be in that situation but thankfully I had some idea of what to expect. The plane will be extremely loud and distracting but it will safely fly. During takeoff my window opened immediately after the CA (Captain) called '80 knots, thrust set.' I was PF and saw the window rolling aft. I grabbed the window handle with my right hand while continuing to fly. I maintained runway centerline and described what happened by shouting cross cockpit to allow the CA to have the information and make an appropriate reject decision. About 10 knots before V1 the CA took the aircraft. I couldn't hear him verbally call V1 due to the cockpit noise and open window. Perhaps I didn't hear him call V1 because he had already taken the aircraft. Regardless it was loud and my audio panel wasn't set up to compensate for the noise.When the aircraft rotated I immediately assumed the role of Pilot Monitoring. He shouted to raise the landing gear and I did. The CA flew and took the radios because I had shouted cross cockpit that I couldn't hear ATC well enough to communicate. Both of us had to compensate because of the noise. The CA selected heading select and turned left to our assigned heading of 360 and elected to select VNAV and Center Autopilot Command almost simultaneously.The CA requested to stop climb around 5,100 MSL and informed me that we would return to ZZZ. Around this time I had determined that as long as I held the window with a good amount of strength it wouldn't roll open. I adjusted my interphone and ATC freq to Max volume so that I could hear. I then asked the CA if he was ready to run the After Takeoff Checklist and we did. Everything from that point forward was standard and in order except that the CA had to turn the Standby Attitude Indicator to ILS mode because I had one hand holding the window, the CA [advised ATC], and did the radios. After we landed all roles were normal and the taxi in was standard.This situation is dynamic. I think perhaps a better verbal transfer of aircraft control on takeoff roll but we effectively handled the situation. I thought the CA was going to reject the takeoff. By the time he processed what was going on he decided it was safer to continue the takeoff. It was loud and we coordinated the best we could in this situation.
ASRS:1823199.s: During takeoff, the First Officer's R2 flight deck window opened at 110 knots, causing extreme noise and communication loss. The Captain took control, continued the takeoff, and returned for a safe landing after determining the window could not be closed in flight.

ASRS:1823273.n: We were operating ZZZ-ZZZ1. Our APU was INOP. We took off climbing out of around 7,000 ft. we got a Gen 1 Off caution message followed by a IDG Disc status. I was flying so I had the Captain run the QRH for the Gen 1 caution. The QRH called for the APU to be turned on, ours was INOP. We [advised] with ZZZ Center then talked about our next step, we looked at different airports and most airports on the east coast were 300 ft. or less overcast, with thunderstorms to the west. We messaged Dispatch and Maintenance about what was going on, they told us to air return to ZZZ. The Captain made the announcement with the flight attendants and passengers and kept them informed. We made a normal ILS landing into ZZZ and switched airplanes and made it to ZZZ1 2 hours later.[The cause was] Gen 1 failure, APU INOP, only working off one generator. Communication between pilots, passengers, ATC, dispatch and Maintenance Control was very good, we were all on the same page.
ASRS:1823273.s: Flight ZZZ-ZZZ1 experienced a Gen 1 failure and IDG disconnect with an INOP APU while climbing from 7,000 ft. The crew coordinated with ATC, Dispatch, and Maintenance to return to ZZZ, where they executed a normal ILS landing and switched aircraft.

ASRS:1823284.n: Large fuel truck, possibly # (NUMBER) came around the end of the concourse and into the alley as we were taxiing outbound. The fuel truck stayed outside of the protected white and in the aircraft lane until abeam the nose of our aircraft. In the meantime we we were given taxi clearance out of the alleyway and were rolling. The fuel truck then darted towards our wingtip but did not cross the white line to the protected area. From my vantage point, I did not think there was sufficient clearance and had to slam on the brakes. Incident reported to Ramp Control (they did not care).Reported to ZZZ Ops.We checked with cabin crew to see if we had any injuries (none).Recommend full size aircraft only enter and exit this alley way on center line if Ground Ops vehicles continue to ignore protected area white line on ramp and continue to drive around our wing while on the east line. I cannot determine clearance of wingtip from flight deck of these vehicles driving around wing.
ASRS:1823284.s: A pilot taxiing outbound reported a large fuel truck darting toward the aircraft's wingtip while remaining outside the protected white line, forcing an emergency brake application. No injuries occurred, but the pilot noted insufficient clearance and recommended that full-size aircraft use the centerline to avoid similar ground vehicle conflicts.

ASRS:1823292.n: Human organs (kidney) transported on flight deck in violation of FOM 2.1. Cargo personnel asked if a package containing a kidney for transplant could be transported on the flight deck. The Captain gave permission and I concurred, however while in route to ZZZ2 we discovered this was not allowed without an escort per the FOM.On my part, this incident could have been avoided through more familiarity with the FOM. Apart from that, a section in the pilot reference cards for cargo and hazmat would be helpful.
ASRS:1823292.s: The Captain and a crew member allowed cargo personnel to transport a kidney on the flight deck without an escort, violating FOM 2.1. The crew discovered this error en route to ZZZ2 and attributed the incident to insufficient familiarity with the FOM.

ASRS:1823384.n: While descending via the CHINS4 arrival into BFI (Seattle/King County Boeing Field), on the segment between 'HUMPP' and 'AUBRN', passing approximately 14,500 ft. MSL at 250 kts. IAS, I encountered wake turbulence. Temporary loss of control was experienced as the aircraft rolled right, back left, and strongly back right again - with the final bank angle in the roll estimated to be beyond 30 but not more than 50 degrees wing down to the right before I could fully react. During the course of the roll and recovery, automation (including autopilot and auto throttle) was disengaged, and at no time did the EGPWS 'BANK ANGLE' warning sound. I stopped the roll and regained controlled flight with full and smooth application of left aileron, while adding power and climbing out of the perceived vortex. Once clear, automation was restored, the event briefed amongst the crew, and I instructed the PNF (Pilot not Flying) to radio Seattle Approach indicating we had 'encountered wake turbulence' and that 'we were attempting to re-establish on the arrival'. The Approach Controller acknowledged the transmission and advised we were following a Boeing 737-900 series sequenced for SEA (Seattle). From there, a normal descent and approach was conducted to the destination airport. No aircraft faults/failures/malfunctions/warnings, nor exceedances were experienced at any time before, during, or after the event. I was aware of the altitude and spacing regarding the traffic ahead on the arrival, with use of TCAS indications and relative altitude, as well situational awareness provided by our aircraft's INAV display. Spacing and distance appeared more than adequate considering the flight conditions, as the preceding aircraft was consistently indicating around 2,500 ft. below our level and well ahead on the arrival. At no time were we given advisories from ATC in regards to traffic ahead, nor caution on wake turbulence.This event was truly unexpected, however, I must credit flight training providers with modeling extremely accurate wake turbulence simulation scenarios that helped me to quickly identify, and recover properly from this real life upset. Experiencing this is a reminder that wake turbulence can be encountered during a descent profile - especially on an RNAV arrival with 'at-or-above/below' vertical crossing restrictions that could result in brief level offs at slower airspeeds which could lead to preceding aircraft generating stronger than expected vortices.
ASRS:1823384.s: The pilot encountered wake turbulence while descending on the CHINS4 arrival to BFI between HUMPP and AUBRN at 14,500 ft, causing a temporary loss of control with a bank angle exceeding 30 degrees. The upset occurred behind a Boeing 737-900 despite adequate spacing, but the crew recovered flight and completed a normal approach without aircraft faults.

ASRS:1823387.n: We were cleared for takeoff RWY XX up to 2,000 [feet]. After rotation I see the shadow of and airplane go overhead as if it was landing on RWY XX TCAS started alerting for 'Traffic', I told the PIC to stop climbing and turn left being that the Aircraft Y was on the right of us and above. Aircraft Y turned right and all is well.
ASRS:1823387.s: The crew, cleared for takeoff to 2,000 feet, observed Aircraft Y overhead and received a TCAS 'Traffic' alert. The pilot stopped climbing and turned left while Aircraft Y turned right, resolving the conflict.

ASRS:1823392.n: During takeoff at ZZZ we were conducting a training flight using a [large] unmanned aircraft under a [military] COA (Certificate Of Authority). Immediately after takeoff on upwind runway XX our [Visual Observer], notified us to immediately level off due to a potential collision with a Helicopter. The Helicopter flew directly over our departure end of runway at approx. 300 feet narrowly missing us on upwind by approx. 100 feet.
ASRS:1823392.s: During a military training takeoff of a large unmanned aircraft at ZZZ, a Visual Observer directed an immediate level-off to avoid a helicopter. The helicopter crossed the departure end at approximately 300 feet, narrowly missing the unmanned aircraft by about 100 feet on the upwind leg.

ASRS:1823412.n: Lost engine on take off, landed on same runway as took off. During landing roll used intersection #1 to exit and clear runway.
ASRS:1823412.s: The pilot reported losing an engine during takeoff and landing back on the same runway. The aircraft exited and cleared the runway using intersection #1 during the landing roll.

ASRS:1823418.n: Aircraft X had landed [Runway] XXR and stopped on the runway to question the exiting instructions. This delay in exiting caused the next [Runway] XXR arrival to go around. Then, an airport vehicle requested permission to inspect the runway because there's some local airport procedure to sweep the runway behind a [type aircraft]. There was a full sequence of arrivals to [Runway] XXR and [Runway] XY. Then, while the Local Controller was sorting out the Aircraft X arrival, the succeeding go-around, and the airport vehicle, Aircraft Y ([Runway] XXR) and the Aircraft Z ([Runway] XY) tied at the intersection. ASDE-X (Airport Surface Detection Equipment) alarmed, Local Controller issued a late go-around.Actual time on position may not have been a factor, rather the lack of staffing to open other positions and reduce the Local Controller's workload. There were only two of us in the tower at the time, simply because no one else was available. We had asked, and been told that we would be getting more people at XA:30z. Positions in the TRACON were also combined, and despite the fact that management had kept 3 tower-certified controllers down [in the TRACON] to 'get time', one controller was working both the runways Arrival position, and vectoring the final to Runway [Runway] XY having to sequence in with the intersecting [Runway] XXR arrivals. The search for more controllers is on-going. What else can one do, when asking for more staffing, and being told to just wait? I was working Local Controls combined. I had Aircraft X land Runway XXR. I told the aircraft to exit the runway at taxiway. An airport vehicle asked to check the runway behind the Aircraft X as per our SOP (Standard Operating Procedure). Aircraft X then stopped at taxiway on the runway an asked if I was sure I wanted him to clear there as he is a [type aircraft]. I said affirmative. It was then too close for the next arrival to land safely so I sent him around. I then got the airport vehicle on to the runway but had to have him exit early as more arrivals were too close. It was then that the ASDE-X (Airport Surface Detection Equipment) alarmed informing me that the next [Runway] XXR arrival and [Runway] XY arrival were in conflict. I sent the [Runway] XXR arrival, Aircraft Y, around. Aircraft Y was about to touch down when he executed the go around. I had become distracted by the situation with Aircraft X and vehicle. By the time I was made aware of the tie between the [Runway] XY arrival and [Runway] XXR arrival the ASDE-X had alarmed. I would give more space behind Aircraft X to do the runway sweep and maybe have local controls split during the push.
ASRS:1823418.s: A Local Controller, working alone due to staffing shortages, issued a late go-around to Aircraft Y after ASDE-X alarmed on a conflict with Aircraft Z. The incident was caused by the controller's distraction while managing Aircraft X's delayed exit and a runway inspection vehicle.

ASRS:1823429.n: Wind was gusting to 15 knots at ZZZ, and the Citation seemed unsure on if they wanted to land at ZZZ or go somewhere else. They got all the way to about 3 minutes from the field before they stated that they had the field in sight and wanted the Visual Approach. They had been assigned present heading and to maintain 9 thousand, but then I cleared them for the Visual Approach. Shortly after the aircraft informed they were VMC and were just going to do local maneuvers while they 'come up with a plan'. They had not begun their descent, and I asked if they were cancelling IFR, and they said no. I told them 'approach clearance cancelled, maintained 9 thousand' and I neglected to give them routing. A hit (radar update) or two goes by and they make a slight left turn and I assign them a heading for terrain. A few hits later, they made a turn into the 9700 foot MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) at 9 thousand feet. The pilot was cleared for the Visual, and the last thing I expected them to do was to turn about 160 degrees away from the airfield. They're allowed to climb, descend, and turn, on a Visual Approach, but they're required to keep the field in sight, which they obviously can't do on that easterly heading, so I'm not sure why they turned that far east. Additionally, I don't think a Visual Approach clearance enables an aircraft to just hold and 'come up with a plan'. I get updates every 12 seconds, and I kept waiting, and hoping, that the pilot would fly their assigned heading. I'm not sure how long it took for him to be established on the turn, but if I had updates every second, I would have known he wasn't taking my turn, and climbed him. This airspace area needs an Approach Control. I believe that if there had been faster updates on the data block, I would have taken different action.
ASRS:1823429.s: An ATC controller cleared a Citation for a visual approach at ZZZ, but the pilot turned 160 degrees away from the airfield while maintaining 9,000 feet. The controller attributed the near-miss with terrain to slow radar updates and the pilot's failure to keep the field in sight.

ASRS:1823435.n: Radar controller, no D-side (Radar Assist), significant weather and deviations south of ZZZ. Skydiving aircraft off of ZZZ1 with VFR advisories from Center. Aircraft was performing operations most of the day, multiple jumps, in and out of radar. The location that the operations were occurring were approximately the ZZZZZ intersection on the ZZZ RNAV XX arrival and the ZZZZZ1 fix on the ZZZ [RNAV] Departure. During the incident, Runway XX was active with the Departure in use and aircraft were departing to the north and making a left turn to the southwest, which put them in the approximate location of the skydive operations. The skydiving aircraft [Aircraft Z] was told numerous times that their location was directly in the way of IFR departures and arrivals into ZZZ. ZZZ is and was very busy with IFR traffic at this time. Tower called for two releases on IFR air carrier Aircraft. The first air carrier departed, and ended up being in the same location as the skydiving aircraft. I issued a traffic alert to both aircraft. That was Aircraft X. The second air carrier, Aircraft Y then departed and if memory recalls, I had stopped that aircraft at 9,000 feet on departure anticipating the same scenario as Aircraft X. I again issued traffic, with the skydiving aircraft being at approximately 12,500 feet at this time. The skydiving aircraft then reported that jumpers were away, with the air carrier aircraft directly below. The air carrier pilot reported seeing jumpers in the air and turning to avoid at approximately 6,000 feet below terrain, to which I replied roger.I have brought this up to managements attention, the day of by notifying the FLM (Front Line Manager) who in turn notified the OMIC (Operations Manager in Charge). We have also forwarded the info to the LSC (Local Safety Commitee). Local airspace has gotten involved and we have opened up the Skydiving LOA (Letter of Agreement) to rewrite the LOA and hopefully make some changes. In my opinion, the jump zone needs to be relocated to a safer spot away from ZZZ IFR traffic.
ASRS:1823435.s: A radar controller issued traffic alerts when an IFR air carrier departed into a skydiving zone near ZZZ, causing the carrier to turn at 6,000 feet to avoid jumpers at 12,500 feet. The controller attributed the conflict to the skydive location overlapping active IFR routes and recommended relocating the jump zone.

ASRS:1823473.n: I operated out of MMUN last month and on takeoff we experienced a dip in the runway just at rotation, nothing concerning but definitely got your attention. You could tell that they had been re-paving the runway and the dip appeared to be where the old surface met the new surface. Yesterday I operated again out of MMUN Runway 12R. It was my FO's leg and I briefed him on the dip in the runway at rotation that I experienced last month. I thought that by now they had finished their paving project and we would not experience this again. The dip in the runway was there and it was much worse. It was jarring and certainly put a strain on the aircraft tires and landing gear. I believe the asphalt is settling and has caused the dip to become deeper.
ASRS:1823473.s: A pilot reported a worsening runway dip at MMUN Runway 12R during rotation on two separate takeoffs, caused by settling asphalt where old and new pavement surfaces meet. The jarring impact strained the aircraft's tires and landing gear, with the condition deteriorating between the first and second occurrences.

ASRS:1823482.n: Flight XXXX ZZZ arrived at ZZZ, was given taxi direction to take [taxiway] north line to Gate XX. As A/C made the turn from [taxiway] to the north line, a tractor with 3 loaded cargo dollies in the VSR moving from south abeam Gate XY to north in the direct on [taxiway] committed to shoot the gap between out bound aircraft. Controllers on duty noted tractor not giving way to the inbound flight. Advised Flight XXXX to STOP. Tractor was observed weaving out of the VSR lines and entering the non-movement area near Spots XX and XY cutting off the aircraft and near missing a major incursion. Inbound Flight XXXX from ZZZ1 was coming inbound to gate. As it was coming into the north line to the gate, a cargo runner almost came into contact with the nose gear of the aircraft. The cargo runner had to divert his path in order to avoid the aircraft.
ASRS:1823482.s: Flight XXXX taxiing to Gate XX nearly collided with a cargo tractor and three dollies that failed to yield and entered the non-movement area. The controller ordered the aircraft to stop, and the cargo runner diverted its path to avoid contact with the nose gear.

ASRS:1823506.n: In VFR conditions and clear of clouds on final approach to Runway XXL in ZZZ. ATC vectored us behind two other aircraft on final for the same runway and assigned us a speed of 160 kts. The aircraft was already configured with approach flaps and slowing. Tower advised that the aircraft in front of us had slowed further and advised us to slow to minimum approach speed. We fully configured the aircraft for landing and continued to slow. Tower advised we were still 60 kts faster than the preceding aircraft and requested us to do an 's' turn to the north to provide further spacing. The Pilot Flying, using the autopilot, initiated a 90 degree turn to the north (right) and continued to descend. We were clear of any traffic. The parallel runway was closed. About 80 degrees perpendicular to the approach course, using the autopilot, the Pilot Flying turned the aircraft back towards the runway. I, the Pilot Monitoring advised him to slow his descent rate, we were continuing to descend while maneuvering, using the autopilot the Pilot Flying slowed the rate of descent. At about the same instant at 2.5 mi from the end of the runway. Tower stated that he had a 'low altitude alert' on us and he advised us to 'initiate a climb'. The altimeter showed 860 ft above the water. The electronic glide path showed one dot low. The Pilot Flying immediately disengaged the autopilot pilot and applied back pressure to the controls. The aircraft immediately recovered to 1,100 ft agl. The Pilot Flying continued the turn towards the runway and descended on the glide path. At 1,000 ft agl, I, the Pilot Monitoring, reported 'stable'. I confirmed our landing clearance. At 500 ft agl, I reported 'stable'. We continued and landed. There were no TAWS warning triggered by the event. No alarms 'glide slope' or 'terrain to low' triggered.Less automation. Had the Pilot Flying turned off the autopilot for the maneuver and hand flown the aircraft, responding to the rate of descent would have happened in a more timely manner and an altitude low waning would have probably not been triggered. Hand flying would have managed the rate of descent better.
ASRS:1823506.s: During a VFR final approach to Runway XXL, the crew executed an S-turn in autopilot to create spacing, resulting in a low altitude alert at 860 ft AGL due to excessive descent. The Pilot Flying manually recovered the aircraft to 1,100 ft, and the reporter attributed the event to over-reliance on automation rather than hand-flying the maneuver.

ASRS:1823508.n: We had coordinated on a ZZZ to ZZZ1 out and back for extra gas so we wouldn't have to shut down the engine at ZZZ1. We had a quick turn and the APU was INOP. After taxiing into the gate without incident, we shut down the left engine and left the right engine running. I got our new release and it said we needed 7.8k gate/6.1k min fuel. We had 6.8k on board and Dispatch gave us a ton extra for holding. I called Dispatch and asked just to take the fuel we had on board and they agreed and sent us a new fuel plan via ACARs. Simultaneously, I had the First Officer go out and tell the ramp we didn't want fuel or external power. He came back and said in informed the Ramp Supervisor. AC power was not applied to the aircraft. We deboarded and boarded without incident. Then about 20 minutes after getting into the gate, while briefing the takeoff, I noticed the AUTO XFLOW INHIBIT message and saw we were taking on fuel. It was less than 300 lbs at that time. I immediately jumped up and opened the galley door and shouted to the fueler to stop because the Right engine was running. It took him approximately a minute to understand what I was saying and he stopped fueling. We took on about 1000 lbs total. I contacted the ramp and he said that they were Other Company and not under his direct control. I informed him I would write up the incident. Rest of the flight was without incident.Have a notice to the pilots and to stations directed specifically at the rampers and fuelers that aircraft cannot Hot refuel. This seems to be more of we're finally busy and COVID is over so we're rusty and rushed. I had a second incident at ZZZ on the return flight. We arrived at the gate in ZZZ without incident. I shut down the left engine while leaving the right one running since we had no APU. The ground crew had trouble hooking up power and before I shut down the second engine, I saw the AUTO XFLOW INHIBIT status message. I had the First Officer immediately head to the galley door to have ramp stop fueling which was just starting. I was mostly deplaned and power was coming up so I killed the engine. The First Officer got the fueler to stop and we took on less than 100 lbs. I discussed with ramp personal reminding them not to start fueling until the engines are shut down. Nothing further of note happened after that.Unrelated, but distracting, update the APU start checklist and remove all items that are duplicates and will be handled under another checklist (told data, doors, trim, fuel check value test, etc.).
ASRS:1823508.s: The flight crew experienced two hot refueling incidents at ZZZ while one engine was running due to an inoperative APU, resulting in approximately 1,100 lbs of unintended fuel. The reporter attributed the errors to ramp personnel rushing and a lack of clear communication regarding the prohibition of refueling with engines running.

ASRS:1823520.n: On final approach, we lost the green hydraulic system. We entered holding to complete the non-normal procedure and get fully configured. We also requested a longer runway and emergency equipment. The landing was made to a full stop because of loss of normal brakes and nose wheel steering. We were then towed to the gate. We experienced a mechanical failure (HYD G SYS LO PRESS) upon our descent into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ1 Arrival beginning approximately outside ZZZ waypoint. I was Pilot Flying, the Captain followed appropriate ECAM actions and checklists following company procedures. We advised ATC based on this ECAM considering our location and situational aspects. We elected to hold over the final approach fix for GPS approach to Runway XX while we completed all of our necessary actions in the interest of safety. Upon completion of these duties, we exited the hold, completed approach and landed successfully coming to full stop on the runway. Based on the mechanical condition of the aircraft as result of systems lost from hydraulic system, we coordinated with company operations to tow us in due to loss of nose wheel steering and deplaned normally. Mechanical malfunction (HYD G low pressure) ECAM.
ASRS:1823520.s: The Pilot Flying reported a green hydraulic system low pressure failure during descent on the ZZZZZ1 Arrival. The crew held to complete checklists, landed with degraded brakes and steering, and was subsequently towed to the gate.

ASRS:1823525.n: Original clearance was to fly the ORKA5 departure with LAS transition. FO was flying. At or near COOPP intersection Center gave us instructions that we understood to be 'fly heading 070 degrees and expect ORCKA and then the BEALE transition'. We set up our FMS for this new transition. Shortly afterward we both heard what we thought was 'cleared direct ORCKA and fly the BEALE transition' and the CA read exactly that back. A few minutes after we had established course to ORCKA center called another flight and directed a stop climb at FL190. We were passing through FL200 for FL230 when we noticed another aircraft on TCAS at 10-15 miles range reach 300 feet below our altitude before descending back down to FL 190. Center then called out that we were off course. CA replied we were direct ORCKA then BEALE Transition as directed. Controller then stated 'No you were cleared ARCUS and the BEALE transition'. ARCUS is the next fix after ORCKA on the ORKA5/BEALE SID and sounds very similar to ORCKA on a VHF radio. No TCAS alerts were initiated and no conflict occurred.The primary factor is the fact that ORCKA and ARCUS, two consecutive points along the ORKA5 SID sound similar over the VHF radio. So similar, in fact, that both pilots heard it wrong when the clearance was first issued and the ATC controller heard it wrong when we read it back.Two suggestions: 1. I recommend that Jeppesen change either ORCKA or ARCUS naming on the SID. 2. When waypoints on a SID sound so clearly similar ATC should phonetically spell out the fix cleared to. Original clearance was to fly to ORKA5 departure with LAS transition. FO was flying. At or near COOPP intersection Center gave us instructions that we understood to be fly heading 070 degrees and expect ORCKA and then the BEALE transition. We set up our FMS for this new transition. Shortly afterward we both heard what we thought was cleared direct ORCKA an fly the BEALE transition and the CA read exactly that back. A few minutes after we had established course to ORCKA center called another flight and directed a stop climb at FL190. We were passing through FL200 for FL230 when noticed another aircraft on TCAS at 10-15 miles ranger each 300 feet below our altitude before descending back down to FL190 LA Center then called out that we were off course. CA replied we were direct ORCKA then BEALE Transition as directed.Controller then stated ' No you were cleared ARCUS and the BEALE transition. ARCUS is the next fix after ORCKA on the ORKA5/BEALE SID and sounds very similar to ORCKA on a VHF radio. No TCAS alerts were initiated and no conflict occurred.The primary factor is the fact that ORCKA and ARCUS, two consecutive points along the ORKA5 SID sound similar over the VHF radio. So similar, in fact that both pilots heard it wrong when the clearance was first issued and the ATC controller heard it wrong when we read it back.Maybe a change to the fixes on the SID.
ASRS:1823525.s: During the ORKA5 departure, the flight crew and controller misheard the clearance for fix ARCUS as ORCKA due to similar phonetics, causing the aircraft to fly off course. Although no conflict occurred, the crew passed another aircraft at FL200 while the controller directed a stop climb at FL190.

ASRS:1823600.n: On departure from ZZZ Runway XXL passing through around 2,800 MSL smoke was observed in cockpit. Smoke event lasted 10-15 seconds. Advised ATC and return to airport was requested. We were switched to Tower frequency and made short approach to [Runway] XXL. Engine was shutdown on ramp inside of taxiway. No smoke or open flames were observed after the initial smoke event.Cause unknown. Aircraft preflight inspection was satisfactory and no smoke/fumes were observed outside of the brief smoke event.
ASRS:1823600.s: Pilots observed smoke in the cockpit at 2,800 MSL during departure from Runway XXL, prompting an immediate return and engine shutdown on the ramp. The cause remains unknown, as preflight inspections were satisfactory and no smoke or flames were seen after the brief event.

ASRS:1823602.n: ALTR FAIL master warning occurred for approximately 1 second during the downwind vector setting up for the ILS XX into ZZZ. Approximately 10 minutes later while approaching minimums on the ILS XX ZZZ, the ALTR FAIL master warning came on continuously. I instructed the student to go-around and fly the missed approach procedure as normal. After a positive rate of climb was established, I silenced the warning and started working on the checklist. The alternator amps were positive when I checked them. The checklist failed to bring the alternator back online without a master warning activation, so I deactivated the alternator and completed the recommended load shedding procedures with the exception of the lighting bus due to being in close proximity of ZZZ1. BATT AMPS was -7. We flew the ILS XYL into ZZZ1 due to poor inflight visibility. The flight was completed without incident, [company] was notified, and aircraft was written up.Reviewing the POH, my best guess as to the cause of the alternator failure is an alternator voltage between 30.5 and 32. The alternator was still providing power with a positive amperage indication while the master warning was active, which leads me to believe that the over-voltage relay was not tripped. Something else caused the master warning to activate. There was no burning smell or other indication of trouble.
ASRS:1823602.s: The pilot and student experienced an intermittent then continuous ALTR FAIL warning during an ILS approach to ZZZ, prompting a go-around and load shedding. The pilot suspects an alternator voltage between 30.5 and 32 volts triggered the warning, though the alternator remained functional and the flight completed safely.

ASRS:1823603.n: We were dispatched an aircraft that had previously been reported with a directional control discrepancy with the right main gear (time frame between this being reported and me getting this aircraft I assume was less than 15 min). This aircraft was not taken off the line for maintenance to check. In the aircraft book I had not seen this discrepancy listed when I opened it. I had gone out and done a preflight of the aircraft and did not see any issue with either landing gear (treads and wheel pressure were all fine and no sign of brake fluid leak). We took off with no incident. We proceeded to ZZZ where we did a few landings. I noted that the aircraft slid a bit which I thought was my new student locking up the brakes. I told him, 'I have controls' and told him to get off the brakes (also visually inspected his feet were off). I assumed it was due to improper use of brakes and we continued to do landings. On our last takeoff at our rotation speed, I noticed the aircraft's right wing dip and an 'odd' experience in the rudder pedals. I believed it was a gust of crosswind (as we experienced this multiple times during our ground reference maneuvers earlier). I took controls and had us climb. However, after thinking about the sensation I got from the rudder pedals I came to the conclusion that my wheel might have been deflated. I decided I wanted to fly back to ZZZ as the runway was longer, wider and ATC could inspect my gear. I came in and Approach addressed me as 'priority aircraft' which I responded that we were not in an emergency as I wanted my tire inspected first before I declared my situation as an emergency (At no point did I declare myself as an aircraft in an emergency). Once I was handed off to Tower I noticed an ambulance and firetruck holding short of the runway. I did a low approach for [Runway] XXR where I was told my gear looked fine. I concluded with a landing and noticed no issue on my landing or taxi. Maintenance followed me back and inspected the tire which they found no issue with.I do respect the fact that as the PIC of this flight I hold the final authority for the safety of the flight. However, this aircraft should not have made it through to be redispatch moments after it was just reported as 'having a discrepancy'. At the time I heard 'Green' aircraft in the pattern. If I was a few minutes early or late a 'Green' could have easily been given this aircraft. Sending a solo student up with an aircraft with known directional control issues very easily could have resulted in a far worse safety report. I believe an outdated software resulted in this. There were a lot of people this problem slipped through and all of us had been trained by the best flight school in the world. I believe any aircraft that has been reported not fit to fly should be marked by the computer system and shouldn't be able to be redispatch. As noted above, this problem had slipped through a number of very well trained personal. Just like the swiss cheese model when analyzing an accidents or incidents. This problem should have been picked up but its wasn't and I believe this highlights a vulnerability in our procedures. This problematic aircraft could have very easily ended up in the hands of a solo student. I would recommend software that allows the dispatcher the ability to straight away remove an aircraft from the line without having to wait for the aircraft's book to be brought in. Or simply marking an aircraft as having been reported as having a discrepancy.
ASRS:1823603.s: The pilot reported that an aircraft with a recent directional control discrepancy was redispatched without maintenance, leading to suspected tire issues during training landings at ZZZ. Although the tire was later found intact, the pilot attributed the near-miss to a software failure that allowed the unfit aircraft to be assigned to a student pilot.

ASRS:1823608.n: Student and I were doing landings on [Runway] 27L before our departure to the practice area at GFK. On one of the patterns, (I believe on the downwind), Tower told us that we needed to keep it a touch and go for jet traffic. We acknowledged but no information was given to where the jet was or what runway it was inbound for. I was looking for the traffic as we moved to short final and did not see it visually or on ADS-B. After completing a shaky soft field landing with a new student, we kept it rolling and at rotation, Tower asked if we could turn crosswind at airport road. It would be right at 30 degrees bank but I felt it was safe so I told them it was possible. At about 2-300 AGL just as I was starting the turn over the road and finishing the reply for the above radio call, I saw an air carrier over the approach lights on short final for [Runway] 35L at near co altitude. I took controls immediately and had to bank nearly 45 degrees to the left in order to avoid a collision with the air carrier. Tower did not seem like it was important to let us know where the traffic was or which runway it was coming in on.Lack of separation and information provided to both aircrews.Better procedures for separating jet and prop traffic especially when using crossing runways. Better communication between ATC and pilot of possible traffic conflicts. Pointing out traffic to aircrews that may be landing close time-wise on intersecting runways.
ASRS:1823608.s: During a student touch-and-go on Runway 27L, the instructor and student nearly collided with an air carrier on short final for Runway 35L at 200–300 feet AGL. The incident occurred because Tower failed to provide traffic location or runway information, forcing the pilot to execute a 45-degree bank to avoid the jet.

ASRS:1823670.n: IFR flight plan filed TVL - ZZZ. 2 pilots. I was the designated SIC and the Pilot Flying for this flight. We elected to depart VFR and obtain our IFR clearance once airborne. We announced our taxi intentions for Runway 36. We noted a few aircraft in the area either landing or flying by the airport. As we held short of Runway 36 at intersection Bravo, we saw an aircraft on our TCAS at 1,700 feet AGL about 4 miles south of the airport heading toward the airport. I visually acquired the aircraft soon thereafter. After hearing no further traffic advisories from other aircraft, the PIC and I agreed to depart Runway 36. The PIC announced our intentions to depart Runway 36 and no further calls (from other aircraft) were initially heard. As we crossed the hold short line, the aircraft that we visually acquired earlier stated their intention to land Runway 36 and began descending. We immediately stopped the aircraft and told the other aircraft we were past the hold short line, but not on the runway surface. The other pilot acknowledged our location and continued their approach to landing. The PIC reiterated that we were already past the hold short line and the other pilot just acknowledged our location. No attempt to increase spacing through S-turns, a 360 or go around was made by the other pilot as we were stopped between the hold short line and the left edge of the runway surface (displaced threshold). Not knowing how fast the aircraft was going to approach the runway, we elected to stay put and maintain visual contact with the landing aircraft. As that aircraft landed, another aircraft (PC-12) announced their intentions to land while on a left base to final. Again, we announced we were past the hold short line but not on the runway surface. They acknowledged our location and continued to land while showing no attempts to increase spacing for us to move our aircraft. After the second aircraft landed, we departed Runway 36 without further incident.
ASRS:1823670.s: Two pilots on a VFR departure from Runway 36 held short at intersection Bravo while two other aircraft landed on the same runway. The departing crew stopped past the hold short line after the landing pilots acknowledged their position but made no maneuvers to increase spacing, allowing the departure to proceed after the landings.

ASRS:1823676.n: On Date at XA15 local Aircraft X had a near miss incident. The other Aircraft Y looked to be a Helicopter. Aircraft X was conducting flight tests in the local area and training in the traffic pattern. They were using Runway XX and using a right traffic pattern. While Aircraft X was descending into the airport the [Visual Observer] noticed the helicopter was headed to ZZZ airport on a NE heading about 200-300 feet AGL. We notified Aircraft X that there was traffic converging in their flight path. At this point Aircraft X completed their landing and was on the upwind Runway XX. At this point Aircraft Y was at the departure end of the runway at 200 feet AGL. We told Aircraft X urgently to turn left and they were about cross paths with Aircraft Y. This wasn't possible because they were too low to the ground. They ended up leveling to pass under the helicopter. Aircraft X and Aircraft Y came within about 20-50 feet of each other. Talking to my other pilot we believe Aircraft Y failed to read the NOTAMS around the local area saying there is UAV activity in the area. Aircraft Y should have never been that low to the ground near the departure end of the runway. Aircraft Y clearly did not see Aircraft X as he did nothing to attempt to climb, descend, or turn.
ASRS:1823676.s: Aircraft X, conducting flight tests in a right traffic pattern, nearly collided with Helicopter Y while descending near the runway departure end. The reporter attributes the 20-50 foot separation to Helicopter Y failing to read local UAV NOTAMs and flying too low without seeing Aircraft X.

ASRS:1823685.n: On a Part 91 repositioning flight we were leveling off at 3,000 feet in contact with Charlotte Approach activating our IFR flight plan. Weather conditions were clear with unlimited ceiling and unlimited visibility despite our destination airport JQF reporting a broken layer at 500 feet. We were loading and activating the approach for our destination airport and had it in sight visually. When I looked up as Pilot Flying out the left-hand window I saw a flash and looked behind the wing to see a high wing aircraft a my 8 o'clock position about 25 feet below me. We did not see the airplane in front of us at any time and had overtaken it as it was flying in the same direction. We were well within the 30 mile mode C veil of Charlotte International yet that airplane did not show up on ADS-B. No evasive action was taken because we had already passed it by the time I saw it. We queried Charlotte Approach if they had a primary target in our vicinity and they said that they did not have any target.
ASRS:1823685.s: During a Part 91 repositioning flight leveling at 3,000 feet near Charlotte, the Pilot Flying visually detected a high-wing aircraft 25 feet below that was not displayed on ADS-B or by Approach. The crew overtook the unseen aircraft without taking evasive action as they had already passed it.

ASRS:1823704.n: I was watching a trainee in Sector X. He was having issues giving a pop up IFR clearance to an aircraft. As he was trying to figure it out I saw Aircraft Y to the south west of the airport at 075 and Aircraft X was headed south bound climbing to 080. I initially thought it would not have been a factor, however, I then heard the trainee give the IFR clearance the wrong altitude and issued a climb into another sectors airspace, IFR. I went and corrected it to avoid a potential airspace violation or worse. As soon as I fixed that situation I saw that Aircraft Y had climbed to 080 and was headed right at Aircraft X. The trainee issued traffic to Aircraft Y and Aircraft Y said he the airbus (Aircraft X) in sight. Aircraft X then said that he was responding to an RA. The trainee then told Aircraft Y to descend for traffic. I keyed up and told Aircraft X to report complete with RA and that the traffic had Aircraft X in sight. Aircraft X said he was going to file a near midair.Aircraft Y should have been capped at a VFR altitude and coordination should have been made to keep Aircraft X climbing. Trainees should be competent at issuing an IFR clearance prior to a control position.
ASRS:1823704.s: A trainee controller in Sector X issued an incorrect IFR clearance to Aircraft X, causing a climb into another sector and a subsequent RA with Aircraft Y. The supervisor corrected the clearance, but Aircraft X filed a near midair collision report due to the trainee's error and lack of coordination.

ASRS:1823717.n: Aircraft X was IFR, level 120, and eastbound.Aircraft X reported Aircraft Y, four hundred feet above, opposite direction, crossing directly above. It was not confirmed, but the pilot believes the Aircraft Y climbed to avoid Aircraft X at the last minute, thus passing above by 400 feet. Aircraft Y was VFR and not talking to any HLN controllers. Aircraft Y later checked on with LC after the conflict was over. There was no time for evasive action by Aircraft X or control instructions from Approach in-between the report of Aircraft Y and the two aircraft passing.HLN is entirely non-radar. Approach cannot and does not see any VFR aircraft, and can only pass traffic if VFR pilots identify themselves. In this case, Aircraft Y did not check on with approach so no traffic was given.Both pieces of traffic were at 120, so they would have been on ZLC's radar and both had ADS-B. HLN does not have access to either of these. If HLN did have access to either one, approach could have called traffic in a timely manner and could have climbed or descended Aircraft X accordingly.HLN needs some form of surveillance, whether it is an ADS-B feed, or a display of already existing radar coverage.
ASRS:1823717.s: A pilot flying Aircraft X IFR at FL120 reported a near-miss with VFR Aircraft Y, which climbed to pass 400 feet above in a non-radar sector. The conflict occurred because the non-radar controller lacked surveillance data to issue traffic advisories since Aircraft Y had not self-identified.

ASRS:1823728.n: I was providing on the job training on Ground 1 when the following event happened. Aircraft X exited [Runway] 25R at J and was instructed to 'taxi via B, L, hold short of K1 and contact City Ramp.' Aircraft X read back the instruction correctly. The developmental made two more calls and in the meantime Aircraft X started to turn from B onto K...one taxiway earlier than instructed. I pointed out the error to the developmental and then the developmental immediately told Aircraft X to stop. (Background: K & L are now City Ramp controlled and the only entry point to the ramp without additional coordination is via L short of K1.)We explained to Aircraft X that they were prematurely turning into the ramp and not following the issued route. Aircraft X responded by saying they had received clearance to continue on K short of K2, however we had never mentioned anything about K/K2. The Controller in Charge coordinated with the City Ramp via the phone and verified that it was safe for Aircraft X to continue northbound on K. Additionally, while this entire scenario was unfolding, Aircraft Y deviated from their taxi clearance (B, K, C, Northroute) and turned onto L. I overkeyed the developmental and told Aircraft Y to 'hold short of K1 and contact the ramp.' After the training session, I reviewed the tapes for both Aircraft X and Aircraft Y's instructions/readbacks. There were no discrepancies with either--each pilot responded correctly and timely to the developmental's instructions but failed to comply.I am writing a report about the operation of this 'LAWA City Ramp' because it continues to cause unsafe proximity events. While I was previously under the impression that the majority of the errors were due to pilot expectation bias and over reliance on familiarity (the old Northroute was on K/L), I now believe that the instructions of the Ramp Tower personnel contributed to Aircraft X's deviation today. See below:When we told Aircraft X that they turned too soon, their response was 'we had further clearance to continue via K short of K2.' It is my belief that Aircraft X called the City Ramp on their second radio while taxiing westbound on B and the ramp personnel instructed them to continue via K short of K2. Aircraft X understood this as a complete change from the instructions we provided and began to turn on K early. If this is approximately what happened, then it needs to be remedied immediately.
