It's unsafe to have non-ATC personnel issuing instructions to aircraft that could be confused with new or amended instructions for how to taxi/proceed on the movement area. The ramp personnel need to clearly define to inbound aircraft that the previous clearance remains the same, but once on L short of K1, they may continue, hold, etc.Additionally, this is about the actions of pilots that turn early onto L/K when they correctly were issued and read back 'the Northroute.' I previously stated that 'I'd recommend additional signage, a change to the charts, or added emphasis in the text of the 'Northroute' that emboldens how N is now the Northroute, not K or L. Or all of the above;' and my sentiments still remain. I believe there was one small change to the Jeppesen map that tried to highlight the new ramp area but bolding the Northroute and re-emphasizing that N is the Northroute could also help prevent this occurrence.
ASRS:1823728.s: An ATC trainee and two pilots were involved when Aircraft X and Y deviated from taxi clearances at LAWA. The reporter attributes the errors to conflicting instructions from City Ramp personnel and pilot expectation bias regarding the new Northroute, resulting in unsafe proximity events.

ASRS:1823740.n: Aircraft Y had just landed and was instructed to hold short of H9 on H to protect for other arrivals that might exit at H9. When I was ready, I taxied Aircraft Y up to hold short of 25R at l. However, Aircraft Y didn't respond. I called him 3 times with no response. I cleared Aircraft X for takeoff on 25R. My assist asked ground control to see if Aircraft Y had switched frequencies and was just about to call approach to see if Aircraft Y had got back to that frequency when we saw Aircraft Y taxiing forward. I called Aircraft Y and verified he would hold short of Runway 25R which he read back with his call sign. Shortly after my assist said 'He's not going to stop!' Momentarily I didn't believe it but quickly went to Aircraft Y and told him to stop. I then immediately cancelled Aircraft X takeoff clearance. Aircraft Y did stop with their nose about at the runway edge. Aircraft X was about at B2 when I cancelled their clearance. Aircraft X was already stopping before ASDE-X (Airport Surface Detection Equipment) alarmed. Aircraft X taxied back for departure and I crossed Aircraft Y. Maybe I shouldn't have departed Aircraft X with Aircraft Y not responding. Aircraft Y was holding on taxiway H short of H9. Aircraft X was told to Line up and wait Runway 25R. Aircraft Y was then told to turn left at H and Hold Short Runway 25R. There was no response from Aircraft Y. The instruction was repeated again to Aircraft Y but still no response. I on Local Assist went to Ground Control to see if they had Aircraft Y on frequency which they did not. I noticed Aircraft Y start moving. Local Control reached out again with and repeated Hold Short Runway 25R. This time Aircraft Y responded and gave a good read back of Hold Short Runway 25R.Aircraft X was cleared for takeoff and started the departure roll. I first noticed that as Aircraft Y was turning at taxiway Lima approaching the hold bars it did not look like they were stopping, and verbal said that. I immediately said again that Aircraft Y is not stopping. Local Control told Aircraft Y to hold position and canceled the takeoff clearance for Aircraft X as they were between B3 and G. Two seconds later the Airport Surface Detection Equipment alarm went off for the occupied runway alert. Aircraft X exited Runway 25R at B4 and taxied back for departure. Aircraft Y continued the cross and went to parking.I don't know what to recommend to prevent this from happening again as all the protocols were followed with correct read backs. I do not know if the Runway Stop Lights were working properly. I know there were issues with that system in the past with the red lights turning off early. But since it was daytime and Lima is not in a direct line of sight for those lights, I cannot know if the system was functioning properly.
ASRS:1823740.s: Air Traffic Controllers cleared Aircraft X for takeoff while Aircraft Y failed to respond to hold short instructions at Runway 25R. Aircraft Y entered the runway, forcing the controller to cancel Aircraft X's clearance just before an ASDE-X alarm triggered, though no collision occurred.

ASRS:1823760.n: At cruise, we had a 'Stab Out of Trim' light. The QRH was run and we determined that we had to land the aircraft using manual trim. We coordinated with Dispatch and ATC for a diversion to ZZZ. An initial decision was made to reduce fuel to max landing gross weight by holding. After several turns in holding and in coordination with Dispatch and Operations Center Chief Pilot, the decision was made to exercise Captain's authority and proceed to ZZZ for an overweight landing, rather than continue to hold for the two hours it would take to burn down to max landing gross weight. We were vectored to a 20 NM final for Runway XXL and had an uneventful approach and landing. Brake cooling was accomplished and we were able to do a normal taxi and park at the gate. Flight Attendants and Passengers were kept aware of our situation with regular updates.
ASRS:1823760.s: The crew experienced a 'Stab Out of Trim' light at cruise, requiring manual trim and a diversion to ZZZ. They elected to perform an overweight landing rather than hold for fuel burn, resulting in an uneventful approach, landing, and brake cooling.

ASRS:1823763.n: During flight preparation at the gate in ZZZ, I received two HAZMAT NOTAC forms for items we would be carrying to ZZZ1. Oxygen cylinders and batteries I believe. I made a mental note to call Dispatch to have remarks added to our dispatch release, but then I got distracted with other events (like servicing requests, weather planning, rushing), and forgot about the HAZMAT.
ASRS:1823763.s: The pilot failed to add HAZMAT remarks to the dispatch release for oxygen cylinders and batteries during flight preparation at ZZZ. This omission occurred because the pilot was distracted by servicing requests, weather planning, and rushing, causing them to forget the required action.

ASRS:1823788.n: Passenger seated over left wing area advised crew with picture of possible damage to left forward wing area. After passengers deplaned, Captain and First Officer examined photo and over wing area and determined that there looked to be possible delamination of outboard left wing slat area. Captain called Maintenance in ZZZ and filed a report. Maintenance came out to inspect and found large area by left wing outboard slat had indeed delaminated and tore out areas of honeycomb structure. Pictures taken. Aircraft taken out of service per Maintenance Control.
ASRS:1823788.s: A passenger reported possible damage to the left forward wing, prompting the flight crew to inspect the area after deplaning. Maintenance confirmed delamination and honeycomb tearing on the outboard left wing slat, resulting in the aircraft being taken out of service.

ASRS:1823837.n: While we departed Ontario, CA on the RAJEE3 departure, ATC asked us to maintain 7,000 feet. Close to the RAJEE checkpoint ATC called two targets:1) [A] Small Aircraft, 12 o' clock, 7 miles, 6,500 feet. 2) A Medium Large Transport 8,000 [feet] at 10 o' clock.We responded searching for the Small Aircraft and called the Medium Large Transport in sight. ATC again called our attention to the Small Aircraft 12 o' clock five miles to which we responded searching. Many other calls not related to us continued over the frequency when we received an RA from the TCAS indicating adjust vertical speed. Looking at the VSI the vertical speed showed to remain level. We spot the Small Aircraft on TCAS converging but only visually picked out the aircraft less than 1/4 mile (hazy outside) at 10 o' clock (not 12 o' clock) passing directly underneath us 300 feet. TCAS indicated clear of conflict as the Small Aircraft passed to our five o'clock. The next call from ATC was traffic passing behind us and climb to 13,000 feet. Meanwhile, the Medium Large Transport passes over us.We indicated to ATC that we received a TCAS RA and that the Small Aircraft passed 300 feet below us. ATC departure acknowledged and passed us to center. ATC could have vectored us off the SID to avoid the conflicting traffic.
ASRS:1823837.s: During departure from Ontario, CA on the RAJEE3 SID, the crew received a TCAS RA while maintaining 7,000 feet due to a small aircraft passing 300 feet below. The pilot attributed the conflict to ATC failing to vector the aircraft off the SID to avoid the converging traffic.

ASRS:1823845.n: On initial approach to Runway XXL, vectored to position ZZZZZ (IAF) 2,600 ft., and reducing speed to180 Kts. ATC cleared us for the approach Runway XXL. Pilot Flying descended below the required altitude to 2,420 feet, While the Pilot Monitoring and I (Observer seat) were giving corrective call outs, the Pilot Flying disconnected the autopilot and corrected the altitude and simultaneously ZZZZ Approach Control gave us an advisory call, which was responded appropriately by pilot monitor. Rest of the approach and landing were uneventful. While being vectored for ILS approach to RWY XXL at ZZZZ, the Pilot Flying momentarily began an early descent through required altitude of 2,600 feet. I, the pilot not flying, and the jumpseat pilot gave immediate verbal corrections. Aircraft descended to approximately 2,420 feet as the Pilot Flying regained situational awareness and applied corrective action to include resetting the MCP altitude, and then reverting to manual control. The recovery was smooth and controlled. As the aircraft was returning to 2,600 feet, ZZZZ Radar Control called to direct climb to 2,600 feet. I responded to ATC while the Pilot Flying completed the recovery. Approach and landing were completed uneventfully. This was the final segment of a 2 leg international flying pairing nearing 17 hours of duty. All crew members were not at their best state of alertness. Original arrival setup was for a STAR coupled to an ILS approach. Flown arrival was very non standard. The aircraft was vectored off arrival path and given clearance to disregard many published mandatory altitudes. This complicated arrival descent planning and may have led to the Pilot Flying losing some situational awareness. ATC Traffic on approach ahead was a potential conflict. This diverted my attention during the approach.Delays in positive corrective action which could have lessened/prevented the altitude deviation were potentially caused by distraction due to traffic call, lessened cognitive performance due to overnight/long duty period, lack of urgency due to VMC weather with runway in view.
ASRS:1823845.s: During a non-standard vector to Runway XXL, the Pilot Flying descended below 2,600 feet to 2,420 feet due to fatigue, distraction, and complex descent planning. The crew corrected the deviation manually while ATC issued a climb advisory, resulting in an uneventful landing.

ASRS:1823851.n: Early descent and low speed condition resulting in go-around. I was the Pilot Flying. Very short flight. Visual approach to RWY 15 at CHS. I was expecting the ILS approach. I missed that the GS for RWY 15 was out of service. We had briefed the OSPRI7 STAR. ATC recleared us direct to the airport and eventually direct MAMAE intersection to join the localizer for [Runway] 15 at 3,000 [feet] ft. Airport was in sight and we were cleared for a visual approach. I armed the approach and when we went into altitude capture at 3,000 [feet] I incorrectly set an altitude below 3,000 [feet] to allow the descent to continue in order to join the glide slope. I then realized we were not receiving the glide slope and were below the FAF crossing altitude at 1000ft. I disconnected the autopilot and stopped the descent. Unfortunately I did not also call for the flight directors off initially. I am relatively new to the equipment. Since we were in landing configuration of course the speed dropped rapidly. We were in landing configuration with the airport and PAPI's in sight but since the approach was unstable I decided to go around. We then flew the RWY 15 RNAV (GPS)Y to a normal landing. It was the third leg of a busy day with thunderstorm avoidance on the first two flights. It is my practice to carefully review the NOTAMs but somehow I missed the GS OTS. I haven't been into CHS as yet and the flight is very short and our ATC clearance had us high from the top of descent.Direct to a new airport on a time compressed flight for a visual at night is never in my opinion a pleasant way to conclude a long day of flying. Upon honest reflection I fully acknowledge I had a strong expectation bias for the ILS to 15. The lack of the GS and the unexpected consequences placed us in a reactionary position which is unacceptable.Our training is clear on how to capture and correct erroneous situations should they occur and we did our best to stop and correct an inadvertently entered unstable position. This was a clear example of the value and necessity of our human factors training. I know these things have happened before and I consider it my professional responsibility to not allow it to happen to me. And yet it did. Recognizing, and fully appreciating how higher than expected workload situations can present themselves is an essential aspect to our work. An increased diligence regarding the review of NOTAMs is a resounding suggestion I'm making to myself for one. Also, the need for particularly increased vigilance when in situations such as this is something I'll never forget.
ASRS:1823851.s: The Pilot Flying missed a glide slope out-of-service NOTAM and incorrectly set a low altitude during a visual approach to Runway 15 at CHS, causing an unstable descent. The crew executed a go-around due to low speed and altitude, subsequently landing safely via an RNAV (GPS) approach.

ASRS:1823869.n: I was the Pilot Flying on Flight XXXX, ZZZ to ZZZ1, DATE. All was normal until takeoff roll. At approximately 110 kts a loud signal began blaring in the cockpit. ECAM was clear of any messages and master caution/warning lights were extinguished so I elected to continue the takeoff. When the After Takeoff Checklist was completed we [advised] with Tower and told them we wanted to return for an immediate landing. I had two jumpseaters that flew the A321 and they were essential assets. They assisted in determining the source of the loud sound which was the EVAC Command Signal and the EMER CALL buzzers going off continuously. Neither the signal or buzzers would silence. Jump seater 1, Captain NAME1, covered the EVAV speaker with his hand trying to muzzle the sound and provided valuable input. I transferred the aircraft to the First Officer and determined that the cabin inter-phone was inoperative and was not able to communicate with the cabin. I directed the jump seater 2, First Officer NAME1, to open the cockpit door and establish communications with the flight attendants and asses the conditions in the cabin. He reported that passengers cabin lights, emergency exit lights, and lavatory smoke detector lights were intermittently blinking on and off. I told him through the cockpit door to tell the flight attendants that we were returning to land and not to evacuate and for the passengers to remain seated once the aircraft stopped. I took back control of the aircraft and we accomplished an over weight landing. After stopping and consulting with the AARF commander we determined it was safe to taxi to the gate. Signal continued to sound until maintenance showed and pulled circuit breakers at the gate. The assistance of my First Officer along with the 2 jump seaters was absolutely essential in successful conclusion to this event. During the event, my confusion of what was actually happening might have been mitigated by a deeper understanding of the CIDS (Cabin Intercommunication Data System) system.I feel that having better systems knowledge would be beneficial to any similar future events. I was the Pilot Monitoring on FLT XXXX, ZZZ to ZZZ1, DATE. All was normal until takeoff roll. At approximately 110kts a loud signal began blaring in the cockpit. ECAM was clear of any messages and master caution/warning lights were extinguished so Captain opted to continue the takeoff. When the After Takeoff Checklist was completed we advised with Tower and told them we wanted to return for an immediate landing. We had two jump seaters that flew the A321 and they were essential assets. They assisted in determining the source of the loud sound which was the EVAC Command Signal and the EMER CALL buzzers going off continuously. Neither the signal or buzzers would silence. Jump seater 1, Captain NAME1, covered the EVAV speaker with his hand trying to muzzle the sound and provided valuable input. I transferred the aircraft to the First Officer and determined that the cabin inter-phone and PA was inoperative and was not able to communicate with the cabin. I directed the jump seater 2, First Officer NAME1, to open the cockpit door and establish communications with the flight attendants and asses the conditions in the cabin. He reported that passengers cabin lights, emergency exit lights, and lavatory smoke detector lights were intermittently blinking on and off. Captain told him through the cockpit door to tell the flight attendants that we were returning to land and not to evacuate and for the passengers to remain seated once the aircraft stopped. Captain took back control of the aircraft and we accomplished an over weight landing. After stopping and consulting with the AARF commander we determined it was safe to taxi to the gate. Signal continued to sound until maintenance showed and pulled multiple circuit breakers at the gate.Causal factor was a failure of CIDS computer. Maintenance has to research more causal factors on their end.Procedure on ECAM for CIDS computer failure. Nothing was displayed in ECAM during entire event.
ASRS:1823869.s: During takeoff of an A321, a continuous EVAC signal and EMER CALL buzzers sounded with no ECAM warnings, caused by a CIDS computer failure. The crew returned for an overweight landing after jumpseaters identified the fault and assisted with cabin communication while the cabin interphone remained inoperative.

ASRS:1823883.n: Low altitude alert from AFW Tower during night visual approach to [Runway] 16L from the south. We entered a left downwind to [Runway] 16L, turned base early due to traffic ahead, and descended initially to 1,000 feet AGL. At the alert from ATC, we cross-checked our altitude, intercepted the glide path from below but inside the instrument FAF, and landed uneventfully. Turning earlier than what would have set us up at the instrument FAF and attempting to interpolate a visual descent path, cross cockpit, at night. Set up for a left base at AFW at 1,500 feet AGL rolled off for the turn to final and slowly descended to 1,000 feet AGL to join up on the ILS glide slope for [Runway] 16L. During the rollout received a call from ATC saying they were getting an altitude alert and heck our altitude. At no point during the rollout did we go lower than 1,000 feet AGL and rolled out on final on glide path. Landing was uneventful. We were on a visual and turned inside the FAF for traffic. As a result we were lower than normal during the final turn.
ASRS:1823883.s: The flight crew received a low altitude alert from AFW Tower during a night visual approach to Runway 16L after turning base early for traffic and descending to 1,000 feet AGL inside the FAF. The crew intercepted the glide path from below and landed uneventfully, attributing the alert to being lower than normal due to the early turn.

ASRS:1823905.n: On a flight landing in EWR, the ATIS advertised the Stadium Visual to Runway 29. Although the environment was busy due to the airspace congestion, everything was working out smoothly and well. Approach mentioned to us a few different aircraft along the way to use caution for due to wake turbulence and we did use caution for the several large aircraft we saw during the terminal phase of the approach. I do not recall, however, my Pilot Monitoring later said the Tower upon clearing us to land issued another caution for wake turbulence for a 747. I did not see any flying aircraft that would pose any wake turbulence threat. The approach was normal and I was right on my target speeds. I closed both throttles all the way during the flare, and both engines settled all the way to idle. The tires were maybe an inch or two from the surface, the yoke back bumping the stop, all the flying air gone from the wings, touchdown imminent, [when] a large gust from the left shoved the aircraft aggressively to the right. The gust raised the left wing up and also the whole aircraft up into the air several feet. When the gust reached the tail, it shoved the vertical stabilizer right moving the nose left. The centerline of the runway went from centered on the nose gear to well outside the main gear near the left wing tip. There were two gusts one right after the other, both the same and having the same effect on the aircraft. I immediately shoved both throttles all the way forward and countered with the controls to maintain orientation. I don't recall calling the go-around, but my Pilot Monitoring says I called it right away. The air was smooth after the two gusts, the plane settled some towards the ground as it gained momentum. Once everything was straightened out and the airplane with some flying speed now climbing from the runway instead of closing toward it, I realized my right arm was still holding the throttles against the stop. Knowing that could be very bad for the engines, I looked inside to see how badly they were over revving and simultaneously pulled them back off the stop some. I never got the chance to see because I noticed the left engine sitting at idle while the right engine was making full power. That's when I realized my right leg was holding about 80% right rudder travel in. The gear was up and the flaps sitting at 15 degrees and we were making only 125 knots. Then after several more seconds, the left engine began to slowly make its way through the 50%'s, 60s, 70s, 80s, and finally into the low 90% of N1 speed. With everything back to normal, we cleaned up the aircraft and settled in for the next approach. ATC again offered us the Stadium Visual to 29 but said the ILS 22R was available. We took the ILS 22R. ATC never asked us why we went around. We did not make any communications to our team in the cabin until after shutdown. The origin of the gust was immediately very clear to both of us in the cockpit. It was jet blast from jet engines pointed at our flight path during our touchdown, departing aircraft on 22R beginning their takeoff roll were blasting the landing zone of 29 with their engines. Perhaps the cautionary statements we received from ATC for wake turbulence were referring to jet blast from airlines beginning to roll on the ground and not from wake turbulence from aircraft in flight. Had I been aware this was the case, I would have never accepted 29 as a landing option. The 22R & L runways cross Runway 29, so I envisioned aircraft departing across our landing path as they took off on the 22s. So I would see them and be aware of the timing for jet blast and wake from landing aircraft. However, instead, airlines were making intersection departures after the 29 intersection, shortening their takeoff distance. So instead of crossing our path, they were starting from our left and starting their takeoff roll, and moving away to our left. I never looked left during my landing, so I don'tknow what was there blasting us, I'm guessing something big. Of note, due to high fuel price in EWR, we were heavy, just a few hundred pounds under max landing weight. I would first suggest not landing small jets on [Runway] 29 at EWR when 22s are departing in the way they were. I wasn't familiar enough with EWR to know how dangerous the circumstance would be, I've landed on 22s in years past. I would also suggest the left engine acceleration be repaired to an acceptable level. Waiting 15 - 20 seconds for an engine to give power in fight is not acceptable. If neither engine had given power for that amount of time, I do not believe a touchdown without major damage would've been possible. Even still, it took everything the aircraft had in it plus everything humanly possible I could do to prevent an accident.
ASRS:1823905.s: During a landing approach to EWR Runway 29, the crew encountered severe jet blast from departing aircraft on Runway 22R, causing a go-around. The pilot noted that delayed left engine acceleration and the unexpected ground-level jet blast nearly resulted in an accident.

ASRS:1823935.n: Initial climb from SBA, ATC assigned 8,000 feet. I was hand flying the airplane and leveled at 8,000 feet per ATC instruction. After we leveled I noticed another aircraft on the ND traffic display showing 200 feet below us, right after that I heard ATC asking another aircraft to confirm they are descending. I'm not sure what they replied because we then got the traffic. As the traffic aircraft warning is going off I then noticed the other aircraft had climbed to our altitude of 8,000 feet then we got the TCAS RA descend descend now, I quickly pushed the nose over into the green band. Because of the high work load I over heard the captain saying I got the aircraft in sight and to follow the guidance, I then quickly saw the aircraft out the captain front window also descending into us from the left (around 7,600 [feet]) then we got another TCAS RA to Climb, Climb now, I started pitching up into the green band. I understood our procedures and did exactly that. It was a bit stressful to know our TCAS is trying to help us by getting away from the other aircraft but now that aircraft also doing what TCAS was initially telling us. I believe the heading we were assigned from ATC and the heading the other aircraft was on, ATC incorrectly assigned to someone and it didn't help that the other airplane wasn't following ATC instruction. After the clear of conflict I returned to 8,000 feet then we went over to departure and continue the climb.
ASRS:1823935.s: During initial climb from SBA, the crew encountered a TCAS conflict with another aircraft at 8,000 feet that descended into their path despite ATC instructions. The pilot executed opposing TCAS RAs to avoid collision, attributing the incident to incorrect ATC heading assignments and the other aircraft's failure to follow clearances.

ASRS:1823945.n: Inadvertent switching off of IR1 mode selector which deactivated that associated ADIRU. ADR and IR data not available. This occurred during flight one of day two of an initial Captain upgrade. The trainee came off the B777. He has been with our company for many years. The three legs of day one was extraordinarily busy. It was immediately clear to me during those three legs he had studied hard during training and had mastered much of the material. On the first two legs of day one I had a LCA (Line Check Airman) in-training watching me conduct the line check as part of that LCA's upgrade training. I commented to the new LCA not all trainees will be so well prepared as this one.This flight was leg four of the IOE and the first flight of day two. Our transportation to the airport was 15 minutes late and there was a detour so we arrived at the aircraft about 30 minutes prior to departure. Normally, I introduce myself to all the FAs (Flight Attendant). However, because we were on IOE, [we] were somewhat late to the aircraft and on Release 6. I only introduced myself to the FM. I felt I did not have time go to the back to introduce myself to the FAs assigned to the rear of the aircraft.We had been in the seat for approximately 3 hours. The upgrade Captain requested I ask the FM to prepare the meals and that we would then take a restroom break when the meals were ready. I did so. The FM called us about 25 minutes later to state the meals were ready. The upgrade Captain offered me the opportunity to use the Lav first. I declined and said he should go first and I would then go. The door chime rang and then I heard a knock. That knock is not standard. However, it occurs occasionally with legacy Company 2 flight attendants. We put on our masks. I saw the upgrade Captain move to get out of his seat, stand up, and let the FA in while he then left the cockpit. I noticed nothing odd about his movement out of the seat and to the rear of the cockpit. I saw out of the corner of my eye the FA was standing near the rear of the cockpit just behind and to the right of the Captain's seat, a normal position for a relief FA.My concentration then focused on something else. I think it was because we were getting ready to enter a large area of convective activity. I might have been looking at WSI and comparing that to what I was seeing on the weather radar. Why my gaze was generally focused forward and right I am not sure, but it was. I planned to brief the relief FA about this weather and its possible effect on their service in a few minutes. It was at that point, maybe 30-45 seconds after the upgrade Captain had left the cockpit, that for lack of a better description, 'all hell broke loose.' The cockpit went from a completely benign environment to one of confusion. The startle effect was in full force. The first warning was a continuous repetitive chime and the warning lights flashing. I immediately looked at the E/WD (Engine/Warning Display) and noted about 4-5 ECAMs listed, primary secondary and independent failures in both red and amber. I silenced the CRC (Continuous Repetitive Chime) by pushing [the] master warning light. That silenced the CRC. However, there still was an aural alert going off that I could not silence, which created a fair bit of consternation on my part. I look at my PFD and saw the FMAs were wrong. I then saw the AP (Autopilot) was off and that there was nothing where I expected to see the AT (Autothrottle) condition. I noted the aircraft climbing slightly and corrected that. I knew the AP disengaged for some reason but didn't know why. I thought about engaging AP 2 but then thought that may create new problems, so I elected to hand-fly until the ECAMs were sorted out. I saw we were no longer in NAV but again, wasn't sure why. I did see that the aircraft didn't diverge much from the 'green line' so lateral stick inputs weren't necessary. At this point ATC called to ask us something about recycling the transponder. We wereon speaker at that time, I responded we had a problem and to standby.I then noted the airspeed increasing and pulled the TLs (Thrust Lever) back, I didn't want to add an over-speed to our problems. This silenced another aural sound. I do not recall seeing a Thrust Locked ECAM or FMA which I thought would have been the source of the alert I couldn't silence. I glanced at the Captain PFD (Primary Flight Display) and ND (Navigation Display) and saw they didn't look right.The aircraft was reasonably stabilized now but, in my mind, because the ECAMs were displayed, the situation wasn't. I then told the FA to recall the trainee Captain to the cockpit. He opened the door, looked and then closed it, and said he was in the bathroom. I told the FA I knew that and I wanted him back in the cockpit now. He then had the FM knock on the Lav door. The trainee Captain returned to the cockpit and the relief FA left. The trainee Captain was incredulous when he looked at the E/WD. I told him I was hand-flying, had the aircraft and radios, and that he was to handle the ECAMs. It was at this point I noted we were about 20 knot slow, well within flying speed but slow for planned speed. I had overcompensated for my worry of overspending the aircraft. I pushed the power back up. Airspeed had fallen out of my cross-check. The trainee Captain methodically and correctly went through the ECAMs. As I recall the first several ECAMs had no action items, one ECAM had us switch the air data switch to three. At some point during this, ATC stated they now had data on us and asked if we needed assistance. We told him we were completing a procedure and to standby. Once the status messages were read and the ECAM procedure completed, I reached up to engage AP two. It did so. I armed the AT and then moved the TLs to the climb detent to engage it. Our ATC clearance was to proceed direct to a fix so we reinserted that. I don't recall having to pull or push to capture our assigned altitude but I can't be sure.It was now maybe 4-5 minutes after the initial event where I could take a breath. I recalled the ECAM and saw the ADR 1 fault. I then looked over to the ADIRS panel and saw IR mode selector one was in the OFF position. It, of course, was on for the flight up until some point in [the] last few minutes. I asked the trainee Captain if he recalls hitting the switch with his head or back as he left his seat. He said no. I then thought perhaps the switch was defective. This aircraft came to us as a through flight. We did not have to turn them on so we had no knowledge of how that switch felt by turning it on. We again discussed it and he stated he didn't recall even touching the overhead panel while leaving the seat.Because I didn't introduce myself to the FAs at the rear of the aircraft prior to the flight, I wasn't sure which FA came to the cockpit during our break. I asked the FM to ask the FA who came to the cockpit to call us on the interphone. That FA did and I asked him if he recalled touching anything on the overhead panel, he stated he did not. What I found unusual was that during the event, the FA seemed very nonplussed by the cacophony of sounds in the cockpit. I would have expected a FA to at least ask what was going on, but maybe he was somewhat shocked by what he saw and heard during his short time in the cockpit.The trainee Captain and I discussed that I would write up the ECAM and then conference Dispatch and Technical Support Maintenance Control to provide further details of what we thought may have occurred. I wanted the switch looked at but also didn't want Maintenance to search for a problem which might not exist. I ACARS'd Dispatch with the request and he set up the conference call. The communications with Technical Support Maintenance Control were reasonably good and he captured exactly what I wanted him to know and he appended it to our write-up. Since the Captain's displays were significantly degraded, we switched PF/PM roles. Fromthat point we continually deviated for weather, were put in holding, and changed our alternate three times. We over-burned by almost 5500 lb on this flight, more than on any flight I have been on in [an] Airbus. It was an understatement to say this was a busy flight. I don't know how this happened. The final flight of the day was a termination. As the trainee ran that checklist and turned off the IRUs, he stated he couldn't believe how he accidentally managed to switch that style of switch - pull and turn - off by getting out of the cockpit.I am disappointed in myself for not more thoroughly reviewing the flight manual for ADR 1 fault after things had settled down. We did not have a GPWS TERR FAULT light and no ECAM direction to switch it off so it remained on. We discussed that threat in that we were now the aircraft's GPWS system and to be cognizant of the terrain. We also discussed changing the transponder to position 2 but did not do so because there was no ECAM direction to [do] so and ATC noted no anomalies in our reporting. Also, once I saw the IR mode selector switch in the off position, I should have considered reviewing the NAV IR fault non-normal even though we didn't have that ECAM. I did not do a word search in the flight manual for ADR. Had I done so, I would have seen that there may be RVSM limitations associated with its failure and should have gone to the FOM for further information. I recall many years ago, our Line Manager at the time, wrote up in his weekly update a similar event. As I recall he wrote the trainee somehow managed to hook the window shade into that same switch and turned it off. That of course didn't happen here.
ASRS:1823945.s: During an initial Captain upgrade flight on a B777, the trainee Captain inadvertently switched off the IR1 mode selector while leaving the cockpit, deactivating the associated ADIRU. This caused multiple ECAM warnings and autopilot disengagement, requiring the check airman to hand-fly while the trainee completed procedures to restore systems.

ASRS:1823946.n: We were on departure, level at 8,000 feet on ATC Vectors. ATC called traffic at our 10 o'clock. We visually acquired the traffic and at about that time, we received a TCAS TRAFFIC DESCEND. The First Officer promptly disconnected the auto pilot and followed TCAS guidance and I reported 'Maneuvering TCAS RA' to ATC. The small aircraft target (high wing single engine) then began descending. Shortly thereafter, we received a TCAS CLIMB NOW command which the First Officer promptly complied with. At this point, the small aircraft also changed path and started climbing. The small aircraft maneuvered laterally away from us finally. Once we were clear of conflict, I told ATC we wished to report a Near Mid Air Collision, we re-engaged the autopilot and continued our flight. I messaged Dispatch and I verbally briefed Flight Operations after we landed.
ASRS:1823946.s: During departure at 8,000 feet on ATC vectors, the crew received TCAS RA commands to descend and climb to avoid a high-wing single-engine aircraft. The crew manually followed TCAS guidance, the other aircraft maneuvered away, and the incident was reported as a Near Mid Air Collision.

ASRS:1823948.n: While turning onto the lead in line to the gate, a maintenance pickup failed to yield to our aircraft, forcing our abrupt stop to avoid a collision. LGA Ramp was notified. Airport authority personnel met the aircraft at our request. The driver of the vehicle was cited by the airport authority. Company Operations was also contacted.
ASRS:1823948.s: During the taxi to the gate at LGA, a maintenance pickup failed to yield, forcing the aircraft to stop abruptly to avoid a collision. The vehicle driver was cited by airport authority personnel, and Company Operations was notified.

ASRS:1823988.n: Captain [was] Pilot Flying. He briefed the OSPRI arrival and ILS to [Runway] 15. ATC kept us high, then Cleared for the straight in visual. Gear, flaps and speed brakes out to get down. We both missed that the glideslope was out of service on the ATIS. We realized we were too low and leveled off around 1,000 feet. At some point we got the low energy speed warning. We had left the speed brakes out. Retracted them. Disconnected the FD's. Captain called for a go around. Preformed the GA and returned for the RNAV 15. Busy day flying around storms. Last flight at night. Short flight. ATC keeping us high. Expectation bias to the ILS. I had recently been to CHS at night and the ILS was working. New Captain to [aircraft], all his other time was in Boeing aircraft. My failure to trap our errors earlier. I will create more effective barriers going forward. For example: Request ILS/RNAV approaches vs visual at night. Get delay vectors when ATC keeps us high.
ASRS:1823988.s: The crew missed that the glideslope was out of service during a night visual approach, causing them to descend too low and trigger a low energy warning. The Captain initiated a go-around due to expectation bias and the new Captain's lack of aircraft experience, returning for an RNAV approach.

ASRS:1824040.n: We took off out of ZZZ to ZZZ1 for a night ETOPS flight. Everything was normal. Although the crew was current, all hadn't flown much in the past XX months due to COVID. We briefed this fact and were aware that we would all have to be on our toes due to the fact that our flying skills were rusty.The flight was normal. We operated the flight very close to the flight plan.After a normal approach and smooth landing, we taxied to the gate. After shutting down the engines and performing the Parking Checklist, we were surprised to see an overweight landing message being printed. We had landed approximately 700 pounds overweight.We sent the appropriate overweight landing code and I called local maintenance to report the issue.
ASRS:1824040.s: The flight crew operated a night ETOPS flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 and landed approximately 700 pounds overweight. The overweight landing message appeared only after engine shutdown, prompting the crew to send the appropriate code and notify local maintenance.

ASRS:1824051.n: We started our taxi out from gate. As we turned away from the gate a water(?) /service truck passed in front of us close enough for us to apply brakes. The driver was looking at his phone and never saw us.
ASRS:1824051.s: During taxi out, a water or service truck passed in front of the aircraft, forcing the crew to apply brakes. The reporter stated the truck driver was looking at his phone and failed to see the aircraft.

ASRS:1824081.n: We were descending on the arrival into ZZZ. We were descending at a high speed programmed into the FMC. I have over 10,000 hours flying the Next Gens and am comfortable with that descent profile. This was my first MAX flight. Somewhere in the descent the FMA changed without warning to MCP SPD (Mode Control Panel Speed). It went unnoticed. I have witnessed many Next Gens revert to VNV SPD (Vnav Speed), but never MCP SPD. There is a significant difference, in that MCP SPD gives no altitude protection. I have never seen anything like this. Somewhere around ZZZZZ/11000, we received a radio call and became distracted as the aircraft descended through 11000. I did not catch the deviation until 10,000 and momentum and recovery took us to about 9,500 feet. I disconnect all automation and hand flew the recovery as I tried to figure out what had just happened. We reported the deviation to ATC and continued to ZZZ without incident.I do not know why this happened. I can only guess that somehow LVL CHG (Level Change) was inadvertently selected. Another theory is that VNV could not keep up and reverted to MCP SPD. This happens sometimes in the Next Gens, but it always reverts to VNV SPD, which is much safer. On arrival to ZZZ in VFR conditions. Arrival information was checked by both pilots for altitude and speed restrictions prior to descent. Aircraft was cleared by approach to descend via the arrival with a bottom altitude of 8,000 feet. The crossing restriction at ZZZZZ is 11,000 feet. Prior to reaching ZZZZZ the crew saw the aircraft was in Lvl Chg (Level Change) mode instead of VNAV and was descending through 10,000 feet. The Captain (Pilot Flying) took the controls, disconnected the autopilot and returned to altitude. The FO (Pilot Monitoring) notified ATC of the deviation but no conflicts existed and was handed to the next controller. Upon checking the FMS the First Officer determined the altitude restriction was still active at ZZZZZ for 11,000 feet. The crew briefly discussed the incident and possible errors but did not determine how or when the autopilot entered Lvl Chg mode during the descent.
ASRS:1824081.s: During a descent into ZZZ in a MAX aircraft, the crew inadvertently entered Level Change mode, causing an unmonitored descent below the 11,000-foot restriction at ZZZZZ to 9,500 feet. The Captain manually recovered the altitude, and the First Officer notified ATC, though the cause of the mode change remained undetermined.

ASRS:1824108.n: While at cruise at 35,000 feet in Cairo control airspace, we began to receive a series of Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting messages- ATC Fault, Unable RNP and Terrain Position. We referenced the Quick Reference Handbook for each message but were unable to clear the faults. We asked ATC if they saw any issue with our transponder and they replied that they saw no problems. Shortly after crossing from Amman control to Jeddah on airway Y415, we received the FMC message 'Verify position'. We saw that we were off the airway to the left and ATC asked if we were on the airway. The First Officer and I put our range scales to 5 miles and noted that the left side showed us approximately 3 to 5 miles left of course, First Officer side showed the same distance to the right of course.We checked the FMC position reference pages and saw that GPS position was blank and substantial errors on the other positions - FMC, IRS and Radio. We advised ATC of the GPS failure and could not determine which source was accurate. ATC said we were showing right of course. I selected GPS off then on, selected HDG (heading) select to manually steer to course. Reselected LNAV. Nothing seemed to be working. I asked for direct to a fix further down the airway. No VORs were on this airway to use for navigation. I repeated switching heading to LNAV but the aircraft symbol did not move closer to the course line as if it was frozen. We were continually advising ATC and monitoring position reference as GPS was now intermittent and RNP-ANP errors were constantly changing. Eventually GPS began to work and we were able to get back on course. This entire time we never received any EICAS or FMA indications of any faults such as 'GPS', 'IRS Nav Only', 'LNAV'. ATC passed the information to subsequent ATC and they offered vectors if needed. After position MOGON, navigation functions all appeared normal for the remainder for the flight.
ASRS:1824108.s: The flight crew experienced intermittent GPS and navigation failures at 35,000 feet in Cairo airspace, causing the aircraft to drift off airway Y415 without EICAS alerts. After manually steering and cycling systems, GPS function restored, allowing the crew to return to course with ATC assistance.

ASRS:1824132.n: Preflight, taxi, takeoff and initial climb were normal. We were flying the ZZZZZ RNAV departure when at approximately 15,000 feet the aircraft displayed a Level 2 alert, CABIN INFLO LO. I was acting as Pilot Monitoring so I began to reference the QRH, but the alert extinguished after only a few seconds. As a matter of course my First Officer and I took note of the QRH procedures for this alert should it reappear. A few moments later we heard a loud squeal seemingly emanating from below the flight deck. This in itself wasn't entirely unusual in an aircraft of this vintage, but the noise was soon followed by a level 1 alert, CABIN RATE. I again referenced the QRH and we found that, indeed, cabin altitude was rising. Passing approximately FL 210 we heard a loud BOOM and the cabin altitude increased its rate of climb. We shallowed our rate of climb to around 1,000 fpm to allow us to process the problem. Given the rate of increase in cabin altitude it was clear to me that we were about to exceed 10,000 feet, and I verbalized to my First Officer to get ready to don O2 masks. This was followed by a Level 3 alert, CABIN ALTITUDE. We donned masks, established crew communications, and I instructed our jump seater to don her mask as well (and comm was established with her). I asked ZZZ Center for a level off at FL 240 (our next available FL). Roles were established with my First Officer continuing as Pilot Flying and I as Pilot Monitoring. We followed QRH procedures for the CABIN ALTITUDE alert but it was clear that the cabin altitude could not be controlled. I [advised] with ZZZ Center and requested an immediate descent and turn back to ZZZ. We were given clearance to 9,000 feet and a left turn back to the airport. My First Officer began an IDLE descent with full spoilers while I set up navigation. Once in contact with ZZZ Approach we were offered any runway landing south. Given that our weight was well below max landing weight we accepted RWY XXR. During the descent I built and briefed the ILS approach, and as cabin altitude went below 10,000 feet we doffed masks and resumed communication on boom mics. I instructed our jump seater that she could do the same. ZZZ Approach inquired as to whether I wished to continue as a [priority] aircraft, but given that cabin altitude had stabilized and we had no other issues I declined the status (CFR did not roll). At approximately 25 nm from the airport I assumed the role of Pilot Flying. My First Officer did an excellent job in depressurizing the aircraft during the remaining descent IAW limitations. Landing, rollout and taxi in were uneventful. After landing it was discovered that the Avionics Compartment Access door under the nose of the aircraft had come open in flight. Maintenance discovered that the Avionics Compartment Access door seal failed allowing the door to open in flight. I don't have a good answer for this one. These are aging aircraft and anomalies are to be expected. I am unaware of current maintenance practices in regards to inspecting these door seals, but perhaps a greater emphasis needs to be put on those inspections.
ASRS:1824132.s: The flight crew experienced a rapid cabin altitude increase during climb due to an open avionics compartment access door caused by a failed seal. They donned oxygen masks, descended to 9,000 feet, and landed safely after maintenance confirmed the door opened in flight.

ASRS:1824194.n: Flying on A321S when [Flight Attendant] #3 showed me that her exit at 2L is partially blocked by a row of seats. There is no protective position if an evacuation happens. You cannot grab assist handle to get into protective position. We approached the Captain who was a bit shocked to see this. Then the Captain asked a maintenance person who stated that the blocking of the exit should not be. Also stated that he had never seen this before today. The row adjacent to exit needs to be removed for safety reasons. Please review this aircraft for our safety.
ASRS:1824194.s: A flight attendant reported to the Captain on an A321S that exit 2L was partially blocked by a row of seats, preventing a protective position. A maintenance technician confirmed the obstruction was improper and stated the adjacent row must be removed for safety.

ASRS:1824212.n: I was advised by Person X that I had loaded an unidentified Hazmat parcel on Aircraft X with no NOTOC. I was the only one involved.Apparently, the event occurred because I supposedly loaded a Hazmat PPS without a NOTOC on Aircraft X. After discussing this with a manager I went back in the NOTOC System and saw no NOTOC was planned for that flight for that date.Once the event was identified even though it was exactly a week later, I spoke with the manager and advised him I was filling out a report.Suggestion - Double checking boxes for DG labels [since no NOTOC was issued].
ASRS:1824212.s: The reporter, acting alone, was advised they loaded an unidentified Hazmat parcel on Aircraft X without a NOTOC. Investigation confirmed no NOTOC was planned for that flight, prompting the reporter to file a report and suggest double-checking DG labels.

ASRS:1824225.n: Helicopter crew experienced a near midair collision with a small unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) during an active search and rescue case. Crew queried other responding agencies about UAV employment as part of the search effort and increased altitude. No other UAV sightings were reported during the remainder of flight.
ASRS:1824225.s: Helicopter crew conducting a search and rescue mission experienced a near midair collision with a small unmanned aerial vehicle. The crew queried other agencies regarding UAV use and increased altitude, with no further sightings reported for the remainder of the flight.

ASRS:1824268.n: Reporting an NMAC [that] occurred at ZZZ, 900 MSL on short final for XXL. Aircraft X, Cessna 172N, on VFR flight plan ZZZ1-ZZZ-ZZZ2-ZZZ1. Home based in the greater San Antonio area. Other aircraft, two pilots on deck - Aircraft Y, Bombardier CL-600.Incident happened on short final for Runway XXL. Separation of 50 ft. or less horizontally at 900 MSL until other aircraft took evasive action veering hard right. I reported midfield for XXL per ATC instructions, was informed of other traffic 8 miles out, and was cleared to land. Confirmed clearance and repeated radio call. Aircraft Y was silent on comms since my clearance. Unable to see Aircraft Y until evasive action was taken 50 ft. behind me and reported over comms. From understanding of comms between ZZZ ATC and Aircraft Y after evasive action was taken, aircraft was shooting RNAV approach for XXL and failed to report and make last call at ZZZZZ and was not cleared to land. Weather conditions at time of incident ZZZ 22011G17KT 10SM SCY041 33/22 A2998.
ASRS:1824268.s: A Cessna 172N on short final for Runway XXL at 900 MSL experienced an NMAC with a Bombardier CL-600 due to the latter failing to report position or receive landing clearance. The CL-600 veered hard right to avoid a collision after appearing 50 feet behind the Cessna.

ASRS:1824282.n: On departure from DCA as gear came up the aircraft right wing dipped 25 deg due to wake turbulence. The wake turbulence was confirmed by the pilots. The severity of the wing dip is the reason I am submitting as a passenger as this was a close call to a major mishap. With wing deflection as great as occurred at low altitude the only thing that prevented a mishap was the rapid correction displayed by the pilots. I am unaware of ATC takeoff clearance and any cautions. I am unaware of the type aircraft departing prior to our departure and the time interval. I am.also unaware of the winds and direction. I only observed the result of the wake turbulence and felt compelled to report it.
ASRS:1824282.s: A passenger reported that during departure from DCA, the aircraft's right wing dipped 25 degrees due to wake turbulence as the gear retracted. The pilot's rapid correction prevented a mishap, though the passenger was unaware of the preceding aircraft, wind conditions, or ATC clearances.

ASRS:1824343.n: The RPIC was standing near the lateral middle of the bridge and flew the Skydio 2 under the deck to inspect the underside. When the drone was well under the bridge, lost link occurred. The drone initiated an RTH but was unable to find a path home, so it maintained a static hover under the bridge. The RPIC moved to the side of the bridge and regained link and then safely returned the aircraft. Flight mode was manual (no 3d scan or autonomous flight plan). Operations were discontinued after this incident.
ASRS:1824343.s: The RPIC flew a Skydio 2 under a bridge in manual mode when a lost link triggered a failed Return-to-Home, causing the drone to hover statically. The RPIC regained control by moving to the bridge's side, safely recovered the aircraft, and discontinued operations.

ASRS:1824357.n: Just prior to departure, we were informed that ground personnel had loaded two aircraft batteries in the proper containers. Captain was given the HAZMAT form, which he endorsed, then push back to fly the leg. After airborne, the Captain realized that there was a required dispatch amendment, so he immediately notified Dispatch to get the proper amendment. The flight continued to destination without any further issue related to this COMAT.
ASRS:1824357.s: The crew departed with two aircraft batteries loaded in proper containers but realized a required dispatch amendment was missing after becoming airborne. The Captain notified Dispatch to obtain the amendment, and the flight continued to the destination without further issues.

ASRS:1824392.n: During cruise flight, the Master Caution light illuminated with the #2 engine driven B hydraulic system light. We ran the QRH and turned the pump off, and also noted that the B system indicated approximately 3000 psi but zero quantity. We discussed the possibility that although technically the conditions were not yet met per the QRH, there was a strong possibility that entire B system had likely failed or was failing and notified Dispatch via ACARS that it was a possibility. We ran the weight data for landing in ZZZ with the B system inop, and came up with approximately 1,300 feet of stopping margin with max manual braking. We let Dispatch know that even with a hypothetical total loss of the B system, ZZZ was still acceptable and they concurred with our stopping margin calculation. The B system held steady with approximately 3000 psi until we started our descent into ZZZ with approximately 120 miles to go. As we were descending, the psi of the B system quickly dropped to near zero and the ELEC 1 B pump Low Pressure light illuminated, along with the Flight Control B Low Pressure light. We ran the QRH for Loss of System B and calculated brake cooling, which advised staying off the gate for 30 minutes.We advised Approach of the situation and asked for delay vectors for checklists and CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) trucks to be present at the end of the runway to check brake temps and condition after landing. We landed on the runway at the end and shut down engines at the request of CFR. CFR noted that hydraulic fluid was leaking from number 2 engine and brake temps were above 500 C. They were also concerned about hydraulic fluid on the hot section of #2 engine aerosolizing and advised we wait for cooler temps for ramp safety. CFR advised that although the brakes had cooled acceptably they were still concerned about the possible aerosolizing of hydraulic fluid from #2 engine hot section and advised we wait another 10 minutes. This all led to a lengthy ground delay but we did the best we could to keep the flight attendants and Passengers informed. In our judgement it was the safest course of action to follow CFR recommendations.
ASRS:1824392.s: During cruise, the flight crew managed a #2 engine-driven B hydraulic system failure that worsened during descent into ZZZ. After landing, Crash Fire Rescue detected hydraulic fluid leaking from the #2 engine and high brake temperatures, causing a ground delay to prevent fluid aerosolization.

ASRS:1824413.n: On final approach to runway 08 at BUR, approximately one mile south of BUDDE intersection, a stationary drone was spotted at approximately 3,000 ft MSL and ATC was notified. Established on localizer and glideslope with zero deviation, the First Officer observed an unreported drone hovering to the south of BUDDE FAF on the approach to Runway 08. The drone was at our altitude as we passed BUDDE. We immediately reported this to Tower and after we landed the Tower Controller asked us to report additional information to the Ground Controller, which we did right after completion of the Parking Checklist.
ASRS:1824413.s: The First Officer spotted a stationary drone at 3,000 ft MSL south of BUDDE while on final approach to Runway 08 at BUR. The crew immediately notified ATC and provided further details to the Ground Controller after landing.

ASRS:1824447.n: Flight took off from ZZZ and at 8,000 feet they had GA traffic in sight. The TCAS went off telling them to descend-they complied. It switched to climb and they did. Crew advised me that flight attendants and passengers were not aware. Crew advised me they were filing the necessary reports.
ASRS:1824447.s: The flight crew experienced a TCAS resolution advisory at 8,000 feet after sighting general aviation traffic, requiring them to descend and then climb. The crew noted that passengers and flight attendants were unaware of the event and stated they were filing the necessary reports.

ASRS:1824465.n: Bag arrived to ZZZ with battery not removed prior to checking in. Bag was taken and customer reminded of hazards. Customer stated that bag was checked plane side due to no space.
ASRS:1824465.s: A passenger checked a bag containing a battery at ZZZ without removing it, citing lack of space at the plane side. Staff intercepted the bag and reminded the customer of the hazards.

ASRS:1824526.n: I knew it was going to be a struggle getting out of ZZZ with all passengers on board when I saw the take-off performance. At 40C the margin between PTOW (Planned Take-off Weight) and MTOW was 1100 lbs. My First Officer (FO) was terrific, but it was his first trip since IOE, he had 18 hours on the airplane at the start of the sequence, and had not flown prior to training for about 8 months. In addition, it was only my second time flying the ZZZZZ departure, which has three at or above altitudes on it, which is a new thing in ZZZ. I live in ZZZ, and consequently fly out of there a great deal. All previous RNAV departures used to have at or below altitudes on them (to keep clear of inbound aircraft), so it never used to be an issue worrying about making altitudes on the SID. At the aircraft, I was already concerned about two things: brake temps and having to bump passengers. I asked my FO to pull us up numbers for 41 and 42C, just in case it got hotter, as it was likely to. In addition, I believe the winds were swinging around - runway XXR had a tailwind component at one point, so I was also looking for numbers for XYL, but due to terrain, the only runway that worked at all was XXR. I noticed that we would be unable to make the restrictions and asked the FO to ask for altitude relief on the SID as soon as he contacted ground. In my experience, asking for altitude relief at other airports was never an issue, so I was not overly concerned. We pushed back, and naturally were over PTOW. I asked the FO to request a new take-off performance for 41 and 42C. We eventually landed on a Flaps 1 take-off performance requiring thrust bump which got us legal for takeoff. All this occurred during the short taxi from the terminal to runway XXR.By the time we reached number 1 holding short of the runway, I realized we had forgotten to ask for the altitude relief on the SID. I asked the FO to do so as we were taking the runway. The controller, upon hearing the request, told us to taxi clear and get a new clearance. By this time there were 6-8 aircraft in a queue for takeoff, and our brake temps were over 150 degrees. My main concern was that if we had to leave the runway, it would get too hot to accommodate the load, and by the time we taxied for another 30 minutes, the brakes would be too hot for takeoff. So, glancing down at the FMS, which showed that we would miss the altitude restrictions by 5-700 feet, I knew that if we delayed cleanup, we could easily make those restrictions. I told the controller that we could manage the departure, and he again cleared us for takeoff. I told my FO that since we were at the max performance envelope of the airplane, he should rotate very gently. As we were rolling down the runway, my attention was fixed on the EGT, as I had not done a bump takeoff before, and the engines were exactly on the edge of the red. He did as I asked, and as a result, we were very fast on the initial climb segment. As we climbed out, I was fixated on the altitude. Once it became clear that the 5,000 ft altitude (I think around 4,500 feet MSL) I relaxed a bit and told him we could clean up. He set climb power (which was a much greater reduction than normal due to the thrust bump) and I reached for the flap lever and set flaps up. At this time we were still wings level. I was so fixated on the altitude, and our airspeed shortly after takeoff was so much higher than usual that I didn't take a good look at the airspeed indicator. I believe that I retracted the flaps very early. VLS (lowest selectable speed) jumped by perhaps 40 knots, and we ended up about 20 knots below VLS. Naturally, we were now facing rapidly rising terrain, and the SID commanded a right turn. My FO started to turn, and now instead of being below VLS, we were in alpha floor. I instructed my FO to lower the nose, but it wasn't happening quickly enough, so I grabbed the side stick and pushed the nose over, at the same time requesting him to let go. There was a momentary DUAL INPUT" annunciation and a momentary noticeable low speed buffet which lasted perhaps a second. We lost perhaps 300 feet of altitude as I got the airspeed back. We were able to make all of the altitude restrictions and I don't believe there were any deviations from the SID. Once we recovered, the only other item remaining was how to get the auto throttles out of alpha floor. Eventually, we turned them off (match and mash) and back on again and that got the system back to normal.I was using my knowledge of past experience flying the old SIDs. They didn't have airspeed or at or above altitudes, and my experience in the past that asking for altitude relief on a SID was not a big deal. In addition, I was flying with a brand new (very sharp) but inexperienced FO, who was relying entirely on my experience. I was also pushing to accommodate the load without having to remove passengers and/or cargo, and was worried about the brake temp issues, causing me to push to get off the ground as soon as possible.I made several errors. The first one was not notifying clearance delivery early of our inability to make the altitude and/or airspeed restrictions on the SID. In the past, ZZZ used to have a procedure for A321 aircraft to delay climb power/flap retraction to 3,000 AGL. I think if we had used that procedure, we probably would have been able to make the altitude and speed restrictions on the SID. That procedure is gone. Second, when we finally did request relief on the SID (by this time we were on the runway) and the controller told us to clear the runway and get a new clearance, I should have done so, even if it had caused us further problems with brake temp and/or takeoff weight. Third, having taken the decision to take off because I was certain we could delay cleanup, thus making us legal for the SID, I should have taken over flying duties. This would have alleviated my FO's task saturation, as I was far more experienced in the airplane. This would still have been sub-optimal, but I am confident the takeoff would have been uneventful. Fourth, once I retracted the flaps and we were below VLS, I should have put the flaps back to Config 1. So, there were many errors on my part, but an early intervention with clearance delivery would have solved everything. I believe there should be a warning to the A320 Fleet about the new SIDS, and that at high temperatures careful note should be taken of the danger of not being able to make altitude restrictions on any SID with at or above altitudes, especially early in the SID, and that relief should be requested at the gate with clearance delivery. Also to note: green dot speed (min maneuver) was 245 with flaps up, so the only way to maintain 230 knot speed at ZZZZZ waypoint is at config 1. Again, the old requirement to clean up at 3000 AGL would have solved this."
ASRS:1824526.s: The Captain and First Officer of an A321 at ZZZ airport took off with a thrust bump to avoid passenger offload but failed to request SID altitude relief early. The Captain's premature flap retraction caused an airspeed drop below VLS and an alpha floor activation, requiring manual recovery to avoid terrain.

ASRS:1824559.n: After takeoff, during a turn to a heading of 270 degrees, we received an ALT and IAS cross-side miss-comparison. The autopilot also would not engage when commanded and I hand flew up to 5,000 ft. After leveling off, and receiving instructions to climb, I called for the autopilot again and it connected. During the climb, we kept receiving the IAS and ALT notices and leveled off at 16,000 ft., FL260, and FL320. We also noted a 200 ft. discrepancy between altimeters at one point. We leveled off at these altitudes because of the miss-comparison. After leveling off, for a minute the miss-compare would go away and we would continue the climb. During the climb and at one of the level-offs, we tried using our alternate static sources. This seemed to work on the Captain's side but the miss-compare came back when we started to climb again. The Captain then ran the airspeed unreliable checklist to see if it would be any help but nothing in the checklist seemed to be a fit for the problem we were encountering. The cause of the problems was not obvious and the checklist did not seem like it was of any help. Also, during the climbs, the FCP was not usable. All of the windows for airspeed, heading, and altitude only showed - - - -.With the problems we were having and not being able to identify the cause combined with the prospect of having to hand-fly and the encounter weather, we felt that continuing to ZZZ1 was not an option should the problems become worse. If we did in fact have an unreliable airspeed, we would be directed to disconnect both AFS and FD switches off which would mean having to leave RVSM, which would lead to higher fuel burns and hand-flying in heavy thunderstorms. [The problem was identified] when the amber IAS and ALT alerts were presented on our PFDs (Primary Flight Display). If I had to guess I would say that the aircraft had some sort of computer issue that was presenting the airspeed and altitude to the displays with differing data and a comparator caught the difference and alerted us. Our first reaction was to fly the plane. I started asking the Captain what his airspeed was as I figured that was more important than altitude. Once we were at a safe altitude and maintaining a safe airspeed, we began to troubleshoot and discuss the problems. There is nothing that we could have done as pilots to prevent this. On the climb out the EIS detected intermittent ALT and IAS miss-comparisons between Captain and FO's (First Officer) PFD (Primary Flight Display). Stopped climb at 16,000 ft., the issue went away. We then decided to continue to climb but had to stop at FL260. I had the FO put his STATIC AIR to ALT. Problem went away for about 1 minute and then came back. I then selected Captain STATIC AIR to ALT. This time, the issues went away for a few minutes. We decided to continue the climb but had to stop at FL320 because the problem came back. I ran the emergency non-alert AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE checklist, but the issue was not resolved. At 27100 ft., Captain's IAS/MACH 336/.830, FO's IAS/MACH 330/.816. At every level change attempt FCP window indicated - - - -. The altitude difference between [the] Captain and FO was over 200 ft. Since AP (Autopilot) #2 was deferred and if we disconnected AP #1 we would not be able to remain in RVSM, we contacted company and returned to ZZZ. No emergency or special handling was required. [The problem was identified by the] amber IAS and ALT on Captain's and FO's upper left-hand corner of the PFD. [The cause was] failure annunciations… cross-side miss-comparisons generated when the EIS detected significant differences between the displayed data of the Captain's and First Officer's instruments AIRSPEED and ALTITUDE. [The response was to] climb to [a] safe altitude, maintain speed, and attempt to address the issue at hand. Maintenance issues cannot be forecasted.
ASRS:1824559.s: Pilots experienced intermittent airspeed and altitude cross-side miss-comparisons and Flight Control Panel failures during climb after takeoff. Unable to resolve the issue or safely continue to ZZZ1 due to weather and RVSM constraints, they returned to the departure airport.

ASRS:1824592.n: We went through a fume event on Aircraft X. It only affected F/A's [Flight Attendant] #1 and #3. The fume felt like a severe piercing acrid, mentholated winter-fresh smell. It started slowly and it rapidly increase to the point in which our eyes started watering, and our throats, and noses became irritated. Initially we both thought either of us was chewing on a winter fresh gum for our breaths. We then asked each other: 'Are you chewing gum?' we both said 'NO!' At that moment the odor/fume got excruciatingly pungent. The fume event lasted for about 5 minutes. We both complaint of having a growing headache. After landing, we both spoke to the Captain about our symptoms. The Captain wrote a mechanical report on the aircraft, and he will follow it up with another report.I am however, requesting for both F/A's to get checked medically through airline protocols, to see if we are fit to continue on our sequence.I am strongly advising for the two F/A's affected on this incident to get check out by medical staff.
ASRS:1824592.s: Flight Attendants 1 and 3 on Aircraft X experienced a five-minute fume event during flight, characterized by a severe acrid odor causing eye watering, throat irritation, and headaches. The Captain filed a mechanical report, and the affected crew members are requesting medical evaluation to determine fitness for duty.

ASRS:1824624.n: I had a near miss with Aircraft Y, who was not communicating on the CTAF frequency. He flew overhead of my helicopter extremely close from my 5 o'clock to my 10 o'clock when I noticed him as he passed overhead. I communicated with ZZZ1 up in ZZZ2 regarding the event, and was told they would respond to me shortly. I gave it about 10 days and called them back. They told me I'd have to file something with the FAA to get some sort of resolution or response. I fly every day in the summer in this particular area and it frightened me considerably.The event occurred about 3-5 miles east of ZZZ on the north side of ZZZ3 and south of ZZZ4 at approximately 3500 ft. My heading was flying west and Aircraft Y flew over me coming from the north.
ASRS:1824624.s: A helicopter pilot reported a near miss with Aircraft Y, which flew overhead from 5 to 10 o'clock at 3500 ft while not communicating on CTAF. The pilot contacted ZZZ1 and ZZZ2 but was advised to file an FAA report for resolution, noting the event caused significant concern.

ASRS:1824631.n: Taking off Runway 17 (North End) of 1K1 airport. Lots of activities at the airport during the fly-in. Folks walking across North ditch to gain access to the restaurant. Performed run-up and check list between North end and fuel service area (staying clear not to prop blast pedestrians walking through the ditch on the North end. Started take-off roll full power, lifted tail wheel... and just then I see a motorcycle take off down the left (East side of the runway). I'm at full power flying a 450hp tail dragger. Not an option to just chop the power. I pulled over to the right side (West) of the runway and continued the take-off. After reaching 60 knots lifted off gaining speed and began climb out just past mid-field. Continued following West edge of runway in case emergency procedures were required (engine failure). There was zero coordination or expectation of a motorcycle jumping out on the runway. I handled the situation as safely as possible maintaining distance but also gaining speed for climb out. I believe I made the safest choice to maintain visibility (Cowling of a 450hp tail dragger), continue gaining airspeed and then maintaining a steady climb out with options if failures were to happen.
ASRS:1824631.s: The pilot of a 450hp taildragger at 1K1 airport encountered a motorcycle entering the runway during takeoff roll. The pilot maintained full power, veered right to avoid the vehicle, and continued the climb out along the runway's west edge.

ASRS:1824644.n: Student Pilot was coming in to land on Runway XX. Winds were variable at approximately 4 knots at the time, skies clear. Instructor witnessed the landing from inside the line office. It appeared to be stable and smooth. Student intended to do a touch and go. Student went off the runway into the grass on the left side of Runway XX. Instructor drove the line truck to check on student who was in the grass with the engine idling. Instructor told student via radio to shut down the engine and secure the aircraft. Student was not injured and visual damage to the aircraft appeared to be impact to the left fairing. Student told instructor that he had a good landing but when he applied power the plane veered to the left. In a follow-up phone call to the student later in the day, student reported no injuries or pain. This was the students second landing of the day. He did one touch and go earlier in the day, and then departed to the practice area before returning. Student has soloed twice before this. Student has 2.8 solo hours. Student has progressed in his training, shown interest in learning and completed the written exam.
ASRS:1824644.s: A student pilot with 2.8 solo hours veered off the left side of Runway XX into grass during a touch-and-go attempt after applying power. The student reported the aircraft veered left upon power application, resulting in left fairing impact damage but no injuries.
